en: Preface to the Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, composed by the śramaṇa Jinnan, a successor to the ancestral lineage residing at the Shangsheng Chan Monastery in Fuzhou.

Since the image season had already returned, the Way and its arts were split asunder; those who sought to clarify the mind mistakenly identified conditioned sensory objects as the self, thereby being turned by external things.
Among those who study the Dharma through logic and doctrine, there are many who are vainly proud of their extensive learning yet lack the power of the Path.

Those of rare talent and magnificent capacity all end up like travelers steaming sand or hungry men who merely describe food. The King of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi foresaw this clearly and extensively expounded this secret scripture to rescue them from their inverted delusions.
Through refining and awakening them, his tireless compassion reached every corner; yet for those of initial capacity in this degenerate age, [the task remains difficult].

It is rarely possible to exhaustively investigate [this matter]. Master Huan of Wenling spent his entire life in seclusion behind closed doors, setting aside worldly interests to accompany only the sages of the yellow scrolls.
Through profound searching and extensive inquiry, he relied upon these skillful means as rafts to explore the Tathāgatagarbha;
he traversed the ocean of omniscience to reach the ground of ultimate reality. Desiring to share this with those of like mind, he composed this commentary. Formerly, Yuegai...
"Monk, once I asked the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja about the meaning of 'Dharma-offering. Bhaiṣajyarāja replied: 'The profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas are difficult to believe;
they are pure and untainted, capable of enabling sentient beings to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment and remain free from the works of Māra.'"
If one skillfully explains this sutra by relying on the meaning rather than the words, on wisdom rather than consciousness, on the definitive meaning rather than the non-definitive meaning,
and on the Dharma rather than the person— thereby causing ignorance and birth-and-death to be utterly extinguished without any mark of extinction—
this is called the supreme offering of the Dharma. Having received this instruction, Candracchattra attained thorough penetration.
Having attained the wondrous Way and unimpeded eloquence, he followed and disseminated the wheel of Dharma turned by Bhaiṣajyarāja,
transforming a hundred trillion people and establishing them in non-retrogression toward supreme enlightenment. Once Huánshī had reached the wondrous Way, he looked up in admiration to Yuègài, who,
regarding the wheel of Dharma turned by Śākyamuni Tathāgata— specifically the *Avataṃsaka* at the beginning and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* at the end— as well as this...

The *Śūraṅgama* is the unsurpassed jewel-seal; it employs skillful means and robust characteristics for discernment, utterly transcending language and departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
It rests solely upon the meaning and never relies on persons. Awakening to the cataract of vision and the illness of perception, one finds them vast and devoid of even the slightest obscuration;
thus, one remains unstained by the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. May I cause this to circulate without end; those transformed by it will be beyond counting.
Tens of millions. It is just like lighting one lamp to ignite hundreds of thousands of lamps, causing all who were in darkness to become illuminated, yet the light never comes to an end.
Therefore, I have composed this preface and introduction to assist in its circulation, thereby making offerings of Dharma through the ink and paper of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Written on an auspicious day during the Mid-Autumn Festival in the first year of the Jianyan era at Shanji Hall.

Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā from the country of Ujjayinī;
the bodhisattva precept disciple and former Minister of Justice and Concurrent Vice President of the Secretariat and Chancellery,
Fang Rong of Qinghe, acted as the scribe.
The Monk Jiehuan of Wēnlíng Kaiyuán Lian Temple Explains the Title of the Sūtra △ Section Three: General Explanation of the Sūtra Title.
The fruit-body of the Tathāgata is inherently such; why should it depend on secret causes? The path-function of the Bodhisattva is... [its function is] without...
What constitutes the myriad practices? There is no cause and no practice; there is no cultivation and no realization; there is neither understanding nor lack of understanding.
All names and characteristics, whether great or small, are not established. This is the true Śūraṅgama, ultimately firm and solid.

It is simply because the Tathāgata is hidden within the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse mind) of sentient beings that he is not revealed except through the secret cause. Sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are submerged in...

Regarding the seven destinies, there is nothing among the myriad practices that is not cultivated. Thus, the Awakened Sovereign revealed to them the Great Dharma, so that they would not be lost in minor paths and might silently attain the essence that transcends all boundaries.
He illustrated this through the metaphor of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa, so that they would not be hindered by the perception of forms and might reach the ultimate subtlety of the Unsurpassed.
He pointed to the secret cause of the Tathāgata, so that they might clarify their original nature.

O Wondrous Mind! Know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon this as their primary cause. This clarifies the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization, enabling one to awaken to the ultimate Dharma.
Know that all sages rely upon this to realize the fruit, even unto the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva’s ten thousand pure practices;
there is no phenomenal phenomenon that does not reach its ultimate consummation in the firmness of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

It is indeed indestructible; therefore, it is titled *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.
Generally, there are five titles, of which three are presented here now, as they are concise yet comprehensive.
As for what is called "the ocean of universal knowledge," "the wondrous lotus king," and "the mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions," these constitute the other two.

The so-called *Siddhārthapātra* (悉怛多般怛囉), the Supreme Jewel Seal, the Pure Sea-Eye, and the Consecration Verses—these three are interconnected. *Siddhārthapātra* means "White Parasol" (*Sitātapatrā*).
It is the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, vast and untainted, the essence that universally covers the Dharma-realm; this sutra is precisely this mind.
This is the seal of the mind; it is the eye of the mind. By sealing with this Jewel Seal, one causes the seventy thousand dharmas to all accord with the fundamental mind.
By illuminating with this Ocean Eye, one realizes that the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and realms are all the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thereby, one realizes the Bodhicitta and enters the ocean of Buddha-wisdom, becoming a Sovereign of the Wondrous Lotus, acting with mastery over the myriad realms of defilement and purity.

It blooms and becomes the Mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions. In lands as minute as motes of dust, it descends and is born according to conditions, until it achieves the fruition of virtue and receives the stage of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Thus, all things that are ultimately firm are fully present within me.
*Śūraṅgama* is translated here as "the ultimate firmness of all things," and is also called the "division of the vigorous aspect."

It is distinct. "All things are ultimately [empty]" has already been explained as before. The remainder—referred to as the "Vajra-observation, awakening, clarity, and analysis"—begins with the investigation of the mind and the discernment of vision, and concludes with the destruction of the aggregates and the expulsion of demons; there is nothing that is not the vigorous activity of discerning phenomena.
The sūtra is merely the text that expresses these meanings. To express is like a fish-trap (śuṅga). Knowing that the sūtra is a trap, one should follow it...

All commentaries upon it are merely fishing traps; they are not the fish themselves. Students must be careful not to mistake the trap for the fish, and only then can the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* be truly attained.
△ Second, a general account of the commentarial divisions (*ko-p'an*).
From the Tang through the Song dynasties, there have been more than ten schools of commentary and exegesis on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Among those I have seen or know of are:
Master Xuán of Chángshuǐ, Master Yuán of Gūshān, Master Dù of Míndú, Master Yǎn of Chángqìng, and Master Yuè of Lètán.
The Master [Zhi] follows the exposition of Emperor Shu (Wang Zhen) and Zhang Guanwen; even those who have only recently seen it can roughly discern his underlying intent.

However, regarding his classification of the scriptures, he maintains that the *Sūtra of King Prasenajit* and the *Sūtra of King Vīradeva* belong to different eras and were not taught all at once in a single assembly.

Furthermore, in his doctrinal judgment (*panjiao*), he restricts himself to events such as those concerning the *Dharmodgata* and Yaśodharā, concluding that these occurred after the *Lotus Sūtra*. This, I, a fool, have privately...

I am doubtful; please allow me to first inquire about this. Now, things carried away in the night ravine can vanish as quickly as turning over one’s hand, and the succession of kings can change in the space of a single morning or evening.
Yet the *Śūraṃgama* Dharma-assembly lasted from summer until winter. This should not lead one to insist that the kings were different or to suspect that the assemblies were distinct.
As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, from the time of King Pradīpa onwards, there has been no time when the Buddhas have not preached it. The Bodhisattvas...
There is no time when [the Dharma] is not realized. Since Kṣitigarbha stated that he had heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the wondrous Lotus Sūtra, how could this refer to Śākyamuni alone?
The sūtra records that Mādrī, through the power of a divine mantra, had her passions extinguished; she and Yaśodharā together awakened to their past causes.

Some attained liberation from the bonds of existence, while others received predictions of enlightenment. If one insists that receiving such a prediction must pertain specifically to the *Lotus Sūtra*, [one overlooks the universal scope of the teaching].

Then there must have been a Mādrī at the assembly on Vulture Peak for it to be said that [the two] are identical; furthermore, to claim this is due to the power of a divine spell is clearly not the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Moreover, there is a distinction between the "prediction of the path" (*mārga-vyākaraṇa*) and the "prediction of the fruit" (*phala-vyākaraṇa*).

One suspects that what is spoken in the present sūtra refers only to the prediction of the path, and not to the prediction of the fruit in the *Lotus Sūtra*. This also shows that one should not restrict the bestowal of predictions to a fixed chronological order.
Regarding the statement that the sutra contains "the final instructions," this is merely a concluding rhetorical flourish.

It occurs at the end of the tenth fascicle, marking the conclusion of the Śūraṃgama Dharma Assembly, rather than referring to the final moments before the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Although many such interpretations have been cited by predecessors, they cannot be detailed here;
none of them provide a sufficient standard for structural analysis (*kepan*). If the structural analysis lacks a standard, the underlying principles and meanings will naturally deviate.
Now, judging by the sequence of our Buddha’s establishment of the teachings, it is not yet clear whether this is appropriate. Please allow me to set forth my humble observations.
When the Dharma King preaches the Dharma, there is order and no confusion. First, he teaches the Sudden Vehicle of the One Vehicle to establish the foundation; this is the *Avataṃsaka*.
Next, he teaches the Gradual Vehicle of the Three Vehicles to accommodate various capacities; this refers to the *Āgama*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. Finally...
The teaching of the One Vehicle Perfect Doctrine is expounded to reveal the ultimate reality; this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* is situated within the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, representing the final, ultimate teaching of the true Mahāyāna.

Thus, the methods for cultivating and realizing the secret causes of the Tathāgata and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas are all brought to completion herein. From this point onward, there is no further cultivation or progress; one proceeds directly to the One Vehicle.
This is the perfectly wondrous Way; therefore, in the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is no further discourse on stages (*bhūmi*).

It speaks exclusively of the wondrous Dharma, merely granting predictions of Buddhahood according to the capacities of beings to confirm their realization. Indeed, the Great Matter for which the Buddha appeared in the world reaches its ultimate fulfillment and perfection in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
nothing more can be added. Following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was then preached to uphold the Vinaya and discuss...
It concludes with the eternal. Those who "support the Vinaya" (fúlù) do so to entrust matters to future generations; those who "discuss the eternal" (táncháng) do so to demonstrate true quiescence.
This is merely a matter of final instructions left behind at the moment of death; it does not add anything to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Yet, commentators, failing to grasp the intent of supporting the Vinaya, arbitrarily judge the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* to be posterior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while also claiming it "supports the Vinaya and discusses the eternal."
This is constant. Thus, having already completed one’s cultivation, one cultivates further; having already supported the Vinaya, one supports it again.
To do so is to add redundantly to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before, and to append superfluously to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* after.

This is to invert the order and create redundant branches, thereby confusing the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Now, the matter of cultivation is like sowing and harvesting, or like weeding and tilling. It is like the lotus...

The lotus flower is still in full bloom. Since it is designated as the "Dharma Flower" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) and the "Harvest of Nirvāṇa," one should not be weeding and tilling within the very act of harvesting and gathering.
Furthermore, since it is designated as the "Dharma Flower" that discards the provisional and establishes the real—just as the lotus appears once the flower falls—it follows that this is so.
Then it would be improper for flowers to bloom again after they have withered and fallen away. To prove this by means of the sūtra:
once a destitute child has found the treasure trove, what more remains to be sought? Once those at the illusory city have reached the place of the treasure, why should they proceed further?
After the Buddha of Lamp-Light preached the Lotus Sūtra, he entered parinirvāṇa in the middle of the night; so too did the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, after preaching the Lotus Sūtra.
He then announced his parinirvāṇa before the fourfold assembly. Furthermore, why would he have extended such rambling discourse regarding the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*?

If the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* must necessarily come later, then Ānanda had already exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet here in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* his outflows are not yet exhausted;
he was deemed capable of receiving the Buddha’s prediction during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet here in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* his power of the Path is not yet complete.
Having already first realized the wondrous Dharma, yet not knowing the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*);

having already established oneself in the Buddha-way, yet being turned back by those [afflictions] and drowning in brothels—all this is a perversion of the natural order, for such a principle is inherently impossible.

Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is judged to follow after the *Prajñāpāramitā*. This is because, following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the study of wisdom (*prajñā*) flourished while the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was not yet fully established;
some individuals became mired in mere erudition and lost the state of right reception (*samyaksamādhi*).

It was then that the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama was revealed to support the Great Wisdom of Prajñā, so that concentration and wisdom might be balanced and both learning and practice brought to completion.
Ultimately, one proceeds toward the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is the purpose for which this *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* was composed.

Examining the general purport of these three sutras, they are all none other than for the sake of the Great Matter (*mahāntam artham*). First, one must rely upon Prajñā to bring it forth; next, one proceeds through the *Śūraṅgama* to practice and realize it;
finally, one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for confirmation. Only then are the capabilities of all Buddhas fully exhausted. Thus, the introduction is indeed...

It is so. However, for guiding one toward the vehicle of dhyāna and resolving upon right view, nothing surpasses the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. Its topical outline follows the conventional pattern, divided into three major sections:
first, the introductory section; second, the main body; and third, the dissemination section. The text of the introductory section is further divided into two parts.
First, the setting and the principal and attendant figures are presented to establish faith and understanding. Next, Ānanda’s manifestation of his traces is presented to initiate the discourse.

The main body of the text consists of five sections. First is the Section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). Initially, through the seven inquiries, the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure luminosity—is revealed (i.e., the first fascicle).
Subsequently, through the eight returns, the wondrously pure seeing-essence is analyzed to reveal the *tathāgatagarbha* (the second [fascicle]).
Third) Subsequently, the mountains, rivers, and myriad phenomena proclaim the true nature of ultimate reality within the supreme meaning (from the beginning of section four to its middle).

All these serve to cause the practitioner to clarify the mind and perceive its nature (*citta-dṛṣṭi-svabhāva*), acting as the secret cause for cultivation and realization; therefore, this is called the "Section on Seeing the Path" (*darśana-mārga-bhāga*). Second is the "Section on Cultivating the Path" (*bhāvanā-mārga-bhāga*).
It first demonstrates the two definitive meanings for the beginner, causing them to examine the causal mind and the resultant awakening, and furthermore, to examine the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The fundamental [nature] serves as the true basis for cultivation (from the fourth chapter to the end). Next, the sequential order of loosening the knots of the six sense organs is shown, so that the mind may understand how to untie them and attain wondrous, perfect penetration;
this constitutes the essential requirement for cultivation (from the fifth to the middle of the sixth chapter). This marks the completion of one cycle of progress for those of sharp faculties.
Therefore, at this point, Ānanda clearly understands the path upon which Bodhi returns, and he says to himself:

Having already awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood, he vowed to deliver those in the final age; he further requested instructions on the establishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa* and the rules for concentrating the mind.

Thereupon, he heard the three types of untainted learning (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi*), the four kinds of discipline (*caturvidha-vinaya*), and the great divine mantras (the sixth and seventh of the six, and the last of the seven).

These collectively serve as the skillful means for cultivation; therefore, they are called the "Section on Cultivating the Path. Third is the "Section on Realizing the Fruit," which begins from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and concludes with...

The Great Nirvāṇa: This section traces the progressive advancement through the fifty-five stages up to the ultimate *miāojiào* (Sanskrit: *samyaksaṃbuddha*), thereby accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way;

hence it is titled the "Section on Realizing the Fruit" (7 end–8 middle). Fourth, the "Section on Concluding the Sūtra": This lists five titles to summarize and clarify the essential purport of the entire work (8 middle).
Fifth, the "Section on Aids to the Path": First, it clarifies that the heavens, hells, and the seven destinies are created solely by the mind; next, it clarifies *śīla* (precepts)...

Within *śamatha*, there are subtle demonic activities (*māra-karman*). Fearing that practitioners might wash their minds with what is not correct, thereby erring and falling, [this section] is therefore called "Aiding the Path" (8.10-end).
Now, one realizes the Path (*darśana-mārga*) and only then cultivates the Path (*bhāvanā-mārga*); having cultivated the Path, one then realizes the fruit (*phala*).
Once the matters of cultivation and realization are completed, the sutra concludes here. The essential teachings of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* end at this point. And as for the world...

The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, further desired that sentient beings who uphold the precepts remain scrupulously pure and free from transgressions, and that true practitioners not encounter divergent paths.
Thus, he taught the dharmas that assist the Way as his final instructions. Consequently, these teachings entered into circulation and culminated in this assembly.
This constitutes a single, comprehensive thread, a continuous chain without interruption; it must not be divided into separate sections or categorized as distinct assemblies.
This is intended to clarify differing interpretations. This is but a general outline; a word-by-word commentary according to the text would provide full detail.

Nevertheless, when viewed by present standards, there are somewhat more instances of contradiction with ancient precedents, and even within the traditional specialized scholarship, inconsistencies cannot be avoided. Only those of broad learning should examine this.

△ Third, the correct explanation of the sūtra text has three parts. First, the introduction has two parts. First, the *samyaksampratyaya-nidāna* (序分) has two parts. First, the time and place of the teaching:
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the city of Śrāvastī.
Such teachings as these I have heard from the Buddha. This assembly relies upon the words established by the Buddha as testimony that there is a Dharma to be transmitted;
it does not necessarily depend on the speech of others. Even the discourse of a single occasion is established because of the Buddha and is universally applicable across all sutras.
Therefore, it is not fixedly specified. Śrāvastī is also called Śāvatthī. Jetavana is equivalent to "Jeta’s Grove.
△ Second, the assembly listening to the Dharma, in two parts. First, the regular followers, in three parts. First, the general heading.

He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus—those who secretly maintained the status of bodhisattvas while outwardly appearing as śrāvakas, and who were called "great bhikṣus" because they had destroyed evil and terrified Māra. There were one thousand two hundred of them.
These were Kauṇḍinya, the three Kāśyapas, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and their like. △ Second, praising their virtues: They were all untainted Great Arhats.
As sons of the Buddha, they maintained the Dharma; they skillfully transcended all realms of existence. They were able to perfect majestic deportment within the lands;

as successors who turn the wheel of the Buddha’s teachings, they were wonderfully worthy of his final entrustment. They strictly purified the Vinaya and established a grand model for the three worlds.
The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) immeasurably delivers sentient beings; it rescues those of the future and transcends all worldly defilements.
Its water of wisdom is wondrously profound and still; because it does not follow after desire, existence, ignorance, delusion, or karma, it is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava).

It is free from birth within the limits of the realms of existence and receives offerings from humans and devas. Having slain the thief of ignorance, it is named Arhat. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* praises the assembly as dwelling therein.

The realm in which all Bodhisattvas’ wisdom dwells; that which protects and upholds the wheel of the True Dharma of all Buddhas—this is what is meant by "the Son of the Buddha abiding in the maintenance [of the Dharma].

Regarding the praise of the assembly in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Having exhausted all fetters of existence, they have attained mastery of mind"—this is what is meant by "skillfully transcending all realms of existence.
Regarding "being able to achieve dignified deportment within the lands": it means manifesting one's body according to each buddha-field with a correct countenance.

He awakened to the nature of things. Among those who followed the Buddha’s turning of the wheel and were worthy of his final entrustment, his Way was able to assist in transformation, and his virtue was sufficient to benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, he strictly observed the *vinaya* to establish a model and manifested an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to deliver living beings.

His intention was not merely to benefit others for a single moment, but was directly aimed at rescuing those of the future, enabling them all to transcend the dust and entanglements of the various realms of existence. This... [Ānanda]... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "此阿", which likely refers to Ānanda, the primary disciple of the Buddha.)
It is difficult to share the virtues of those in the same rank. Generally, the prefaces to the scriptures all arise according to circumstances.
This scripture begins its teaching with Ānanda, showing him falling into a chamber of lust. It seems as though he was unable to uphold the Buddha-dharma or transcend the various realms of existence;

that he failed in dignified deportment and defiled the precepts, becoming unworthy of the final testament to save sentient beings and deliver those of the future. Therefore, it is for this reason that he is lamented alongside [the others].
The virtues of those listed serve to manifest the traces of Ānanda; in reality, there is no deficiency or defilement, for the intent lies in providing deliverance.
△ Third, the listing of names:
Their names were Mahāmati Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, and Pūrṇa...
With Kṣemadattīputra, Subhūti, Upāli, and so forth as their leaders; Śāriputra, whose wisdom was peerless and who was foremost in definitive realization;
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who was perfectly luminous and penetrating, foremost in supernormal powers;
Kauṇḍinya, whose faculties were sharp and keen, foremost in broad learning; and Pūrṇa, who possessed great...
Prajñākūṭa (辯才) was foremost in preaching the Dharma. Subhūti had realized the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) since kalpas past.

Upānanda had attained awakening to the nature of form (*rūpa*) among the six sense objects. As for the twelve thousand members of the assembly, the specific mention of these six names serves to represent the great purport of entering the Dharma.
Now, if one wishes to be ultimately firm and steadfast in all matters, one must necessarily...

Wisdom is the precursor; it definitively discerns all phenomena, causing them to become perfectly luminous and penetratingly clear. Furthermore, one must use extensive learning to unify them and eloquent exposition to clarify them.
When one thoroughly understands emptiness and form, achieving perfect integration and sovereign mastery, this is precisely the primary skillful means of the Śūraṅgama King.
Thus it is concluded. II. The Gathering of the Assembly (in two parts): 1. The Assembly of Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning, along with those at the initial stage of their resolve, all of whom came together to the Buddha’s presence.

At this time, while the bhikṣus were observing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end of the summer retreat, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions consulted him to resolve their doubts; they revered his compassionate yet majestic demeanor, seeking to attain the profound meaning of the Dharma.
*Pratyekabuddha* is translated here as "Solitary Realizer" (*Dujue*). "One beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) refers to the Arhat; the "initial mind" refers to those still in training (*śaikṣa*).

"Self-invitation" (*pravāraṇā*) means that one freely allows oneself to be raised for any transgressions by the Saṃgha. Because one is restricted from visiting the Buddha during the ninety-day period of *pārājika* observance, one consults to resolve doubts at the conclusion of the summer retreat.
Both the self-invitation and the resolution of doubts serve to examine one's virtuous conduct and achievements over the ninety-day period.
Reverently honoring the Tathāgata, he addressed him as "Compassionate and Majestic. "Compassionate" refers to his kindness; "majestic" refers to his awe-inspiring authority.

At that moment, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in tranquil repose, proclaiming the profound mysteries for the sake of the assembly. The pure multitude at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before;
his kalaviṅka-like celestial voice resounded throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
He proclaims the profound mysteries; this is why the *Śūraṅgama* is initiated. It is like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which takes the "Innumerable Meanings" as its point of departure.
The kalaviṅka is a divine bird whose voice is harmonious and elegant; the Buddha’s voice is like it.
△ Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), with Mañjuśrī as their leader.
"Mañjuśrī" is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*); it represents fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*). At the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* assembly, he served as the eye for discerning the Dharma;
therefore, he occupies the position of the leader. II. The Prologue of the Arousing [of the Teaching], in eight parts: First, the Buddha accedes to the King's command.

At that time, King Prasenajit, for the sake of the memorial day of his deceased father, prepared a vegetarian feast. He invited the Buddha to the inner palace and personally went out to welcome the Tathāgata.
He extensively provided rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, and furthermore personally extended an invitation to the great Bodhisattvas.
King Bimbisāra was the King of Śrāvastī. "Palace" (gōngyè) refers to the inner court of the king. He invited the Buddha into this inner court, demonstrating the utmost reverence.
△ Second, the section on the assembly of noble ones.
Furthermore, within the city, there were elders and lay devotees who simultaneously provided meals for the Sangha, awaiting the Buddha’s arrival to respond to their invitation.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the bodhisattvas and arhats to attend to the various hosts of the feast.
△ Third, Ānanda alone was exceptional.
Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation and, having traveled far, had not yet returned; thus he could not wait for his turn in the monastic assembly.
Since there were neither elders nor *ācāryas* with him, he returned alone along the way. On that day there was no alms-food offering; immediately, Ānanda took up his bowl.
As he went through the city begging for alms in succession, he first sought out his final donor to serve as the host for his midday meal;
whether they were pure or impure, of noble Kṣatriya lineage or even Caṇḍālas, he practiced universal compassion toward them all, making no distinction between the lowly and the humble.
He resolved to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings;
this describes the reason for his mistaken entry into a brothel. According to the Vinaya regulations, when a monk travels abroad, he must be accompanied by at least three companions.
One senior elder (*sthavira*) and one preceptor (*ācārya*) are appointed so as to solemnize conduct and prevent errors or omissions. The alms bowl is called the "receptacle" (*pātra*).

The "last donor" refers to one who has not yet provided a meal for the *saṃgha*. Through impartial compassion, one transforms them by regarding them with an equanimous mind, causing them to give with an equanimous mind.
Regarding equality in food, there is likewise equality in the Dharma; it is in this way that [the practice] can be perfected.
There are immeasurable merits [in this]. If one were a Mātaṅga, they would be defiled and lowly; since Ānanda failed to exercise discernment, he fell into error.
The Kṣatriya royal lineage refers to the Cāṇḍālas—those known as "killers"—namely, the families of butchers, slaughterers, pimps, and liquor-sellers.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for being Arhats whose minds were not impartial.
He reverently looked up to the Tathāgata as he elucidated the unobstructed Dharma to resolve all doubts and slanders, and passed through the city moat.
Walking slowly through the city gates, he maintained a solemn and dignified demeanor, reverently observing the rules of purification;
this describes his intention to practice universal compassion. Śūnyatā-jāti (Subhūti) abandoned poverty, while Kāśyapa abandoned wealth;
one was because the wealthy find it easy to give, and the other was to plant seeds of merit for the poor. The Tathāgata rebuked them both, desiring that their minds be free from obstruction.
This is to limit [the practice] and to dispel doubts and slanders regarding unequal observance of the fast. Thus, Ānanda revered and looked up to it with solemnity and respect.
As for the "fast method" (*zhāifǎ*), it refers to begging for alms in a disciplined, dignified, and orderly manner.

Some restrict this to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, claiming it is not a reprimand from the Tathāgata; yet how could they know that the Tathāgata did not reprimand Vimalakīrti alone? △ Fourth, showing the encounter.
Adverse conditions.

At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and was ensnared by the great sorceress Maṭaṅgī, who used the *sāvikāra* mantra of the ancient Brahmā to draw him into her bedchamber. As she physically caressed him, he was on the verge of violating his precepts.
The body [of Śāriputra] was that of Mātanga, a female courtesan. The sorcery transmitted by the heretic Śvāvikāla—here translated as "Yellow-Haired"—is called the "First Brahmā" spell;
it is in fact a demonic artifice. [Śāriputra] was about to have his precept-body destroyed by the lecherous embrace and caressing [of the woman]. Therefore, [the Buddha]...

To physically draw near to those defiled by desire is to violate the essence of pure precepts. As it says later, "Because the mind is pure, one has not yet sunk into ruin," which implies that [the violation] was merely on the verge of being committed.
At the time of the Buddha Emptiness-King, Ānanda made the same resolve for enlightenment as the Buddha; his merit and practice were indeed equal to the Buddha's.
However, because of his original vow to always delight in extensive learning and to protect and uphold the Dharma-treasury, he did not take up the fruit of Buddhahood.
Thus, the manifestation of traces in the present is precisely for the purpose of protection and preservation. For after the *prajñāpāramitā*, the study of wisdom (*prajñā*) flourished;

those who were deluded regarding their own nature pursued only extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without cultivating right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Being turned about by external objects, they were easily defiled by the heterodox;
thus, wandering aimlessly and falling into ruin, the Buddha’s treasury of Dharma would have been in peril of having no means of protection. Therefore, [the Buddha] provisionally relied upon...

I have heard that when the affairs of human depravity and defilement arise, the teachings are established. By means of the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama, one is supported by the Great Prajñā of Wisdom, so that concentration and wisdom may be balanced and study and practice may both be clarified.
Then, inverted delusions can be eliminated and the wondrous, profound stillness can be attained.
One will not be turned by external objects, but rather be able to turn them; thus, one becomes equal to the Tathāgata. You should know, Ānanda, that this is the skillful means.

True compassion! You have condescended for the sake of this late learner to follow in the tracks of the later scriptures; every word is nothing but an exhortation to sharpen one's resolve. △ Fifth, the Buddha’s Compassion Descends to Rescue:
The Tathāgata, knowing that the arts of lust had been employed against him, returned immediately after the meal. The king, along with his ministers, elders, and lay devotees—
They all came together to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
The Buddha usually preaches the Dharma for donors after his midday meal; he has now returned home abruptly, yet the king and his ministers followed him, wishing to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within this light, a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus emerged, upon which a transformation-body Buddha sat in the full-lotus posture and proclaimed a divine mantra.
He commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go to protect [them], so that evil spells might be extinguished. He then led Ānanda and Mātanga back to the presence of the Buddha.

The crown of the head represents the unsurpassed fruit. The light possesses the colors of a hundred jewels; it is called "Fearlessness" because it can intimidate demons and outsiders, such that no being can surpass it.

The World-Honored One does not himself recite the mantra, but rather causes a manifested Buddha to speak from the light upon his crown, thereby demonstrating that this mantra is the unconditioned mind-Buddha and the supreme dharma of the mind. 6. Ānanda’s Rebuttal.
[The Master] said:

When Ānanda saw the Buddha, he prostrated himself and wept with grief, lamenting that since time immemorial he had been devoted solely to much-learning (*bahu-śruta*) without fully perfecting his power of the Way (*mārga-bala*).

He realized that the wisdom of much-learning must necessarily attain right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), whereby the power of the Way is fully perfected and one is no longer captivated by the heterodox. △ Seven.
Seeking this present Dharma,
he earnestly entreated [the Buddha], who then revealed the initial expedient means for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to attain Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
*Śamatha* is called "stopping" (*zhi*). *Samāpatti* is called "contemplation" (*guan*). *Dhyāna* is called "meditative concentration" (*jinglü*).

These are precisely the three contemplations of stillness, illusion, and quiescence within Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanjue*). The contemplation of stillness relies on awakening to extinguish the dust; thus it is for abiding oneself.

The contemplation of illusion proceeds from meditative absorption to initiate action; thus it is for responding to phenomena. The contemplation of quiescence forgets both arising and ceasing; thus it is for eradicating traces. These three—
The harmony of these movements is neither three nor one; therefore, it is designated as "wondrous. It is the primary gateway to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions who attain Bodhi invariably take their initial inspiration from this. △ At all eight times, the assembly delights in hearing it.
At that time, there were also bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with great arhats and pratyekabuddhas from the ten directions, who all wished to hear [the teaching] with joy;
they withdrew to sit silently, awaiting the holy instructions.
The preceding section on the introduction is concluded.

△ Second, the main body of the teaching has five parts. First, the section on the Path of Vision has three parts. First, the discernment of the real and the false as the secret cause [of awakening] has two parts.
First, clarifying how the mind and its perceptions lose their true nature and sink into delusion has two parts. First, revealing the great cause that arises from the defilement of craving.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You and I share the same life-force; our feelings are equal to those of natural kin. When you first resolved your mind within my Dharma, what superior signs did you perceive that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy affection for the world?"
The question regarding the cause for relinquishing craving initiates the following passage. Ānanda was the son of King Droṇodana;
they shared the same parents and were of one root—brothers by natural order.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "I have observed the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, which are supremely wonderful and peerless.
His physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli. I have constantly reflected that these marks are not produced by the craving of desire.

Why is this? The breath of desire is coarse and turbid; it is a mingling of putrid odors, a chaotic jumble of pus and blood, incapable of giving rise to such supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous purple [radiance]."
A mass of golden light. Therefore, out of thirsty longing, he followed the Buddha to shave his head and leave the household life.
This answers the cause of abandoning craving; it reveals that the desires and outflows (āsrava) are coarse and evil, capable of obstructing wondrous clarity. To restore true purity once again—

One should distance oneself from attachment and abandon turbid defilement to give rise to wondrous clarity; this is precisely the *nidāna* (origination) of this sutra, while other explanations are but peripheral.
As for the thirty-two marks, they begin with the level soles of the feet and end with the high and rounded crown of the head.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You should know that all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not understand the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. They employ various false thoughts;
because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic wandering."
Sentient beings revolve through the cycle of birth and death because they do not know their own eternal, wondrous essence of mind, and are instead delusively entangled by thoughts of craving.

Now Ānanda alone is able to recognize this, reflect upon it, and with weary detachment abandon it; for this reason, he is praised as "excellent. II. Clarifying that the cause of inverted delusion lies within the mind and eyes.
1. Questioning and revealing the root of delusion.
If you now wish to investigate the true nature of enlightenment through supreme illumination, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.

Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path, they all depart from birth and death by means of a straightforward mind; for when the mind and its words are straightforward, [liberation is attained].
Thus, from the beginning to the end, through all stages and positions, there is forever no trace of crookedness.

The Way is inherently level and direct; it becomes crooked only due to delusion. Since one intends to investigate the True Path and eliminate inverted delusions, I have therefore commanded that you answer directly.

When the mind and speech are direct, the Way can be reached by a shortcut. This "One Way" means that all [beings]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the available portion.]
"It is the straightforward mind.
Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved upon the path, what did you see as you took the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata as your object?
Who was it that cherished them? Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, such cherishing was done with my own mind."
The eyes. Because one perceives the sublime marks of the Tathāgata with the eyes and gives rise to love and delight in the mind, I resolve to abandon birth and death.
Question: Who is it that loves and delights? This interrogates the root of delusion. Answer: It is due to the "mind-eyes. This precisely reveals the root of delusion. △
Second, investigating the illusory substance:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said, that which you truly love and cherish depends upon the mind and the eyes;
delusion and karma shift and migrate, and everything arises from this."
If you do not know where the mind and the eyes reside, you will be unable to subdue worldly afflictions.
It is like a king who, when invaded by bandits, dispatches troops to eliminate them; those troops must first know the location of the bandits.
Since it is the fault of your mind and eyes that causes you to wander through the cycle of rebirth, I now ask you: where, precisely, are your mind and eyes located right now?
From this point forward, there are seven layers of refutation and demolition, all of which reveal that the deluded mind and deluded views have no substantial reality;

they arise from grasping at objects of perception. This is called the root of beginningless birth and death, and therefore it must be demolished and severed. △ First, [the refutation] regarding being within. (2)
First inquiry.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that the consciousness-mind resides within the body.
Even when one gazes at the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are seen to be on the Buddha’s face. Now, as I observe this floating...”
The sense organs and their four objects reside only within my face. Thus, the consciousness-mind truly dwells inside the body; that is to say, the mind is internal while the eyes are external.
This is true for all beings from ordinary sentient creatures up to the Tathāgata—Ānanda is no exception. These points appear interchangeably in the text.
There are twelve classes of distinct beings, excluding those of earth, wood, space, and dispersed matter, as these do not belong to the category of the eye or the mind. The eye...
The external, floating, provisional earth, water, fire, and wind are formed by means of the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*). When they disperse, they return to these objects;
therefore, they are named after the objects. △ Second, the refutation of the two [theories]. First, citing facts to establish the determination.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall. Look at the Jeta Grove; where is it now?
"World-Honored One," [Ānanda replied], "this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is within the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden; the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall."
To determine the internal and external objects, one should clearly perceive the mind within in successive order.
Ānanda, what do you first see now within this hall? World-Honored One, while in this hall, I first see the Tathāgata.
Next, one observes the great assembly. Looking outward in this manner, one eventually beholds the groves and gardens;
there is a fixed sequence in what is seen first and last. If one intends to destroy the mind that dwells within, one does not first see the interior.

"Ānanda, you gaze at the grove and garden; by what means do you see them? "World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to look from within the hall and see them from afar."

All these matters shall first be established through the citation of scriptural evidence, and subsequently refuted by restating them. △ Second, the formal refutation that [the self] is not internal, in two parts.
First, the instruction to listen attentively:
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden-hued arm and rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head, instructing Ānanda:
And to the great assembly: there is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices.

It is the wondrous path of majestic adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate. You should now listen attentively. Ānanda prostrated himself and humbly received the compassionate instruction.
*Samādhi* is also called *samāpatti* and *samaya*. In this [language], it means "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*).
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is the path traversed by a thousand sages; hence it is called "the one gate. The ocean of wondrous adornment is reached through this; hence it is called "the way. 2.
Refuting the preceding [position] by tracing its implications.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "It is as you have said. While the body is in the lecture hall, with doors and windows wide open and one can gaze afar at the groves and gardens, there are also sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata but see what is outside the hall. Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One, it is impossible for one who is inside a hall not to see the Tathāgata but instead to see the groves and springs;
being within the hall, one ought first to see what is inside.
Ānanda, you are just like this: your mind is all-pervasive and fully cognizant. If that which you currently perceive before you...”

The mind is truly within the body. At that time, one should first understand the internal body. Is there any sentient being who first perceives what is within the body and only afterwards contemplates external objects?

If the mind were located within the body and one could see its internal organs, that might still be plausible. But to lead the assembly and ask them whether they can actually do so—that is utterly impossible.
Even if they cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, they certainly ought to clearly perceive the growth of nails and hair, the movement of tendons, and the throbbing of the pulses.
How can it be that one does not know it? One certainly does not know it internally. How then can one know it externally?
Even if one cannot know the internal organs such as the heart and stomach, why is one not aware of external things like the nails and veins?
Since one does not know it internally, it is certain that it does not reside within.
Therefore, you should know: your claim that the mind which perceives and knows dwells within the body is untenable. This concludes the refutation of the [position that the mind] is inside.
II. [The position that the mind] is outside. This has two parts: 1. The inquiry.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, and I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body. Why is this? It is like a lamp burning within a room;

that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only after that can its light reach the door and the courtyard beyond. Yet all sentient beings do not see [their minds] within their own bodies."
To perceive only what is outside the body is like a lamp placed outdoors; it cannot illuminate the interior of the room. This principle must be clear so that there will be no confusion;
it accords with the Buddha’s definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Could it be that I have fallen into error?

Because this refutation of [the notion that the mind] is not internal further gives rise to false conceptualization—namely, the conviction that the mind exists externally—the second section follows to refute these two views.
First, an analogy is cited to establish the certainty [of the argument].
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "These bhikṣus have just now come from me; they have been begging for alms-food throughout the city of Śrāvastī."
[The Buddha] returned to the Jeta Grove and said, "I have already finished my midday meal. Observe these bhikṣus: when one person eats, do all the others become satiated?
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are arhats, their physical bodies and life-sustaining elements differ;
how could one person cause the multitude to be satiated?"

That food cannot satisfy him; this means that the external mind cannot know the body. When it says "returning to the forest after begging for food," it refers to the multitude who see him before eating.
Therefore, it says, "I have already completed my meal for the night. "Night" (*sō*) implies preparation. There are four kinds of food:

edible morsels (*kavaḍīkāra*), contact (*sparśa*), volition (*manasikāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Morsel" (*dandan*) refers specifically to edible food; it has a physical form that can be grasped and taken up, thereby distinguishing it [from the other three].
It is not the food of thought, nor the food of consciousness. △ Second, the direct refutation that [the mind] is not external.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were actually located outside the body, then the body and the mind would be external to one another."
Since they do not interfere with one another, that which the mind knows, the body cannot perceive; and that which is perceived at the physical boundaries, the mind cannot know.
This demonstrates that [the object] is not external.
"I now show you my hand of tūla-cotton. When you see it with your eyes, does your mind not discern it?
Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "If they are mutually cognizant, why would one be outside [the other]?"
This proves it is not external. Tūla-cotton is white like frost, and the Buddha’s hands are as soft as it;
therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which perceives and knows resides outside the body—is impossible.
△ Section Three: The Hidden Root (2).
Part One: The Interrogation. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has stated, because one does not see within, it does not reside inside the body;
yet because the body and mind know one another and are not separate, it does not exist outside the body. As I now reflect, I know it must be located in a single place. The Buddha—
"Where is this locus now? Ānanda replied, "This cognizing mind, which does not know the interior yet can see the exterior, must, as I have reflected, be hidden within the sense organ."
Furthermore, one may calculate that the mind is hidden within the eye-faculty; this can be clarified by the following analogy:
it is like a person who takes a lapis lazuli bowl and places it over both eyes; although there is an object covering them, it does not obstruct or hinder vision.

Those faculties follow their perceptions and immediately engage in discrimination. Yet, as for this mind of mine that is aware and capable of cognition, it does not see within because it resides in the faculties;
nor does it clearly gaze outward without obstruction because it is hidden within the faculties.
The lapis lazuli cage surrounding the roots is a metaphor for the eye-organ concealing the mind. Because it resides within the organ, the internal viscera are not seen;
yet because the organ is pure, external objects are clearly perceived. Therefore, it is called "hidden within the root. △ Second, the refutation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said, that which is hidden within the root is like lapis lazuli. Suppose that person were to cover their eyes with a lapis lazuli mask;

would they see the mountains and rivers, and yet see the lapis lazuli as well? [Ānanda replied: 'Yes, World-Honored One, if that person were to cover their eyes with a lapis lazuli mask, they would indeed see the lapis lazuli.
The Buddha told Ānanda: 'If your mind were united with the lapis lazuli in this same way, [you would see it as well when looking at objects]. "

If you can see mountains and rivers, why do you not see your own eyes? If you were to see your eyes, the eye would become identical to its object, and thus it could not function as a faculty of perception.
If you cannot see them, how can you claim that this cognizing mind resides within the faculties like a crystal vessel?

This contradicts both fact and principle; it is not a case of the faculty being hidden. As for the failure to establish "conformity" (anuvartana): as stated previously, conformity consists in following after conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Now, since the eye is the object seen, the meaning of "conformity" is not established.
Therefore, you should know that your claim— that the mind capable of conscious cognition dwells hidden within the sense organs like a crystal casket—

is untenable. *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, from the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.*
