△ Section Four: The Obscurity of the Four Āgamas, Part Two.
I. Inquiry. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now further engaged in such reflection: regarding this body of sentient beings, the internal organs..."
The internal cavities are within, while the apertures reside on the outside. Where there is an internal cavity, it is dark; where there is an aperture, it is bright.
Now, when I face the Buddha, I open my eyes and see light, which is called seeing the external. When I close my eyes and see darkness, it is called seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?
Furthermore, wishing to calculate that the mind resides within, one takes the perception of darkness as seeing the internal organs. △ Second, the refutation of the three [positions].
First, regarding external vision:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye?"
If it does not face the eye, then when darkness is before the eye, how could it constitute the "internal"?
If it were internal, then when you are in a dark room without sun, moon, or lamp, that darkness within the room would all be your own entrails.
If it does not face [the object], how can it constitute seeing?
The sequence of first questioning, then challenging, and finally concluding is clear. There are the five spirit-repositories (zàng) and the six transformative viscera (fǔ);
the triple-burner (sānjiāo) is one of these six viscera. △ Second, the internal correspondence.

If one were to set aside external vision and instead perceive internally through internal confrontation, then closing the eyes to see darkness would be called seeing within the body; yet when opening the eyes to see light, why does one not see one's own face?
If one does not see one's face, then internal confrontation is not established.

The objects before one's eyes are called "external seeing. The objects within the body are called "internal facing. Previously, because that which faces the eye was considered external, it could not be established as internal.
Now, even if one sets aside external seeing to constitute internal facing, this would mean the eye is capable of looking back upon itself.
If it can look back upon the body while closed, then when opened, it should likewise look back upon one's own face. If this were not the case—
The principle is not established. △ Third, refutation by concession:
If the meeting were established, then this cognizing mind and the eye-organ would reside in empty space; how could they be said to be within?
If it were in empty space, then since that space is not your own body, the Tathāgata seeing your face now would also have to be your body.
Your eyes already perceive this; therefore, your body should not be capable of sensation. If you insist that both body and eyes possess sensation, then there must be two distinct cognitions.
Then your single body would have to become two Buddhas.
This sequential clarification shows that there is no principle of mutual observation. Since your eye has already known [the object], the body must not be the knower;
as it resides in empty space, it is inherently not your own substance. If you insist that both possess cognition, then they would constitute two distinct entities.

The reason the texts refuting delusion involve much circuitous argumentation is that people’s mental perceptions have lost their truth and are so deeply mired in delusion that, when confronted with an inquiry, they become frantic and lose their footing. As it is said, "The empty and deluded mind possesses many clever views.
Therefore, the Buddha, to counteract such delusion, employs skillful, circuitous arguments to clarify the truth.
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal"—is untenable.
△ Five: Following the Conjunction, Part Two. One: The Interrogation. Ānanda said:
"I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise. Because...
Because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise. As I now contemplate, this very essence of contemplation is my true mind-nature;
wherever it encounters conditions, the mind exists accordingly, yet it is not located within, without, or in between these three places.

This cites the intent of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. It means that by virtue of a single moment of delusion within the ālayavijñāna, the sense-faculties, the body, and the objective world arise through transformation;
this is the arising of dharmas from the mind. Furthermore, when stirred by the winds of objective conditions, the waves of consciousness surge forth;
this is the arising of the mind from dharmas. Through the mutual arising of mind and dharmas, one engages in conceptualization in accordance with those objects.
That is to say, the very point where the essence of mind and mental phenomena conjoin is what constitutes the mind’s presence. △ Second, the refutation of these two.
First, restating the previous position to raise an objection: The Buddha told Ānanda, "You have now stated that because phenomena arise, various kinds of minds are produced; wherever they conjoin,"
As for the mind following after existence: if this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it can conjoin.
If that which lacks substance could nevertheless conjoin, then the nineteen realms would conjoin with the seven sense-objects; this principle is not tenable.

If, however, it does have substance, then when you touch its substance with your hand or eye, as for the mind you perceive—does it emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerges from within, [then...]
Furthermore, when one perceives [the mind] within the body, if it were to come from the outside, one should first perceive the face;
yet, because one immediately takes the substance itself to be the mind, this is merely a superficial conceptualization. Therefore, it is difficult to determine whether its substance exists or not.

If it has no substance, then it is empty of anything more than its name; how could it then correspond [to the body]? It would be like the "nineteenth element" or the "seven particles," which are merely empty names.
If it did have substance, where would it be located such that one could touch it with the body? Thus, it is verified that its substantial reality is actually non-existent.
Ānanda said: "I see with this eye; I know with my mind that it is not the eye. This is because 'seeing' does not constitute the true meaning [of vision].

This explains the previous objection. It means that while the mind can only cognize, one cannot say it sees. He had never realized that the capacity to see resides in the mind, whereas the eyes alone do not see.
The Buddha said: "If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, those who have already died still possess their eyes;
they should all be able to see objects. If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?"

The analogy of the door illustrates that the capacity for seeing resides within the mind; the analogy of death clarifies that it is merely the eyes that do not see. △ Second, a detailed analysis of the correspondence:
"Ānanda, furthermore, if this mind of yours that perceives and knows must have a substantial body, would it be a single entity, or would it be..."
If it were many bodies, they would now reside within your own body; would they then pervade the entire body, or would they not pervade it?
First, four propositions are established, which will be examined and analyzed in detail below. You should know that the True Mind is neither one nor many, and neither pervasive nor non-pervasive.
If it were a single entity, then when you prick one limb with your hand, all four limbs should feel it.
If they all felt it, there would be no specific location for the prick. If the prick has a specific location, then your "single entity" cannot be established.
This refutes [the self] as being a single entity. "Non-abiding" means having no fixed location.
If it were a plurality of entities, then there would be many persons; which entity, then, would be "you"?
This refutes [the self] as being a plurality of entities.
If it were pervasive throughout the entire body, it would be the same as what was previously touched;
thus, it is argued that it is not pervasive. As for "being the same as before," if one touches a single limb, all four limbs should experience sensation.
If it were not all-pervasive, then when you touch your head and also touch your feet, the head would have sensation while the feet should remain insentient.
Since this is not the case for you, it is clear that [the mind] is not non-pervasive. Since these four arguments are invalid, one cannot claim that the mind follows along wherever it makes contact.
It exists. Therefore, one should know that wherever there is a point of conjunction, the mind follows and exists there; it is not the case that such a thing does not exist.
△ Sixth, the two intermediate sections. First, the inquiry.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I too have heard it. When the Buddha was conversing with Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma-princes regarding the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the World-Honored One also said: 'The mind is neither within nor without.

As I reflect upon this, there is nothing perceived within, and there is no mutual cognition of the external. Because there is no cognition within, its existence within is not established; yet the body and mind are mutually cognizant."
To claim it is external is contrary to reason; since the various parts now know one another, yet there is no perception within, it must reside in between.
This is a mistaken interpretation of the Great Teaching. To hold that it is internal, then one would not perceive the internal organs;
to hold that it is external, then the body’s parts would not know one another. Since these two positions are untenable, it must reside between the sense organ and its object. △
Second, the refutation of the two [positions]. First, defining the intermediate state:

The Buddha said, "Regarding what you call the 'intermediate,' that which is intermediate must not be deluded, nor can it be without a location. Now, as you investigate this intermediate, where does it reside?
Does it reside in a place, or does it reside within the body?"
First, I shall address the lower position. "Place" (*sthāna*) refers to the objective domain.
If [the self] were located within the body, it would be at the periphery rather than in the center; if it were in the center, it would be identical to being internal.

The body possesses both the meanings of "center" and "periphery. If [the self] were at the periphery, it could not be considered the center; if it were in the center, it would be the same as the aforementioned case of being internal.
Internally, one should perceive the internal.

If it exists in a location, does it have a manifest sign (*vijñapti*) or is it without a manifest sign? If it were without a manifest sign, it would be identical to non-existence; if it were with a manifest sign, it would lack fixed stability.
Why is this? It is like when a person uses a marker to designate a center: looking from the east, it is west; observing from the south, it becomes north.
Since the substance of the marker is thus indeterminate, the mind ought to be confused and disordered.

This clarifies that the middle position has no fixed location. "To manifest" means to indicate an object for the purpose of making it evident. If things are in a state of confusion, there is nothing from which a middle can be apprehended.
Ānanda said: "The 'middle' I speak of is not these two kinds [of extremes]. It is as the World-Honored One has said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, [visual consciousness] arises.'"
Regarding visual consciousness: the eye possesses discrimination, while the object of form is devoid of cognition. When consciousness arises between them, it is said that the mind resides therein;
that is to say, it does not reside within the body, but rather between the sense organ and the object. △ Second, the formal refutation of "not being in the middle."
The Buddha said: "If your mind were within the sense organs and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both, or would it not encompass both?
First establish your thesis, and then I shall refute it."
If one combines both [the object and the essence], the substance of things becomes confused. Since the object is not the knowing of the essence, they stand as two opposing entities;

how, then, can this be the Middle? To refute the combination of the two is to show that it cannot constitute the Middle. "Object" refers to the sense organs and their objects; "essence" refers to the essence of the mind.

As for "the object is not the knowing of the essence": if the object does not possess the same essence as the knowing, then the sense organs and objects would stand in opposition to the mind, and there would be no intermediate position between them.
Furthermore, if both [aspects] are not established, it is neither knowing nor non-knowing; thus, there is no essential nature. What, then, could constitute the characteristic of the "Middle"?

To refute that which is not inclusive is to show that it cannot be the Middle. If it does not include the sense organ (*indriya*), it is not knowing; if it does not include the object (*viṣaya*), it is not...
"I do not know. Since both meanings are untenable, how can the middle be determined?
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for [the self] to exist in between.
△ Seven: Non-attachment, in two parts. First, the inquiry.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma. You constantly spoke of awakening to and discerning the nature of the mind."
Since it is neither within, nor without, nor in between— having no location at all—
and since that which is entirely free from attachment is called "mind," would you say that my lack of attachment is "mind"?
The Buddha’s intention was to reveal that the mind is fundamentally non-existent and that one should not harbor attachments;
yet now Ānanda is attached even to "non-attachment," which is precisely the clinging of deluded sentiment. △ Second, the refutation.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for your statement that the nature of the mind which perceives, knows, and discriminates has no location whatsoever—consider all things in the world, including space, water, land, and all flying creatures, as well as every object and phenomenon;
these are called 'all. If you do not cling to them, does this state of non-clinging exist, or does it not exist?"
If it were non-existent, it would be the same as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could there be non-attachment?
That which is non-attached cannot be called non-existent. This restates the previous objection, intending to clarify that as soon as there is cognitive awareness, one cannot be without attachment.
Regarding the question "Does it exist or not?"—it asks whether those objective phenomena exist or are empty and non-existent, even though your mind is non-attached. If...
If that emptiness were non-existent, it would be identical to a tortoise’s hair; how then could one speak of "non-attachment" while being attached [to such a thing]?

If there were one who was not attached, then that would constitute an existing entity; therefore, it cannot be designated as "non-existent. These points all recapitulate the objections; what follows is the refutation.

If there is no characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then there is nothing. That which is not non-existent is precisely a characteristic. If characteristics exist, then they are present. How can there be non-attachment?
If things truly lacked characteristics, they would be like the hair of a tortoise. If things are indeed not non-existent, then they inherently possess characteristics.
Knowing that characteristics exist means the mind has a point of attachment; how, then, could this be called non-attachment?
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for there to be a mind of awakening and cognition that is not free from all attachments;

this concludes the refutation of the fetters. The seven preceding investigations have thoroughly exhausted all conceptual attachments. Once deluded sentiments are dispelled, deluded objects naturally cease to exist.
Thus, the true mind and the true vision may be clarified. △ Second, the formal determination of the true mind and the true vision, in two parts.
First, the selection of the true mind, in two parts. First, Ānanda’s sorrowful entreaty.

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am the Tathāgata’s youngest brother. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, even though I have now left the household life, I still rely upon his affectionate indulgence.
For this reason, although I possess much learning, I have not yet attained the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*), nor have I been able to subdue my own mind."
The *Sāṃvarī* mantra was turned against him by those [demons], causing him to fall into a brothel. This was due to his failure to know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because of the previous provocation, he finally realized his delusion and error; he then reproached himself and requested instruction, seeking to reach the true limit.
The intent of what is related here is entirely to warn future followers. "True limit" (*zhēnjì*) refers to the true mind as the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that those of the icchantika class may abandon their barbaric ways.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; the entire great assembly likewise waited expectantly with yearning hearts.

I have reverently heard your instructions, and my mind is as clear as a mirror reflecting water—not merely that it is not obscure, but because I seek the path of *śamatha* to reach the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Once the ultimate reality is revealed, delusive defilements vanish of their own accord; thus, even those of the icchantika nature and the Mlecchas are caused to fall away from their errors. As for the icchantikas: [The text continues: ...they are those who have severed all roots of goodness, harboring no aspiration for the Buddha-way. They are like withered seeds that cannot sprout, or like a stone that cannot grow grass. Yet, by the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, even they may eventually be awakened.

This is why the teaching says: "Even an icchantika can attain Buddhahood. It is not that they possess a fixed nature of non-enlightenment; rather, it is because they lack the conditions for practice in this life that they are so designated. If one encounters a true teacher and applies oneself with vigor, there is no reason they cannot transform their nature and realize the Way. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching never abandons anyone. This is the profound meaning of the Dharma-gate of universal inclusion. Thus, it is said that even the icchantika can destroy their state of being a Mleccha. As for the icchantika... [The text concludes: ...it is through the transformative power of the Great Vehicle that even those deemed beyond salvation are ultimately brought to liberation. This is the inexhaustible merit of the Buddha’s wisdom. Thus ends this passage.
The meaning [of the term] is translated as "severing the roots of goodness. *Mleccha* means "one who delights in filth"; it signifies ruin and destruction.
△ Second, the World-Honored One’s response and instruction has three parts. First, the manifestation of auspicious light and omens.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face. The radiance was so brilliant as to resemble hundreds of thousands of suns.
The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways, and in this manner, lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions were simultaneously revealed.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all worlds were merged into a single realm.
All the great bodhisattvas within those worlds remained in their respective lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.

To reveal the primordial luminosity (*mūla-vidyā*), this omen was first manifested. When it is said that "light of various kinds is emitted from the face-gate," this means that light is simultaneously emitted from the mouth, eyes, ears, nose, and the space between the eyebrows;
it demonstrates that this primordial luminosity manifests through all the sense-faculties (*indriya-dvāra*) without exception.
Because it manifests everywhere, it shines forth in unison and illuminates all at once, like hundreds of thousands of suns throughout the entire Buddha-field.

This is the Dharma-realm itself. As for the "sixfold earthquake," it symbolizes that the ignorance of the six consciousnesses is about to be shattered, thereby revealing the illusory objects produced by karmic bonds.
"The lands of as many atoms as there are appear simultaneously" means that fundamental luminosity shines through clearly, such that delusory dust does not create any obstruction.

"The worlds of the ten directions merge into a single realm" means that the sphere of wisdom manifests perfectly, such that the measure of emotional consciousness poses no hindrance. The Bodhisattvas...
As for the audience who all reside in their own lands: their mental capacity is fundamentally rooted in the mind, and their hearing is fundamentally rooted in the void.
To realize this auspicious radiance is to attain the primordially pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana. △ Second, a general demonstration of that which is deluded.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions.
The seeds of their karma naturally cluster like the *akṣa* fruit. Consequently, practitioners are unable to achieve unexcelled Bodhi;
instead, they may become Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or even follow the ways of external paths, becoming devas, Māras, or the retinues of Māra. All of this arises from ignorance."

There are two fundamental roots for erroneous cultivation. It is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal; even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed.

What are these two? Ānanda, the first is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is that very攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pán-yuán-xīn*—the mind that clings to external objects) that you and all sentient beings currently take to be their own nature. The second is the root of beginningless Bodhi...

Nirvana is the fundamentally pure essence; it is this very consciousness-essence, originally luminous, which is capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet that which is lost amidst those conditions.
Because sentient beings have lost this original luminosity, though they act throughout their entire lives, they remain unaware of it and thus falsely enter the various realms of existence.

The seeds of karma accumulated by sentient beings cause practitioners to fail to achieve the perfect fruit; this is entirely due to practicing erroneously because of ignorance regarding the two fundamental roots.
Therefore, it is necessary to exercise decisive discernment. "Karma-seeds" refers to inverted, deluded confusion, like the akṣa fruit.

"One branch producing three fruits must necessarily grow from the same stem" is a metaphor for how delusion, karma, and suffering—these three lifetimes—must necessarily coalesce. Being unstained by afflictions is called Bodhi; not entering into birth and death is called Nirvana. Because it is neither stained nor involved, it is termed the Primordially Pure Essence.
The essence of consciousness (vijñāna) is the *ādāna-vijñāna*; primordial luminosity is the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and wondrous luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
The faculties, the physical body, the vessel-world, and all conditioned phenomena arise in dependence upon this. Yet, human beings perceive conditions and lose the truth;
thus it is said, "that which is abandoned by conditions. Because of abandoning this, ignorance and non-awakening cause one to enter the various realms of existence in vain.

To speak of the "original substance" as "originally luminous," and further to call it "fundamental luminosity": that which emerges from its own source is called "original"; this directly points to the very essence itself.
[The Buddha] said: "Fundamental. △ Third, the actual provision of definitive discernment, in nine parts. First, raising his fist to pose a question:
"Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of *śamatha* and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now question you again.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm and extended his five fingers, saying to Ānanda: "Do you see this now? Ānanda [replied].

[Ānanda] spoke of "seeing. The Buddha asked, "What do you see? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata raising his arm and bending his fingers to form a radiant fist that illuminates my heart and eyes. The Buddha asked, "By means of what do you see?
Ānanda replied, "I and the great assembly all see with our eyes. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Now answer me: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers to form a radiant fist..."
"I shall illuminate your eyes and mind. Your eyes can see; with what, then, do you perceive my fist as it illuminates?
At each fingertip of the Buddha’s five fingers, there was a mark of a wheel. △ Second, answering by following after delusion.
Ānanda said, "The Tathāgata has now inquired as to where the mind resides. I have used my mind to investigate and pursue it;
that which performs this investigation, I shall take to be the mind."
When the Golden Fist is raised, one must directly recognize fundamental luminosity; if the marks of sensory dust are not yet removed, one continues as before to mistake the thief for one's own son.
△ Third, being rebuked, he was struck with alarm.
The Buddha said, "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind. Ānanda was startled and withdrew from his seat; joining his palms and rising, he addressed the Buddha:
"This is not my mind. What should it be named?"
*Jue* (矍) signifies an expression of alarm and astonishment. △ Fourth, the refutation and demonstration that [these perceptions] are not real.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is the illusory appearance and conceptualization of external objects (*pratyaya*). It deludes your true nature.
Because from time immemorial until this present life, you have mistaken the thief for your son, you have lost your original constancy and thus undergo successive cycles of rebirth."
△ Five: Ānanda was at a loss.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha; because my heart loved the Buddha, he caused me to leave the household life.
Why should my mind be concerned with making offerings solely to the Tathāgata? I would rather travel throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas and..."
"Good spiritual friend, it is by means of this mind that one gives rise to great courage and vigor to perform all those difficult dharmic deeds.
Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it would still be because of this mind.

If what has been revealed here were not the mind, then I would be without a mind and identical to earth or wood. Apart from this awareness and cognition, there is nothing else at all. Why, then, does the Tathāgata say..."

"This is not the mind. I am truly terrified, and there is no one among this great assembly who does not harbor doubt and confusion. I only pray that you will bestow your great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened.
Having long since falsely identified with delusion, I was momentarily startled and disoriented upon hearing this refutation; therefore, I earnestly request further instruction. △
Sixth, demonstrating the existence of the true mind:

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), sat upon the lion throne, rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head, and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always said that all dharmas arise..."
All is manifested by the mind alone. All causes and effects, the worlds, and even their subtlest atoms, derive their substance from the mind.
Ānanda, if one examines the fundamental source of everything that exists within all these worlds—even down to a blade of grass, a leaf, a thread, or a knot—they all possess an inherent nature.
Even empty space has its name and characteristics; how much more so the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind-nature, which is the single essence of all?
The mind is entirely insubstantial, yet because of fear, it is said that there is no mind;
thus, by citing what is commonly spoken to lead beings toward realization, it is shown that the true mind exists.

This enables one to know where to apply oneself. "The mind entering the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" means causing one to awaken to the mind of the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is neither born nor extinguished.
Since the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, it is said that "the arising of all dharmas is manifested solely by the mind.
"All causes and effects" refers to the primary retributions (*vipāka*) within the ten realms; "the atoms of the world" refers to the environments (*bhājana-loka*) of the ten realms.
This is the retribution. Since there is nothing that does not take the mind as its basis for forming its substance, how can it be said that the mindless are the same as soil and wood?
That which is inherently undefiled is called "pure"; that which is defiled yet remains undefiled is called "wondrously pure. All deluded minds—
All receive their nature from this. △ Seventh, refuting false attachments:

If you stubbornly cling to the notion that the nature cognized by discriminative thought and observation must necessarily be the mind, then this mind should exist as a distinct, complete nature apart from all objects of the senses—namely, the spheres of form, fragrance, taste, and touch, as well as all activities.
To discriminate between vitarka and vicāra is precisely to engage in mental speculation. This mind, when separated from sensory objects, has no inherent nature; it should not be grasped as real.
As you now listen to my teaching, this constitutes discrimination arising because of sound. Even if you were to extinguish all [sensory objects], [the mind would still persist].
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—internally maintaining a state of profound stillness—is still but a reflection of the discrimination of dharma-objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).
This explains, based on the six sense objects, that they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). When sensory cognition ceases, the mind becomes profoundly still;
yet that profound stillness is likewise but a reflection of dharma-objects, and it too lacks intrinsic nature.

I am not commanding you to hold that this is not the mind. Rather, you must examine the mind with subtle discernment: if the nature of discrimination exists apart from the external objects, then it is truly your own mind.
If the nature of discrimination has no substance apart from the objects, then it is merely a reflected phenomenon of the discrimination of those objects.
Since objects are not permanent, when they change and perish, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
"In that case, your Dharma-body would be identical to annihilation. Who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
Examine this closely so that you may know it is not the truth. The Dharma-body is precisely the true mind. △ 8. Ānanda loses his composure.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and lost in self-reflection.
Having always clung to their deluded minds, they were suddenly subjected to refutation and rebuke; finding nothing upon which to rely, they were thus overcome with self-disparagement. △ Ninth:
Concluding the Formation of Delusive Error.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "All practitioners in the world who have attained the nine successive meditative absorptions in the present life yet fail to achieve the exhaustion of outflows and become Arhats, do so because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality."
Therefore, although you have now attained much learning, you have not achieved the fruit of sainthood.

The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the extinction concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*) of the two vehicles constitute nine stages. One enters from one dhyāna to the next, practicing them in successive order.
This concludes the selection of the true mind.
△ Second, the Selection of True Insight. Mind is the essence; insight is the function. Mind is the source of all phenomena; insight is the eye of the Way.
Therefore, they are sequentially determined as the secret cause. The text has two parts. First, Ānanda’s sorrowful plea. 2.
First, lamenting over previous failings.
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with deep sorrow. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Ever since I followed the Buddha to resolve my mind on leaving the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and have constantly thought to myself that there was no need for me to practice."
I thought that the Tathāgata had bestowed this samādhi upon me, not realizing that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable.
Having lost my original mind, although my body has left the household life, my mind does not enter the Way; it is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees.
I am moved by what the Buddha has revealed and lament the errors of the past. The World-Honored One’s samādhi was unknown to Kāśyapa; therefore, it could not be bestowed upon him.
One must cultivate this personally within one's own body and realize it within one's own mind. Whether one is deluded or awakened depends on oneself; it cannot be substituted for another.
The parable of the impoverished son who abandoned his father illustrates the loss of one’s original mind.

Today I have come to know this: though one may possess much learning, if one does not practice it, it is equal to having heard nothing at all. It is like a person who speaks of food but can never satisfy their hunger.
The essential method for studying the Way is to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation. Merely hearing without practicing leads ultimately to nothing.
Therefore, it is equivalent to not having heard [the teaching] at all; it is like merely talking about food.

Among the later generations of superficial scholars, there are many who boast of their extensive learning yet lose the reality of practice, deviating from the truth and turning their backs on the Way, all while remaining unaware of their own failings and failing to repent.
Ānanda’s grief and remorse truly serve as a powerful admonition. II. A Second Request for Instruction.
World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for our wretched and destitute state, will give rise to his wondrously luminous mind and open our eyes to the Way.
This reiterates the inquiry into the causes of delusion and seeks further instruction. The two obstacles are those of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cognizable (*jñeya*).
The obstacle of the cognizable obstructs right knowledge and vision; the obstacle of afflictions perpetuates the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), acting as a false entanglement.

If one realizes quiescence and permanence, then afflictions will not arise, birth and death will not undergo change, and the false entanglements will naturally unravel. The "eye of the Way" (*mārgacakṣus*) is precisely true vision.
It arises from the wondrously luminous mind. △ Second, the World-Honored One’s response and instruction in three parts: First, the manifestation of the auspicious light-omen.
At that moment, from the *svastika* on the Tathāgata’s chest, there surged forth precious light; this light shone brilliantly with hundreds of thousands of colors.

Simultaneously pervading all Buddha-worlds as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, [the water] flowed over the crowns of all Tathāgatas in all the precious lands of the ten directions,
and then descended upon Ānanda and the entire great assembly.

To clarify the true vision, the emission of precious light from the *svastika* on the chest symbolizes that right knowledge and insight arise from the wondrous mind of jewel-like clarity (*ratna-prabhāsa-citta*).
The *svastika* upon the Buddha’s chest signifies the gathering of all auspicious myriad virtues;

its light is brilliant, radiant, and magnificent, manifesting in hundreds of thousands of colors, which likewise symbolizes that the wondrous mind’s illumination is fully endowed with the myriad [virtues].

This is virtue. That its light pervades the Buddha-realms demonstrates that it is pure and fundamental by nature. That it universally moistens the crowns of the Buddhas' heads symbolizes what is shared among those at the ultimate fruition.
That it subsequently reaches the great assembly demonstrates what is common to all sentient beings.
This is the true light of the wondrous mind and the eye of the Way; it does not increase in sages nor decrease in ordinary people—it merely manifests in accordance with their capacities. △
Secondly, having granted the request, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I shall now, for your sake, erect the great Dharma banner, and likewise cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions [to do so]."
One attains the wondrous, subtle, and secret mind of pure luminosity and obtains the eye of purity.

The "banner" (*dhvaja*) symbolizes the crushing of heterodoxy and the establishment of the orthodox. The following clarifies the wondrous mind and the pure eye, enabling one to subdue heterodox and divergent views and attain correct knowledge and vision;
this is called erecting the great Dharma banner. Once heterodoxy is crushed and knowledge and vision are rectified, then the wondrous...
The mind can be attained; the pure eye can be obtained. That which exists equally in both sentient beings and Buddhas yet cannot be measured or known is called "wondrously subtle and esoteric.

That which cannot be defiled by impurities and cannot be obscured by darkness is called "naturally pure and luminous. That which perceives apart from the disease of cataracts and illuminates with vast clarity is called the "pure eye.
Part Three: The Direct Provision of Determination (in four sections). First: Question and Answer Establishing the Meaning.
"Ānanda, you previously answered me that you saw the radiant fist. From what cause does this fist possess its radiance? How is it formed into a fist?
And by whom was it seen? Ānanda replied, "Because the Buddha’s entire body is of Jāmbūnada gold, blazing like a mountain of jewels, born of purity, it therefore possesses radiance.
I truly saw it with my own eyes as he bent his five fingers into a fist and showed it to me."
Therefore, he has the mark of joined hands.
When the juice of the Jambu-river tree enters the water, the sand and stones turn into gold; it is like a blazing, crimson flame.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Today the Tathāgata speaks these true words to you: those who possess wisdom must rely upon parables."
And thus they attained awakening. "Ānanda, it is like my fist: if there were no hand of mine, my fist would not be formed;
if there were no eye of yours, your seeing would not be formed. Applying the principle of my fist to the faculty of your eye—does the meaning not hold equally?
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One. Since without my eye there is no seeing of mine, the analogy of my faculty of sight to that of the Tathāgata [is valid]."
The fist and the matter at hand share similar characteristics.
However, the sense organ of the eye does not actually resemble the meaning of the fist; Ānanda, not yet having realized this, indicated they were the same, and thus replied that they are similar.
△ Second, the correct discernment of the true seeing.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "What you say regarding their similarity is not correct. Why is this? It is like a person without hands—their fists are ultimately non-existent.
Yet for one who lacks eyes, it is not the case that seeing is entirely absent. Why so? Try asking a blind person on the road, 'What do you see?
Those blind people will surely answer you: 'Now, before my eyes, I only [see darkness]...'"

One sees darkness; there is nothing else to behold. Observing through this principle, the external object itself is dark; what deficiency could there be in the seeing? To see darkness is simply to see.
Thus we know that blindness is not a lack of seeing; it is merely the absence of eyes.
Ānanda said, "The blind see only darkness before their eyes; how can this be called 'seeing'? The Buddha told Ānanda, "The blind have no eyes and perceive only darkness.
Is there a difference between this darkness and that of a person with sight who is situated in a dark room?

Or is there no difference? [Ānanda replied,] "It is so, World-Honored One. When comparing the darkness of the person in the dark room with that of the group of blind people, there is indeed a distinction."
There is no difference;
the two types of darkness are indistinguishable. Thus, darkness does not arise from the sense organ, but is merely the darkness of the object.
Ānanda, if a person without eyes sees only the blackness before them, and suddenly regains the light of their eyes, they will again perceive various forms within that same objective field.
If various colors are called "seen by the eye," then when a person in the dark sees only the blackness before them and suddenly obtains the light of a lamp,
they should likewise be said to see the various colors of the external objects through the lamp.
This sufficiently demonstrates that seeing resides in the mind and not in the eyes.

If it were the lamp that sees, then the lamp would possess the faculty of vision; in that case, it could no longer be called a "lamp. Furthermore, if it is the lamp that observes, what concern is that of yours?
Therefore, you should know this: just as a lamp can reveal color, yet it is the eye—not the lamp—that sees;
so too, while the eye can reveal form, it is the nature of mind—not the eye—that sees.

This recapitulates the preceding points to clarify that seeing does not depend on the eye. Since knowing and seeing do not depend on the eye, one directly awakens to the nature of seeing, transcends the burdens of form, and attains the pure eye. △ Third, Ānanda has not yet understood.
Although Ānanda had heard these words along with the great assembly, their mouths were silent while their minds remained unenlightened;
still hoping for the Tathāgata’s compassionate voice to provide further instruction, they joined their palms, purified their hearts, and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful teaching.
Because he had somewhat clarified his mental vision, his mouth remained silent; yet because residual doubts still persisted, his mind had not yet attained awakening.
△ Fourth, the Dispelling of Adventitious Defilements, in four parts: first, the inquiry that initiates the discourse.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, marked with the webbed fingers like fine cotton, and opened his five wheel-like fingers.
He instructed Ānanda and the great assembly: "When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Park, I spoke to Ajñāta Kauṇḍinya, the five bhikṣus, and you fourfold assembly, saying:
'That all sentient beings fail to achieve Bodhi or Arhatship is entirely due to adventitious [defilements].'"
You were all deceived by the afflictions of the mundane dust (*rajas-kleśa*). For what reason did you attain awakening at that time and now achieve the fruit of sainthood?
The reason Ānanda’s mind has not yet been awakened is still due to the delusive obstructions of adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*);

it is specifically for this that I have sent [this teaching] to sweep them away. Now, as for these adventitious obstructions: on a large scale, they prevent the attainment of Bodhi; on a small scale, they prevent the attainment of the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The Sage’s compassion is profound; thus, he inquires after the circumstances at the Deer Park so that the multitude may attain awakening.
(As seen in the subsequent text: "The five bhikṣus were Kauṇḍinya, Mahānāman, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, and Vāṣpa.
Initially they attended the Buddha at the Snowy Mountains, but later they practiced the teachings of non-Buddhist paths at the Deer Park. The Buddha first delivered them."
△ Second, Kauṇḍinya explains the meaning of his name.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha: "I am now an elder; among this great assembly, I alone have earned the title of 'The One Who Has Understood'."
"From this, I have realized the two characters 'guest' and 'dust' and attained fruition. World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who stays at an inn to lodge or eat;
once his lodging and meal are finished, he packs his bags for the road ahead and has no leisure to remain. If one were truly the host, they would naturally have nowhere else to go.
Reflecting thus, I conclude that 'not abiding' is called 'guest,' while 'abiding' is called 'host. Therefore, that which does not abide is named..."

This is the meaning of "guest" (*ātithya*). Furthermore, it is like when the clear sun rises in a sky newly cleared after rain; its light enters through a crack in a wall and reveals the various forms of dust within the air.
The substance of the dust moves, while empty space remains tranquil. Reflecting in this way: that which is pellucid and still is called "space," and that which moves is called "dust.
Thus, that which moves is defined as the meaning of "dust. The Buddha said: "It is so."

Kauṇḍinya means "understood" (in Chinese); he was so named because he was the first to attain awakening and understanding. Regarding the metaphor of the "adventitious dust," there is both a general and a specific sense.
Generally, it refers to the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—as well as the two types of delusion—the discriminative and the innate.

These arise and perish according to their objects and lack true permanence; thus, they are all "adventitious. That which defiles the wondrous clarity and turbidly disturbs the tranquil stillness is all "dust."
Specifically, the "guest" is a metaphor for the coarseness of discriminative consciousness (*vikalpa*), while the "dust" is a metaphor for the subtlety of innate [afflictions].

Because they arise and perish without ceasing, they temporarily rely upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as if staying in a lodging house; thus, they are likened to a traveler who has taken up residence in an inn.

As they give rise to delusions and create karma, they depart from the old to move toward the new; thus, they are likened to one whose eating and lodging are finished and who prepares his pack for the road ahead. The true nature (*bhūtatathatā*), however, is eternally quiescent.
Originally, such a thing did not exist; thus, it is likened to a host who has nowhere to go. Coarse obstructions are easily dispelled, but subtle delusions are difficult to clarify.

This must depend upon the celestial realm of one's nature becoming clear and cloudless, so that the sun of wisdom may spread its light. Seizing the opening within the five aggregates, one illuminates the fundamental nature of emptiness.
One then realizes that within this state, one has falsely disturbed oneself. This [disturbance] arises simultaneously with the body and functions concurrently with the mind;
it is subtle, minute, and hidden, and is thus likened to dust in a dark crevice. A traveler in an inn can easily leave behind his baggage, yet dust in a dark crevice is difficult even to sweep away.
One must simply break open the shadows of the crevices so that they become suddenly clear and transparent. However—
Subsequently, they disperse and perish. Thus, the co-arising afflictions must wait until the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are exhausted before they can be completely eradicated.
△ Third, the explanation of the characteristics of the Honored One’s afflictions has two parts. First, showing their coarseness based on the objective realm.
At that moment, the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, bent his five fingers; having bent them, he opened them again; having opened them, he bent them once more.
He said to Ānanda, "What do you see now? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata’s palm, adorned with a hundred jewels, opening and closing in the midst of the assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Regarding what you see as my hand opening and closing in the midst of the assembly, does it belong to my hand?"

"Opening and closing—do you mean that your faculty of vision opens and closes? Ānanda replied, 'World-Honored One, when the precious hands open and close among the assembly, I see the Tathāgata’s own hands opening and closing;
it is not that my faculty of vision itself has opening and closing. The Buddha said:"
"Who moves and who is still? Ānanda replied, "The Buddha’s hand does not remain still, yet my seeing-nature has no stillness;
what, then, could be said to be non-abiding? The Buddha said, "It is so."
Coarse delusions arise and cease in accordance with their objects; therefore, the Buddha’s hand is used as a metaphor for the objects of the mind.
The first question concerning opening and closing clarifies the dust of movement; the subsequent question concerning motion and stillness clarifies the transient guest that does not abide.
Both reside in the object and not in the mind; hence it is said: "The nature is neither opening nor closing; the nature has no abiding in stillness. II. Demonstrating the Subtle through the Body.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from the wheel-mark on his palm, which appeared to Ānanda’s right;
immediately, Ānanda turned his head to look to the right. He then emitted another light, which appeared to Ānanda’s left; Ānanda then likewise turned his head to look to the left.

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "For what reason does your head shake today? Ānanda replied, "I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous jewel-light from his body, which came to my left and right; therefore, as I looked to the left and right, my head moved of its own accord.
"Ānanda, when you gaze at the Buddha’s light and move your head to the left and right, is it your head that moves, or is it the vision that moves? "World-Honored One, it is my head that moves."
The nature of my seeing has no cessation; who, then, could cause it to waver? The Buddha said, "It is so.
Because subtle delusions arise simultaneously with the body, Ānanda’s own head serves as a metaphor for the characteristics that contrast with the nature.
This also clarifies that the wavering dust—the transient guest—is entirely within the characteristics and not within the nature; therefore, it is said that the nature has no [wavering].
If there is stillness, who is there to move? As for not questioning those who do not abide, this is omitted because it follows from what was previously stated.

△ Fourth, the conclusion of the reprimand and the exhortation of the assembly: Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly universally: "If sentient beings again take that which moves to be called 'dust' (rajas),"
That which does not abide is called "guest. Observe, Ānanda: your head moves, yet your vision remains unmoved.
Again, observe me: my hand opens and closes, yet your vision neither expands nor contracts. Why, then, do you now take that which moves to be the body?
Taking movement as their object, from beginning to end, they undergo birth and extinction in every thought-moment. They lose the true nature and act with inverted views;
their fundamental mind loses its truth as they mistake external objects for themselves. Thus they revolve within this cycle, taking upon themselves the process of wandering through saṃsāra.
Through Ānanda, he addressed the assembly, reprimanding them for identifying adventitious dust while neglecting their own original nature (*svabhāva*).

Previously, he had clarified the mind alone; here, he clarifies both mind and objects. All phenomena of mind and objects possess a fundamentally quiescent essence. Apart from this original source, everything is merely adventitious dust.
It is like the opening and closing of a hand or the movement of a head: when these cease, the original essence remains as it is.
In stillness, there is nothing else; thus, all deluded movements are fundamentally unobtainable. Yet you sentient beings take movement for your body and movement for your environment;
this is merely to recognize adventitious dust and lose the true nature, acting in a state of inversion.
This is what is called being summoned into the cycle of saṃsāra. As for the phrase "taking it oneself within," it refers to that which is within the true nature.
Fundamentally, there is no movement; it is entirely what they themselves have taken up. This is intended so that they may awaken at the very place where they are deluded. Alas!

The multitude of deluded beings are rooted in passionate attachment and conditioned by the mind and eyes. Following after adventitious defilements, they have long since taken up the cycle of transmigration for themselves.
True benevolence and compassion provide salvation; their pervasive and vigorous inspiration is indeed ultimate. How nearly could one achieve awakening right within the state of delusion!
