The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling Unfolds [the Meaning] △ Second, Illuminating the Nature of Enlightenment to Directly Cause Realization. First, the Sūtra Master’s Narrative of the Intent:
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil. They reflected upon [their state] since beginningless time...

Having lost my original mind, I falsely identified with the shadows of conceptualization arising from conditioned objects. Today I have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again.
With palms joined, I prostrate before the Buddha and pray to hear the Tathāgata reveal the truth and falsehood, the reality and unreality of body and mind.
The manifestation of both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing clarifies the nature of enlightenment.

This passage describes how the assembly’s minds were moved to realization, expressing their hope that the Buddha would further clarify this point. Previously, you criticized taking movement as the body and movement as the environment;

thus, the true and the false within the body and mind have not been distinguished, nor has their reality or unreality been discerned. Furthermore, you criticized the state of moment-to-moment arising and ceasing for losing track of the true nature.

As for the nature [of things], even those who claim it is neither arising nor ceasing have not yet been able to discern it. Therefore, I wish to clarify these two meanings so that they may be fully elucidated.
△ Second, the eleven sections of questions and answers for elucidation: First, clarifying non-arising and non-ceasing through the transformation of the body;
Second, first, the King Indradyumna’s inquiry.

At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha: "In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I encountered Kātyāyana and Ajita Keśakambalin, both of whom claimed that the cessation and extinction of this body after death is called Nirvana.
Although I have now met the Buddha, I still harbor doubts. How may I manifest and realize this ground where the mind is neither born nor extinguished? Now, this great...
All those with outflows (āsrava) wished to hear it.

To clarify that the ground of the non-arising and non-ceasing of body and mind was initiated by King Bimbisāra, it is shown that the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is fully present within the state of bondage;
yet worldly beings merely follow the transformations of things, and though they may occupy the highest nobility, they ultimately succumb to change.
That he was unaware of his own extinction serves as a warning to King Bimbisāra regarding the arousal of hindrances.

Kātyāyana and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa were non-Buddhist heretics who adhered to the view of annihilationism. △ Second, the Buddha’s illumination of the truth, which has two parts. First, the question and answer distinguishing illusion.

The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body is present now. I ask you again: is this physical body of yours identical to a diamond, eternally abiding and indestructible, or will it eventually decay and perish?
"World-Honored One," [the king replied], "this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction."
"The world is truly precarious and fragile; there is nothing therein that is firm or strong.
The Buddha said, "Great King, you have never before perished. How then do you know of perishing?

"World-Honored One," [the king replied], "although this body of mine, subject to impermanence and decay, has never before perished, I observe before me that from moment to moment it undergoes transition and passes away; it is ever-new and never abides, like a fire."

It turns to ash, gradually wasting away and perishing; its destruction continues without ceasing, leading one to know with certainty that this body must come to total extinction, like a sheep entering a slaughterhouse, stepping closer at every pace toward the ground of death.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King. You are now advanced in years and have grown old; how does your appearance compare to that of your youth?
"World-Honored One," [the king replied], "in my childhood, my skin and flesh were smooth and lustrous; as I grew into adulthood, my blood and vital energy became full."
Now, my declining years are pressed by senility; my physical form is withered and emaciated, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled.
As I approach the end, how can I compare myself to the time when I was in the full vigor of youth?

The vigor of youth does not endure, being like a galloping horse; therefore, it cannot be compared [to anything else]. "A child who has just formed a skeletal frame" refers to one who is so young that they require others for nourishment.
"Skin on the surface" is called *fū* (skin); "the patterns of the fibers" are called *zòu* (pores). "Slumping like the setting sun" means to be in one's late years.
The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical form should not have deteriorated so suddenly. The King replied, "World-Honored One, through subtle and secret transformation, I truly do not perceive it;
yet as cold and heat shift and flow, I have gradually reached this state. Why is this?
At the age of twenty, though I was called young, my countenance was already aged compared to when I was ten. At thirty, I was further declined than at twenty."
Now I am sixty-two years old. When I look back at the time when I was fifty, I appear as robust as ever. World-Honored One, I perceive this subtle shifting;
although there has been such decay, the transition between these stages is limited to ten-year intervals.

If I were to reflect upon it more minutely, would the change be merely every decade or two? In truth, it is a change that occurs year by year. Is it only a change by the year? It is also accompanied by changes month by month.

Transformation. What is meant by "transformation"? It is also called "transition. Through deep reflection and careful observation, one realizes that from moment to moment, between every thought-instant, there is no staying still.
Thus, one knows that this body of mine will ultimately undergo change and perish.
Observe closely the principle of illusion: it shifts and changes in rapid succession, hastening toward its exhaustion. "Exceeding two" refers to sixty-two [kalpas].

Furthermore, limiting it to ten years is a coarse observation based on a broad calculation. When observing minutely from the perspective of the brief moment, in reality, every thought-moment is without cessation.
△ Second, clarifying the true through illusion.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly proceed; you realize and know your own extinction.
At the very moment of this extinction, do you know that within your body there is something that does not perish? King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "I truly do not know."
The Buddha said, "I shall now show you the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. Great King, at what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?
The King replied, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīva. As we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges.
The Buddha said, "Great King, it is as you have said. At the age of twenty, [you were] already diminished compared to..."
"From ten years of age up to sixty, days, months, years, and seasons pass and change from moment to moment.

Thus, when you were three years old and saw this river, by the time you reached thirteen, what was the water like? The King replied, "It was exactly as it was when I was three; there was no difference at all."
Even up to this year at the age of sixty-two, there has been no difference;
despite the various transformations of youth, vigor, old age, and decrepitude, he sees no difference.
This is precisely that which is neither born nor extinguished amidst birth and extinction. Jīvaka—here translated as "Longevity Deity"—brought his son to visit him, seeking long life.
The Buddha said, "Now you yourself lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; your face is certainly more wrinkled than it was in your youth.

As you look at this Ganges River now, is there any difference between this vision and the vision you had when looking at the river as a child—any distinction between childhood and old age? The King replied:
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled.

That which is wrinkled is subject to change; that which is not wrinkled is not subject to change. That which changes undergoes extinction; that which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or death."
How can you undergo birth and death within this [body], yet still cite those such as Maskarin and others who claim that after the death of this body there is total extinction?
Since there is neither birth nor death, this is your true permanence; you should not be deluded by their heterodox doctrines of annihilationism. Maskarin...
Li was a follower of Kātyāyanīputra.
Upon hearing these words, the King gained conviction that after death one abandons this life and proceeds toward a future birth; together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy.
"Having attained what was never before attained, and having been granted this illumination, I have suddenly awakened to the True and Constant, no longer clinging to the view of annihilation.
△ Second, clarifying that there is nothing lost by relying on the hand to correct the inversion; Part One: Ānanda’s Request for Instruction.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt on one knee to address the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, if this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of delusion?"
I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements.
Because of the King’s questions and answers, I have instead stirred up the dust of doubt, thinking that since the nature has arising and ceasing, it can be said to be lost;
yet, if there is no arising or ceasing, how could it be lost? II. The Buddha’s Revelation and Instruction (in two parts). 1. Analogy.
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm; with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda and said, "Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted?
Ānanda replied, "Worldly beings consider this to be inverted, but I do not know which is upright and which is inverted."
This clarifies that all Buddhas and sentient beings share the same single essence; there is certainly no loss or omission therein. It is only based on inverted views that one speaks of loss.
For example, when an arm hangs down naturally, it is considered "correct," yet one might instead regard this as "inverted";

when it is raised upward, it is considered "inverted," yet one might instead regard this as "correct. This is to lose the truth. Viewed from the perspective of the fundamental source, there has never been any loss, nor has there ever been anything correct or inverted. Therefore—
He asked: "Who is upright and who is inverted? [The Buddha replied: "Mudrā means 'hand-seal,' which is one of the thirty-two marks [of a Buddha].
The Buddha told Ānanda: 'If people of the world consider this to be inverted, then by what standard do people of the world determine what is upright?'"
Ānanda said, "If the Tathāgata were to extend his arm, with his hand made of *tūla* cotton pointing upward toward the sky, that would be called 'correct.
The Buddha then extended his arm and told Ānanda, 'If this were inverted, with the head and tail exchanged, people of the world would look at it twice as much.'"
To take what is upright as being inverted is truly a perversion. Yet this inversion is merely a matter of reversing the beginning and the end;
viewed from its own source, there has never been any loss. That worldly people all together double their scrutiny and forcibly create distinctions is sufficient evidence of their delusion.
Thus you should know that your body and the pure Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas are illuminated through comparison:
the body of a Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge," whereas your bodies are termed "inverted by nature."

The arm and the body are originally one; it is through emotional attachment that they are falsely distinguished. The Dharma-body is originally identical; it is through correctness and inversion that it appears as different.

If one forgets emotional attachment and discards correctness and inversion, then the arm and the body will be as they naturally are, and the Dharma-body will be non-dual. △ Second, tracing the origin of delusion.
"Observe closely as you wish: between your body and the Buddha’s body, where is the designation 'inversion' applied? What is called by the name 'inversion'?
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed at the Buddha with fixed, unblinking eyes, unaware of the location of their own bodies and minds' inversion.
I shall now exhaustively investigate the root of this perversion so that you may achieve awakening through reversal; yet the great assembly remains mired in confusion, unaware of its location.
The Buddha, arising from his great compassion, takes pity on Ānanda and the entire multitude, and emits a voice like the ocean tide to address all those gathered there.
"Good sons, I have always said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and the objects upon which they depend, are manifested solely by the mind.
Your bodies and your minds are both things manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence of the wondrous mind."
Why is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, and its jewel-like, brilliant, and subtle nature? You mistake delusion for enlightenment;

this inverted state has no location other than being a manifestation of the mind itself, intended to lead you to enlightenment within the very mind. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers collectively to the five sense organs and the six sense objects.
"Mind" (*citta*) refers collectively to the six consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness. "All conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to the objects perceived by the sense organs and consciousnesses.
These are all dharmas. The mental factors that drive the mind are the thoughts and reflections that give rise to wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions.

As for all objects of perception, they extensively include mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness, the nature and characteristics of the true and the false, and the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox.

All things lack intrinsic nature; they are manifested solely by the mind. Just as a reflection in a mirror is entirely the mirror itself, so too your current illusory body and mind are both manifestations of the wondrously luminous mind-mirror; they are entirely the mind.

You should directly awaken to this wondrous essence without identifying with the illusory and false. Instead, you have abandoned the fundamental wondrousness to cling to the illusory and false—this is to mistake awakening for delusion.

This is the locus of delusion; this is where inversion resides. While the wondrous mind is one, its designations vary greatly because they accord with the differences in their functions according to the teachings.
This clarifies that the objects manifested by the mind are like reflections in a mirror; therefore, it is called the "wondrously luminous true essence.
Furthermore, it clarifies that delusion fundamentally pursues the peripheral; therefore, it is called the "fundamentally wondrous luminous mind. As it is said:

"Fundamentally wondrous" means that it is fundamentally and inherently wondrous, not requiring cultivation or effort. "Mind" (*citta*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*) are mutually designated as essence and function.
Mind arises clarity from the wondrous; it is perfectly integrated and illuminating, like the light of a mirror.
Therefore, it is called the "perfectly luminous wondrous mind. Nature is wondrous within that very clarity; it is profoundly still and tranquil, like the substance of the mirror. Therefore...

It is said: "The wondrous nature of the jewel-brightness becomes obscured and darkened, resulting in emptiness. Within this darkness of emptiness, the coagulation of obscurity forms matter. Matter is intermingled with false conceptualization; the characteristics of these thoughts constitute the body."

Gathering on objects, they waver within; rushing outward, they flee in wild abandon. Taking this state of dark confusion and agitation as their true nature, they are deluded into regarding it as their mind, firmly convinced that it resides within the physical body.
They do not realize that from the physical body outward, it extends through the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth.

All these are things within the wondrously luminous true mind. It is like discarding a clear, vast ocean hundreds of thousands of miles wide and instead identifying with a single floating bubble, claiming that this tiny bubble constitutes the entire tide and exhausts the whole expanse of the sea. You all are people who are doubly deluded.
Just as my hanging down of the hand is no different from its being raised, the Tathāgata calls such a person "one who is to be pitied.
This is precisely the origin of delusion and inversion. The perfectly wondrous and luminous mind is fundamentally neither emptiness nor form; it is entirely nothing but true awakening.
Due to the sudden arising of false objects, it becomes a state of obscurity and gloom. Thereupon, the essence of awakening is transformed into inert emptiness.
The obscuration of wondrous luminosity constitutes delusory form. Once emptiness and form are established, conceptual appearances compete to arise.

As form and conception intermingle, they subsequently become the characteristics of the body. Delusory conditioned vapors accumulate therein; internally, one is tossed about by conceptions, while externally, one rushes toward objects.
This is merely the mark of being turbidly disturbed by various delusory conditions and sensory dust, yet people take it to be themselves.

The essence and nature of the mind—could this not be delusion? Having once fallen into such delusion, one resolutely believes the mind exists within this illusory physical form, never realizing that the wondrously luminous true mind encompasses heaven and earth and swallows all phenomena.
To instead identify it within this tiny body is no different from abandoning the boundless ocean of lands to recognize only a single bubble.
To regard the entirety of the tidal body as having the capacity of the vast ocean—this is to mistake the correct for the inverted, like one who views things through a single slice.
Therefore, the matter of "hanging down the hand" is cited to conclude [the argument], clarifying that this is taking the correct for the inverted.
△ Second, the refutation of the "shadow of conditions" (yuan-ying) to distinguish and clarify confusion. Part One: Questioning the confusion.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

"Though I have received from the Buddha such wondrous sounds and have awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the fundamental, ever-perfect, and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I nevertheless perceive the Buddha’s current preaching of the Dharma with my conditioned mind.
While I truly gaze upon You, I have merely obtained this mind; I do not yet dare to recognize it as such."
This is the fundamental source-ground of the mind. I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim the perfect sound to uproot my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way.
By hearing the sound of the Dharma, I have awakened to the wondrously luminous mind, which is fundamentally perfect and pervasive, with nothing left unaccounted for;

thus it is called the eternally abiding ground of the mind. Yet, my emotional attachments remain coarse and my insight is not yet refined; I still take the perceiving mind that conditions what is heard as [the self].
The nature realized herein is precisely that which ordinary people doubt and confuse within their minds, making it difficult to uproot. Therefore, I pray that the Buddha will pull it out for me.
△ Second, the Buddha’s proclamation and instruction has two parts. First, recognizing conditions and losing the truth.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is likewise conditioned, and you have not attained the nature of the Dharma.
That which discriminates based on sound is merely the conditioned mind, not the truth of the mind.
That which perceives delusively based on objects is merely the conditioned dharma, not the nature of the dharma."
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another. That person, because of the finger, ought to look at the moon.
If they instead observe the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar orb, but also lose the finger itself? Why is this?
Because they have taken the finger used as a pointer to be the bright moon. Would they not only lose the finger, but also fail to distinguish between light and darkness?

For this reason, one takes the substance of the finger itself to be the nature of the moon’s brightness; yet since the two natures of light and darkness cannot be discerned [as distinct], you are likewise so.

Because you falsely recognize based on external objects, you become increasingly deluded regarding conditions, and in every matter you lose the truth. △ Third, distinguishing that conditions have no inherent nature.

If you consider this discriminative mind that perceives the sounds of my Dharma-teachings to be your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess a discriminative nature even apart from those discriminative sounds.
It would be like a traveler staying overnight at an inn: he halts briefly and then departs; he never remains there permanently.
Yet the person who manages the pavilion has nowhere to go; thus he is called the "pavilion master. This is also like that: if it were truly your mind, it would have nowhere to go.
How then could it be devoid of sound and lack a nature of discernment?

The discriminating mind that takes objects as its conditions is devoid of intrinsic nature and is like a passing guest; the eternally abiding true mind has nowhere to go, for it is like the innkeeper.

Thus, it is not only the discriminating mind that discriminates sound; it also discriminates my appearance, yet when separated from all forms and characteristics, it is devoid of the nature of discrimination.
In this way, up to the point where all discrimination is entirely absent, it is neither form nor emptiness.

Kauśalya and others mistook this for the "Dark Principle" (Tattva). This was spoken to extensively clarify the intention of Ānanda. "Discriminating the sound" refers to the mind that takes sound as its object;

this is precisely what awakens to the Buddha’s Dharma-sound. "Discriminating my appearance" refers to the mind that takes form as its object; this is precisely what accords with [the mind] that gazes upward in reverence.
This is so. "And so forth" refers to the inclusion of all six sense-objects and their reflected images, which are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because everything is entirely non-existent, they are not form (*rūpa*); because they falsely appear in dependence upon conditions, they are not emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since they are neither form nor emptiness, they are obscure and indistinguishable.
Not only do the non-Buddhists confuse them for the "dark principle" (*tattva*), but even students of our own tradition reach this point and remain utterly bewildered.
Furthermore, *Kūṣmāṇḍa* is simply another name for *Maskarī*.

If one is free from the conditions of all phenomena and possesses a nature devoid of discrimination, then your mental faculties each have their own place of return; how, then, can [the self] be the master?
This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. △ Fourth, showing that the nature of seeing has no place of return based on the eight objects; this has two parts.
First, Ānanda’s inquiry:
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature each has a place of return, then why does the Tathāgata speak of the wondrously bright, original mind?"
"Why is there no returning? I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me:
the wondrously luminous original mind is precisely the essence of seeing. △ Second, the Buddha’s proclamation and instruction.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for this faculty of seeing of mine which you perceive—the very source of clarity—although this seeing is not the wondrous, subtle, and clear mind, it is like a second moon;
it is not a reflection of the moon. You should listen attentively, for I shall now show you the ground from which there is nothing to be returned."
Furthermore, when you observe my statement that "the essence of seeing is bright and clear," I am entirely referring to Ānanda’s seeing of objects.
This essence of seeing emerges from the wondrous, bright, and pure mind; therefore, it is said that although it is not the wondrous mind itself, it is like a second moon.

The two moons are in reality one body; they appear as distinct only because of mental fabrication. This is analogous to how the essence of vision and the wondrous mind are fundamentally without two aspects, yet are made dual by the person who perceives them.
Since the reflection of the moon actually possesses two distinct forms, it is said that [the second moon] is not real.
Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east. When the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance;
at midnight, during the dark fortnight when clouds and mist shroud the heavens, it becomes dark and murky again. Through the openings of doors and windows, one sees through;
between the walls and the eaves, one perceives obstruction. In places where distinctions are made, one perceives conditions; yet throughout the vast emptiness, it is everywhere present.
Emptiness. When the signs of turbidity appear, it is shrouded in dark dust; when it clears and the mist subsides, one again beholds its purity.
Ānanda, you have observed all these changing phenomena. Now I shall cause each to return to its original source. What is this original source?
Ānanda, these various transformations: clarity returns to the sun; why is this? For there is no clarity without the sun; clarity depends upon the sun, and therefore it returns to the sun.
Darkness returns to the dark moon; penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and buildings; discrimination returns to its conditions;
the stubborn void returns to space; turbidity returns to dust; and clear brightness returns to a cloudless sky. Thus, all things in the world...

There is nothing that does not fall within these categories. As for the eight kinds of objects you perceive—the clarity and darkness, the openness and obstruction, the empty space, the dense fog, and the clear atmosphere—each returns to its own eight causes.

As for the nature of the seeing-essence that can observe these eight kinds, to what place would it return? Furthermore, that which perceives these conditions arises from the discriminating mind; thus, one perceives both form and mind.
This is due to conditions.

Why is this? If one returns to light, then when it is not light, one no longer sees darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the seeing itself is without distinction.
This explains that there is no returning. If there were something that returned, it would depart with the object; once gone, one would no longer be able to see.
Objects naturally differ from one another, yet the nature of seeing has no distinction; thus, it is clear that seeing does not follow the objects.
All those things that can be returned naturally do not belong to you. As for that which cannot be returned, if it is not you, then who is it?
This conclusively demonstrates that the non-returning is your true nature, what is called "the body alone revealed amidst the myriad phenomena."

Thus you should know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure. It is you who have become deluded and distressed, losing your fundamental nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth;
within this birth and death, you are constantly adrift and submerged. For this reason, the Tathāgata calls you one worthy of compassion.
This concludes the section on binding [the mind], reprimanding, and awakening. **V. Determining the True Nature of All Phenomenal Appearances (in two parts):** **1.
Ānanda’s Follow-up Question:** Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has nothing from which it can return, how can I know that it is my true nature?"
Although you know that the essence of seeing has no place to return, it currently appears to be mixed with external objects and you have not yet been able to discern them clearly.
△ Second, the Buddha provides definitive resolution in five parts; first, a general description of the function of seeing.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now ask you this: although you have not yet attained the purity of the outflows-free state, by relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, you see the first dhyāna without obstruction.
Yet Aniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as clearly as looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand;
the various bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds; and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions perceive even the finest motes of dust."
In the pure land, there is nothing that is not within the range of vision; yet sentient beings, though they see through with penetrating clarity, do not exceed the span of a few inches.
This description consists of five parts: first, the śrāvakas; second, the arhats; third, the bodhisattvas; fourth, the Tathāgatas; and fifth, sentient beings.

This clarifies that although the cognitive capacities (*jñāna-mātra*) of the four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings differ, the essence of their seeing (*darśana-sāra*) is no different;

thus, all can be resolved through the immediate investigation of objective phenomena. Ānanda’s vision had not yet departed from desire, which is why it was said he had "not yet attained untainted purity" (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*).

The First Dhyāna is the head of the Realm of Form (*rūpa-dhātu*), being the Heaven of Those Free from Desire (*vītarāga-deva*). Aniruddha was an Arhat who had attained the untainted state through cultivation.
The heavenly eye can see throughout the great trichiliocosm; thus, it views Jambudvīpa as if it were but a single grain.

As for the statement that sentient beings do not exceed the measure of a few inches, this means that [the heavenly eye] cannot reach across even the barrier of a curtain. △ Second, the definitive discernment of objects.
Ānanda, let us now, together with you, observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell, surveying everywhere across water, land, and air.
Although there are various forms and images, whether obscure or bright, none of them are anything other than the obstructions left behind by the discrimination of external objects.
You should, in this regard, distinguish between self and other. Now, as I lead you to select from within these visions, who is my true essence? Who is...?
Regarding objects and phenomena:
first, the objects and phenomena are identified; next, they are to be discerned.
Ānanda, exhaust the source of your vision from the palaces of the sun and moon—these are objects and not you—up to the Seven Golden Mountains that surround [Mount Sumeru].
Observe closely: although there are various kinds of light, these things are not you. Gradually observe further:
clouds rising, birds flying, wind stirring, dust rising, trees, mountains, rivers, grasses, weeds, humans, and livestock—all these things are not you.
"Exhaustively reach the source of your vision; cause it to be scrutinized with utmost diligence and truth. Above, reach the sun and moon; below, reach the Cakravāḍa mountains;
in between, reach all myriad things; cause each and every one to be carefully examined. △ Third, the formal demonstration of the nature of seeing.
Ānanda, although these various natures of things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are all equally beheld by your pure essence of vision.
Thus, while the categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing is without difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly your own nature of seeing.

The previous question asked how one may know this to be my true nature (*tathatā*). This demonstrates that while the myriad objects of experience appear as distinct, their underlying non-distinction is seen;
this non-distinction is precisely your true nature. This true nature surveys the coarse and turbid without being mixed with the refined;
it traverses the ten thousand differences without deviating from its wondrous subtlety; it perceives the furthest and the nearest alike, for it is equally luminous. △
Fourth, the discernment that seeing is not an object.
If seeing were an object, then you would also be able to see my seeing. An object can indeed be seen;
this reiterates the previous point that all things are objects and not you, providing a further clarification.
If you see the same as I do, it is called "seeing me. When I am not being seen, why do you not see the place where I am not seen?
Those who see the same rely on the traces of things; those who do not see rely on the essence that transcends things.
If you say that you and I see one and the same thing, this is merely seeing my seeing—it is nothing more than a trace. It is when I transcend things that...
When you look for it, where is its substance? Since it cannot be found anywhere, it is certainly not a material thing.
If you see that which is not seen, naturally it is not the characteristic of that "not seeing."
This is an exhaustive argument. Even if one were to falsely claim that they can see my "not seeing," it would ultimately not be that same characteristic of non-seeing.
For that characteristic of non-seeing is not within the reach of vision.
If you do not perceive the ground of non-perception, it is naturally not a thing; how could it not be you?
Since seeing is not a thing, it is your true nature.
Furthermore, at this very moment when you see objects, since you see the objects, the objects also see you; their essential natures would then become confused and intermingled.
In that case, you, I, and all the world would fail to be established as distinct entities.
Furthermore, regarding the confusion between objects and the self, we have already discerned that seeing is not an object. If seeing were an object, then objects would possess the faculty of seeing;
consequently, the natures of sentient and insentient beings would become intermingled and indistinguishable. Therefore, it is said that they cannot be established.

Standing up, he said: "It can be clearly seen that this is not a physical object. Generally, in the world, "sentient beings" and "the vessel-world" refer collectively to both the animate and the inanimate.
△ Fifth, restating the manifestation to provide the final answer.
Ānanda, if when you see it were you and not I, then since this nature of seeing is all-pervasive, who else could it be but you?
Why do you doubt your own true nature? If you consider your own nature to be unreal and seek the truth from me, you are mistaken.
This restates the preceding [argument] to reveal the true nature. "This is you, not me" clarifies that the essence of seeing is not intermingled with external objects.
If you awaken to the fact that the essence of seeing is not intermingled with objects, you will realize that the nature of seeing is vast, pure, and all-pervading throughout the Dharma-realm;
this is precisely your own true nature. Why do you doubt its authenticity and seek its verification from me? This concludes [the section].
The answer addresses the question: "How can it be known that this is my true nature? Regarding the phrase "nature, you":
it means that nature can take you as its object, just as it is said that nature pervades all minds. 6. Clarifying that the True Body is Primordially Beyond All Limitations.
Part One: Ānanda follows up with his question.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing must be me and nothing else, then when I and the Tathāgata were observing the Palace of the Supreme Treasury of the Four Heavenly Kings and dwelling in the palaces of the sun and moon, this seeing was all-pervasive and encompassed the entire Sahā world.
Yet, upon returning to the vihāra, I saw only the monastery; entering the hall of the pure mind, I beheld only the eaves and corridors. World-Honored One, this seeing is like..."
"It is so. Its substance was originally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm; now that it is within this room, it fills only this single room.
Is it that this vision has contracted from the large to the small? Or is it that the walls and buildings have constricted it and severed it? I do not know where the truth of this matter lies.
I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and expound upon it for me."

This question is posed by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power to perceive the affairs of the first dhyāna; it arises from doubting whether the essence of vision expands or contracts according to the breadth or narrowness of what is observed.
This is because one has not yet attained direct realization, but instead merely attempts to measure it with the limited capacity of the conceptual mind.
The palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings are as vast as that which can be seen when aligned with the sun and moon;

therefore, while the *saṃghārāma* throughout the Sahā world is narrow, its gates and halls are even narrower. A single realm is precisely the Sahā world. △ Second, the Buddha’s clarification, in three parts.
First, the direct instruction:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "All worldly activities, whether great or small, internal or external, each belong to the objective fields before one.
One should not say that seeing expands or contracts."

"All worlds" refers to categories such as the sense organs, the physical body, and the environmental realm; "large and small, internal and external" refers to categories such as a single world-system or a single room;
and "all activities" refers to categories such as expansion and contraction, or compression and severance. This collectively enumerates all phenomena.

All these belong to the external objects before one; they do not, of their own accord, intersect with my spiritual awareness. Therefore, whether the external objects before one are large or small, the vision neither expands nor contracts.
It is like a square vessel, within which a square void is seen. I ask you again: as for this square void seen within the square vessel—
Is space fixed in shape, or is it not fixed? If it were fixed, then when placed in a separate round vessel, the empty space within should not be round.
If it were not fixed, then when contained within a square vessel, there should be no square space. You say that you do not know where this principle resides.
The nature of reality is thus. How can there be "being within"?
The vessel is a metaphor for the external objects; the emptiness is a metaphor for the essence of seeing. When the vessel has squareness or roundness, the emptiness undergoes no change.

Since it undergoes no change, how could there be expansion or contraction? As for what is meant by "being within": the essence of seeing is suchness (*tathatā*); it admits no room for the delusions of the emotional mind or the sensory vessels.
It is liberation, Ānanda.
If one wishes to cause that which has no squareness or roundness to enter [the vessel], one need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the substance of space itself has no squareness.
One should not say that the location of the spatial characteristics of emptiness must be further removed.
By departing from sensory dust and contemplating the nature, one spontaneously attains the original truth without the need for strenuous effort. 2. Dispelling Sentimentality:
If it were as you ask—that when entering a room, one contracts the vision to make it small—then when looking up at the sun, would you not have to stretch your vision to equal the face of the sun?
Furthermore, if building a wall or a house could sever the vision by obstructing it, then when a small hole is pierced through it, would there not be a trace of continuity?
This interpretation is not correct.
Since it cannot be drawn out, it certainly cannot be shortened; since it cannot be continued, it certainly cannot be severed.
As this meaning is not so, there is no use for emotional conjecture. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding themselves as external objects and have lost their original mind.
Being turned by these objects, they perceive the great as small within this state. If they can turn objects [back toward themselves], they will be identical to the Tathāgata;
their body and mind will be perfectly luminous and unmoving within the site of enlightenment, such that upon the tip of a single hair, they can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
To mistake oneself for an object means that one loses one's true nature and follows after sensory objects. To be turned by objects means that, because of this, one falls into inverted delusions.
Being turned by objects is like empty space changing according to the shape of its vessel; thus, within this state, one perceives the large as small.
Yet, in the end, one remains a sentient being. One who can "transform objects" is like removing the vessel to contemplate the emptiness within;
thus, the mind itself is perfectly luminous and universally contains all lands, becoming identical to the Tathāgata. For the lands upon the tip of a hair are fundamentally neither small nor large;

the principle of containment does not require supernatural transformations. It is simply that when the emotional attachments to the vessel-like world are removed, it manifests before one in its vast, open clarity. △ Seven.
The Clear Vision and its Conditions Share the Same Sublime Essence. Part One: Ānanda Doubts Their Difference.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my sublime nature, and if this sublime nature is now present before me, then vision must be my true self.
What, then, are my current body and mind? For now, my body and mind are divided..."
There is another reality. He saw that there was no distinct differentiation from his own body, and thus he repeated his previous question.
That which was previously pointed out among all things as "this exquisite, bright clarity" is truly your seeing-nature;

it is this very wondrous nature now present before me, distinct from the body and mind. And yet, [the body]— *Note: The final sentence fragment "And yet, while the body... appears to be an incomplete thought or transition leading into a further argument regarding the relationship between the physical form and the seeing-nature.*

Regarding the claim that the mind possesses substantial discrimination: you say the mind has discrimination, yet you perceive it as non-discriminative, thereby distinguishing it from the body and establishing them as separate entities.
If this "real self" were truly my mind, it would cause me to see it now; seeing that the nature of vision is the real self while the body is not the self—how does this differ from the Tathāgata?
Regarding your previous objection that "an object can see me," I entreat you to bestow your great compassion and clarify what I have not yet understood.
If the seeing that occurred previously were truly my mind, then that [object] would be the true self while this [body] would not be the self;

for the seeing would reside in the object and not in the body. Thus, it would be that object which could see me. All of these points are difficult to discern because they arise from deluded sentiments.
△ Second, the Buddha’s harmonious reconciliation in three parts. First, a detailed analysis and demonstration in four parts. First, a general refutation of the preceding doubts.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "What you have just said—that the seeing is before you—is not the true meaning."
△ Second, the reprimand for failing to discern that [the object] is not real. First, the discernment that the object does not exist as such a vision:
"If it were real, and you truly saw it before you, then this essence of vision would have a specific location and could not be said to be without indication."
Furthermore, as we now sit together in the Jeta Grove, surveying the groves, the streams, and the halls,
from the sun and moon above down to the Ganges River before us— now, in front of my lion throne, point with your finger and describe these various features.
The "obscured" refers to a forest; the "luminous" refers to the sun; the "obstructed" refers to a wall; the "penetrating" refers to empty space.
In this manner, down to the smallest blade of grass, tree, or hair—though they differ in size—whenever there is form, there is nothing that cannot be pointed out.
If you must identify that which sees before you right now, you should point it out with your hand with certainty: what is it that sees? Ānanda, you should know this.
If space is the seeing, since it has already become seeing, what is space? If a material object is the seeing, since it has already become seeing, what is the material object?
You should minutely peel away and analyze the ten thousand phenomena to extract the fundamental source of the bright, pure, and wondrous faculty of seeing.
Point it out and show it to me, so that it may be as clear and free from delusion as those other objects.

To thoroughly discern all things such that no such vision exists—whether they be empty space or material objects—one must comprehensively cite the teachings on form and emptiness to analyze them in detail.
First one speaks of the "essence of seeing," next of the "source of seeing," and finally of "refined seeing"; this seeing is fundamentally...
Because it refers to the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind, it is generally termed "essence" (*jing*). Because it emerges first from the mind, it is called "seeing.

Because it points to the substance by means of its function, it is called "the essence of seeing" (*jian-jing*). Because it points to the function by means of the substance, it is called "the essence of vision" (*jing-jian*). "Forest and stream" (*lin-qu*) is synonymous with "forest and spring" (*lin-quan*).

Ānanda said, “World-Honored One, here in this multi-storied lecture hall, reaching as far as the Ganges River, looking up at the sun and moon, pointing with my hand, and surveying with my eyes—all that I point to are objects; there is nothing therein that is the seeing-nature.
World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, how much less could I, a beginner Śrāvaka still possessed of outflows, or even a Bodhisattva, perceive the seeing-nature within the myriad phenomena?”
Previously, when dissecting and examining the essence, one perceives a self-nature that exists separately, distinct from all things. The Buddha said, "It is so, it is so.
Since objects do not possess this perception, even a Great Sage cannot dissect and distinguish it within the object itself; the intention must be to separate it from the object.
This knot has no such thing as a "seer. △ Second, distinguishing that objects have no "non-seer":
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda: "As you have said, there is no essence of seeing that exists apart from all objects with a separate self-nature;
thus, among those objects you point to, there is no such thing as a seer."
Having established that the previous statement contains no such [visual] seeing, you must now point to what is not seeing.
I tell you again: as you and the Tathāgata sit in the Jeta Grove, look further at the groves and gardens, even down to the various distinct forms of the sun and moon;
there will certainly be no visual essence (*darśana-vijñāna*) that responds to your pointing. You shall then discern, among all these objects—
"What is it that is not seeing? Ānanda replied, "I truly see this entire Jeta Grove, yet I do not know what within it is not seeing.
Why is this? If the tree is not seeing, how can one see the tree? If the tree is itself seeing, how can it be a tree?
This applies even unto the sky: if the sky is not seeing, how can one see the sky? If the sky is itself seeing, how [can it be the sky]?"
"What is empty? I further contemplated that within these myriad phenomena, even the subtlest manifestations of light are none other than seeing.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
Previously, I answered that I did not know because the meaning could not yet be definitively established. If the tree were not seeing, how could it be this tree? If...
This is precisely "seeing. The tree should be named "seeing. Why is it named "tree"? However, the previous assertion that what is severed is non-existent as "seeing" does not accord with reason;

therefore, one further reflects that there is nothing that is not "seeing. Since neither of these two meanings is fixed, and the Buddha permits both, this is because the characteristics of form, emptiness, and so forth are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent and thus truly impossible to designate definitively.
Therefore, the subsequent text says: "These various objects and images, as well as this essence, are fundamentally the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant essence of Bodhi.
Within it, there is originally no meaning of 'is' or 'is not. △ Third: The beginner is at a loss.

At that time, the great assembly—none of whom were yet those beyond training—upon hearing these words of the Buddha, were utterly bewildered and did not understand the beginning or end of their meaning;
for a moment they were struck with terror and lost their composure.
Suspecting that the Buddha’s response to the two points was not definitive, Ānanda lost his composure. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s compassionate consolation and parable:
The Tathāgata, perceiving that Ānanda’s spirit was distressed and cowed, gave rise to compassion and comforted Ānanda as well as the great assembly.
"O sons of good family, the Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth; he teaches exactly as it is, without deception or falsehood.

This is not the fourfold equivocation regarding immortality of Makkhali Gosāla. You should contemplate and investigate this with earnest attention, so as not to be unworthy of your sorrowful longing."

"His spirit and thoughts changed and were struck with terror" means that he was immediately filled with alarm and lost his composure. "True words," and so forth, refers to the two meanings answered above;
these are words that accord with reality and teachings of suchness (*tathatā*), not deceptive arguments.

Regarding the four kinds of evasive equivocation used by the heterodox *mārga*, see the passage on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) at the end of the volume. [I am] deeply humiliated [by my own inadequacy]. △ Second, Mañjuśrī requests clarification from the Buddha.
This was intended to reveal that seeing and its objects are like flowers in the sky; within them, there is fundamentally no meaning of "is" or "is not.
Therefore, he answered according to the question using the word "like" (tathā). However, this is not something that can be reached by the limited wisdom of those in training;
thus, the great assembly was bewildered and lost their bearings, necessitating Mañjuśrī’s request for clarification.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
this great assembly does not yet understand the Tathāgata’s elucidation of the two kinds of refined vision— the seeing of form and the seeing of emptiness— and their respective meanings.”
As for the "two kinds," they refer to the essence of the faculty of vision and the preceding objects—form and emptiness—which are two distinct meanings.
World-Honored One, if these preceding objects such as form and emptiness were the seer, there should be something pointed out;
if they were not the seer, there should be nothing beheld. Yet now I do not know where this principle leads, and thus I am filled with alarm and fear. It is not that... [I am at fault].
My past roots of goodness have been meager and slight; I only pray that the Tathāgata, through his great compassion, will illuminate this for me:
what are these various objects and this essence of seeing fundamentally? Within them, there is neither "is" nor "is not."

I repeat my previous state of being at a loss for words; I pray that you will clarify this. △ Third, the formal demonstration of the identical essence has three parts. First, the formal determination of what is illuminated.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: "The Tathāgatas and Great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, within their own abiding..."
Within samādhi, the seer, the objects of seeing, and the perceived characteristics are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be "is" or "is not" within this?
"Abiding in one's own samādhi" refers precisely to the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* (the foremost heroic concentration) of intrinsic nature.

When a sage dwells within this concentration, they clearly perceive that all phenomena are nothing other than the single, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening; there is never anything that is not it. This is the direct answer to the question posed.

"Seeing" refers to the sense organ (*indriya*). "The object of seeing" refers to the objective field (*viṣaya*). "The marks of what is conceived" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). These three—the organ, the field, and consciousness—[are thus explained].

This encompasses all phenomena. Now, if one can realize that all conditioned dharmas are fundamentally the single precious awakening (*ratnabodhi*), wherein there is neither "is" nor "is not," then the deluded mind’s attachment to shadows of conditions—its prior sentiments of true and false, real and unreal, inversion, and its discriminating doubts regarding difference—will suddenly and utterly dissolve.
△ Second, revealing the absence of "is" and "is not. First, the illustration by analogy.
“Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: apart from you, Mañjuśrī, is there another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī? Or is there no Mañjuśrī?
“Thus it is, World-Honored One: I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such Mañjuśrī.”
This demonstrates that the single true dharma-nature is fundamentally devoid of right and wrong.
"One such as you, Mañjuśrī" refers to the essence that is fundamentally without right and wrong. To say "there is another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī" implies there is no [true] Mañjuśrī;

this clarifies that because one entertains notions of right and wrong, one consequently loses the original truth. Therefore it is said: "I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no Mañjuśrī of right and wrong. This is because...
If there were such a thing as "is," then I would not be the Real. What is called "having 'is' and 'is-not'" leads to confusion and the loss of the mind.
Why is this? If there were "is," then there would be two Mañjuśrīs. Yet, although I am not without Mañjuśrī today, within this there is truly no duality of the characteristics of "is" and "is-not."
This explains and establishes the preceding meaning. Thus, these two clarify that where there is "is," there is also "is not.

However, from the phrase "Yet I" (*ran ni*) onwards, it clarifies that although one does not establish "is," one likewise does not fall into "is not"; within the very essence of reality (*dharmatā*), there are truly no two characteristics. △ Second, the combined manifestation.
The Buddha said: "This wondrous clarity of vision and these various empty objects are likewise so. Originally, they are the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind.
It is through delusion that they appear as form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing. They are like a second moon:
which of them is the real moon, and which is not?"
The wondrous, luminous seeing is like what is called "you, Mañjuśrī. The conditions of empty objects and seeing are like what is called "this Mañjuśrī.
The bodhicitta is like what is called "the true Mañjuśrī. Form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing are like what is called "the two Mañjuśrīs.
Because all these arise based upon the pure, perfect true mind, they are like a second moon.
The substance is entirely empty; there is no room for debate or interrogation. To know that there is no room for debate is for right and wrong to vanish.
Mañjuśrī, it is simply the one true moon; within it, there is naturally neither "this is the moon" nor "this is not the moon."
However, when the true substance is manifested, the "is" and "is not" vanish of their own accord. △ Third, the conclusion addressed to the assembly:
Therefore, what you now perceive as being identical to or distinct from sensory objects, and which you variously manifest through conceptualization, is called deluded thought (*vikalpa*).

You are unable to transcend "is" and "is not" within it; yet, because of this essential, true, wondrously enlightened, and luminous nature, you are able to transcend the pointing at "this" and "not-this."

"Seeing" refers to the dust; it points to deluded defilement and deluded objects. To observe the dust and thereby produce illumination is like using a finger to point at a finger—it ultimately sinks into deluded thought and fails to transcend the duality of right and wrong. To produce illumination from the refined and true is like using "not-a-finger" to point at a finger;
one can thus transcend right and wrong, attain non-discrimination, and emerge from both "finger" and "not-a-finger," such that the words "right" and "wrong" are both extinguished.
