The Secretariat Director Fang Rong of Qinghe transcribed this under the direction of the Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lotus Temple in Wenzhou. Section Two:

Clarifying the Tathāgatagarbha through the Six Entrances (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Previously, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) were clarified; here, the six entrances are clarified. This section has two parts.
First, the general heading.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
The six sense organs absorbing their objects are called "entrances. II. Specifically explaining the six [entrances]. 1. The eye-entrance (three parts). A. Arising based on the True [Suchness].
"Delusion!
Ānanda, that very act of staring with the eyes until they become strained— both the eyes and the strain— are equally the manifestation of the fatigue of enlightenment through fixed gazing."
"That very person" refers to one within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) who, through staring with wide-open eyes, becomes fatigued and perceives illusory flowers;
this is the same as the delusion of one with clear vision entering [the state of exhaustion]. However, the eye is but a floating organ, and fatigue arises from staring;

within the nature of Bodhi, both are entirely illusory and false. Therefore, it is said: "They are equally the appearance of fatigue arising from the staring of Bodhi. △ Second, distinguishing that the delusion has no reality.
Based on the two kinds of delusive objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises in the midst of them; it draws in these objective phenomena and is termed the "nature of seeing.
Yet this seeing, apart from those two objects of light and darkness, ultimately has no substance.

Vision arises because of objects; it draws in objects because of the sense organ. Thus, there is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). Yet, apart from objects, it has no substance; this is sufficient to know that it is false and illusory.
In this way, Ānanda, you should know that this vision does not come from light or darkness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced in space.

Why is this? If it came from light, then darkness would immediately cease upon its arrival, and one should not perceive darkness. If it came from darkness, then light would immediately cease upon its arrival, and there should be no perception of light.
If it were produced from the sense organ itself, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness. Thus, the essence of seeing has no inherent nature of its own.

If it emerged from empty space, then when it looks forward at external objects, it should return to see the sense organ; furthermore, it would be empty space itself observing [itself]. How could this be?
"Regarding your entry:
it must be neither light nor darkness. This means that if there were no light or darkness, then seeing would have no inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it appears to arise from light and darkness, rather than arising from the sense organ itself. △ Third, realizing the false as the true.
Therefore, you should know that the eye-entrance is illusory; fundamentally it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Since it has no origin, it is neither caused nor spontaneous; it is fundamentally the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
The remaining five [senses] follow this example. △ Second, the ear-faculty has three parts. First, the arising of delusion based on the truth.
Ānanda, it is like a person who blocks their ears tightly with two fingers; because the ear-faculty is fatigued, sounds arise within the head.
Both the ear and the fatigue are, in equal measure, the signs of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.
The finger is fundamentally without sound; the ear is fundamentally without hearing. It is through the false interaction of their characteristics that sound arises within the head.
The delusion of the ear’s engagement is exactly like this. One must rely on the analogy of the finger to clarify that all sounds are fundamentally non-existent;
they arise from false contact. Yet, whether there is contact or no contact, both are silent. Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha is inherently true and wondrous. The ear [is likewise so].

The cause of the eye’s fatigue is obstruction, and so on, up to the cause of the mind’s fatigue being habituation; these delusions are identical to the eye’s fatigue, and thus they are all metaphorically described as "staring until [fatigue] arises.
△ Second, distinguishing that delusion has no reality:
Based upon the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises within the center. It draws in these objective phenomena, which is called the nature of hearing.
This hearing is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects, movement and stillness.
Hearing arises because of movement and stillness, just as seeing arises because of light and darkness.
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this hearing does not come from stillness or motion; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?

If it came from stillness, it would cease as soon as motion occurs, and one should not perceive motion. If it came from motion, it would cease as soon as stillness occurs, and there should be no awareness of stillness.
If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither motion nor stillness. Thus, the essence of hearing is fundamentally...

There is no self-nature. If [the ear] were to emerge from emptiness and possess the nature of hearing, it would not be empty space. Furthermore, if emptiness itself hears, what concern is that for your faculty of hearing?
To say that it possesses the nature of hearing means that because there is something heard, it establishes the nature of existence. △ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true.
Therefore, you should know that the ear-entrance is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
△ Third, the nose-entrance (in three parts): First, the arising of delusion based on the True.
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching it for a long time, fatigue arises, and they perceive a cold sensation within the nose.
Based on that sensation, they distinguish between penetration and obstruction, emptiness and solidity, and so on, even extending to various fragrant and foul odors.
Together with the nose and the resulting fatigue, these are all but the appearance of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.

"Accumulation" (*chù*) refers to the gathering of qi. Cold exists because of accumulation; without accumulation, it is fundamentally non-existent. The delusions of the nose's inhalation are all like this.
Other mental functions may be inferred by analogy with what precedes. △ Second, distinguishing that delusion has no reality.
Based on the two kinds of false objects—openness and obstruction—the faculty of hearing arises in their midst and inhales these objective phenomena; this is called the nature of smelling-hearing.
This hearing, apart from those two objects of openness and obstruction, ultimately has no substance. One should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction.

It does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why? If it were to come from the passage, then when the passage is blocked, hearing would cease; how then could one know that it is blocked?
If it exists because of the blockage, then when there is no blockage, there would be no hearing. How then could it manifest the perception of fragrances, odors, and other tactile sensations?

If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no such thing as a passage being blocked or unblocked. Thus, the faculty of hearing is fundamentally without self-nature. If it were to emerge from space... [is] this...
When hearing occurs, it will naturally turn back to smell your own nose. Since emptiness itself possesses the faculty of hearing, what concern is this for your sense-faculty?
It has no reality whatsoever. △ Third, realizing that the delusory is itself the true.
Therefore, you should know that the nose-faculty is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
△ Four: The Tongue-Faculty (Three Parts). One: The Arising of Delusion Based on Reality.

Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking them repeatedly until they grow weary, if that person is ill, there is a bitter taste, whereas for one who is healthy, there is a slight sensation of sweetness.
Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, it is revealed that when the faculty of the tongue is at rest, its nature of neutrality is ever-present.
Furthermore, both the tongue and its weariness are equally manifestations of the fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi.
Kissing is neither bitter nor sweet; it exists only through the delusion of exertion. Therefore, when there is no movement, its inherent blandness remains constant.
The delusions of the tongue-sense base (*jihvā-āyatana*) are all like this. △ Second, the analysis that delusions lack reality.
Due to the two kinds of false objects—sweet, bitter, and bland—the faculty of cognition arises within them, absorbing these objective images; this is called the nature of knowing taste.
This nature of knowing taste, separated from those three objects of sweet, bitter, and bland, ultimately has no substance. It is thus, Ānanda.

You should know that this perception of bitter and bland tastes does not arise from the sweet or the bitter, nor does it exist because of the bland; furthermore, it does not emerge from the tongue-root, nor is it produced from empty space. Why is this?
If it arose from the sweet or the bitter, then when the bland taste is perceived, [the former] would cease; how then could one perceive the bland?

If it emerged from the bland, then when the sweet is perceived, [the former] would perish; how then could one perceive the two characteristics of sweet and bitter? If it were produced from the tongue... necessarily...
There is no sweetness, blandness, or bitterness among sensory objects; thus one knows that the root of taste has no intrinsic nature. If it arises from space, then space itself would have the taste;
it would not be known by your mouth. Furthermore, if space were to know it itself, what would it have to do with your sense-faculties?
For example, prior to its arising, it has no reality. △ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true:
Therefore, one should know that the tongue-sense field is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
△ The five bodies enter into three. First, the arising of delusion based on the Truth.
Ānanda, it is like a person whose one cold hand touches another hot hand. If the power of the cold is greater, the hot hand follows the cold;
if the efficacy of the heat prevails, the cold hand becomes hot. In this way, by means of this contact of combined perceptions, it is manifested.

Detached from cognition, when the engagement with conditions appears to be established, it arises from the contact of exhaustion; both the body and this exhaustion are equally the signs of exhaustion manifested through the fixed gaze of Bodhi.

The body is the locus of entry for contact, yet contact has no self-nature; it is like two hands, one cold and one hot, coming into contact with each other—neither of which possesses inherent existence.

The fixed principle is this: it is known to be false that the foot [perceives]. Since the hand does not touch itself, but perceives touch because of contact, it is called "the touch perceived through contact.
Since contact does not contact itself, but knows contact because of separation, it is said to be "manifested through the knowledge of separation.
As for "engaging with conditions such as formation" and so forth, this means that by engaging heat with cold, one attempts to make the cold become hot; this too is merely the exertion of touch. △
Second, to discern that the false has no reality:

based on the two kinds of false objects which are difficult to harmonize, the faculty of awakening arises in the interim; it draws in these objective images and is termed the nature of cognitive awareness.
This essence of cognition, when separated from or conjoined with, and apart from the two objects of opposition and compliance, is ultimately without substance.

Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this cognition does not come from separation or conjunction; it does not exist through opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense organs; nor is it produced from space.

Why is this? If [the sense-faculties] come together when in union, they must have already ceased when separated; how then could one perceive separation? The two characteristics of opposition and conformity are likewise so.

If [cognition] were to emerge from the faculties, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of union, separation, opposition, or conformity; thus, the cognition of your body would fundamentally lack self-nature.
If it were to emerge from space, then space itself would possess cognition and awareness; what connection would that have with your sense-faculties?
△ Third, realizing that the delusory is itself the true.
Therefore, one should know that the body-faculty is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
△ Sixth, the three aspects of the mind-faculty: first, the arising of delusion based upon the true.
Ānanda, it is like a person who sleeps when weary; having slept soundly, they awaken. Upon encountering sensory objects, they remember them;

losing that memory is forgetfulness. This is their state of inversion. Birth, abiding, change, and extinction—these are absorbed within the process of conditioning and return to the source, never exceeding one another.
What is called the faculty of mental cognition (*manas*), together with the mind and its weariness, is likewise a state of exhaustion manifested through the fixed gaze of Bodhi.

The mind-faculty (*manāyatana*) presides over recollection and cognition. Since recollection and cognition arise during both waking and sleeping, it is by relying on these states of sleep and waking that they are clarified.

Taking up recollection constitutes arising; losing it constitutes cessation. They abide within the interval between these two. Having taken it up, one recollects; having lost it, one forgets. This is called inversion.
One inhales and habituates oneself to delusive objects, which then return to the mental faculty (*manas*). Thus, the preceding thought and the succeeding thought follow in succession.
They are continuous; thus, it is said they do not transcend one another. This is the characteristic of the entrance of the mind. 2. Discerning that the deluded has no reality:
Based on the two kinds of deluded objects—arising and ceasing—the faculty of cognition gathers within and draws in internal objects, such that seeing and hearing flow against the current.

The nature of awareness that does not reach the objects of the flowing [consciousnesses] is called the "nature of cognitive awareness. This nature of cognitive awareness is ultimately without substance, as it is detached from the two sensory objects of waking and sleeping, or arising and ceasing.

Since the *manas* (mental faculty) presides over cognitive awareness while its sense organ remains latent within the body, it is said that the "cognitive consciousness resides in the center. The *manas* then attaches itself to the mental objects (*dharmas*).
Because mental images arise from within, it is said that one "sucks in and gathers internal objects" (*āntaraviṣaya*). Mañjuśrī states: "The term 'dharma' refers to internal objects.
These are precisely the reflected images of past dharmas; they are also called "fallen-away objects" (*patita-viṣaya*). In the Abhidharma, they are termed "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*);
all of these are internal objects. "Flowing against the current" refers to retrogressive cognition. Since the mind governs the five sense faculties, it is termed "seeing."

I have heard that while the five sense-faculties can only follow along with present objects as conditions, only the mental faculty can turn back to perceive the objects of the five faculties—realms they cannot otherwise reach—just as one recollects the scenes of a dream; the five faculties are incapable of reaching such [past] realms.
Know this, Ānanda. You should know that this faculty of cognitive awareness does not come from waking or sleeping; it does not exist through arising or ceasing;
it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space. Why is this? If it came from waking, it would cease immediately upon sleeping—what then would there be to sleep?

If it must exist when one is awake, it would be as non-existent as nothingness when it ceases—who would then experience that cessation? If it existed through ceasing, then [it would arise from] arising...

It is immediately extinguished and non-existent; who then knows that which arises? If it emerges from the sense organs, then its two states of waking and sleeping would open and close along with the body.

Apart from these two forms, this conscious knower would be like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature. If it were born from space, it would simply be the consciousness of space; what would it have to do with your faculties?
Though one interrogates and examines this repeatedly, it possesses no real meaning whatsoever. The *Liezi* says: "In waking, the form opens; in sleep, the form merges.
Thus it is said that the two aspects of waking and sleep follow the body in opening and closing. △ Third, realizing that the delusory is itself the true.
Therefore, one should know that the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
△ Third, revealing the Tathāgatagarbha through the twelve bases (āyatanas), in two parts: first, the general statement.
Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
The six faculties and the six objects are called the twelve bases. II. Specifically explaining the six [faculties]: 1. The base of the eye and form. 3.
First, citing the characteristics and questioning the basis.
Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. What do you think?
Do these forms arise first and are then seen by the eye, or does the eye arise first and then perceive the characteristics of forms?
The trees, groves, springs, and ponds are form (*rūpa*). That which is able to perceive these is the eye. △ Second, the analysis that the location has no reality, in two parts.
First, the analysis based on the sense organ:
"Ānanda, if it were the eye-organ itself that produced the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to dissolve. If it were to dissolve,"
It reveals that everything is utterly non-existent. Since the marks of form (*rūpa*) are absent, who can perceive the substance of emptiness? Emptiness is likewise so.
If the eye could produce form, then the eye would be the nature of form. However, when perceiving emptiness, since the marks of form are absent, the nature of form should dissolve.
Once the nature of form within the eye has dissolved, it reveals that everything is utterly devoid of form.

This is indeed so. Furthermore, the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) manifest in mutual dependence. Since the characteristic of form does not exist, by what means could emptiness be manifested?
Therefore it is said: "Who clarifies the substance of emptiness? Thus, the calculation that the eye produces the locus of form is an error.
That emptiness is likewise is because, by analogy with form, emptiness also has no fixed locus. △ Second, the analysis based on the object.

Furthermore, if visual consciousness were produced by the dust of form, then when one contemplates emptiness—which is not form—the seeing would immediately perish. Once it has perished, it is entirely non-existent;
who then could discern empty space from form?
If form were able to produce seeing, then at the time of contemplating emptiness, seeing would have nothing from which to arise; therefore, it is said to perish. Once it has perished...
There is no seeing. Who can clarify that space and form [are one]? Thus, to reckon that form arises from the locus of the eye is an error. △ Third, realizing that delusion is itself truth:
Therefore, one should know that seeing and the emptiness of form both have no location; that is, the two loci of form and seeing are both illusory.
This is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
△ Second, the sense field of the ear and sound: First, citing the characteristics and questioning the locus.
"Ānanda, listen further to this Jeta Grove: when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled. The bell and drum..."
Sounds continue in succession from before to after. What do you think? Do these sounds come to the side of the ear, or does the ear go to the place of the sound?

Can this coming and going be discerned such that there would be a real location? II. Distinguishing that the Location Has No Reality. This has two parts: first, distinguishing based on the sense organ.

Ānanda, if this sound comes to the vicinity of the ear—just as I am now begging for alms in the city of Śrāvastī—it is because I am not present in the Jeta Grove. This sound must come to the location of Ānanda’s ears;
otherwise, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas who, upon hearing the bell, all came at once.
Regarding the place of eating:
it is like when I enter the city, the Jeta Grove is no longer "with me. This is analogous to how when a sound comes to the side of the ear, there is no sound elsewhere;
yet, since a thousand people all hear it, the locus of the sound has no reality. △ Second, the analysis based on the object.
Furthermore, if your ear were to travel to the location of the sound— just as I have returned and am staying in the Jeta Grove, such that I am no longer present in the city of Śrāvastī—
and your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is being struck when the bell-sound simultaneously arises, [where would you hear it?]
One should not hear them all simultaneously; how much less so the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within that garden?
Just as when I return to my garden, I am no longer in the city, so too, if the ear were to go to the location of the sound, it would be absent from other places.
Yet, since one hears diverse sounds [simultaneously], the ear must lack substantial reality.
If there is neither coming nor going, there is likewise no hearing.
The preceding and following arguments regarding delusion all serve to dispel the conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind. △ Third, realizing that delusion is itself the True.
Therefore, you should know that hearing and sound both have no location; thus, these two locations—hearing and sound—are empty and false.
Originally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
△ Section Three: The Sense Base of Odors (Ghrāṇa-gandhāyatana). Part Two. First:
Raising the Characteristics and Questioning the Locus. "Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner.

If this fragrance were to burn even a single *zhu* [of weight], its scent would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī. What do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood?"
The sandalwood [incense] arises from your nose; does it arise from space?
△ Second, the analysis of the lack of reality in its location has two parts. First, the analysis based on the sense organ:
"Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced from your nose, and is thus called 'produced by the nose,' it should emerge from the nose. Yet the nose is not..."

Regarding sandalwood: how can there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose? To say that you "smell the fragrance" implies it enters through the nose; yet if the fragrance issues from within the nose itself, to speak of "smelling" it is not logically tenable.
To calculate that the nose arises [from fuel] is a delusion. △ Second, the analysis based on the object:

If it were produced from emptiness, since the nature of emptiness is eternal and constant, fragrance should be ever-present; why then would one rely upon burning this withered wood in an incense burner?

If it were through burning that [the fragrance] existed and yet was not produced from the wood, then when it arises from the wood, this fragrant substance would become smoke due to the burning; if the nose were to perceive it, it ought to encounter the scent of that smoke.
The smoke rises into the air and has not yet traveled far; within forty li, how is it that the fragrance is already perceived?
The substance is wood, but the smoke is not the wood. Apart from the wood and apart from the smoke, one perceives the fragrance at a further distance of forty li.
How could it be born from wood? Since it is neither the nose, nor space, nor wood, it has no real location. △ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true:
Therefore, one should know that the fragrance, the nose, and the act of smelling all have no location; thus, both the act of smelling and the fragrance are empty and false.
This is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
△ Fourth, the sense-field of the tongue and flavors, in three parts: First, stating the characteristics and posing the question.
Ānanda, when you regularly carry the alms bowl among the assembly during the two times of the day, you may occasionally encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter; this is called...
"Supreme flavor. What do you think? Does this flavor arise in space, arise within the tongue, or arise within the food?
△ Second, the analysis of the lack of reality in the location [of perception], in two parts: first, the analysis based on the sense organ.
Ānanda, if this flavor were produced in your tongue and remained within your mouth, you would have only one tongue.
At that time, since your tongue has already become the flavor of ghee, it should not change when encountering black rock honey. If it does not change, it cannot be called "knowing flavors.
If it does change, then the tongue is not a single entity; how then can a single tongue perceive many flavors?
Since it has no fixed substance, the flavor does not arise in the tongue. This refers to rock honey and granulated sugar, which are as hard as sand and stone.

**2. Discernment Based on the Object:** If [the flavor] were produced within the food, the food would lack consciousness; how then could it know itself? Furthermore, if the food knew itself, it would be identical to the food consumed by another.
How could this have anything to do with your knowledge of the name and flavor?
Food does not know itself; it is through the tongue that flavor is known. Even if food were able to know, such knowledge would not reside in you, and it would thus be the same as another's food;
you would have no involvement in it. How, then, could it be called "knowing flavor"? Since this reasoning is untenable, flavor does not arise from food.
If it were produced from emptiness, you would be devouring empty space; what flavor could it possibly have?
If that emptiness were to have a salty taste, once your tongue was salty, your face would also be salty, and the people of this world would be just like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness.
If one does not know the bland, then one neither recognizes the bland nor perceives the salty. If there were nothing known at all, how could it be called "taste"?
Space has no taste and cannot be distinguished; therefore, one relies on saltiness to distinguish it. △ Third, realizing that the false is itself the true.
Therefore, you should know that both the sense of taste and the tongue, along with the act of tasting, have no location; thus, both tasting and flavor are equally empty and false.
Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor do they possess an inherent nature.
△ Section Five: The Sense Base of Tangible Objects. Part Three: First, the section posing the question regarding the characteristics of the example.
"Ānanda, you habitually rub your head with your hand every morning. What do you think? Regarding this sensation known through rubbing, who is it that performs the touching?
Does the capacity to touch reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head?"
△ Second, the analysis of the location [of contact] as being without reality, in two parts: 1. Analysis based on the hand:
If [contact] resides in the hand, then the head is without cognition; how, then, could there be contact?
2. Analysis based on the head.
If it were located in the head, the hands would be useless; how then could they be called "contact"?

Contact arises from the interaction between the faculty and the object—the subject and the object mutually responding. Yet, the reason we specifically clarify it as depending on the faculty is to demonstrate that all phenomena are of one essence.
Because of the deluded differentiation between subject and object, there is deluded contact. Yet, whether it resides in the hand or the head, it has no fixed location;
thus, both the body and the locus of contact are entirely illusory.
If each were separate, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies. If the head and the hand arise from a single instance of contact, then the hand and the head must be one entity.
If they are one entity, contact cannot be established. If they are two entities, with which one does the contact reside?
It cannot reside in the agent, nor can it reside in the object; it is not possible for empty space to enter into contact with you.
Second, the combined analysis of the two bases of body and touch shows that both are without substantial reality. Regarding "touch being unestablished," this means that touch requires two things;
since one alone is not established, it is neither the object nor the agent. Thus, it is said that both are without substantial reality. △ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true.

Therefore, you should know that the sensation of touch and the body both lack a fixed location; thus, both the body and touch are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature of their own.
△ Section Six: The Three Natures of the Mind and the Sense-base of Dharmas. First, raising the characteristics to inquire about their locus:

"Ānanda, regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral natures that you constantly take as objects within your mind, which give rise to the laws of phenomena—do these phenomena arise from the mind itself, or do they exist separately from the mind in some other location?"
Good and evil are the mind that cogitates upon objects; the indeterminate is the mind that remains in a state of dull stagnation.

The mental faculty (manas) does not go beyond these three types of objects as it draws in internal dust to form the dharmas that serve as its objective support; hence it is called the "principle of generation. II. Discerning that the sense bases have no reality.
This has two parts: 1. Discerning according to the faculties.

Ānanda, if the dharmas were identical with the mind, then they would not be objects; they would not be what the mind takes as its objective support. How then could they constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)?

Since the dharmas are already identical with the mind, they do not belong to the realm of external objects; therefore, they are not objective supports and do not constitute the sense-field of the mind (*manāyatana*). 2. Discernment based on the object.
If there were a separate location apart from the mind, then would the self-nature of phenomena be conscious or unconscious? If it were conscious, it would be called "mind";

being distinct from you yet not an external object, it would be identical to the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of others. It would be you and it would be the mind; how could your mind then be dualistic with respect to you?

If it is not known, then since this object is neither form, sound, fragrance, flavor, nor touch—neither conjunction, disjunction, cold, nor heat—and is distinct from the characteristic of empty space, where could it possibly reside?
Now, within the realm of form and emptiness, there is no indication of its presence; nor should there be anything further between humans and the external void.
If the mind is not an object of perception, from what basis is its locus established?

If mental objects (*dharmas*) lack specific characteristics, they are manifested through cognition by the intellect (*manas*). Therefore, one must ask: is it known or unknown? If it is known, it belongs to the mind;

however, its essence differs from yours [the opponent's], and furthermore, it is not an external object (*viṣaya*), thus it is equivalent to the measure of another’s mind. Even if it were unknown, this...
Since the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) is not form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it arises specifically through cognition. Now, since it is not itself cognition, where could its locus possibly be?
Since it is not manifested within form or emptiness, it should not exist outside of form or emptiness; moreover, emptiness itself has no exterior.
Thus, the mind’s objective condition (*ālambana*) in the sphere of the intellect (*manāyatana*) is ultimately without reality. △ Third, realizing that delusion is [identical to] the [true nature].
Truly so.
Therefore, you should know that both phenomena and the mind have no location; thus, both the mental faculty and phenomena are equally false and illusory.
Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
△ Fourth, clarifying the Tathāgatagarbha through the eighteen *dhātus*, in two parts. First, the general introduction:
Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the eighteen *dhātus* fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?

The sixfold sets of faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are each divided into internal, external, and intermediate categories, which are termed "elements" (*dhātu*). II. Specifically explaining the six [faculties]:
A. The three elements of the eye and form. 1. Stating their characteristics and questioning the elements.
Ānanda, as you understand it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions.

Does this consciousness arise because of the eye and thus have the eye as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of visible forms and thus have visible forms as its constituent element?
Sleeping consciousness consists of the eye-faculty and its objects. Based on the investigation of the mind, it is said that when consciousness arises within them, the mind resides therein;
therefore, it is stated, "As you have explained. II. Distinguishing that the elements lack reality has three parts. First, distinguishing based on the faculties.

Ānanda, if [the visual consciousness] arises because of the eye, then in the absence of form and space, there would be nothing to distinguish. Even if your consciousness were present, what would you have it serve?
Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white; since there is nothing to indicate it, how could a boundary be established?

If consciousness were caused by the eye alone and there were no empty space, then consciousness would have no object of perception, vision would have nothing to manifest, and the sensory element (dhātu) would have no basis for establishment;
thus, it would not be caused by the eye. △ Second, the analysis based on the object.
If [your consciousness] arises because of form, then when space is devoid of form, your consciousness should cease. How then could your consciousness cognize the nature of empty space?
If form undergoes change, you likewise cognize that the characteristics of form are shifting; yet if your consciousness does not shift, from what basis would the realms be established?
If [consciousness] arises because of form, it should perish along with the cessation of form; when form ceases and emptiness appears, consciousness should no longer be cognizant.
If it nevertheless remains cognizant, then while the characteristics of form undergo transformation, your consciousness alone persists. Being solitary, it has no neighbor;
how then could a realm be established? It does not arise because of form. This concludes the citation of the objection.

If it changes along with [the object], then the characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*) are inherently non-existent. If it does not change, then it is constant; yet since it arises from form (*rūpa*), it should not be able to cognize the location of empty space.

If it changes, it has no essence, and thus the characteristics of the elements are inherently non-existent. If it does not follow change, then the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is eternally one. It should...

First, regarding form: it should not be perceived as empty. This principle is also untenable, for [consciousness] does not arise from form. △ Third, the analysis of the conjunction of the sense organ and the object:

if both types [of consciousness] were produced by the eye and form together, then when they conjoin, there would be a separation in the middle; when they separate, there would be a union of two. Thus, their essential natures would become confused and disordered.
How is the realm (dhātu) established?
If the eye and form conjoin, they together give rise to the consciousness-realm; thus it should be half-conscious and half-unconscious, and is therefore called "separated in the middle.

If it is separated in the middle, it is half-conjoined with the faculty (indriya) and half-conjoined with the object (viṣaya); therefore, it is called "conjoined in two ways. Thus one investigates and exhausts these two meanings.
None of these constitute a realm. △ Third, realizing that the delusory is itself the true:
Therefore, one should know that the eye and forms serve as conditions to produce the eye-consciousness realm; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the eye, forms, and the realm of form—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Since it is neither dependent on the eye nor dependent on form, all delusions are eliminated together, and the nature of the storehouse-consciousness manifests of itself. The remaining five [senses] follow this same principle.
△ Second, the ear and sound element (three parts). First, citing their characteristics to inquire about the element.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that the ear and sound serve as conditions for the arising of ear-consciousness—
does this consciousness arise because of the ear and thus take the ear as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of sound and thus take sound as its constituent element?
△ Second, the analysis that the elements lack substantial reality, in three parts. First, the analysis based on the sense organs:

"Ānanda, if [hearing] were produced by the ear, then when the two characteristics of motion and stillness are not present before it, the organ would fail to constitute cognition; there would necessarily be nothing known.

Since even cognition itself would not be established, what form or appearance could consciousness have? If one takes the ear as the hearer, then because there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing would be non-existent."

What is established? How can the ear’s shape, its various colors, and the tactile object be called the "consciousness element"? From what, then, is the "ear-consciousness element" further established?
To discern individually is called "knowing"; for the ear’s shape to encounter sound is called "hearing. Both arise through movement and stillness. If...

There is neither movement nor stillness; each is devoid of any established entity. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore it is said that knowledge itself is not established—how, then, could consciousness have any form or appearance?
Hearing is merely the physical form of the ear perceiving the various colors and sounds of objects; it is not the auditory consciousness itself. Therefore it is asked:
"How can the physical form of the ear be called the element of consciousness? 2. Distinguishing [the elements] based on their objects.
If consciousness arises from sound, and consciousness exists because of sound, then it would have no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would perish.

If you grant that consciousness arises from sound and that the characteristic of sound exists because of hearing, then hearing should hear the consciousness; if it does not hear [the consciousness], it is not a sense-element (*dhātu*).

If it is claimed that consciousness arises from sound, then consciousness would exist because of its object and would have no relation to the sense organ. Yet, if it does not depend on the organ, how could one know the location of the sound?
To claim that sound depends on hearing is to grant [the very point we dispute]. Furthermore, if consciousness arises from sound, then sound is identical to consciousness;
in that case, hearing should hear consciousness itself. If, however, it does not hear it, then it fails to fulfill the definition of a sensory element (*dhātu*). All [of this follows].
This is not possible.

When there is hearing, the sound and consciousness arise together; once consciousness has been affected by the hearing, who is it that knows this hearing-consciousness? If there were no knower, it would ultimately be like grass or wood.

Consciousness is the agent of hearing, and sound is the object heard. If consciousness itself were truly the hearer, then consciousness would be identical to the sound, and having already become the object...

[Question: "I hear. [Answer: Who is it that hears? Therefore it is said: "Who knows the consciousness of hearing? If there were no one who knows the act of hearing, then one would be like grass or wood;
yet this is also untenable. △ Third, the analysis of the conjunction of the sense organs and their objects.

It should not be that the Śrāvaka [element] is mixed with others to form a middle element (*madhyama-dhātu*). Since there is no middle position for an element, from what then could the characteristics of "internal" and "external" be established?

Relying on the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), it is already incorrect to discuss them individually; nor should these two be combined to form the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) as a middle position.
Since the middle position does not exist, how can the boundary elements be established? △ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true.

Therefore, you should know that the ear-consciousness element arises with the ear and sound as conditions. Since these three locations are entirely non-existent, the triad of the ear, sound, and the sound-element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
△ Third, the threefold analysis of the nose and odor elements. First, raising the characteristics to inquire about the elements:

"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that the nose and odors serve as conditions to give rise to nose-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the nose, taking the nose as its element, or does it arise because of the odor, taking the odor as its element?"
△ Second, the analysis that the elements have no reality, in three parts. First, the analysis based on the sense organs:
"Ānanda, if [the faculty] arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose?
Do you take it to be the physical form of the two nostrils, or do you take it to be the nature of olfactory cognition and its movement?"
The "claw-shaped" refers to the appearance of the nose; its movement and its smelling constitute the nature of the nose.

If one takes the physical form of flesh, that fleshy substance is simply the body. Since the cognition of the body is contact (*spraṣṭavya*), it is called the body and not the nose; what is called contact is simply an object (*viṣaya*).
The nose itself has no name; how, then, can it be established as an element?
If one calls it a "body of names," it is not the nose; if one calls it "contact," it belongs to the sensory object. Thus, the nose has no name.
If you take the act of smelling as the cognition, then in your mind, what constitutes that cognition? If you say the flesh constitutes the cognition, then it is merely the cognition of the flesh.
The original contact is not the nose; it takes emptiness as its cognition. If emptiness is self-cognizing, then the flesh must be without sensation.
If this were so, then empty space would be you, and your body would have no cognition. In that case, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence today.
Since the cognition of flesh belongs to the body, the original contact cannot belong to the nose; since the cognition of empty space belongs to emptiness, the flesh ought to be without sensation.
Furthermore, if empty space were your body, then Ānanda’s body would now be empty and have no location.
This calculation that consciousness arises because of the nose is erroneous. △ Second, the analysis based on the object:

If fragrance constitutes the knowing, then that knowing belongs to the fragrance itself; what concern is it to you? If fragrant or foul odors must arise within your nose, [then the smelling would belong to the nose].
Thus, those two kinds of flowing vapors—fragrance and stench—do not produce the *eranda* tree or sandalwood; these two substances do not come forth.
You must smell your own nose yourself to determine whether it is fragrant or foul.
If the cognition belongs to the fragrance, then the nose does not participate in the cognition; thus, the cognition would not belong to the fragrance.

If the fragrance were produced by the nose, then wood should have no fragrance. Furthermore, when the stench of *eranda* and the fragrance of sandalwood do not arrive, what odor would the nose produce?
Thus, fragrance is not produced by the nose. This reckoning that consciousness arises because of fragrance is erroneous. △ Three.
To distinguish between the sense organ and its object:

that which is foul is not fragrant, and that which is fragrant should not be foul. If both fragrance and foulness could be smelled simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.
When I question you, there appear to be two Ānandas; which of them is your true self?
If the objects were two, then the sense organs would likewise have to be two. All of this is merely the conceptualization and discrimination of the discerning mind.
If the nose were one, then fragrance and stench would not be two; if stench becomes fragrance, then fragrance in turn becomes stench. Thus, the two natures do not exist.
From what are the elements (dhātu) established?
If the faculty and the object were one, then their objective natures would mutually cancel each other out; from what, then, could the elements be established?

If [consciousness] arises because of fragrance, and consciousness exists because of fragrance, then—just as the eye possesses seeing yet cannot perceive the eye itself—it is because consciousness exists because of fragrance.
One should not know fragrance. If one knows it, it is not produced from fragrance;

if one does not know it, it is not consciousness. Visual consciousness exists because of the eye; since the eye is not seen [by itself], [visual consciousness does not arise]. Olfactory consciousness exists because of fragrance; one should not know fragrance.
If you say it can be known, then it is not produced from fragrance; if you say it cannot be known, then it cannot be called consciousness. In all cases, this is not so.

It is so. If fragrance were not cognized as existing, the fragrance-element (gandhadhātu) would not be established. If consciousness did not perceive fragrance, then the element would not be established by reason of fragrance.

If fragrance did not depend upon the sense organ, the fragrance-element would not be established. If consciousness did not perceive fragrance, the consciousness-element (vijñānadhātu) would not be established.

Since there is no intermediate space, internal and external cannot be established. Those various natures of hearing are ultimately false and illusory—this refers to the intermediate realm of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu), as well as the internal and external realms of the nose and fragrance (ghrāṇa- and gandha-dhātu). △ Third, realizing that the delusory is itself the true.
Therefore, you should know that the nose, odors, and the nose-consciousness element arise with one another as conditions; yet in all three locations, they are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the nose, odors, and the nose-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
△ Fourth, the triad of the tongue and taste elements. First, the inquiry into the characteristics and elements:

"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand—the tongue and taste as conditions giving rise to tongue-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the tongue and thus have the tongue as its element, or does it arise because of taste and thus have taste as its element?"
△ Second, the analysis that the elements have no reality, in three parts. First, the analysis based on the sense organs:

"Ānanda, if [taste] were produced by the tongue, then all the sugarcane, *ume* plums, *hāridrā*, rock salt, *śuṇṭhī*, ginger, and cinnamon in the world would have no taste at all. Try tasting your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter?"
Sugar cane and so forth are cited as examples of the five flavors.
If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste it? The tongue does not taste itself; what, then, could possess cognition? Thus, the nature of the tongue is not bitter.
Taste does not arise by itself; how then can a constituent element (dhātu) be established?
Taste is experienced through the tongue. If the tongue were inherently bitter, there would be no one capable of tasting it; what, then, would constitute the essence of consciousness?

If the tongue were inherently bland, it would not depend on an object, and taste would have no basis for arising. Without taste and its counterpart, from what could a constituent element be established? This...
To reckon that the realm [of consciousness] arises because of the tongue is an error. △ Second, the analysis based on the object:

If it were to arise because of flavor, then consciousness itself would be the flavor, just like the tongue-organ; in that case, it should not be able to taste itself. How then could consciousness discern what is flavor and what is not flavor?
Consciousness itself constitutes the taste; that is to say, consciousness is identical to the taste. This is analogous to the tongue faculty, meaning that consciousness does not taste itself.

Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single entity. Since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise possess multiple entities. If the essence of consciousness were one, [it could not perceive multiple tastes].

The substance must necessarily give rise to taste. When salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together with various changing characteristics, they become a single flavor and should thus be without differentiation.
Since there is no differentiation, it cannot be called "consciousness. How, then, can it further be called the "tongue-flavor-consciousness element"?
Space should not give rise to your mind-consciousness.
Since consciousness arises because of taste, then when there is much taste, the consciousness should also be many; when the taste is one, the consciousness should also be one.
"If its substance must arise from taste" reiterates the certainty that consciousness has taste as its cause. "Saltiness, blandness, sweetness, and pungency being all of one taste" [is the example].

If the consciousnesses formed were of one flavor, they would also have to be one. Since distinct consciousnesses are thus one and distinct flavors are thus identical, there would be no differentiation.
Where there is no differentiation, there is no consciousness; where there is no consciousness, there are no realms. This notion that the cause of the realms arises from flavor is false.

Various flavors are called "harmonious combination" (*saṃyoga*); their fundamental flavors are called "co-arising" (*sahaja*); and their transformed flavors are called "alteration" (*vikāra*). △ Three.
The union of the sense organ and its object is analyzed:
when the tongue and flavor meet, there is fundamentally no self-nature within them; how, then, can a realm arise?
When the organ and object merge and blend, their self-nature is indeterminate; from what, then, could a realm be produced? △ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true.
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-consciousness element arises with the tongue and flavors as conditions; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the triad of the tongue, flavors, and the tongue-consciousness element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
△ Section Five: The Threefold Nature of the Body and Tangible Object Realms. First, posing a question regarding the characteristics of the realms:

"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you have clarified—that in dependence upon the tangible, body-consciousness arises—does this consciousness arise because it is produced by the body and thus has the body as its realm, or does it arise because it is produced by the tangible and thus has the tangible as its realm?"
△ Second, the analysis that the elements have no reality, in three parts. First, the analysis based on the sense organs:
"Ānanda, if [consciousness] were produced because of the body, there would necessarily be no dual conditions of contact and separation for its observation; what, then, would the body cognize?"

Initial and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are simply body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). They take the two conditions of contact and separation as their objects. △ Second, the analysis based on the object:
If they were produced by touch, there would necessarily be no such thing as "your body. Who, then, apart from the body, could perceive contact and separation?
Without a body, one does not know union or separation; thus, this is due to the body and not due to the object. △ Third, the analysis of the conjunction of the faculties and their objects:
Ānanda, objects do not touch cognition; it is the body that knows there is contact. To know the body is itself contact; to know contact is itself the body. This is contact.

It is not the body; thus, the body is not contact. The two characteristics of body and contact have fundamentally no location. When combined with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself;
when separated from the body, they are merely phenomena such as empty space. Since neither internal nor external can be established, how could a middle be posited?
Since a middle cannot be further posited, and the natures of the internal and external are empty, from whom would your consciousness arise to establish its realms?
"Objects do not touch cognition; it is the body that knows there is contact. Mere contact cannot produce cognition; it is because of the body that one then knows contact.

This clarifies that body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) is manifested through the conjunction of the sense organ and its object. When they are conjoined, one should know that the body is contact and contact is the body.
If the body were identical to contact, then the body would no longer be the body. If contact were identical to the body, then...
Contact and non-contact are mutually exclusive; because the body and contact displace one another, they have no fixed location.

When conjoined with the body, there is no locus for contact, and thus it becomes the body itself. When separated from the body, there is no function of contact, and thus it is identical to empty space.

Thus, the positions of internal, external, and intermediate are all unestablished. Even if one were to say that consciousness arises dependent on contact, from what basis could the "elements" (dhātus) be established?
△ Third, realizing that the delusory is itself the real.
Therefore, one should know: when body-contact serves as a condition to give rise to the sphere of body-consciousness, these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the triad of body, contact, and the body-sphere are fundamentally not produced by causes and conditions, nor do they possess an inherent nature.
△ Third, the six consciousnesses, mind, and the dharma-realm (three sections). First, raising the characteristics to inquire about the realms:

"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand—the mind and dharmas acting as conditions to produce mental consciousness—does this consciousness arise because it takes the mind as its cause and the mind as its realm, or does it arise because it takes dharmas as its cause and dharmas as its realm?"
△ Second, the analysis that the elements have no substantial reality, in three parts. First, the analysis based on the sense faculties:
"Ānanda, if consciousness arises dependent upon the mind, then within your mind there must be something thought of that brings forth your mental faculty.
If those preceding phenomena did not exist, the mind would have nothing from which to arise. Being formless apart from conditions, for what purpose would consciousness be used?"
Mental consciousness arises from that which is thought; the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) arises from the objects of dharma (dharma-viṣaya). Both of these belong to the preceding objective realm.
Apart from this, the faculty would have no form and consciousness would have no function. Since they must depend on the objective realm, it is a delusion to reckon that the faculty produces them.

Furthermore, as for your consciousness-mind and the nature of the various faculties of deliberation and discrimination: are they the same or different? If they are the same, then what is the deliberative faculty produced from?

If they are different, then since they would not be the same as the deliberative faculty, there should be no object of cognition. If there were no object of cognition, how could the deliberative faculty arise?

If there is something perceived, how can one speak of "consciousness" (vijñāna) and "mind" (manas)? Only the two natures of identity and difference fail to be established; how then could the realms (dhātu) be posited?

Furthermore, if one distinguishes between the faculties and consciousness, they become confused and cannot serve as the causal basis for the realms. "Consciousness" refers to the mind-consciousness (mano-vijñāna); "mind" (manas) refers to the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) which functions through deliberation and discernment.
If they were identical, there would be no further distinction between subject and object; if they were different, there could be no consciousness. Since these two are thus conflated...
If they are indiscriminate, they already lack intrinsic nature; thus, the realms would have no basis for establishment. II. Discernment Based on Objects:
If [the faculties] arise due to dharmas, then the various phenomena of the world do not depart from the five sense objects.
Observe these dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch; their characteristics are distinct and correspond to the five organs, rather than being subsumed by the mind.
Your consciousness definitely arises in dependence upon dharmas. Now, observe closely: what is the nature of each dharma?

If one is separated from form and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—transcending all these characteristics—ultimately nothing can be found.
When they arise, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when they cease, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together.
The five sense objects each correspond to the five faculties of eye, ear, and so forth, and are not subsumed under the mind.

The five phenomena each depend on conditions such as form and space, and ultimately possess no real substance. Since they are neither subsumed under the mind nor possess any real substance, how could they possibly give rise to mental consciousness?
Since the cause itself does not exist, what kind of form or characteristic could the consciousness produced by that cause possess? Since no such characteristic exists, how could the realm arise?

Previously it was said that consciousness arises with dharmas as its cause; now, since that which serves as the cause arises and ceases in accordance with conditions, it lacks any inherent reality of its own.
Then, consciousness arises based on these. Furthermore, what would its form be? If its form does not exist, then the element (*dhātu*) would also perish.
△ Third, realizing that the delusive is itself the true:

Therefore, one should know that with the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) as conditions, the element of mind-consciousness (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*) arises. Since these three locations are entirely non-existent, then the mind and the mental objects...
And the three [realms] including the mind-realm (*manodhātu*): fundamentally they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
Since they are neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, this is called the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
From the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Definitive Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Essential Explanations, Scroll Five.
