Yinwu. Cuō (pronounced with the initial *ch* and the finals *huó*). Mèi (pronounced with the initials *m-* and *ì*, second tone). Zhuàng (pronounced *zhāng*). Zhū (pronounced *shū*). Jì (pronounced with the initials *c-* and *yè*). Ruò (pronounced with the initials *r-* and *yuè*).

Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas. Scroll Six.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā from the kingdom of Ujjayinī;
orally received by Fáng Róng of Qīnghé, former Grand Master for Rectifying Proposals and concurrently Minister of State Affairs, and disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling provides an explanation [of this section]. △11.
Extensively citing the seven elements to broadly demonstrate the *tathāgatagarbha*. Previously, by taking the immediate example of the body, the *tathāgatagarbha* was revealed;

now, based on the four categories of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), sense-fields (*dhātu*), and elements (*dhātu*), it is clarified that although one has awakened to the single body, the myriad phenomena have not yet been fully integrated.

Since the faculties and their objects are already distinct, the nature of seeing is not yet perfected. Here, by further taking up various external things to perfectly demonstrate the hidden nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), one relies upon the seven great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and consciousness—to clarify that they cause one to awaken to the fact that self and others share the same root.

Thus, it is understood that while they are not a single identical entity, every phenomenon is perfectly accomplished and every particle is all-pervasive. As the *Dharmadhātu-gāthā* says: "If a person wishes to know..."
The principle of true emptiness: the True Suchness within the body extends universally without; sentient and insentient beings share a single essence;

everywhere is identical to the True Dharma-realm. This is the purport of the "Seven Greats. They are called "Great" because their nature is perfectly pervasive, encompassing and containing the ten directions.
As for why there are seven: the generation and completion of the myriad dharmas do not depart from these four [elements].
They are "Great" because they are established based upon emptiness; it is because of the faculty of sight that there is perception, and because of consciousness that there is cognition.
The first five [elements] are possessed by insentient things, while the latter two are shared by sentient beings. Now, by citing these seven, all phenomena are encompassed.

Since the seven elements all arise through the transformation of consciousness, they are subsumed under consciousness. Consciousness, in turn, is the deluded manifestation of luminosity within the fundamental nature of awareness.
This is the Awakened One. Once that which is falsely established arises, it gives rise to the false capacity for perception; thus, there are the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Yet the nature of those great elements was originally neither water nor fire, nor was it space or consciousness; they are entirely the substance of the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting according to karma.
As it is with the seven great elements, so it is with all phenomena: all that we rely upon and our own bodies were originally neither the sense organs nor the physical body, nor were they...
The vessel-world is entirely the manifestation of following one’s karma; its nature is truly perfect and harmonious, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing.
Thus, when Ānanda received the Buddha’s instruction, his body and mind became vast and open, attaining freedom from all obstructions.

He clearly realized that all things in the world are identical to the wondrous mind, encompassing the ten directions. Looking back upon his illusory body, he found its arising and ceasing to have no source, and thus attained [liberation].

The fundamental wondrous mind is eternally abiding and indestructible. This concludes the second major section, which truly elucidates the essential purport and the secret causes for cultivation and realization.
This section has two parts; first, Ānanda initiates the inquiry.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often taught that all the various transformations in the world arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, specifically through the manifestation of the four great elements in combination. Why then does the Tathāgata now reject both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity?
I do not yet understand to what this meaning refers. I only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings."
The Way is the definitive meaning, a dharma free from conceptual proliferation.

This [section] concerns questions and challenges based on the provisional teachings. It explains the principle of the spontaneous arising of the seven great elements from the four great elements as the causal conditions.
△ Second, the World-Honored One provides the response in three parts. First, the compassionate admonition.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Because you previously felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall now reveal the ultimate truth for you."
Why do you further entangle yourself with the causes and conditions of worldly frivolous discourse and delusive conceptualization?

Although you are well-versed in the teachings, you are like a man who knows the names of medicines but cannot distinguish them when the actual medicine appears before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied.
Extensive learning is like a prescription for medicine; the meaning of the Truth is like the actual medicine. △ Second, the granting of the answer:
"Listen attentively now! I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so as to enable those who will practice the Mahāyāna in the future to penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command.
To know that the seven elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha is called penetrating the true mark. △ Third, the direct answer has two parts.
First, the general answer:
"Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world. Ānanda," [he continued].
If the essence of those great elements were not a composite, they would be unable to intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not mix with material forms.
If they were composites, they would be like transformations, wherein beginning and end mutually constitute one another, and arising and ceasing continue in succession.
Birth and death, death and birth; life and death, death and life—like a whirling firebrand, there is no rest.
Although provisional teachings speak of "harmony" (*saṃyoga*), they possess no ultimate reality.

For if that Great Nature were not harmonious with its effects, it would be like empty space, which does not harmonize with various forms; yet this is surely not the case. If it were indeed harmonious, then it would be identical to those myriad things.
Furthermore, it is not the case that transformations form a continuous succession through mutual dependence, for these are all successively illusory. A whirling firebrand has no substantial reality;
this serves as a metaphor for the appearance of illusory phenomena forming a continuous succession.
Ānanda, it is like water turning into ice, and ice returning to water;
this directly demonstrates the principle that the Great Nature is neither harmonious nor disharmonious. Since this serves as the introduction to the subsequent text, he calls out to him once again.
Now, how can water combine to form ice? How can ice blend to become water? The nature of the seven elements does not arise from combination;
it is merely that they manifest according to karma. Thus it is. △ Second, the specific answers to the seven [elements]. First, the earth element. Third.
First, as for the illustration:
observe the nature of earth. That which is coarse is the great earth; that which is subtle is the minute particle, down to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest atom).

If one were to break apart the boundaries of those ultimate material particles, they would be found to be composed of seven parts. If one further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is simply the nature of emptiness.
Although these manifest colors can be analyzed into emptiness, they cannot be recombined; this is intended to show that the nature of earth is not a composite.
The subtlest part of a particle is called a *paramāṇu* (atom); what is subtler than that is called an *aṇu* (extreme atom); and what is subtler still is called a *sanniveśa* (proximate atom).
An atom (*paramāṇu*) still possesses subtle form; therefore, it is called the "limit of form" (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*).
When an atom is analyzed into seven parts, its subtle form becomes almost non-existent; therefore, it is called the "near-atom" (*anu*). △ Second, the clarification.
Ānanda, if these atoms were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that it is from empty space that the characteristics of form arise.
First, I shall establish the principle; below, I shall clarify it.
You have now asked: "Is it because of combination that the various transformed phenomena of the world arise? Observe this for a moment.
A single atom (paramāṇu): by how many spaces must it be combined to exist? It cannot be that atoms combine to form an atom.
Furthermore, when an atom is analyzed into space, by how many material forms (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) must space be composed?
This clarifies that the various marks of transformation are not composite phenomena.
If form were to combine, the combined form would not be empty; if emptiness were to combine, the combined emptiness would not be form. Form may still be analyzed [into its constituent parts].
How could emptiness be combined?
If form were combined, it should not be called empty; if emptiness were combined, one should not be able to analyze form.
Knowing that emptiness is not a combination, one knows that form is not a combination either. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.
You originally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;

it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and manifests according to the capacity of what they know, appearing in accordance with their karma. The world is ignorant of this.

Delusion acts as the causal condition and the nature of spontaneity; all these are merely the conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind. They exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.

The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is such that the myriad dharmas are one and the same; yet, as they manifest in accordance with conditions, they appear to be different, thereby giving rise to the names of the "Seven Greats."

This is merely a distinction in terminology between essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*). "True emptiness" (*zhēn kōng*) is the essence of the single suchness (*yī rú*). Therefore, all seven elements (*qī dà*) are described as true emptiness.
The seven elements are precisely the function that accords with karma. Thus it is said: "the true form of the emptiness of nature," up to "the true consciousness of the emptiness of nature.
Because essence and function are non-dual, they are mentioned in mutual dependence upon one another; because they do not depart from the wondrous nature, each and every one [is so described].
This refers to its nature (*dharmatā*). Being neither defiled nor pure is called "purity" (*viśuddhi*). Being neither harmonious nor disharmonious is called "original suchness" (*prakṛti*).

Being nowhere not present is called "pervasive" (*vyāpin*). Since it is neither defilement nor purity, yet can give rise to the seven great elements and all phenomena, [it is the fundamental substance].
It is merely that things manifest according to karma, in accordance with the mind, and in response to its capacity. Later it says: "If you clarify emptiness, then emptiness appears;
if you clarify earth, water, fire, or wind individually, then each of these appears. This is the matter of responding to the mind and its capacity.

Because one turns one's back on awakening and unites with the dust of the senses, one gives rise to worldly toil (*rajas*). Because one extinguishes the dust and unites with awakening, one gives rise to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This is the manner in which things manifest according to karma. As for the characteristics of the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—and the subtle principles of their myriad forms, none fail to manifest in accordance with conditions and in conformity with karmic responses. Yet, these observed phenomena are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described;

the observed nature is fundamentally real, consisting solely of wondrous, enlightened clarity. This principle transcends emotional conceptualization and does not admit of arbitrary conjecture. Therefore:

All verbal expressions are devoid of ultimate meaning. Therefore, regarding the First Noble Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), any conceptualization of the mind leads to error, and any movement of thought results in deviation.
Only by remaining at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts and without employing the conscious mind to discriminate or calculate can one then achieve resonance with it.
The other six [elements] are the same as this. △ Second, the Fire Element (three parts): 1. Stating the Source.
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe the households within the city that have not yet eaten:
when they wish to cook their food, they take a magnifying lens in their hands and seek fire from the sun.
Fire has no self-substance; it assumes form by depending on objects, and is therefore said to be "without self. A sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) is made of cast copper;
it resembles a mirror but is concave. △ Second, the clarification.
Ānanda, that which is called "conjunction" is like myself and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who now constitute a single assembly.
Although the assembly is one, if one examines its basis, each individual possesses a body; each has a clan from which they were born and a personal name.
For example, Śāriputra is of the Brahmin caste, while Uruvilvākāśyapa is of the Kāśyapa caste, and so on.

Ānanda, this is the clan of the Gautamas. Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, when one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun, does this fire emerge from within the mirror, does it emerge from the tinder, or does it come from the sun?
Ānanda, if it were the sun that comes, it would naturally burn the moxa in your hand; the trees and forests from which it originated should all likewise be consumed by fire.
If it were produced from within the mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror and ignite the moxa; why then does the mirror not melt?
Since your hand grasping it shows no sign of heat, how could it ever liquefy? If it were produced from the moxa itself, what need would there be for the light of the sun or the mirror?
Fire arises only after these elements come together;
when one analyzes these various names of "combination," each has its own fundamental source—this is true combination.
When one analyzes the name "fire" as a "combination," it lacks any fundamental source for each part—it is not a combination. *Uruvilvā* means "Pumpkin Grove. Kāśyapa...
"Pā" means "tortoise," and "Gautama" means "most excellent on earth," or alternatively, "of the solar lineage.
You should observe this carefully: the mirror is held by the hand; the sun comes from the heavens; the moxa is produced from the ground. From what direction does the fire travel to arrive here?
The sun and the mirror are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the fire of the flame exists of its own accord without a source.
The three substances are vastly separated; fire has no fixed location. All such measurements are merely false reckonings. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification:
You still do not know that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire—pure and fundamentally so.
It pervades the entire dharma-realm. In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it manifests according to the measure of what they know.
Ānanda, you should know that when a person holds a mirror in one place, fire arises in one place; yet when held throughout the dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire world.

Since it arises throughout the world, how could it have a fixed location? It is manifested according to karma. The people of the world lack understanding and are deluded into thinking it is caused by conditions or is of a spontaneous nature; all of these are...
The discerning and calculating mind of consciousness consists only of verbal expressions; it possesses no real meaning whatsoever.
△ Third, the Great Water. First, the indication of its source:

Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy. For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was the seer Kapila... [the text continues with the story of] Jāṭila... [and so forth].
The Rishi Aṭṭhaka, the Mahāsattva Paduma, and other great masters of illusion sought the essence of the moon to compound their illusory medicines.
These masters, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, held a *fangchu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.
Does this water emerge from within the gem, does it exist spontaneously in the air, or does it come from the moon?
If one seeks it, it flows; if not, it ceases. This is what is meant by the impermanence of flowing and ceasing. The four, such as Kāpila and others, were all non-Buddhists skilled in magical arts.
"The essence of the Great Yin" refers to the water within the moon. Before the full moon, it is called "white"; at midday, it is called "day.
"Fāngzhū" is the pearl for collecting water, which is the same as the "yin-suil" (the sun-crystal). II. Clarification.
Ānanda, if [the water] came from the moon, it would still be able to cause the pearl to produce water from afar; all the trees and forests it passes through should likewise discharge flowing streams.
If they flow, what need is there for the *fangzhu* (concave mirror) to produce it? If they do not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon.
Regarding the phrase "does not flow, etc.": if the forest trees do not emit flowing water, one knows that the water does not descend from the moon.
If it were to emerge from the pearl, then this pearl should constantly produce flowing water; why then wait for the middle of the night to receive the white moonlight?
If it were produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless; from humans up to the heavens, all would be submerged and drowned.
How, then, could there still be those that travel on water, land, or through the air?
The water does not come from the moon, nor does it emerge from the jewel; it is not born from space. It is inherently pervasive and is not a product of combination.
You should observe this more closely: the moon ascends from the heavens, the jewel is held in the hand, and the water basin that receives the jewel was originally set out by a person.
From what direction does the water flow here? The moon and the water-crystal are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the water-crystal exists of itself from nowhere.
This follows the same logic as the passage on the fire element. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.
You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
According to the minds of sentient beings and responding to the measure of their cognition, if one person grasps a pearl in one place, water will emerge in that same place.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it manifests as beings filling the Dharma-realm; born filling the world, how could it have a fixed location? It appears according to karma.

Beings in the world lack understanding and deludedly regard it as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature; all of this is merely the conceptualization and calculation of the conscious mind.
All these are merely words; they possess no real meaning whatsoever.
First, it says, "You originally did not know. Next, it uses terms such as "still," "yet," "clearly," "entirely," and "formerly.
Finally, it again uses the term "originally" (*yuan*). The initial statement—that you were fundamentally deluded—is the reason for your ignorance. When this is further clarified...

Furthermore, because the meaning was not yet fully conveyed, he next used the word "you" (猶). Later, when he again provided clarification and the listener still did not understand, he used the word "shang" (尚).

Because understanding remained elusive, he used the word "wan" (宛). Because there was total lack of understanding, he used the word "quan" (全). Because the lack of understanding was extreme, he used the word "zeng" (曾).

Because there was ultimately no understanding, he finally used the word "yuan" (元). The initial intent was one of leniency; the final intent was one of censure. Thus, the gradations of severity follow a proper order.
...Indeed. △ Fourth, the Great Element of Wind, in three parts.
First, the indication of its essence: "Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.

When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī robe moves and reaches a person nearby, whereupon a subtle breeze brushes that person's face. Does this wind emerge from your *kāṣāya*?"
The corner of the *saṅghāṭī*. It emerges from empty space and appears upon the person’s face;
when the robe is brushed, it moves, and when the robe hangs down, it is still. This is what is meant by "movement and stillness are not constant"—it is the *saṅghāṭī* Dharma robe.
△ Second, the clarification.
Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of my *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind; as the robe flutters, it should then separate from your body.
Now, as I preach the Dharma in this assembly with my robe hanging down, look at my robe: where is the wind?
There should be no place within the robe where the wind could be hidden.
I argue that it does not emerge from the robe.

If it were born from empty space, then while your robe remains motionless, for what reason would there be no breeze? Since the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, the wind should likewise arise constantly.
If there were no wind, empty space would perish; if wind could be seen to perish, what would the state of perished space be like?
If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called empty space. Since it is named "empty space," how could wind emerge from it?
This refutes the claim that [the wind] arises from empty space. If empty space were to perish, then even when there is no wind, space itself should cease to exist.

Furthermore, if the wind arose spontaneously from the face it brushes against, then it should brush against you as well; and if it arose from the face after you adjusted your robes, it should likewise brush against you.
What is meant by "wiping away the inversion"?
It means that one discerns that [the wind] does not arise from that face; it does not emerge from the clothing, nor is it produced from space.
Since it does not arise from that face and has no source whatsoever, it is not a product of combination.
Examine this with careful scrutiny: your adjustment of the robe resides within you, while your face belongs to that other person. Space is tranquil and does not participate in movement.

From which direction does the wind stir and come here? The natures of wind and space are distinct; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the nature of wind exists of itself without a source.
Third, they do not intermingle; their two natures are separated. One seeks the source of the wind, yet it is so profound that it cannot be investigated.

It is truly said that this is the fundamental pervasiveness manifesting according to karma. To claim that the nature of wind is the "wind-mind" (vāyu-citta) is an error. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.
"You are completely unaware that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognition.

Ānanda, it is like when you alone slightly move your robe and a subtle breeze arises; it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm, fills the lands, and extends everywhere in the world—how could it not exist?"
Regarding their locations, they manifest according to karma. The world is ignorant of this and is deludedly attached to them as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness. They consist only of words and have no real meaning whatsoever.
Regarding the terms "Dharmadhātu" and "Buddha-field": the term "Dharmadhātu" refers to the entire realm in relation to a single person, while "Buddha-field" refers to it in relation to clothing.
△ Fifth, the four great emptinesses: first, the indication of the source.

Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through matter. It is like a place far from the river in the city of Śrāvastī, where various Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Purohitas, Caṇḍālas, and others, have newly established a dwelling and dug a well to seek water.
When they have removed one foot of earth, there is then one foot of empty space within it. Thus it is.
Even when one has excavated the earth to a depth of one zhang, there is still one zhang of empty space remaining within; the depth of this space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth removed.
Is this space produced because of the earth being removed, or does it exist because of the act of digging, or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?

Dugging into the earth, one finds emptiness; this is what is meant by "manifesting through form. In the Western Heaven (India), among both the noble and the common, the clans are divided into four castes, similar to the four classes of people here [in China]. The Kṣatriya are the royal caste; the Brāhmaṇa are those of pure resolve;
the Vaiśya are merchants; and the Śūdra are farmers. These are called the four castes. The Pāraśava possess sharp faculties; the Caṇḍāla...
"Duo-luo-kui" means "butcher. This, moreover, is a matter of the distinction between the wise and the foolish. **2.
Clarification.** Ānanda, if this space were produced spontaneously without a cause, why was it not unobstructed before the earth had been excavated?

Why did one see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration? If it arose because of the earth, then at the time the earth was being excavated, one should have seen space entering [the hole]. If the earth...

Regarding the statement that space first emerges without entering [the earth]: how could space emerge because of the earth? If there were no entering or emerging, then space and earth would fundamentally have no different causes.
If they were not different, they would be identical; if they were identical, then when the earth emerged, why did space not emerge as well?
To have no distinct cause means to be of one essence.
If the space were produced by digging, then the space would not be produced from the earth. If it were not produced by digging, then the digging itself would be produced from the space.
How do you perceive emptiness?
It cannot be established through causes, nor can it exist apart from causes.

Examine this further with meticulous attention; observe it with thorough and repeated scrutiny. The excavation follows the movement of the person's hand in various directions, while the earth shifts according to the ground.
From what source does such empty space arise? One cannot excavate emptiness from within solidity, for the void and the solid do not function as cause and effect. They are neither blended nor joined;
thus, it is illogical that empty space could emerge of itself without a source.

This instructs one to examine in detail that [the nature of reality] is not produced by causes and conditions but is spontaneous (*svabhāva*). "Carving out emptiness from the void" means carving out emptiness from within the real and the void.
All the aforementioned skillful dialectics serve to eliminate the false conceptualizations of the conscious mind and reveal the perfectly interfused true essence.
△ Third, the Synthesis.
If this nature of space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind presently manifest are likewise called the five great elements.
Their nature is truly interfused and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

This explains the meaning of the assembly and connects it to the preceding text. From what has been clarified above, one knows that apart from the harmony of causes and conditions, the nature of emptiness is perfectly pervasive and is not a phenomenon of arising and ceasing.
Since this is the case for the "one great" element, so it is for all others; therefore, the text speaks generally of earth, water, fire, and wind.
As for the phrase "manifest before you," it is intended to cause one to realize clarity through every encounter with phenomena, without seeking elsewhere.
Ānanda, your mind is clouded and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate empty space:
does it emerge? Does it enter? Is it neither emerging nor entering?

If one realizes that the nature of space is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally has no coming or going, then one realizes that the nature of the four great elements is truly perfect and harmonious, fundamentally having no arising or ceasing. △ Fourth, the conclusion by analogy.
"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.

It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognition. Ānanda, it is like a single well’s emptiness:
the emptiness arises within one well, yet the empty space of the ten directions is likewise so; it fills the ten directions—how could it have a specific location? It follows karma."
I have discovered that the world is ignorant, deludedly taking causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature to be real;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and devoid of any actual meaning.
“Emptiness” and “awakening” are also different designations for essence and function. Since essence and function are non-dual, they are mentioned in mutual dependence.
The emptiness of a single well is a metaphor for the nature of a single dharma; the emptiness of the ten directions is a metaphor for the nature of all dharmas.
By observing the many through the one, and by observing others through oneself, their nature is without distinction; it is merely the false discrimination of physical forms and vessels. △ Six: Views.
Section Four: One Exemplar.
Ānanda, seeing and awareness have no inherent cognition; they exist because of form and space. It is as when you are now in the Jeta Grove: in the morning it is bright, in the evening it is dark;
even if it were midnight, it would be light during the bright fortnight and dark during the dark fortnight. Thus, brightness and darkness alike depend upon seeing.
Analyze this: does this vision coexist with light, darkness, and the great void as a single entity, or is it not a single entity?
Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different?
The essence of seeing and cognition is fundamentally devoid of knowing. △ Second, the clarification:
"Ānanda, if this seeing were originally one with light, darkness, and empty space, then the two entities of light and darkness would mutually negate each other;
there would be no light when it is dark, and no darkness when it is light."
The first part provides a general indication; the second provides a detailed analysis. "The characteristics vanish" means they mutually cancel one another.
If seeing were identical to darkness, then when light is present, seeing would vanish. If it were necessarily identical to light, then during darkness it ought to cease.
If it ceases, how can one see light or see darkness? If light and darkness are distinct, yet seeing has no arising or ceasing, how can identity be established?
This demonstrates that they are not of one substance.

If this essence of vision is not of one substance with darkness, light, and empty space, then when you separate from light, darkness, and empty space to analyze the source of vision, what form or appearance does it take?
Apart from light, apart from darkness, and apart from empty space, what is this source of vision like?
Turtle hair and rabbit horns; light, darkness, and empty space—these three things are all distinct. From what could "seeing" be established? This argues that they are not of different substances.

Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they ever be the same? Apart from these three, nothing exists; how could they ever be different? To distinguish between space and seeing [is a fallacy].
Originally it has no boundaries; how could it not be the same? In seeing darkness and seeing light, its nature does not change; how could it not be different?
This explains that it is neither the same nor different, yet neither non-different nor different. That which does not change means that while light and darkness shift, the seeing does not change.
Examine this further; examine it minutely and in detail. Scrutinize it with precision and observe it closely:
light comes from the sun, darkness follows the dark moon, pervasion belongs to empty space, and obstruction returns to the great earth. From what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise?

This causes one to examine thoroughly that nature which is truly perfect and harmonious, such that it does not involve any delusions. To discern deeply is called "examination" (*shen*); to deliberate with precision is called "thoroughness" (*xiang*);

to accord with principle is called "truth" (*di*); and to look with clarity is called "contemplation" (*guan*). Initially, regarding the earth element alone, it says "you contemplate" (*ni guan*); regarding fire, it says "contemplate with truth" (*di guan*).
Subsequently, it says "further contemplate with truth" and "examine and contemplate with truth. This continues until the repetitions reach their limit.

Regarding the statement that "consciousness turns back and forth," its meaning is the same as [the terms] "evasive speech" (*yuan yan*), "incomplete speech" (*quan yan*), and "repeated speech" (*zeng yan*), and so forth;
this is because it turns back and forth in ignorance, is utterly ignorant, and is profoundly ignorant.
Seeing perceives emptiness as stubborn; it is neither a fusion nor a union. It cannot be that the essence of seeing emerges from nowhere on its own.
You should know that its nature is perfectly round and all-pervasive, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. △ Third, the Comprehensive Synthesis.

If one perceives, hears, knows, or realizes that their nature is perfectly pervasive, fundamentally unmoving, and unshakable, one should know that the boundless, unmoving space, together with the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally termed the six great elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*). Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha.
Fundamentally, there is neither arising nor ceasing.

As illustrated by the preceding passage on harmonizing [the teachings], Ānanda, your nature is mired in samsāra; you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should...
Contemplate this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they arising or ceasing? Are they identical or different? Are they neither arising nor ceasing? Are they neither identical nor different?
Arising, ceasing, identity, and difference all depend upon delusory objects; yet that which is neither arising nor different does not depart from deluded conceptualization. To depart from these...
Delusion is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha. △ Fourth, the conclusion and clarification:
You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, and the clarity of awareness and the essence of seeing, are fundamentally pure by nature.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it accords with the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition.

Just as the faculty of sight perceives throughout the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognitive awareness of touch—all these wondrous virtues are brilliantly pure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling the ten voids;
how could they have any fixed location? They manifest in accordance with karma. The world lacks knowledge and is deludedly grasped as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously.
All of these are merely the conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind; they consist only of verbal expressions and lack any real meaning.
Regarding "the nature-vision" (*xing-jian*) and so forth, these are also mentioned by way of the mutual dependence of essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*).

Although having vision and awareness is the fault of the clarity of awareness, the essence is in fact the nature-vision, and the function is in fact the essence of awareness. This is illustrated by one example, which applies to the remaining faculties as well. I have [examined] this.

Contact (*spraṣṭavya*) refers to the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*), which only perceives when in conjunction with flavor; thus it is also called contact. The perception of contact and the cognition thereof are the body and the mind.
△ Seven: The Four Great Elements of Consciousness. First, the indication of the essence.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects.
These three—the faculties, the objects, and consciousness—are all mutually dependent upon false appearances.
Now, as you survey this assembly of noble ones, let your eyes move through them one by one; as your eyes look around, they are merely like reflections in a mirror.
There is no separate analysis; you must identify them one by one among them: "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," "This is Maudgalyāyana," "This is Subhūti," and "This is Śāriputra."
This demonstrates the essence of distinct discernment.
This consciousness cognizes: does it arise from the seeing-faculty? Does it arise from the objective-sign? Does it arise from empty space? Or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?
This refers to the faculty of sight; its objects are the marks [of form]. △ Second, the clarification:
"Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within seeing, then as with darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four would necessarily not exist.
Fundamentally, your seeing would not exist. If the nature of seeing itself does not exist, from what could consciousness arise?"
This clarifies that brightness does not arise from seeing.
If your nature of consciousness were produced within the objective form and did not arise from seeing, then you would neither see brightness nor see darkness.
When light and darkness do not enter the field of vision, there is neither form nor space. Since those characteristics do not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?
Light does not arise from the characteristic;

if it were to arise from space, it would be neither a characteristic nor a seeing. Without seeing, there is no discernment, and one would be unable to know light, darkness, form, or space for oneself.

It is not that characteristics are extinguished as conditions; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place where they can be established. Abiding in these two non-existences, emptiness is the same as nothingness.
Existence is not the same as a substantial thing. Even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would you distinguish?
This clarifies that [consciousness] does not arise from emptiness. If it were to arise from emptiness, it would neither be a characteristic (*nimitta*) nor a vision (*darśana*).

If it were not a vision, there would be nothing to discern; if it were not a characteristic, there would be no object of perception (*ālambana*). If there is no object of perception, how could the perceiving subject be established?
Furthermore, situated between this absence of characteristics and absence of vision, if the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*) were empty, it would be like the hair of a tortoise.
If the substance of consciousness were existent, it would not be the same as material objects; since it lacks its own substance, how could it possess function? Therefore it is said:
"What is there to be discriminated?
If it were to emerge suddenly without any cause, why does one not perceive the bright moon at midday?
This clarifies that it is not without cause.
You should examine this further, scrutinizing it with great subtlety: you see that it relies upon your pupils and projects itself toward external objects; thus, its form can be described as existing.
If they do not arise through mutual formation, from what source would consciousness emerge? Consciousness moves while vision remains still; they are neither blended nor conjoined.
The same applies to hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. It is not possible that consciousness arises from no cause whatsoever.
Seeing relies upon the faculty; the appearance relies upon the object. That which emerges can be characterized; that which does not emerge is not a mark.

From what, then, would consciousness emerge? Consciousness has discrimination and is thus active; seeing is without discrimination and is thus still. Consciousness is active while seeing is still; their natures are distinct and separate.
Seeing and consciousness are separated from one another; the same applies to hearing and knowing. None of these are a combination, nor are they spontaneous. This is therefore...
The nature is truly perfect and harmonious; it does not involve any delusions. △ Third, the reconciliation:

If this consciousness-mind is fundamentally without origin, one should know that its capacity for discernment, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is complete, tranquil, and its nature does not derive from external sources.
Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious.
All are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

This "consciousness-mind" (shixin) refers collectively to the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu). "Discriminating seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" refers specifically to the six consciousnesses (ṣaḍvijñāna).

Incorporating those such as space, it comprehensively unites the seven great elements and extends laterally to all phenomena. Since they fundamentally have no origin, they are serene, perfect, and pervasive.
As it is so for earth and the others, so it is for every single thing in the world, including sentient beings.

Not only are earth and the others called "great," but even grass, weeds, dust, and a hair may be called "great. Their true nature is perfectly interfused and fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.

This has been explained in detail in the preceding text; the essential meaning is all gathered here. Therefore, from the fundamental roots and objects, the myriad dharmas are comprehensively integrated and universally understood.
Ānanda, your mind is coarse and flighty; you have not realized that seeing, hearing, clarity, and cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should...
Contemplate these six sense bases and the consciousness-mind: are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent? Are they neither the same nor different? Are they neither empty nor existent?

The essence of consciousness is profoundly hidden; one should contemplate with subtle and profound reflection rather than coarse superficiality. When one contemplates until the truth is attained, then awakening occurs.
This is the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha. △ Fourth, the conclusion and clarification:

You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminously intelligent; it is the awakened, luminous, true consciousness. This wondrous awakening is profoundly still and serene.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and encompassing the ten voids, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma;

yet the world is ignorant and deludedly regards it as having the nature of causes and conditions or as being spontaneous. All of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness; they exist only as verbal expressions.
There is no substantial reality whatsoever;

all cognition arises from the luminosity of the nature. Therefore, it is called "the luminous knowledge of the nature. Although cognition bears the fault of being a conscious luminosity, its essence is truly real.
Therefore, it is called "true consciousness of conscious luminosity. Essence and function are non-dual; truth and delusion are one truth. Thus...

By alternating [the citations]. △ Third, the assembly attains realization. From the beginning of the second fascicle where [the teaching] was first revealed until this point is the section on "Attaining Realization.
This text has two parts: first, the narrator of the sutra describes the realization.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds completely cleared away, attaining freedom from all obstructions.
Each member of this great assembly personally realized that their own mind pervaded the ten directions and perceived the emptiness of the ten directions.
Just as one observes the object held in the palm of one's hand, so too all things existing within the world are none other than the wondrous, luminous, and primordial mind of Bodhi.
This essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions. When one turns back to observe the body born of one’s parents, [one perceives it as such].

It is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions, appearing and disappearing; or like a single bubble floating upon a vast, tranquil ocean, arising and ceasing without trace.
Thus, one clearly knows for oneself that one has attained the fundamental, wondrous mind, which abides eternally and is never extinguished.
Prostrating to the Buddha with palms joined, he experienced what he had never before attained. Before the Tathāgata, he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.

From his initial resolution of mind and views, through the subtle [dharmas], the aggregates, the sense bases, and the seven elements, he elucidated these in manifold ways to cause [beings] to realize that the myriad phenomena of the vessel-world are, in their very essence, entirely the true Suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha. This is called the subtle and wondrous revelation. Having...
Realizing that the nature of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is truly perfect and harmonious, the body and mind become vast and empty, attaining freedom from all obstructions.

Realizing that wondrous enlightenment is profoundly still and pervades the entire Dharma-realm, each person comes to know for themselves that their own mind extends throughout the ten directions. This profound stillness of awakening pervades and encompasses the ten voids;
thus, one perceives the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as a leaf held in the palm of one's hand. The true nature of the myriad dharmas is fundamentally...
Because of the Tathāgatagarbha, all that exists is none other than the wondrous mind.

Upon awakening to the fact that the scope of one's fundamental mind is as vast as this, one looks back upon the deluded body; it is as minute as a speck of dust and as illusory as a bubble, suddenly becoming nothing at all.
Having clearly awakened to and attained the fundamentally wondrous and eternal mind, he was profoundly gratified and spoke a verse in praise and gratitude.
△ Second, Ānanda’s Verse Praise, Part Three: First, the Praise and Gratitude; Second, the Initial Praise.
"The Wondrously Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One, the Śūraṅgama King, is rare in the world.
"Wondrously Profound, Total-Mastery" refers to the essence of the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature that is clear, perfect, wondrous, and still.

This is what was repeatedly referred to previously as the "wondrous enlightenment, profoundly still, immovable, all-pervading, encompassing and containing the ten voids. Although this is inherently possessed by all people, it must nevertheless depend upon—

It is from the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi that [this power] is manifested. Once Ānanda had personally attained awakening, he realized that the reason the Buddha is called "Buddha" is precisely because of this alone;
therefore, he offered praise in these terms. The ocean of awakening is perfectly clear and still, such that no thing can disturb it—this is called "wondrously profound.
The hidden mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions—this is called "total retention" (dhāraṇī). Its essence is tranquil like space.
It is eternally abiding and indestructible; thus it is called "Immovable. Possessing these qualities, it alone is honored throughout the three realms.

By virtue of this, it serves as the King of all Dharmas. Even if one were to seek such a being in the world, it would be difficult to find; truly, it is rare indeed. △ Next, the expression of gratitude.
It dissolves my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas; without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, I attain the Dharma-body.

Since beginningless time, I have been deluded regarding the Truth and have mistakenly identified with the illusory reflections of conditions—this is precisely what constitutes the inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas.
Once I receive this instruction and clearly realize my original mind, I shall not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.

Offering this body and mind to every dust-mote world, this shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities;
so long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter *nirvāṇa* here.

Having realized one's own nature, one feels a profound sense of gratitude for the grace of its illumination; thus, one vows to achieve something meaningful, propagating the Way to benefit sentient beings as a way to repay the Buddha’s mind.
To aspire to attain the fruit of sainthood is the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*); to return and deliver the multitude is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*).
The simultaneous operation of wisdom and compassion, vast and inexhaustible, is what is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*). One vows to enter the five...

"Not attaining nirvana amidst the turbidity" is the effect of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). Relying upon this [mind] to repay [the Buddha's] kindness, he therefore requests the Buddha to act as witness.
△ Second, the repeated request.
O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions,
so that I may quickly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having offered praise and thanks, he again requested the subsequent teaching, hoping to exhaustively sever the obstacles of afflictions and fulfill his vow for the fruition.
To sever the obstacles of afflictions, one must rely upon heroic and fierce wisdom-power and the virtue of great compassion; therefore, he invoked these qualities fully in his earnest request.
Previously, the illumination of the mind revealed the Tathāgatagarbha, which first destroys the coarse delusions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); next, it was necessary to resolve...

It penetrates doubts and obstructions to open the gate of cultivation and realization. By severing the subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the path of cultivation, one scrutinizes and eliminates them completely before ascending to supreme awakening.

From the fourth fascicle onward, it resolves and penetrates doubts and obstructions while subduing discursive攀缘 (*pān-yuan*); this is precisely the method for scrutinizing and eliminating subtle afflictions.
Once inverted conceptions have been dissolved, one suddenly attains the Dharma-body; having already realized the fruit, one yet further aspires and seeks.
Furthermore, regarding the further elimination of subtle delusions: there are seven aspects of the Buddha-fruit, namely:
*bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *tathatā*, *buddhadhātu*, *amala-vijñāna*, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

That which is called "attaining the Dharma-body" means that one partially attains *bodhi* and personally realizes the Buddha-nature. After realizing this nature, one must carefully eliminate the subtle [delusions].
Delusion causes both arising and ceasing to cease, and both ceasing and arising to become quiescent, thereby harmonizing with the *nirvāṇa* of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Pure and white, perfectly concentrated, it harmonizes with the *amala-vijñāna*. Vast and all-encompassing in its illumination, it harmonizes with the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
When the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the seven fruits are fully perfected, this is what is called "ascending to unsurpassed enlightenment. As for students today:
Having attained only two of them, one suddenly forgets the remaining five; thus, one lightly discards the teachings and no longer practices cultivation or severance.
When, then, will birth and death be stilled? When, then, will defilement be purified? When, amidst this constant clamor and turmoil, will there be sudden, vast clarity?
Obscured and dim, when will there be perfect illumination? Even if one has realized the nature of mind, the outflows of conditioned habits cannot be avoided from arising again.
I know that their inverted perceptions remain as they were, and will likely double over the course of billions of kalpas; this is truly lamentable.
Upon hearing this teaching of the ultimate Śūraṅgama, you should joyfully exert yourselves and strive to bring all things to ultimate completion.
...and so forth. △ Third, the general conclusion:
"The nature of Śūnyatā (Śunyata) may perish, but the Śakara-mind does not waver.
Śūnyatā here means "emptiness," and Śakara means "solid" or "firm. This refers to the fact that while the nature of emptiness has no substance and might [seemingly] vanish, [the mind remains].
They shall perish. My mind is firm and resolute; it shall never waver. This is based on the power of the *samādhi* of the *Śūraṅgama*;
I bind myself by my previous vow, swearing that I shall ultimately reach the end without falling back. When the aspirational mind is thus established, only then can the holy fruit be expected.
The Buddha’s grace can be repaid.
