Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty. Scroll Seven.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā of the country of Ujjayinī;
the bodhisattva-precept disciple and former Minister of Justice and Concurrent Vice President of the Secretariat and Council of State,
Fang Rong of Qinghe, acted as the scribe.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling explains:

Third, profoundly investigating the myriad dharmas to resolve and penetrate doubts and obstructions. Entering the Way takes the realization of one’s nature as the foundation; understanding all phenomena follows next.
This is because even if one realizes one’s nature, if one does not understand the myriad dharmas, one will encounter obstructions at every turn. Therefore, regarding this elucidation:

After the mind’s vision had revealed the Tathāgatagarbha, Pūrṇa again presented his doubts to exhaustively investigate the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth, so that every dharma might be decisively understood and rendered free from all doubt and obstruction;
only then could one proceed with cultivation in accordance with the Way. The text has three parts. First, Pūrṇa’s inquiry: among the ten great disciples, Ānanda was preeminent in learning.

Pūrṇa expounds the Dharma, each [disciple] occupying the foremost position. [The Buddha] first employs Ānanda to provoke those with much learning and deluded wisdom, so as to cause them to give rise to right view;
he then employs Pūrṇa because these various doubts are obstructed and stagnant, requiring the mediation of exposition to be cleared away.
Both are the skillful means of the Sage responding to specific capacities. The text has two parts; the first describes the arising of doubt.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, rising from his seat in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground,
joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue,
you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth."
First, he praises the preceding Dharma; next, he sets forth his state of doubt. It crowns the three vehicles and governs the myriad dharmas, and is named the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Although the World-Honored One has always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, now he hears the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
It is like a deaf person who, from more than a hundred paces away, attempts to listen for the sound of a mosquito; what he cannot see, how much less can he hear?

Although the Buddha has proclaimed this clearly to remove my delusions, I still do not yet fully understand the ultimate meaning of these principles and have not yet reached the stage free from doubt.
What was previously proclaimed is profound and far-reaching in its meaning; yet those whose faculties are dull and inferior are like a deaf person hearing the sound of a gnat at a hundred paces.
Since even those with the capacity for the foremost Dharma are still dim-sighted, it is no wonder that those of middling or inferior faculties harbor doubts.
This is why Pūrṇa manifested his uncertainty and made his request.
World-Honored One, although those such as Ānanda have attained awakening, their habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated.

As for us who have attained the state of no-outflow within this assembly, though we have exhausted all outflows, even now, upon hearing the sound of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, we are still beset by lingering doubts and regrets.

Ānanda’s habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated; thus, it is possible for him to harbor doubts. Yet, if Pūrṇa, having already exhausted all outflows, is still entangled by doubt and regret, then the state of the rest of the assembly can be inferred from this.
Part Two: The Actual Question, in two sections. First: Asking how the pure nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) gives rise to various phenomena.
World-Honored One, if all sense organs, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements heard of in the world are, as you say, the Tathāgatagarbha— pure and inherently so—
how is it that the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise, undergoing successive transformations and flowing on from end to beginning?

If it is pure, it should be devoid of all marks (*nimitta*); if it is primordial, it should be devoid of flux. △ Second, the question: how can the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), each being omnipresent, be mutually accommodated?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that the fundamental nature of earth, water, fire, and wind is perfectly interfused, pervading the *dharmadhātu*, serene and eternally abiding.
“World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is all-pervasive, how can it accommodate water? If the nature of water is all-pervasive, then fire cannot arise.
Furthermore, how do you explain that the two natures of water and fire both pervade space without one subduing or extinguishing the other? World-Honored One, the nature of earth is obstructive.”
Emptiness is void and pervasive; how is it that both are universally present throughout the Dharma-realm? I do not know the direction in which this meaning leads.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will flow forth great compassion to dispel the clouds of delusion for me and for the great assembly. Having spoken these words, [he remained silent].
Prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground, he yearned for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
Both questions arise from doubts concerning the preceding four sections on the seven elements.

His intention was that because the nature and its characteristics appear contradictory and principle and phenomena seem mutually obstructive—this being a genuine point of stagnation for ordinary minds—he posed these questions in the hope of attaining a definitive resolution. △
Second, the Tathāgata’s definitive response has two parts: first, a general permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and had attained the stage of no-more-learning.
Today, for the sake of this entire assembly, the Tathāgata proclaims the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning, so that you in this assembly—
the śrāvakas of fixed nature and all those arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and have turned toward the Mahāyāna— may understand it.
All shall attain the ground of the extinction of the One Vehicle, the true *araṇya* and the locus of correct practice. Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you.

There is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and there is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). To escape the mundane and darken the profound reality, to transcend sentimentality and depart from delusion—these are the three worldly [truths].

There is. The two vehicles that transcend the world cannot fathom it with their minds of cognitive objects; this is called the true nature of ultimate truth within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This is precisely what the following text means by "discerning true awakening through enlightened clarity" and "exhausting all delusions through the realization of their source," until mountains and rivers no longer emerge and water and fire no longer encroach upon one another, such that the body contains the ten directions and every hair...
The manifestation of all lands and realms is the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Those śrāvakas of fixed nature who sink into emptiness and pursue quiescence have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness; they are practitioners at the initial stage of learning (*śaikṣa*).

When they turn toward the Great Vehicle, they become arhats of great resolve. This ground of the cessation of the One Vehicle is the true destination that transcends the disputes of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, "āraṇya" means "free from clamor and confusion.
Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, listened in silence.
II. The actual answer, in two parts: 1. Answering regarding the origination of the various marks. First, clarifying the source.
The Buddha said, "Pūrṇa, it is as you have said. If it is fundamentally pure and quiescent, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Have you not constantly heard the Tathāgata proclaim that 'the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous' and 'fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous'?
Pūrṇa replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One. I have constantly heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning."
"Nature-awareness is wondrously luminous; original awareness is luminously wondrous. These are alternative designations for the essence and function of the myriad dharmas.

That which can nature all things is called "nature-awareness"; the wondrousness of nature-awareness manifests as luminosity, which is that which emerges from its own substance and appears within the myriad dharmas.
That which is the basis of nature is called "original awareness"; the luminosity of original awareness is contained within wondrousness, which is [that which] from its own...
To employ [phenomena] while returning to the profound stillness of the single reality is the way. Once these two meanings are understood, essence and function are one awakening;
things and self are one wondrousness; and there will no longer be any differentiation between various appearances.

The Buddha said, “When you speak of ‘awakened clarity,’ does this mean that the nature itself is clear and is thus called ‘awakening,’ or does it mean that awakening is not inherently clear and is therefore called ‘clear awakening’?
I shall now raise the former meaning to question you, so as to determine whether this is understanding or delusion. Now, as for what you call ‘awakening’ and what you call ‘clarity’—”
What do you think? Is it because this nature is fundamentally luminous and inherently unclouded that it is called "awakening" (*jue*)?
Or is it because the nature is itself not luminous and one awakens it by means of mental effort that it is called "luminous awakening"?
That which is inherently luminous and unclouded is true awakening; that which is awakened through mental effort is deluded awakening.
Pūrṇa said: "If this lack of illumination were called awakening, then there would be nothing illuminated.

Pūrṇa’s intention was that one takes the nature of illumination to be awakening, rather than taking the lack of illumination to be awakening; therefore he said, "If this lack of illumination were [awakening], then there would be nothing illuminated.
However, not knowing that within the entanglements there is that which is illuminated, one falls into deluded awakening, leading to an endless cycle of delusion.
Karma arises from this. Therefore, it is said below: "Awakening is not that which is illuminated; because of illumination, an object is established.
Once the delusory object is established, your delusory subjectivity arises."
The Buddha said: "If there is nothing to be illuminated, then there is no ignorance of enlightenment.
The delusion of enlightened awareness arises from that which is to be illuminated.
To have something before one is not true enlightenment; to have nothing before one is not true ignorance. Furthermore, this ignorance is not the nature of the profound clarity of enlightenment."
Because awakening is free from subject and object, that which has an object is not awakening. Because it illuminates and comprehends all marks, that which lacks an object is not non-illumination.

If the fruit were not illumination, one could not call it the nature of profound, luminous awakening. One should know that having an object and lacking an object, being illumination and not being illumination—all are false conjectures;
they are ultimately not the true state where the wondrous is the illumination and the illumination is the wondrous. △ Second, the narrative.
Regarding the two types of delusion: the first three arise from the subtle.
The nature of awakening is inherently luminous; it is through delusion that this luminosity becomes "awakening-as-illumination.

What was previously called "the wondrous luminosity of the nature of awakening" is here termed "the nature of awakening is necessarily luminous. This is because profound stillness and silent illumination are what is meant by "wondrous."
"Clarity. To insistently seek to know through forceful effort is called "necessarily clear" (*bì míng*); this is false. If it were wondrous clarity (*miào míng*), it would be true;

if it is necessarily clear, it is delusion. Thus, delusion constitutes the awareness of clarity. This is precisely the initial phase of the first of the three subtleties—the deluded consciousness. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Because one does not truly know that the dharma of True Suchness is one, the mind moves unconsciously. This refers to this very phase.

Awakening is not something that can be illuminated; it is because of the act of illumination that an object is established. Once the object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. Within that which is devoid of identity or difference, a blazing diversity is created.
True awakening is fundamentally without subject or object; yet, because there must be illumination, a false perception of objects arises. Once subject and object are established, the mind...
Because objects are mutually differentiated, there is no identity within difference that blazes forth as distinct; this is the characteristic of transformation.

Because it differs from that which is differentiated, identity is established based on difference. When identity and difference are manifested, based on this, one further establishes neither-identity-nor-difference.
Thus, through such disturbances, they wait upon one another and give rise to weariness; this weariness, prolonged, gives rise to dust, which muddies their own characteristics.
Taking that burning diversity as "difference," they further establish "sameness" based on these marks of difference.

Again, because there is both sameness and difference, they further establish "neither sameness nor difference. Within the single true essence, these things never existed from the beginning; they all arise from...

Subject and object are falsely established through mutual opposition, thereby agitating the emotional dusts of the senses. Consequently, the wondrous clarity becomes turbid and the wondrous stillness becomes defiled;
the signs of the obscuration of emptiness and form thus emerge. This is the manifestation of phenomena (*nimitta*).

The three preceding [categories] belong to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), while the following six coarse states arise as their branches and leaves. △ Second, the arising of the six coarse states.
From this, the dust of worldly toil and the afflictions of defilement are aroused;
these are aroused by the three subtle states. "Dust" refers to defilement; "toil" refers to agitation; and "affliction" refers to the distress of anxious torment.

Delusion and confusion constitute affliction (*kleśa*). This refers to the general characteristics of the four gross states: wisdom (*jñāna*), continuity (*saṃtati*), grasping (*upādāna*), and conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

From here downward, the continuity of the world and the continuity of sentient beings constitute the characteristic of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). The continuity of the fruits of karma constitutes the characteristic of suffering bound by karma (*karmabaddha-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*).
III. The three aspects of the resulting fetters (*bandhana*). 1. General explanation.

Arising constitutes the world; stillness forms empty space. Empty space is uniformity; the world is differentiation. In that state, there is neither uniformity nor differentiation, for truly conditioned phenomena are false perceptions.
When false perception moves, it gives rise to weariness and agitation, thereby producing dust. Thus, arising constitutes the world. When false perception is suppressed, it becomes inert and dull.

Because it is profound and obscure, stillness becomes empty space. That the single emptiness of the dharma-realm is called "sameness" (tóng), while the myriad differences of sentient beings and their environments are called "difference" (yì)—this is the blazing manifestation of difference within that which has neither sameness nor difference.
Therefore it is said: "That which lacks both sameness and difference truly consists of conditioned phenomena.
Part Two: A Detailed Explanation, in Three Sections. One: The Initial Arising of the World-System.

Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation; thus there is the wind-circle that supports the world. From emptiness arises agitation, and from the firmness of clarity arises obstruction.
That which is the golden treasure is the firmness established by awakened clarity; thus there is the gold-circle that maintains the lands.

The solidified awareness becomes a precious gem; it is stirred by the wind of radiance. As the wind and the gold rub against each other, there arises the nature of fire-light as a transformative phenomenon.

Moisture is produced from the brilliance of the gem, and the fire-light steams upward, thereby forming a water-wheel that contains the worlds of the ten directions. Fire surges upward and water descends.

Intermingled and arising together, they become firm. The moisture becomes the great oceans; the dryness becomes the continents and sandbanks. For this reason, within those great oceans, flames constantly arise;
within those continents and sandbanks, rivers and streams constantly flow. When the power of the water is weaker than the fire, it solidifies into high mountains.
Therefore, when mountain rocks are struck they become flame; when melted they become water. Earth-nature is inferior to water, yet it draws forth grasses and trees.
Thus, forests and thickets, when met with fire, become earth; through compression, they become water. These mutual delusions arise, each serving as the seed for the other.
By these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
The myriad phenomena naturally undergo transformation through the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). These five elements arise from deluded awareness; thus, the world originates.
It begins with the clarity of awareness and depends upon wind, earth, water, and fire to generate all things. True awareness—
The wondrous emptiness is fundamentally neither luminous nor obscure. Due to delusion, it is taken as luminous awareness; consequently, there arises obscurity within emptiness.

As luminosity and obscurity incline toward one another, one fails to perceive the movement of the mind. Thus it is said: "Luminous awareness and obscure emptiness interact to form agitation. Therefore, there arises the wind-circle.
The world’s lowest stratum rests upon the wind-circle; therefore, it is called the "support of the world. Regarding the phrase "arising from emptiness, there is agitation, etc.":
due to the dullness of emptiness, a stirring thought arises; through the firm attachment of awakened clarity, an obstruction is established, which evokes the manifestation of gold.

The earth’s lowest stratum arises supported by the gold-circle; therefore, it is called the "maintenance of the land. Regarding the phrase "firm awakening achieves the jewel, etc.": due to firmness...

The awakening to delusion causes agitation; contact gives rise to afflictions, which in turn evoke fire. Within the two realms—internal and external—what was raw is transformed into what is cooked, and what exists is transmuted into non-existence;
all these are transformations of the fire element (tejas-mahābhūta). Therefore, it is said that its nature is one of transformation.

Regarding the phrase "precious clarity produces moisture" and so forth: from the perception of solidity, consciousness arises; this is steamed by afflictions. Accumulated emotions give rise to craving, which evokes water (ap-mahābhūta).
Furthermore, worlds reside within the great ocean; therefore, it is said that they "contain the realms of the ten directions. As for the phrases "fire ascending and water descending," etc.:
deluded awakening arises in turmoil, and deluded consciousness flows perversely. Through their mutual entanglement, obstructions are established, and thus the earth is brought forth.

Since the nature of earth is solidity and obstruction, it is called "establishing solidity. Its elevations become mountains, and its depths become oceans; both are earth. A mound of water is called...
Continents; sandbars are called *tan*. All these originate from deluded awareness and are moved by the five elements.
Therefore it is said: "Delusions arise in interaction, serving as seeds for one another. Earth and water produce wood; wood and earth produce metal; metal and wood produce fire.
Fire and metal produce water; water and fire produce earth. At the beginning of the world, consciousness arises from the radiance of awareness, forming water;
the dullness of emptiness coagulates into form, forming earth. Their mutual dependence creates movement, which becomes wind and wood—this is precisely how earth and water give rise to wood.
Furthermore, from the soil of empty obscurity arises movement, which becomes wood; through its solidity and luminosity, it establishes obstruction—this is the generation of metal from wood and soil.
The remaining text is very clear: soil is produced by water and fire, just as a child receives the vital energy of its parents.
Therefore, fire arises within the sea and water pours into the sandbars. According to the Five Elements (*wǔxíng*), when the "I" overcomes another, it takes that as its wife;
only after the husband is weakened do Yin and Yang harmonize to produce offspring. Thus, when water is weakened, fire becomes the mountain; when earth is weakened, water becomes wood.

The "blazing fusion" (*yànróngmíng*) refers to the division of the elemental energies of fire and water; the "burning and twisting" (*shǎojiǎomíng*) refers to the division of the elemental energies of earth and water.
This is the cause for the continuous succession of this world-system. △ Second, the commencement of sentient beings.

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, this delusion of clarity does not come from another; it is the fault of the awakening-clarity itself. Once that which is delusory has been established, the principle of clarity cannot transcend it.
For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not surpass form. Thus, the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth are accomplished.

From these, the functions of seeing, sensing, hearing, and knowing are separated. Through common karma they entwine one another, and through their union and separation, the transformations of the world are formed.

To clarify delusion means to point out that while the luminous awareness is firm and clear, it is the delusion of "shaking" that luminosity which arises; there is nothing else, for it is simply the deluded mind of awakened luminosity that is at fault.
In the wondrous principle of true luminosity, there is fundamentally no subject or object; it is originally one, perfectly interfused, and pure precious awakening.
Because that which was falsely established has come into being, it subsequently becomes an obstruction. Thus, the principle of clarity does not transcend [the senses].

Because it does not transcend them, hearing and the other faculties become falsely restricted; form, fragrance, and the other six sense-objects become falsely defiled; and the six consciousnesses of perception and cognition become falsely divided.
Since these three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—constitute the nature of karma, they give rise to deluded karma. Thereupon, they are alike...

The binding, merging, and separation of karmic characteristics constitute transformation; this is the beginning of the six paths and four modes of birth. Those of "common karma" are the womb-born and egg-born classes;
because the karma of the three—the parents and the self—is identical, they bind and adhere to one another, resulting in birth.

Those of "merging and separation" are the moisture-born and transformation-born classes; they do not depend on parents, but arise solely from the karma of the self. Either by merging with moisture, a form is produced, or...
They are wriggling and crawling creatures. Some depart from their physical forms and undergo transformation, such as the classes of beings in celestial prisons or among ghosts.

When they perceive bright colors, consciousness arises; through clear vision, perceptions are formed. Diverse views give rise to aversion, while shared perceptions result in attachment. This flowing attachment becomes the seed [of rebirth].

The conception of an image serves as the embryo. Through sexual union, life is generated, attracting those of similar karma; thus, by means of causes and conditions, there arise the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.
Birth occurs through womb, egg, moisture, or transformation according to what is appropriate. The egg-born arises solely from mental conception; the womb-born arises because of emotional attachment.
Moisture causes union through sensation; transformation causes separation through response. Sentient thoughts of union and separation alternate and change one another;
all karmic retributions follow their respective ascent or descent. By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
That which is illuminated by deluded vision manifests deluded forms; this is called "vision illuminating and forms arising. This arises because the mind produces the objective realm.

Because of illumination, vision arises, and because of vision, perception arises; this is called "illumination, vision, and perception being established. This arises because the objective realm produces mental affect.
When vision differs, the objective realm is contrary, and thus aversion is formed. When perception is the same, the mind is compliant, and thus love is formed. (3)
The mutual pouring of desire is called "flowing. The convergence of the three perceptions is called "receiving. Desire is the root of saṃsāra; therefore, the flowing of desire constitutes the seed.
Perception is the medium for transmitting life; therefore, the reception of perception forms the embryo.
It arises by means of sexual union and is attracted through shared karma. This is the beginning of taking birth and relying upon a physical substance. Within the womb, there are five stages.
It undergoes a transformation every seven days. *Kalala*—translated here as "coagulated mucus"—is the appearance during the first week.

*Arbuda*, translated as "bubble," is the appearance during the second week, continuing through to *peśī*, *ghana*, *praśākhā*, and so forth. Regarding the four modes of birth: the egg-born corresponds to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*);
the womb-born corresponds to feeling (*vedanā*); the moisture-born corresponds to contact (*sparśa*); and the transformation-born corresponds to separation (*vibhoga*). Therefore...

It is said that these correspond to their respective conditions. Disordered thought is called *saṃjñā* (perception); the binding of affection is called *vedanā* (feeling). When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) attaches, it is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*);

through conjunction with moisture, birth occurs. When the physical form departs, it is called "separation" (*viyoga*); through separation, one dies here and is born there. Feeling, perception, conjunction, and separation—all modes of birth possess these.
This is spoken of in terms of the majority of cases. Why are egg-birth (*aṇḍaja*) placed first? Because at the initial movement of thought and perception, affectionate attachment arises.

It arises subsequently, and furthermore, it includes those born from wombs, moisture, and transformation. This text discusses "perception" (*saṃjñā*); this refers to defiled perception within the internal realm, not pure perception within the external realm. It discusses "transformation";
this refers to transformation through the karma of molting or metamorphosis, not the wondrous transformation of mind-born beings (*manomaya*).

Regarding the mutual transformation and alternation of emotional attachment and perception, or union and separation: sometimes emotion transforms into perception, and union transforms into separation; there is no fixed karma.
Furthermore, the egg-born can easily become womb-born, and the moisture-born can easily become transformation-born; there is no fixed substance.

Thus, the karmic retributions one receives may lead to ascent or descent, with no fixed destination. This is the cause for the continuity of sentient beings. △ Third, the initial arising of the fruits of karma.

Pūrṇa, when ideation and craving form a common bond, and one cannot separate from that craving, then the succession of parents, children, and grandchildren in all the worlds continues without end. These are rooted in desire and greed.
Parents and children do not gather together except through affection; they are not born except through desire.

When craving and attachment grow together and greed cannot be halted, then all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, from transformation, from moisture, or from a womb—devour one another according to their relative strength.
These things have the greed for killing as their root.
Among those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, the weak are devoured by the strong. Driven by greed, they commit killing;
humans eat sheep, and when the sheep dies, it becomes a human; when the human dies, they become a sheep. This cycle continues through ten successive births.
Life after life, they devour one another; their evil karma arises together with them, persisting until the end of the future.
These beings take their origin in the greed for theft.
To take what is not given is called theft. Furthermore, to take it secretly is also called theft. When humans eat sheep, they take what has not been given.
When sheep die, they become humans and come to devour one another; this is "taking by stealth" (*yin*). That which devours one another in the world is entirely the result of theft and greed.
Lust, killing, and theft—these three constitute the roots of karmic fruition.
"You owe me my life; I shall repay you for your debt. Because of these causes and conditions, we shall remain within birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
You love my mind; I cherish your form. Because of these causes and conditions, we shall remain in bondage for hundreds of thousands of kalpas."

The preceding section clarified the basis of karmic results; this section clarifies the causes of their continuity. Debt is the cause for killing and stealing; affectionate attachment and sensual craving are the causes for sexual misconduct.
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct alone constitute the three fundamental roots. By these causes and conditions, the characteristics of karma and its results are fully integrated.
This concludes the summary. △ Third, the conclusion of the answer:
"Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of the luminous clarity of awareness that clearly knows.

Because of this knowing, appearances arise; they are born from deluded vision. The various conditioned phenomena, such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth, undergo successive transformations and flows because of this."
This is false and illusory; it ends and begins again.
This summarizes the preceding text to conclude that the karmic fruits of worlds and sentient beings all have their fault in the "clarity of awakening" (*jue-ming*).
"Clarity of awakening" refers to the inherent awakening that must be clear. To clearly know this nature is what constitutes the delusion of "clarifying awakening."
"The manifestation of arising" refers to that which is established through the interaction of causes and conditions. "Deluded vision" refers to the production of your deluded subjectivity.
This "falsehood" points to the luminosity of awareness (*jue-ming*). The previous question asked: "How did the mountains, rivers, and so forth suddenly arise, ending and beginning again?
This [passage] fully restates those words and answers by pointing to the luminosity of awareness. △ Four: Following the Footsteps to Raise Doubts and Difficulties.
2. First, Pūrṇa’s objection. Pūrṇa said:
"If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrously enlightened and luminous, and is neither increasing nor decreasing in relation to the Tathāgata’s mind,"

Without apparent cause, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arose. Now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, luminous awareness of emptiness, when shall the habitual outflows of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever arise again?

"Wondrous Enlightenment" refers to the essence that is devoid of both reality and delusion. "Fundamentally wondrous, enlightened, and luminous" refers to that which arises as delusion based upon the True.
The essence of enlightenment in sentient beings is no different from that of a Buddha; yet, without cause, they suddenly give rise to various conditioned phenomena.

If this is so, once the Tathāgata has realized empty enlightenment, how could conditioned phenomena ever arise again? This is indeed a point of confusion for ordinary minds; therefore, [the text] specifically...
This is a rebuttal. △ Second, the Buddha’s thorough and exhaustive explanation has five parts. First, having awakened, one is no longer deluded.
2. First, the illustration clarifies this. The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Suppose there is a person who is lost, and in a certain village, he mistakes south for north.
Does this delusion exist because of delusion itself, or does it emerge from awakening? Pūrṇa replied: "Such a lost person does not [arise] because of..."

Delusion does not arise because of awakening. Why is this? Delusion originally has no root; how, then, could it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not produce delusion; how, then, could it arise because of awakening?

"Village" (*zhùluò*) refers to a market town; the *Hànshū* (Book of Han) does not record the burning of villages. "Village" is a metaphor for the nature-portion (*xìngfèn*), while "north and south" are metaphors for delusion and inversion.
However, since north and south cannot be easily changed from the outset, the nature-portion is fundamentally without inversion. Therefore it is said: "Delusion originally has no root;
awakening does not give rise to delusion."
The Buddha said, "Suppose that person who is lost is in the midst of his confusion when suddenly someone who has attained awakening points it out to him and causes him to awaken.
Pūrṇa, what do you think? Even though this person was previously lost, would he become lost again in this village? "No, World-Honored One."
△ Second, the combined explanation:
"Pūrṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are also like this. This delusion has no root; its nature is ultimately empty.

Originally there was no delusion, yet it appeared as if there were the awakening to delusion. When awakening realizes delusion, delusion is extinguished; once awakened, delusion does not arise again."

This reveals that awakening is not delusion. Since there was originally no delusion from the beginning, yet one speaks of awakening from delusion, this is called "awakening to the delusion of delusion.
II. The Subtle Emptiness Without Habituation. This has two parts: first, the illustration by analogy.
It is also like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky; when the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Suppose there were a foolish person who, at that spot in the empty sky where the flowers had vanished, waited for the flowers to reappear. Do you consider this person to be foolish or wise?

The cataract is a metaphor for deluded vision; the flowers are a metaphor for the mountains and rivers. The extinction of the flowers in the sky is a metaphor for the wondrous, empty, luminous awareness.

Pūrṇa said: "In emptiness there were originally no flowers; it was deluded vision that gave rise to their appearance and disappearance. To perceive the extinction of the flowers as the emptiness itself is already a perversion."
To issue a further edict [on this matter] would truly be madness. How can one further label such a madman as either ignorant or wise?
II. Combined Manifestation. The Buddha said:
"According to your understanding, why do you ask: 'When will the wondrously enlightened, luminous emptiness of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas [be realized]? "
Furthermore, mountains, rivers, and the great earth emerge [from it].
Since you have now understood this analogy, why do you still harbor your previous doubts? △ Third, the fruition-awareness is unchanging:
It is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; once that gold is pure, it can never again become alloyed.
△ 4. The fruit and virtue of non-arising:
Just as wood that has become ash cannot again become wood.
△ 5. Conclusion of the answer.
The *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are likewise thus.
*Bodhi* is the fruit of awakening; *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of virtue. When the fruit reaches the state of being unchanging and unborn, it can be known that habitual outflows (*āsrava*) do not arise.
Regarding the meaning of the four parables: the first two clarify that there was originally no delusion in the past, and that delusion arises from false imagination.
Arising. The latter two clarify that through the realization of the false conditions of habitual outflows (*āsrava*), these are then permanently severed.

If one were to cite only the former analogy, there might be the fear that the false would not obstruct the true, and that delusions could extinguish themselves spontaneously, leading to the attachment of nihilistic denial.

If one were to cite only the latter analogy, there might be the fear that awakening is fundamentally not pure and that its nature is inherently subject to arising, leading to views of defilement. Therefore, the four analogies are presented together so that [the practitioner] may understand.

Although delusion and enlightenment are both illusory, they do not preclude cultivation and realization. △ Second, answering the question regarding the mutual containment of the four great elements, in two parts. First, the restatement:
"Pūrṇa, furthermore, you have asked: 'The fundamental nature of earth, water, fire, and wind is perfectly interfused and pervades the entire Dharma-realm. This is your doubt."

The natures of water and fire do not mutually suppress or extinguish one another. Furthermore, it is questioned that empty space and the great earth, both of which pervade the entire dharma-realm, cannot possibly coexist within one another.
△ Second, the answer has two parts. First, a brief clarification of the capacity to contain. First, citing an analogy.
Pūrṇa, it is like empty space: its essence is not composed of manifold characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics.

Empty space is not the characteristics themselves, yet all characteristics arise in dependence upon space. The true essence is not the four great elements, yet the four great elements gather the true essence to form themselves.
Since they were originally neither water nor fire, they do not obstruct one another. This is the general heading; what follows is the specific explanation.
Why is this so? Pūrṇa, that great void becomes bright when the sun shines upon it; it becomes dark when clouds gather; it moves when the wind stirs it;
it becomes clear when the weather clears; it becomes turbid when vapors condense; it becomes a haze when dust accumulates; and it becomes a reflection when water settles.
This demonstrates the various characteristics. Below, the mutual containment is clarified. "Mái" refers to wind and rain mixed with dust.
What do you think? Do such diverse conditioned characteristics of various regions arise because of those [conditions], or do they exist within emptiness?
If it were produced by that [sun], Pūrṇa, then when the sun shines, since it is the light of the sun, the worlds of the ten directions would all share the same solar color;
why then do we still see the orb of the sun in the sky? If it were the light of space, space should illuminate itself;
why then does no radiance arise during the night when there are clouds and mist? You should know that this light is neither the sun nor space. It is not...

Space and the sun are distinct. When one contemplates their characteristics, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described; it would be like inviting empty flowers to form empty fruit. How can you question the meaning of their mutual sublation?
When one contemplates their nature, it is fundamentally real—nothing but wondrous, enlightened clarity. This mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity was not originally water or fire;
why then do you ask how they could be mutually exclusive?
Since the perceived forms are illusory, their submergence and destruction are likewise illusory. When one contemplates their nature as the single truth, there is nothing that is not encompassed.
As they manifest wherever conditions arise, it is said they appear in "different regions"—referring to the sun, clouds, and so forth. △ Second, the combined manifestation.
The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this. If you manifest it through space, then space appears;
if you manifest it through earth, water, fire, or wind individually, then each of these appears; if you manifest it through them all together, then they all appear together.
This is like space, which is not a characteristic; it does not reject manifestation.
When you say "you take emptiness as the illumination," if we speak in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), it is like digging a well to bring forth space, or striking flint to produce fire.

If we speak in terms of karma, it is like the arising of the world, or stillness forming empty space, or the friction between wind and metal producing light and heat. If we speak in terms of the mind...
If one falsely gives rise to the view of emptiness, then emptiness appears. It is the same for earth, water, fire, and wind. Therefore it is said:
"If each is individually manifested, then each appears individually. "Each" refers to preceding and succeeding; "together" refers to simultaneity.
What is meant by "appearing together"? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.
When two people look at the sun in the water together and walk off in opposite directions—one to the east and one to the west—each has a sun that follows them.

Since there was no fixed standard to begin with, one should not raise the objection: "This sun is but one; how can it go in different directions? If each person has their own sun, then they are indeed dual. How... [is this possible]?
Why do they appear as one? They revolve in delusion and are without any basis for reliance;

this explains the phenomenon of simultaneous appearance. Just as the shadow of the sun varies according to the person, so too do the seven elements (mahābhūta) manifest differently in accordance with conditions.
Previously, there was no fixed standard; thus, one should not raise objections. △ Second, a detailed explanation of their mutual manifestation in three parts. First, manifestation following delusion:
"Pūrṇa, you have used form and emptiness to oppose and supplant one another within the Tathāgatagarbha, and thus the Tathāgatagarbha has followed [along with them]."
Because the emptiness of form pervades the entire Dharma-realm, within it, the wind moves, the sky is clear, the sun is bright, and the clouds are dark. Sentient beings are deluded and distressed;
turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of sensory objects, they give rise to worldly toil and the appearances of the mundane world.
To lose the true essence and differentiate from the conditioned shadows is called "turning one's back on awakening and joining with the dust.

To realize that appearances are fundamentally illusory and to contemplate that nature is fundamentally real is called "extinguishing the dust and joining with awakening. II. Manifestation Based on Reality.
I unite my wondrous, luminous, unceasing, and unborn nature with the Tathāgatagarbha; yet the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, enlightened luminosity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, the one becomes the immeasurable, and the immeasurable becomes the one; within the small, the large is manifested.
The large manifests within the small; without moving from the site of enlightenment, one pervades the worlds of the ten directions. The body contains the infinite space of the ten directions;
upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests jeweled royal lands, and sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
Form is emptiness; it is the illusory appearance of the world. Wondrous clarity is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).

Both are manifested from the Tathāgatagarbha and are fundamentally one and perfectly interfused. It is only because sentient beings turn their backs on the Truth and unite with delusion that they are confined within the narrow bounds of worldly appearances.
Because the Buddhas extinguish delusion and unite with the Truth, they wondrously attain the function of True Suchness. Thus, the one and the many are mutually...
It is so. The small and the large contain one another; the jewel-adorned lands are manifested upon the tip of a hair, and the turning of the Dharma wheel occurs within a speck of dust.
In every matter there is no obstruction; every dharma is suchness (tathatā). This is because when observing characteristics, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out;

when observing nature, it is fundamentally true, and thus there is nothing that is not accommodated. △ Third, the perfect integration through detachment from identity. First, the perfection based on substance.
By extinguishing the dust and unifying with awakening, one gives rise to the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature of True Suchness.
Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha—the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and circular mind—is neither mind, nor space, nor earth, nor water, nor wind, nor fire.

Although one extinguishes the dust and manifests the truth, such that the one and the many, the small and the large, can all be as they are, the fundamentally wondrous and perfect essence has from the beginning undergone no change or variation;
therefore, it is neither mind nor fire, and so forth, up to neither mundane nor supramundane phenomena.
"Neither mind nor fire" refers to the seven elements (mahābhūta) and the five aggregates (skandha). Mind is the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu), which subsumes the five aggregates.
It is not the eye; it is not the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It is not form; it is not sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomena. It is not the element of eye-consciousness;
and so on, up to and including the element of mind-consciousness.
That is to say, it is not the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), nor does it include the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

It is neither knowledge (*vidyā*) nor ignorance (*avidyā*), nor the exhaustion of ignorance. In this manner, it extends even to being neither old age nor death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death.

This is not the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas. Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda), desiring to overturn ignorance (avidyā) into clarity (vidyā).
These twelve links possess both the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of being abandoned through cultivation; this [text] mentions them together.
It is not suffering, not its origin, not its cessation, nor the path; it is not knowledge, not attainment, and not the Dharma of the śrāvakas.
The śrāvakas cultivate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, taking knowledge as that which realizes and the fruit as that which is attained.
It is not dāna; it is not śīla; it is not vīrya; it is not kṣānti; it is not dhyāna;
it is not prajñā; it is not pāramitā.

This is not the dharma of a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva cultivates the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). These are giving (*dāna*), morality (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), vigor (*vīrya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). *Pāramitā* means "crossing over."
In this way, it extends even to what is not the Tathāgata, not the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha, and not the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Tathāgata" is translated here as "Thus-Come One. "Arhat" is translated as "Worthy of Offerings."
Samyaksaṃbodhi means "Right Universal Knowledge," which is the third of the Ten Epithets.
It is not Great Nirvāṇa; it is not permanent, not blissful, not self, and not pure.
These are not the dharmas of the Buddha’s fruition. "Permanence, bliss, self, and purity" constitute the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Because these are neither mundane nor supramundane, this concludes the preceding section and introduces the following.
From the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) up to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), these are mundane dharmas. From the pratyekabuddhas...
Reaching Great Nirvana, it becomes the supramundane dharma. △ Second, the Perfect Identity of Function:

It is the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally luminous and wondrous mind. It is identical with mind; it is identical with space; it is identical with earth; it is identical with water; it is identical with wind; it is identical with fire.
It is the eye; it is the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. It is form; it is sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects. It is the sphere of visual consciousness;
and so on, up to and including the sphere of mental consciousness. It is clarity and ignorance, and the exhaustion of clarity and ignorance;
and so on, up to and including old age and death, and the exhaustion of old age and death. It is suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. It is knowledge; it is attainment.
It is dāna; it is śīla; it is vīrya; it is kṣānti; it is dhyāna; it is prajñā; it is pāramitā.
In this way, it extends even to tathāgata, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha, and mahāparinirvāṇa;
it is permanence, it is bliss, it is self, and it is purity.
Although its essence is without change, its function is suchness; therefore, mind is identical to phenomena and phenomena are identical to mind.
△ Third, the simultaneous realization of the perfect and the merging:
because both are identical to the mundane and the supramundane, they are the wondrously luminous fundamental mind of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is free from both identity and difference.
This is both non-identity and identity;
being non-identical yet identical, and being identical yet non-identical. It is wondrously beyond the reach of mind and speech, and cannot be fathomed by measurement.
This passage may appear contradictory, yet each statement has its own specific referent. The first says, "The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind," which refers to the self-substance.

The former statement, "the primordial and luminous mind is wondrous," speaks from the perspective of its function. The latter statement, "the wondrously luminous mind is the source," speaks by unifying both essence and function.
This fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind is the root rather than the branch; it is total rather than partial; it is the mind rather than a material object.

This is the truly pure and wondrous essence; therefore, it is not any phenomenon (*dharma*). The primordial luminosity of the mind is wondrous: this "primordial" is not the fundamental source, and this "luminosity" is not the essence.
It is the wondrous function of suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is identical with all phenomena. The primordial source of the wondrously luminous mind—

This is the wondrous clarity; this is the source of the mind. When the provisional and the wondrous are viewed together, one is neither attached to identity nor to difference, and thus is neither identical nor non-identical.
When the wondrous reaches this state, essence and function are perfectly merged, and conceptualizations are utterly severed;
thus, the wondrous nature of the hidden mind becomes vast and free from all blemish. △ Third, the conclusion and reprimand of false speculation.
How can beings within the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have transcended the world,
use their minds of limited knowledge to fathom the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata, or employ worldly language to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?

I have composed this wondrous work to transcend the limitations of mind and speech, yet I must caution against its false interpretation. For as soon as one directs the mind or stirs a thought, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma.
It is like the lute, the harp, the *konghou*, or the *pipa*: though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skilled fingers, they can never produce music.
It is the same for you and all sentient beings: the precious, awakened true mind is fully complete in each and every one.

Just as when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal manifests its radiance, so too when you briefly stir your mind, the afflictions of worldly toil arise first. This is because you do not diligently seek the path of supreme enlightenment.
Those who cherish the Lesser Vehicle consider a small attainment sufficient.
Although the lute possesses its full range of tones, they do not sound forth without a finger; although the human mind is inherently perfect, it does not awaken without a teacher.

The various methods previously employed to reveal the *tathāgatagarbha* are precisely the Buddha’s pressing of the fingers. When the myriad phenomena of body and mind are thus engaged, they become manifest in their very place.

This is precisely the radiance of the Ocean Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi). Yet, when Pūrṇa and the others produced interpretations according to the words, their doubts and anxieties became turbulent;

this was the initial arising of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). This resulted from their failure to seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment and the fault of cherishing the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Now, when a master strikes the point directly so that it is immediately clear, students compete to give rise to wild, deluded interpretations based upon it.
All this arises because the defilements of emotion are easily stirred, causing one to become involved in doubt and delusion.

If one were to know the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, then a single utterance and a single response would suffice to clear away heaven and earth; how then could there be any further worldly toil? As the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* says:
The myriad phenomena of Jambudvīpa all appear within the ocean; therefore, it is named the "Ocean-Seal" (Sāgaramudrā). △ Fourth, following the traces to resolve doubts and difficulties, in two parts:
first, Pūrṇa’s doubt and difficulty; second, his initial question and challenge. **First, the Question and Challenge:**
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata are identical in our perfect, luminous, true, wondrous, and pure mind; we are both complete and without duality.
Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusion and have long remained in saṃsāra. Although I have now attained the Noble Vehicle, I am still not yet ultimate."
"World-Honored One, all delusions have been completely extinguished within You; You alone are wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata:
for what reason do all sentient beings give rise to delusion? How do they obscure their own wondrous clarity and undergo this drowning in saṃsāra?"

This question is posed by building upon the previous statement regarding the individual perfection [of each]. Having already realized non-duality, the further manifestation of deluded sinking becomes even more evident;
yet, one does not know the origin of this delusion. Therefore, he requests an exhaustive investigation into its cause. Part Two: Answering the Difficulties (in three sections).
Section One: Tracing the Origin of Delusion (in two parts). Part A: Citing an Analogy.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unexhausted.
I shall now question you again regarding various matters manifest in the world. Have you not heard of Yaśoda in the city of Śrāvastī? One morning, he suddenly looked at his face in a mirror;
seeing the head in the mirror with its brows and eyes clearly visible, he grew angry and rebuked his own head for not being able to see its face."
They took him for a *chīmèi* (a mountain-demon) and, without cause, ran about wildly. What do you think?
For what reason did this man run about wildly without any apparent cause? Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind was deranged; there was no other cause."
Yajñadatta was a madman who, out of attachment to his head in the mirror, rebuked himself and ran about in a frenzy.

This serves as a metaphor for how, by clinging to reflected images, one becomes deluded regarding one's original reality and falsely follows the cycle of transmigration. △ Second, the application to the Dharma.

The Buddha said: "The wondrous awakening is perfectly luminous; its fundamental nature is perfectly luminous and wondrous. Since it is now termed 'delusion,' how could it have a cause? If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion?
From these various false thoughts, they mutually cause one another; from confusion to further confusion, they have passed through dust-like kalpas.
Even if a Buddha were to illuminate this for them, they would still be unable to turn back."
The wondrous enlightenment is perfectly complete; this refers to my being no different from the Tathāgata in perfect fulfillment.

It is fundamentally a perfect, luminous wonder, meaning it is fundamentally without deficiency and fundamentally without delusion. This is the original face of every person. Alas, how can one treat it as dual through delusion and allow it to be deficient?
Thus, one distinguishes between "self" and "other," forcibly giving rise to love and hatred; various delusions follow one another, leading to further confusion.

The wheel does not turn back. Such is the cause of delusion; the cause exists because of delusion itself. Consciousness is deluded without an external cause, for the false has no basis upon which to rely.

Since it has never even arisen, what is there to be extinguished? One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream; though the mind may be sharp and lucid, [it remains as such].
For what reason would one wish to grasp at objects within a dream? All the more so, these things are without cause and fundamentally non-existent.
Pūrṇa regretted his own past adherence to false imaginings, yet he had claimed that the World-Honored One’s various delusions were completely extinguished.
This seemed to imply that delusion has a cause and that delusion can be extinguished. Therefore, [the Buddha] spoke to him in this way.
It is like that person in the city, Yan-liao-da-duo (Yajñadatta), who, for no reason at all, became terrified of his own head and ran away.
When his madness suddenly subsided, his head was not to be found outside; even if his madness had not subsided, what would he have lost? Pūrṇa, such is the nature of delusion:
by what cause could it exist?
This section restates the analogy to further clarify that delusion has no cause and thus nothing can be extinguished. △ Second, the exhortation to cease the conditions for delusion:

"If you merely do not follow after the three kinds of continuous succession—worldly karma and its fruits, and sentient beings—the three conditions will be severed, and the three causes will not arise.
Then, the nature of madness in your mind, like that of the yakṣa Yajñadatta, will naturally subside."
Sentient beings and the karmic fruits of the world are all the luminous reflections of the wondrous mind; they are like the head seen in a mirror—delusory upon conceptualization.
Therefore, by not following after conceptualization, the nature of madness naturally subsides.

To take sentient beings and the karmic fruits of the world as the "three conditions" means that the deluded mind arises by taking them as its objects. To take killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the "three causes" means that the deluded...
The mind exists because of these causes. What is meant is that from various deluded thoughts, they successively cause one another;
therefore, when they are severed and do not arise, the nature of madness naturally subsides. △ Third, the cessation of delusion and the manifestation of reality.
Cessation is itself Bodhi. This supremely pure and luminous mind has always been coextensive with the Dharma-realm; it is not obtained from others.
Why rely on arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?
This means that by merely departing from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*). "Ken" (肯) refers to the tendons between the flesh and bone;
"qing" (綮) refers to the small knots within the flesh and bone that can be pried open. In the *Zhuangzi*, it says: "The butcher never once struck the sinews, tendons, or knots.

Here, "ken" and "qing" are used as metaphors for severing the subtle knots of delusion. This arduous cultivation and realization is undertaken solely because of delusive confusion; once the causes of delusion are [eliminated]...
Since the fetters of one's own delusions are naturally eliminated, there is no need for strenuous effort.
It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within their own garment, yet remains unaware of it while wandering in poverty and exposure in a foreign land.
He wandered about begging for food; though he was truly impoverished, the pearl had never been lost.

Suddenly, a wise person pointed out the pearl to him, whereupon his wishes were fulfilled according to his heart and he attained great wealth. Only then did he realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.

It is like the manifestation of the true when delusion ceases; there is no need for laborious cultivation or realization. △ Second, Ānanda’s doubts and difficulties, in two parts. First, the question and difficulty:
At that moment, Ānanda, amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose, and addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, you have just now said..."

Regarding the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct: because these three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise. When the mind clearly realizes this, the nature of madness naturally subsides.
This subsiding is itself *bodhi*; it is not obtained from another. Thus, the principle of causes and conditions is perfectly clear and evident.

Why would the Tathāgata suddenly discard causes and conditions? It was through causes and conditions that I attained awakening in my mind. World-Honored One, why should this principle apply only to us?
There were young śrāvakas in training, such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and Subhūti, who were present in this assembly;
having heard from the aged brahmin the causes and conditions regarding the Buddha, they resolved their minds toward awakening and attained the state of being free from outflows (anāsrava).
This successively builds upon the preceding text to raise an objection, resolving the doubts of later students.

The previous statement that "when conditions cease, causes do not arise" refers to the principle of direct cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Why, then, was this previously stated position abruptly discarded?
As for those who followed the old Brahmins—such as Subhūti and others—they all came from non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) in their later years.

If you now state that bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svayambhū*) taught by Kauśārī and others in Rājagṛha would constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
We pray only that you will deign to show great compassion and dispel our confusion.
If one were now to abandon causes and conditions, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) attachment to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) would be justified.
Following Pūrṇa, Ānanda was again made to pose questions because, once all dharmas have been clarified, there can be no further obstruction to spiritual progress.

To demonstrate the gateway to cultivation and realization, he was thus employed as the appropriate interlocutor to initiate the discourse. II. Answering the Objections (in five parts). First, following the previous pattern:
Tracing back to the root, the Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as with the case of the man in the city named Yanjadatta.

If the causes and conditions of his madness were to be extinguished, then his non-mad state would naturally emerge. The principle of causes and conditions and of spontaneity is fully exhausted in this."
Once the cause of madness has ceased, the nature of spontaneity emerges. Prior to the state of madness, both were fundamentally non-existent.
Viewed from this perspective, all that is called "causality" or "spontaneity" was originally non-existent; they all arise solely from deluded madness.

Therefore it is said: "The principle is exhausted here. **II. Detailed Explanation of the Erroneous Establishment.** This has three parts. First, refuting spontaneity by means of causes and conditions:
"Ānanda, if the head of Yajñadatta were originally spontaneous—if it were originally spontaneous by itself, such that there was no 'spontaneity' apart from the self—then for what reason..."
Because of these conditions, he was terrified and ran about frantically.
As for "natural," it means that from the beginning it is spontaneously so by nature, not dependent upon causes and conditions.

If it were fundamentally natural, then whether one were frantic or not would have no basis in reality and would not be of itself. Why, then, would it further depend upon the condition of looking into a mirror before [realizing its state]?
"He runs about wildly. This is the natural fallacy of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). △ Second, refuting dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by means of spontaneity:
"If the head is 'spontaneous,' why does it go mad because of dependent origination? Why does it not lose [the head] because of dependent origination? The original head is not lost."
The madness and fear emerge delusively, yet there has never been any change; why rely on causes and conditions?
If one was originally not mad and only became mad due to causes and conditions, then if one were originally not lost, one should likewise not become lost due to causes and conditions.
Since the head is not lost, it is specifically due to the madness; thus, the calculation of causes and conditions falls away. △ Three.
The manifestation of delusion is established;
its root is natural madness. Since there was originally the potential for mad terror, before one became mad, where could that madness have been hidden? When not mad, it is simply natural.
The head is fundamentally without delusion; why then do you run about in a frenzy?
If madness and fear were based on nature, then madness and fear would be inherently existent; yet, since there is nothing hidden [within them], they are not inherently mad.
If madness and fear were not based on nature, then the head would originally be without delusion;
why then would one run about in a frenzy? Thus, it is neither inherently mad, nor is it not inherently mad. From this, one can know that nature is the cause.
The discourse on conditions is entirely a false construction. △ Third, causing one to realize the true mark (*dharmatā*):
If one realizes that this is one's original head and recognizes it as such, then both "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity" are equally mere frivolous arguments (*prapañca*).
Therefore, I say that when the three conditions are severed, that itself is the bodhicitta.

If one awakens to the original truth, then one knows that all delusions are fundamentally unrelated to it. For one who perceives the true nature, all delusive conditions are suddenly and utterly severed.
It is for this reason that one attains great liberation. △ Fourth, showing the absence of frivolous discourse.
The Bodhicitta arises; the mind of arising and ceasing ceases. This is merely arising and ceasing. When both ceasing and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*).
If there were something "spontaneous," then this would clarify that the spontaneous mind arises and the mind of arising and ceasing ceases; yet this too is arising and ceasing.

That which is without arising or ceasing is called spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Just as in the world, when various phenomena are blended and unified into a single entity, it is called the nature of combination;
that which is not a combination is termed the nature of original suchness (*tathatā*). Original suchness is not "such," and combination is not "combined."
It is neither conjunction nor separation; it is neither both nor neither. Only this phrase is called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Within the *bodhicitta*, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing, nor is there any spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

If one says that the *bodhicitta* arises while the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases, this is merely arising and ceasing, not the *bodhi*. If one says that both arising and ceasing are exhausted, there is no [attainment of] merit.
Regarding the claim that there is a "natural" [state] within the functioning of the Way: based on this, it would clarify that the natural mind arises while the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases;
yet this too is arising-and-ceasing and is not Bodhi. Furthermore, you instead point to that which is without arising-and-ceasing and name it "natural."

All of these are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). For example, it is because there is a mixture that one speaks of "combination," yet one points back to what is not combined and calls it "original nature.
These are all dharmas of conceptual proliferation established through false opposition.
One should simply cause both "is" and "is not," "combined" and "not combined," to be entirely transcended, such that there is neither a mind of detachment nor a mind of non-detachment.
This is truly the path of effortless non-action, the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far beyond reach; they cannot be realized through your diligent cultivation over kalpas.

Even if you were to memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, with their pure and wondrous principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, it would only increase your conceptual proliferation.

This rebukes their false conceptualizations and frivolous discursive proliferation (*prapañca*), which make it difficult to accord with Bodhi; hence it is said that Bodhi is far distant and cannot be realized by you.
Though you may uphold many sutras, they only increase your frivolous discursive proliferation. △ Fifth: Summarizing the Faults and Exhorting to Practice.

Although you have explained the principles of causality and spontaneity with such certainty and clarity that people of the world acclaim you as the foremost among the learned, even with this accumulation of habituation from hearing the Dharma over many kalpas, you could not escape the peril of the Mātanga woman.
Why then wait for my Buddha-peak divine mantra? The lustful fire in the heart of the Mātanga woman was instantly extinguished, and she attained the stage of Anāgāmin within my Dharma.
You shall form a forest of diligence; the river of craving will dry up, and you will be set free.

Therefore, Ānanda, though you may throughout kalpas retain the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments in memory, it is not equal to cultivating untainted karma for a single day and remaining far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.
Causes and conditions are spontaneous; they are beneficial for debate but not for the Path. Extensive learning is foremost among worldly things;

it is beneficial for reputation but not for reality. Therefore, even if one has cultivated and maintained [the teachings] for many kalpas, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for a single day.
Untainted karma is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. One who attains this samādhi eternally extinguishes all outflows (āsrava) and thus leaves behind the suffering of hatred and attachment.
For example, Maṭaṅga was formerly a courtesan; through the power of the divine mantra, her lustful desires were dissolved, and she is now known by that name within the Dharma.
The bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī and Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, together awakened to their past causes.

Knowing that throughout successive lifetimes they had suffered due to craving and attachment, they cultivated untainted goodness through a single moment of thought; thus, some were liberated from the bonds of existence, while others received predictions of their future enlightenment.

This clarifies the swift efficacy of uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as an impregnating influence (*vāsanā*). "Mātanga" is translated here as "intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti*); thus, she is called the Bhikṣuṇī of Nature.

Her "past causes" refer to the causes of suffering rooted in craving throughout successive lifetimes. She has emerged from the entanglements (*saṃyojana*) of Mātanga; she is the one who received the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) of Yaśodharā.
How can you deceive yourself? You still linger in viewing and listening.

I reprimand Ānanda to cause him to abandon the root of suffering and cultivate the path of non-outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*), so that greed and attachment shall no longer reside within his mind and eyes.

From the initial discernment of the true and the false to the illumination of the nature of awakening, and even down to the profound investigation of the myriad dharmas and their definitive resolution—

To resolve all doubts and remove obstructions, these serve as the initial expedient means to ensure that one's faith and understanding are authentic, thereby constituting the mind of the causal stage.

Once the causal mind is truly authentic, it is possible to perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage; therefore, the preceding sutra concludes here and a separate section begins below.
Essential Exegesis of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
