Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā from the kingdom of Udyāna;

the Bodhisattva-śīla disciple Fang Rong of Qinghe, formerly the Grand Master for Rectifying Discourse and concurrently the Vice President of the Secretariat and the Chancellery, received the oral transcription.
The Monk Jieru of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling: △ Second, the Essential Truths of Practice.
Ānanda had seen his nature but was not yet able to enter realization; it was as if he had encountered a magnificent mansion but could not find its door.
He therefore requested instructions on the expedient means for practice. The previous demonstration of the true foundation was the site of that magnificent mansion.
This demonstrates the essential truth; it is the gateway to the magnificent hall. The text has two parts: first, the essential truth for untangling the knots;
second, Ānanda’s formal request.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the gateways to the second meaning, as I now observe the world, I do not understand..."
"World-Honored One, if one does not know the root from which a knot was tied, I believe that person will ultimately be unable to untie it.

World-Honored One, it is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training: since beginningless time, we have been born and extinguished together with various forms of ignorance.
Although we have attained such roots of goodness through much learning and are called 'those who have left home,' we remain as distant from the truth as a day [is from the night]."

"Malaria" (malaria-like affliction). This refers to the second section of the preceding gate, which causes one to examine the root of karma. The text says: "If one does not see what has been bound, how can one know its release?
Therefore, this is cited here as a request. "All ignorance" (avidyā) encompasses both the fundamental and the derivative [aspects]. Only then can one [temporarily...]
I prostrate myself. Yet, as I have not been able to sever [the fetters] forever, it is like a tertian malaria; this is because I do not know the essential method for binding and untying them.
I pray only that you, in your great compassion, will take pity on me who am drowning in suffering. Today, what constitutes a "fetter" within my body and mind, and from what is it called "liberation"?
"May all sentient beings suffering in the future also be freed from saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly, shedding tears and raising his mind in sincere devotion, awaiting the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
The fetters and delusions of body and mind are truly the root of future suffering and hardship. The source for unraveling these fetters is truly the essential means for escaping the cycle of saṃsāra.
△ Second, the True Compassionate One’s instruction has four parts. First, the Golden Hand strokes the crown of the head.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training,
and also for the sake of all future sentient beings as a cause for transcending the world and as eyes for the future, used his hand of Jambūnada golden light.
"Mahānanda," he said, first touching his crown;
this signified the supreme revelation. Second, the auspicious light appeared as an aid to manifestation:
at that moment, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, and the Tathāgatas, as numerous as motes of dust, who dwelt within those worlds...
Each possessed a jewel-light that issued from their crowns. Simultaneously, these lights came from those worlds to the Jeta Grove and descended, bathing the crown of [the Buddha’s] head.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
As for the "six quakes," they consist of shaking, rising, surging, roaring, trembling, and striking; these signify the breaking of the delusive knots of the six sense faculties.

The light from the crowns of all Buddhas pouring over the crown of Śākyamuni’s head demonstrates that they together have realized the supreme Dharma of the Crown. Therefore, he subsequently proclaimed to Ānanda with a single voice.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly all heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice and in unison to Ānanda:

"Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and know the root of the fetters that causes you to revolve in birth and death—the innate ignorance—it is none other than your six sense faculties; there is nothing else. Furthermore, if you wish to know unsurpassed Bodhi..."
It shall cause you to swiftly realize the blissful liberation, the wondrous, eternal tranquility. Furthermore, these are your own six sense faculties and nothing else.
That all speak with one voice and in unison is to show that the Buddhas’ deliverance from birth and death and their realization of Bodhi all stem from this essential point.
“Co-arising” refers precisely to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). Regarding “birth-and-death and wondrous permanence share the same cause, the six sense faculties”:

when one establishes knowledge within seeing and hearing, one revolves through birth-and-death; when there is no seeing within seeing and hearing, one realizes wondrous permanence, as will be explained below.
△ Third, Ānanda’s inquiry.
Although Ānanda had heard such sounds of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet clear.
He bowed his head to the Buddha and said, "How can it be that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both these same six sense faculties and nothing else?"
△ Fourth, the correct demonstration of the essential truth, in two parts. First, the general demonstration, in two parts. First, the prose section:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky."

Ānanda, it is because of objects that cognition arises, and because of the faculties that appearances exist. Appearance and seeing have no inherent nature; they are like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other.

Therefore, when you now establish cognition within your seeing and knowing, this is the very root of ignorance. When seeing and knowing are free from [the notion of] seeing, this is precisely nirvāṇa—untainted, truly pure.
How could anything else possibly be admitted therein?
The faculties and their objects are fundamentally real; thus they are said to share a common source. Bondage and liberation are both illusory;

thus they are said to be non-dual. Dream-consciousness has no beginning; thus it is likened to flowers in the sky. Material objects and environments appear as existent; thus they arise from the sensory fields. Cognition exists because of the faculties and their marks;
these faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are like a bundle of reeds, leaning upon one another. Although they possess coarse appearances, their essence is entirely empty.
Therefore it is said that when appearances meet, they have no inherent nature and are like intertwined reeds. Since they lack self-nature, they transform according to conditions.
Thus, if one establishes a mind of cognition and perception within these appearances, it binds one to the root of ignorance (*avidyā*).

If, within these appearances, one realizes the delusion of "seeing" and awakens to the absence of such seeing, this is resolved as the true purity of *nirvāṇa*. Now, since it is called "true purity," how could one possibly allow for the establishment [of a conceptual mind] therein?
[He] understood. Therefore it was said: "How can other things be further admitted within this? This generally demonstrates that false knots arise based on the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.
However, if the deluded consciousness does not establish itself, the false knots will naturally unravel; this is the essential method for untying the knots.
Thus, those who study the Way must strive to eliminate the afflictions of consciousness. II. Verse Recitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Regarding the textual divisions: *geya* (Sanskrit) means "verses to be chanted," which are verses corresponding to the prose (*gadya*).
*Gāthā* means "recited verses," which arise independently without corresponding prose. The text has two parts. △ First, the *geya*.
In true nature, conditioned phenomena are empty; because they arise through conditions, they are like illusions.
Unconditioned phenomena have no arising or ceasing; they are as unreal as flowers in the sky. Words of falsehood reveal the various truths, yet both falsehood and truth are equally false.
Since neither is truly real, how can there be a seer and that which is seen? In between, there is no substantial nature.

Therefore, if within the true nature of the "mutually supporting reeds" all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty, then the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are fundamentally empty; this verse illustrates that the source of the sense organs and their objects is one and the same.

If all dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) are illusory, then bondage (*bandhana*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) are likewise illusory; this verse illustrates that there is no [inherent] bondage or liberation.

Second: Since the phenomena of arising and ceasing are all non-existent, deluded consciousness is fundamentally non-existent. This verse shows that the nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.
Since deluded phenomena do not exist, even "the Real" cannot be established. If one says that the Real is revealed by means of the deluded, then the Real would likewise be identical to the deluded.
When both the Real and the non-Real are already doubly negated, how could seeing and the object seen possibly persist?

You should know that both lack substantial reality and are like intertwined reeds; this verse shows that the naturelessness of the perceived and the perceiver is identical to that of intertwined reeds.
The binding and the unbinding share the same cause; for the sage and the ordinary person there are not two paths. Observe the nature within the intertwined reeds.
Neither emptiness nor existence—both are negated. Delusion and obscurity are precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).

When illumination is manifested, one is liberated. The binding and the untying share the same cause; Between the sage and the ordinary person, there are no two paths. The verse [states] that these are simply the six sense faculties and nothing else. "Observe this below":
this restates that the faculties and objects have no substance, being merely due to deluded binding. "Delusion and obscurity below": this verse concerns knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
To establish knowledge is itself ignorance; when fundamental knowledge perceives that there is nothing to be seen, this is *nirvāṇa*. II. Gāthā:

The sequence for untying the knots Is such that when the sixth is untied, even the one [root] perishes. By choosing the faculty of perfect penetration, one enters the stream and achieves true enlightenment.
This follows upon the meaning of the preceding "untying the knots" and initiates the subsequent passage on "perfect penetration. When the six knots are untied, the faculties are uprooted;
when the one [knot] is lost, there is profound stillness and perfection. By selecting the perfect faculty, one enters the stream of the sages and realizes the fruit of sainthood.
"The ādāna-vijñāna is subtle; its habitual tendencies form a violent torrent. Fearing that [beings] might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly taught it.
This verse explains the origin of the initial arising of the sense-faculties' knots. Ādāna means "grasping" or "sustaining," referring to the grasping and sustaining of seeds.
The arising of its active manifestations is the initial phase of the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*; therefore, it is called "subtle. Containing seeds constitutes its "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*);
the accumulation of waves of consciousness constitutes its "flood. It is from this that the profound stillness is divided, and it is from this that knots arise.
This consciousness relies upon *tathatā* (Suchness) while conjoining with birth-and-death; it is intermingled between the real and the false. Therefore, it is said:
It is neither truly real nor truly unreal. If one were to take it as truly real, one might fear becoming deluded by habitual tendencies and thus erring on one’s own account;

if one were to take it as not truly real, one might fear becoming deluded regarding one’s own nature and seeking it externally. Therefore, within the provisional teachings for those of lesser capacity, this was not revealed.
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The ādāna-vijñāna is exceedingly subtle; all seeds form a turbulent stream. I [do not] [reveal it] to ordinary beings..."
I do not expound this to the foolish, fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self. The "divine self" (ātman) clung to by non-Buddhists is precisely this consciousness.
When one's own mind grasps its own mind, that which is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon; when one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not illusory.
"Even that which is not illusion does not arise; how then can illusory phenomena be established?

This verse explains the essential method for entering the perfection by unraveling the knots. All dharmas are manifested solely by the mind, yet within them one grasps and clings, falsely forming the root-knots.
This is the mind taking hold of itself, whereby non-illusion becomes illusory phenomena. By means of this...

Because of false grasping, there is illusion and non-illusion. If one does not falsely grasp, even non-illusion does not exist. Since non-illusion itself is absent, how could illusory phenomena exist?
When illusory phenomena do not arise, the sense organs and their objects are suddenly purified, and perfect penetration manifests before one.
This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening,
the Illusion-like Samādhi by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning with a mere snap of the fingers. This Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
This verse summarizes the essential truth. This Dharma-gate is unstained by purity and untainted by defilement; it is named the "Wondrous Lotus.
When the roots, objects, fetters, and delusions encounter it, they dissolve; it is named the "Vajra-King Awakening," which is itself both conditioned and unconditioned.
When emotions cease and conceptualizations are severed, this is called the "Samādhi of Illusion-like Reality.

By practicing and advancing according to this, one may transcend the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) in the mere blink of an eye and enter the Perfect Stage (*pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*). The *Abhidharma* refers to this as the "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*).

It is through this that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions emerge far beyond birth and death and swiftly realize quiescent permanence; therefore, it is said: "The Bhagavans of the ten directions..."
The Path to Nirvana. The title Bhagavat possesses six meanings: namely, sovereignty, brilliance, majesty, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility.
II. Detailed Explanation, in two parts: 1. A further request.
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha-Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction—
consisting of *geya* and *gāthā*, interwoven with exquisite purity, wondrous, refined, and lucid— felt their minds and eyes opened and enlightened, and they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
The two verses are sung together to express their mutual excellence; thus it is said they are "intermingled yet refined.
Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said: “I have now heard the Buddha’s words on the unobstructed great compassion, the pure, wondrous, eternal, and true nature.
Yet my mind has not yet fully grasped the sequence for loosening the knots so that the six may be resolved and the one vanish. I pray you will bestow your great compassion upon me.”
Again, out of compassion for this assembly and those of the future, he bestows the sound of the Dharma to wash away deep-seated defilements.

His unimpeded great compassion speaks of universal salvation. The "nature-purity, wondrous permanence" and the "true phrases of the Dharma" refer to discourse that accords with the nature, wherein both truth and falsehood are forgotten.
"Deep-seated defilements" refers to subtle fetters and delusions. △ Second, the skillful demonstration.
Second: First, showing the cause for the formal assembly.
At that time, the Tathāgata, upon the lion throne, adjusted his inner robe (nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī), gathered his outer robe (saṃghāṭī), and took up a seven-jeweled stand.
He reached out his hand toward the table, took the flowered scarf offered by the deva Kāpila, and before the great assembly, tied it into a single knot.
Showing it to Ānanda, he asked, "What is this called? Ānanda and the entire assembly replied to the Buddha together, "This is called a knot.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata folded and knotted the flowered scarf again, forming another knot, and asked Ānanda once more, "What is this called?"
...and so forth. Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying: "This is also called a 'knot.

In this manner, by successively folding and overlapping the flowered handkerchief, a total of six knots were formed. As each knot was completed, [the Buddha] took the knot formed in his hand and held it up, asking Ānanda:
'What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly likewise answered the Buddha in succession: 'This is called...'"
*Jie* (knot): This refers to the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, the inner robe; and the *saṃghāṭī*, the great outer robe. *Kāpāla* means "time-portion," referring to the cloth offered by the Yāma Heaven.
*Wan* (to wind) and *jie* (to knot) signify binding and entanglement. The cloth is a metaphor for the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*); the winding is a metaphor for deluded movement (*vikalpa*).
The six knots are used as a metaphor for the six delusions. To inquire into each one in detail is to cause [the listener] to realize that all deluded movements constitute the karma of bondage.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When I first tied the cloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally but a single strip."
"Second, third... why do you all call these 'knots'? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One, this cloth made of precious silk threads, though originally a single entity, according to my contemplation, receives the name of one knot when the Tathāgata ties it once;
if it were tied a hundred times, it would ultimately be called a hundred knots. How much more so for this cloth, which has only six knots? "
"It does not reach seven, nor does it stop at five. Why then does the Tathāgata allow only for the first [knot], while the second and third are not called 'knots'?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This precious flowered cloth—do you know that this cloth originally consists of only a single strand?
When I tied six knots, there were six knots. Examine this closely: the substance of the cloth is the same, yet because of the knots, there are differences."

"What do you think? When the first knot was formed, it was called the 'first. In this way, up until the formation of the sixth knot—now that I wish to designate the name of the sixth knot as the 'first,' would you agree? "No, World-Honored One.
As long as the six knots exist, the name of this sixth one can never become the first. Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence through many lifetimes, how could I make this sixth [knot]..."

Regarding the names of the knots, the Buddha said: "It is so. Although the six knots are distinct, if one traces them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth;
yet by making them disordered, they can never truly be formed [as separate entities]."
The single substance of True Suchness is neither different nor the same; yet the six roots of delusive bondage are stubbornly clung to as distinct.
Thus it is with your six faculties: within ultimate sameness, they give rise to ultimate difference.
This concludes the summary. △ Second, showing the essential method for unraveling [the knots], in two parts. First, the general exposition:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "If you truly find these six knots unsatisfactory and wish for them to become one, how can this be achieved?"
Ānanda said, "If this knot remains, disputes will arise: within it, one will naturally think, 'This knot is not that,' or 'That knot is not this.
If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and the knots did not arise again, then there would be no 'this' or 'that';
they would not even be called 'one,' so how could 'six' be established? The Buddha said, "The dissolution of six and the disappearance of one is also like this."
It is not established. This means that because they do not arise as bees, they cannot constitute a single entity. One wishes for them to become one, yet there is nothing that is not resolved.
When fetters and delusions do not arise, then identity and difference are completely extinguished; therefore, it is said that they cannot even be called "one. How then could "six" be established?

Because your mind-nature has been deluded since beginningless time, false perceptions have arisen. As these false perceptions arise without ceasing, the toiling faculty of sight gives rise to the dust of phenomena.
It is like having blurred vision when the eyes are fatigued, causing illusory flowers to appear; within the pure, brilliant, and essential clarity, these arise in disorder without cause.

All that exists in the world—the mountains, rivers, and great earth, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana—is nothing but the inverted, illusory appearance of those blurred flowers born of weary delusion.
The preceding section clarified the principle of the afflictions and karma that are bound; this section clarifies the deluded mind that performs the binding.
The binding of the deluded mind to false objects is like the sight of phantom flowers by one with fatigued eyes. Therefore, it is said that they are all "deluded and exhausted.
△ Second, a detailed exposition.

Ānanda said, "This knot is identical to a binding; how can it be untied? The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth with his hand and pulled its left side to one side, asking Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One.
He then rotated his hand and pulled the right side to one side, again asking Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "I..."
Now, pull with both hands from the left and right; yet you cannot untie it. By what skillful means can it be untied?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if one were to untie it at the center of the knot, it would immediately fall apart. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at the center of the knot."

"Pulling alternately at the left and right is a metaphor for relying on the partial teachings of expedient means while remaining ignorant of the essential truth; this merely results in excessive and frantic toil.

Therefore, if one wishes to resolve this frantic toil, one must resolve the frantic mind. Once one knows how to resolve the frantic mind, one will no longer depend on partial expedients, and the cultivation and realization of the essential point will be achieved."
Ānanda, I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse, composite appearances of the world.

The Tathāgata illuminates both mundane and supramundane phenomena, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their respective conditions. Thus, even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows its number.
He perceives all that appears before him: the straightness of pines and the curvature of thorns, the whiteness of cranes, and so forth.
Wu Xuan: "In all cases, one must clearly understand the fundamental cause. Therefore, Ānanda, according to your own mind, choose among the six faculties.
If the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sensory objects will naturally cease. When all delusions are extinguished, what need is there to wait for the unreal to vanish?"
This causes one to rely on supramundane right wisdom to discern the fundamental causes of the faculties and fetters, thereby liberating them.

If one attains right wisdom, not only can one know the fundamental causes of the faculties and fetters, but even the myriad species throughout the sands of worlds will all have their origins fully understood.
"Ānanda, I now ask you: these six knots in this *karpāsa* cloth appear before you; could they all be untied simultaneously? No, World-Honored One.
These knots were originally tied one after another; today they must be untied in that same sequence.
Although the six knots share the same substance, the knots themselves did not arise at the same time. Therefore, when they are untied, how could they be removed all at once?"
This demonstrates that the six faculties cannot be liberated all at once, but must proceed through their proper sequence.
The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense-faculties is likewise so. When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation from phenomena (*dharma-vimukti*). Once liberated from phenomena, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise; this is called the Bodhisattva’s [progression] from the three..."
Through this samādhi, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
One realizes that all fetters of affliction (*kleśa*) arise from attachment to a self; thus, by being unattached to a self, one leaves behind the obstacle of afflictions.

This is the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). One realizes that all fetters of the knowable (*jñeya*) arise from attachment to phenomena (*dharma*); thus, by being unattached to phenomena, one leaves behind the obstacle of the knowable.

This is the attainment of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), termed "liberation through phenomena. When both person and phenomena are simultaneously liberated, this is termed "universal emptiness" (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*).

Yet even universal emptiness is extinguished; when the mind has nothing further to arise, one emerges from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At the outset, Avalokiteśvara, within the faculty of hearing, entered the current and lost the objects of perception. The two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly ceased to arise; thus he first attained liberation from the person.
It is emptiness. Thus it gradually increases until that which hears and that which is heard are both exhausted. When hearing is exhausted, one does not dwell therein;

when that which perceives and that which is perceived are empty, one achieves liberation through the Dharma. When the awareness of emptiness is perfectly fulfilled, that which empties and the emptiness itself are extinguished; this is the non-arising of all that is empty.

When arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one; this is the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). △ Second, the essential method for entering the Perfect [Vehicle], in two parts:
first, the restatement of the request.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, attained perfect clarity and penetration through wisdom and were freed from all doubt. At that time—
With palms joined, they prostrated at his feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear;

we have attained a sense of unimpeded ease. Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' perishing, we have not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration, World-Honored One."

We have drifted and wandered in exile, left orphaned and exposed for accumulated kalpas. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated becoming fellow members of the Buddha’s celestial kin?

We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk suddenly encountering a compassionate mother. If, through this meeting, the Way is realized, the secret words we receive will be identical to our original awakening.

"In that case, there would be no difference between this and not having heard it at all. I pray you will deign to show great compassion and bestow upon me the secret adornment, fulfilling the Tathāgata’s final instruction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and withdrew to conceal his inner intent, hoping for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
The perfect penetration of awakened wisdom resides within the single mind. Having already received your instruction, my body and mind have become luminously clear;
yet, as for the fundamental root of perfect penetration that merges with all phenomena, I have not yet fully mastered it, and thus I hope for the Buddha’s secret transmission.
"Secret words" refers to the words that clarify and manifest awakened wisdom. "Secret Adornment" refers to the essential mystery of the fundamental root of perfect penetration. Awakened Wisdom.
"Perfect Penetration (Yuantong). It is inherently possessed by me; therefore, although it was restored through the secret words, it remains identical to my original awakening.
Had the secret adornment not been revealed, it would have been no different from never having heard it at all; thus, I sought a separate instruction.

The twenty-five sages each awakened to perfect penetration within the faculties, objects, and the seven elements. This shows that the fundamental root is darkly interfused with all phenomena. The Buddha did not manifest [this]..."

It is said that while the teaching is expounded through the assembly, this is called "mysterious transmission" (*mingshou*). To withdraw and conceal the secret mechanism is precisely what is meant by "stopping discursive thought and concentrating the mind.
Part Two: Extensive Demonstration, in four sections. First, the general exhortation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great bodhisattvas and the great arhats who had exhausted their outflows within the assembly:
"You bodhisattvas and arhats, having been born into my Dharma and attained the state of no-more-learning, I now question you."

At the initial arousal of the mind, one awakens to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). Which among these serves as the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), and by what skillful means does one enter *samādhi*?
The twenty-five gates of perfect penetration consist precisely of the eighteen realms and the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Since the seven great elements are themselves derived from the eighteen realms, they are not mentioned separately here. Now, the myriad phenomena of the faculties and their objects are entirely subsumed within these eighteen realms and seven great elements; therefore—

This has been set forth in detail, desiring to enable the practitioner—amidst the various phenomena of the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world—to attain true, perfect penetration at all times, whether in moments of distress or leisure, without the slightest obstruction.
△ Second, the detailed explanation has five parts. First, the six sense objects through which one attains awakening, with six sub-sections.
First, the sense object of sound.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“While we were in the Deer Park and at the Kukkuṭārāma, we witnessed the Tathāgata first attain the Way. Through the Buddha’s voice, we realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, ‘I am the first to have attained understanding,’ the Tathāgata confirmed me by naming me Ajñāta. Thus spoke the Wondrous Voice.
"Secret and Perfectly Round. I attained Arhatship through sound. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme.
Because Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya attained perfect enlightenment through sound, it is called "Mysterious Sound, Secret and Perfectly Round. As stated below: "Mysterious Form, Secret and Perfectly Round."

The subtle fragrance is dense and perfect; because of the flavor, awareness becomes luminous. The subtle touch proclaims clarity, and the subtle Dharma opens up illumination. The meaning of the text is the same as this.
Regarding the twenty-five gates, the fact that the sense-object of sound is listed first indicates that it was the primary teaching-body of this region.
The Kukkutārāma was built by King Aśoka to welcome the Buddha. △ Second, the sense-object of form.
Upāliṣada immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I too, upon observing the Buddha's initial attainment of enlightenment, contemplated the mark of impurity and gave rise to great revulsion. I realized that the nature of all forms arises from impurity;
that white bones and subtle dust return to emptiness; and that both emptiness and form are non-dual, thereby attaining the path of no-more-learning. May the Tathāgata grant me his seal of approval."
"My name is Niṣadha. Once all coarse forms have been exhausted, the wondrous form becomes subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through the characteristic of form.
When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of form is supreme."

Pāṇiśata (the "Hand-Grasper"). This refers to the nature of the sense-object of odor; it derives its name from awakening to understanding through odors. In the past, this person had much greed and desire.

The Buddha instructed him to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). By contemplating this physical body as being entirely empty and insubstantial, he attained perfect enlightenment through the medium of form.
△ Third, the sense-object of fragrance.
The youth Gandhahastin immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to carefully contemplate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena. At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting.
I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. I contemplated this scent and perceived that it was neither wood nor space."
It was neither smoke nor fire; it departed without attachment and arrived from nowhere. By this, my conceptual mind dissolved and I realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).

The Tathāgata conferred upon me the name "Incense Purity" (*Gandhavimala*). Dusty vapors suddenly vanished, and wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive. Through this Incense Purity, I attained Arhatship.
When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, Incense Purity is supreme.

He surveyed all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and, through the cause of the Perfected Incense, attained the stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*); thus he was named "The Youth. Regarding his "taking leave of the Buddha to dwell in seclusion":

he sat in quietude (*yansuo*) to obscure his traces, purifying his mind to engage in contemplation. Since both wood and smoke are non-existent, and coming and going do not exist, the mind has no object of perception (*ālambana*).
Thus, by means of this, his mental activity dissolved and he manifested the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*); because the dust-like vapors were extinguished.
This refers to the subtle fragrance being dense and perfect. △ Fourth, regarding the sense-object of taste:
the two Dharma-Princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, along with five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since beginningless kalpas, I have served as a skilled physician for the world.
With my own tongue, I have tasted the herbs, trees, metals, and stones of this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand.
Thus I thoroughly know their tastes—bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—as well as their various combinations, natural properties, transformations, and whether they are cold or hot."
Whether they were poisonous or non-poisonous, he was able to know them all completely. He served the Tathāgata and thoroughly understood that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent;
it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor is it separate from the body and mind. By discerning the causes of taste, he attained awakening.
The Buddha-Tathāgata conferred upon him and his brother the names of the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, and they now serve as Dharma princes within this assembly.

By means of the clarity of the sense of taste, one ascends to the stage of a Bodhisattva. When the Buddha inquired about the perfect penetration [of the senses], I testified that the cause of taste is supreme.

Having perfected the merit of skillful salvation, one is worthy to succeed to the rank of a Buddha and is named a Dharma Prince (*dharmaputra*). Having served as a physician for vast eons, one has always been skilled at saving people.
As for what is called "discerning the cause of taste," it means to thoroughly understand the nature of taste and thereby realize that it is neither empty nor existent.
The "perfect cause that transcends [the specific sense objects]" refers to the fundamental root of universal penetration; it does not mean the cause by which one attains awakening.
The previous mention of the cause of form and the subsequent mention of the causes of water and phenomena are all the same as this. △ Five: The Sense Object of Touch.
Bhadrapāla and his sixteen companions, the bodhisattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life. Once, during the time for bathing the Sangha, we entered the bathhouse according to custom;
suddenly we realized the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes the body, yet in between these two, there is perfect stillness."

I attained the state of non-existence; my past habits were never forgotten, continuing until the present time when I left the household life under the Buddha and attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).
That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla. Through the manifestation of wondrous touch, I dwell as a son of the Buddha. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, [this was my response].
As I have realized it, contact (*sparśa*) is the supreme cause.
Bhadrapāla—also known as Bhadrapāla—whether washing away the dust, washing the body, or within both the dust and the body, there is nothing at all to be attained;
for all are false contacts and false perceptions. Thus, by attaining non-existence, the wondrous contact is proclaimed and clarified, and one becomes a Buddha in truth.
Son, this is called the "Abode of the Buddha-Son. Because he is well able to guard [the mind], causing delusions not to arise and causing awakening not to waver, he is named Bhadrapāla.
△ Sixth, the objects of the mental faculty (dharmaviṣaya).
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light, and the others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa."

I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice it. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics, lit lamps to maintain the light, and applied purple-gold leaf to the Buddha’s images.
From that time forth, in life after life and birth after birth, my body has always been perfectly full and a mass of purple-gold light.
These bhikṣuṇīs of Purple-Gold Light and the others were my kinsmen; we all resolved our minds for enlightenment at the same time.

I contemplate how the six sense-objects in the world are subject to decay and transformation; by cultivating cessation through emptiness and stillness alone, my body and mind can pass hundreds of thousands of kalpas as if it were the snapping of a finger.
Through the dharma of emptiness, I have attained arhatship. The World-Honored One has declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta.
The sublime Dharma has been clarified for me, extinguishing all outflows. Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, this is what I have realized.
The Dharma-cause is supreme.

Mahākāśyapa, the Great Kaśyapa of Radiant Light, possessed a body of golden hue whose brilliance eclipsed the sun and moon. By contemplating the transformation of sensory objects (*dharmāyatana*), he realized the emptiness and stillness of all phenomena.

He subsequently cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to extinguish the faculty of mind (*manas*), so that it no longer took sensory objects as its object. Thus he attained [liberation].
Because there is no arising or ceasing, he has transcended hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the time it takes to snap one's fingers. He now awaits Maitreya on Mount Kukkuṭapāda;
it was for this reason that he entered this samādhi. *Dhūta* means "to shake off"; he took this as his name because he was able to shake off the dust of dharmas.
II. Enlightenment through the Six Sense Organs (five parts). 1. The Eye Organ.
Aniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep.
The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying that I was of the same class as beasts. Upon hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself.”
For seven days I did not sleep, and consequently lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One then showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination.
Without relying on my eyes, I perceived the ten directions; their essential reality was transparently clear, as if looking at fruit held in the palm of one's hand.

The Tathāgata certified me as an Arhat. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, according to what I have realized, by turning back the faculty of sight and following its source, this is the foremost method.

Aniruddha—here translated as "Free from Poverty"—was the son of King Śuklodana. He attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which delights in seeing illumination; this is precisely the concentration of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-samādhi*).

Once this concentration is perfected, it manifests as the four great pure forms (*catvāri mahābhūtāni śubharūpāṇi*) originating from half the head. It penetrates all obscurations of darkness and illuminates the great trichiliocosm.
Therefore, it is said that his essence is perfectly true and profoundly luminous. To "revolve the vision and follow the source" means to turn back from delusion and rest in the fundamental.
Truly so. △ Second, the specific designation following the faculty of hearing. Third, the faculty of smell:
Cūḍapanthaka rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am deficient in recitation and retention;
I lack the nature of great learning. Although I first encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the household life, I could not remember even a single verse of the Tathāgata."
"Oṭṭha, for one hundred days, I was able to let go of what came before while grasping at what came after, and let go of what came after while grasping at what came before.

The Buddha, out of compassion for my folly, instructed me to dwell in retreat and regulate the inhalation and exhalation of breath. As I then observed the breath, I scrutinized the subtle moments of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
My mind suddenly opened up and attained great non-obstruction. Eventually, with the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), I became an Arhat and sat upon the Buddha’s seat."

[He attained] the lower [fruit], thereby achieving the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration (*pariṣuddha-mārga*), he replied: "According to what I have realized, by reversing the breath and following emptiness, this is the foremost.
Cūḍapanthaka (translated here as Jìdào, "Successor of the Path") was the bhikṣu who recited the *broom*; in his past lives, he had been stingy with the Dharma.
Their retributive nature was scattered and dull. The Buddha instructed them to count their breaths to collect the mind;

thereby, they realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent through their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. Consequently, they turned back from arising and ceasing, followed the unborn and empty, and attained perfect realization. △ Fourth, the tongue faculty.
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have committed verbal karma;
during past kalpas, I habitually mocked śramaṇas. Consequently, in birth after birth and life after life, I suffered from the affliction of ruminating like an ox.

The Tathāgata has shown me the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor pure mind-ground. Having attained this, I have extinguished the discursive mind and entered samādhi, wherein I contemplate the cognition of flavors."

Neither a substantial entity nor a material object, he should contemplate so as to transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally detached from body and mind, and externally having cast off the world, he distances himself from the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) like a bird escaping from a cage.
Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, his Dharma-eye becomes pure, and he attains the state of an Arhat.

The Tathāgata personally certified him as having attained the path of no-more-learning. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the senses, [Kauṇḍinya] replied: "According to what I have realized, returning the taste and revolving the faculty of cognition—this is the foremost.
Kauṇḍinya (which is translated here as "ox-chewer") was so named because he habitually mocked his past retribution; the Buddha granted him this name to prevent slander.
The rosary causes one to constantly recollect the Buddha; this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Mind-ground.
It can extinguish mental objects and enable entry into right concentration (*samāpatti*). Furthermore, through the teaching of contemplating the tongue-root as it tastes flavors, one enters the Way.

One contemplates that the cognition of the tongue does not arise from its own substance, nor does it exist because of external objects. When delusive conditions are simultaneously severed, it is called attaining the extinction of the mind and entering *samādhi*. [The assembly...]
That sentient beings wander in the cycle of existence and remain within the outflows (*āsrava*) is due to the uninterrupted continuity of mental objects.

By extinguishing the mind and severing these objects, one transcends all outflows and leaves behind the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Not clinging to the flavors of sensory dust and not following deluded cognition—this is called "returning to flavor and revolving cognition.
△ Five: The Body-Faculty (*kāya-indriya*).
Piliṅgavatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I followed the Buddha into the Way.
I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the various things in the world that are not to be enjoyed. While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gates;
I did not notice that a poisonous thorn had pierced my foot on the road, causing my entire body to ache. As I reflected..."
"I understood. I understood this profound suffering. Although the sensation perceived pain, the perception of the pure mind was free from the sensation of pain.
I further reflected: how could there be two simultaneous perceptions within this single body? Before long, as I focused my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty.

Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and I attained Arhatship. I received the personal seal of certification and realized the state of No-more-learning. The Buddha asked about the perfection [of the mind].
"Penetrating. As I have realized, pure awakening that leaves the body behind—this is the foremost.
Pindola Bharadvaja spoke of 'residual habits,' which refers mostly to the habit of conceit (*māna*). 'Unpleasant matters' refers to all things that are suffering.
One contemplates the nature of unpleasant phenomena and encounters unpleasant matters; thereupon, one correctly observes them as such."
There is knowing; therefore, one knows this profound pain. Although the mind that possesses knowing can perceive profound pain, conversely, the pure mind has never experienced the sensation of pain.
Yet, as these two modes of awareness coexist, that awareness is not yet singular. Therefore, one contemplates further and advances until bodily contact is entirely extinguished;
thus, all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted in emptiness, and one knows that both [pain and its perception] are simultaneously stilled.
Therefore, pure awakening transcends the body. △ Sixth, the faculty of mind.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind has attained non-obstruction.
I recall my own births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; even when first in my mother's womb, I immediately knew emptiness and stillness. As...
Thus, even unto the ten directions, space is realized as empty; he also causes sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness.

Having received the Tathāgata’s awakening to the true emptiness of their own nature, they attain Arhatship through the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness. They suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and are sealed as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Liberation through the emptiness of nature is my supreme [attainment]. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, [it was] as follows...
That which I have realized: all marks enter into non-existence; that which is not is exhausted in non-being. Turning the dharmas back to nothingness—this is the foremost.
Subhūti, having understood emptiness throughout vast eons, it is not limited to a single lifetime. Because one realizes the body is empty and still, the mind attains non-obstruction.
Because one penetrates past lives and realizes that objects are empty and still, the ten directions become empty. Thus, one awakens oneself and awakens others.

It also causes sentient beings to realize emptiness; however, this is merely the emptiness realized by the Hīnayāna, wherein the true emptiness of the awakened nature has not yet been fully perfected.

Therefore, by now elucidating the true emptiness of the awakened nature, one is able to suddenly enter the ocean of the wondrous nature of precious luminosity and true emptiness, departing from the views of the two vehicles and attaining the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha.
All characteristics enter into non-existence; both subject and object are exhausted. This is because they are integrated within the ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness.
All conditioned phenomena revolve back to the ultimate non-being; this is because they return to the ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness.
