Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā from the kingdom of Ujjayinī; orally received by Fáng Róng of Qīnghé,
former Grand Master for Rectifying Propriety and concurrently Minister of State Affairs under the Chancellery and Secretariat, and disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling Unveils [This Commentary].
△ Part Three: The Six Consciousnesses Entering Enlightenment. 6. First, Eye-consciousness.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “For kalpas upon kalpas, my mind...”
His vision became pure. Thus, through births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he attained unimpeded mastery upon a single insight into all the various mundane and supramundane transformations.
On the way, he encountered the Kāśyapa brothers following one another; they proclaimed the causes and conditions for awakening to the boundlessness of the mind.
He left the household life under the Buddha, and seeing that the clarity of his awakening was perfect, he attained great fearlessness and achieved [enlightenment].
The Arhat [Mahākausthila] said: "I am the eldest son of the Buddha; born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma.

When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the mind and vision emit light, and when that light reaches its limit, knowledge and vision are perfected. This is the foremost."

The mind sees through the visual consciousness. Because consciousness is pure, all things are clearly and penetratingly perceived. Because the mind is boundless, its vision and awakening are perfectly luminous.

Regarding the statement that "the mind’s vision emits light, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowledge and vision": it is because the mind’s vision brings forth illumination that it universally illumines all phenomena.
Kāśyapa and his brothers refer to Uruvilvākāśyapa and the others; some say they encountered Aśvajit and heard [his teaching].

Verse: That is merely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the Hīnayāna; it is not what is grasped by perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom, and his reputation for sound was preeminent;
therefore, he is called the "eldest son. △ Second, the ear-consciousness.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I have previously served as a Dharma prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct those disciples who possess the roots of bodhisattvas to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, and they derive their names from me. World-Honored One, with my mental hearing, I discern all that sentient beings possess.”

Knowledge and Vision. If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth the realization of Samantabhadra’s practice within their heart, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, all arriving at that place.
Even if their obstructions are so deep they do not yet see me, I will secretly stroke the crown of that person's head, providing protection and consolation to cause them to...

Accomplishment. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I spoke of its fundamental cause: the mind’s hearing brings forth illumination, and through this, discernment becomes sovereign.

This is the foremost. To act so that there is nowhere it does not reach is called "Universal" (Pǔ). To protect those above and benefit those below is called "Worthy" (Xián). Because it is all-pervasive in its protection and benefit, it is [called] "Ordinary" (Fán).
Possessing great faculties and cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva—all these are called the conduct of Samantabhadra.

"The mind hears and the ear-consciousness cognizes" refers to discerning the knowledge and views of sentient beings and thereby selecting and perfecting the conduct of Samantabhadra. △ Third, the nose-consciousness.
Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I first left the household life and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind remained constantly distracted within *samādhi* and I had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The World-Honored One instructed me and Cūḍapanthaka to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose. When I first contemplated it intently, after three weeks...”

One day, I saw the breath entering and exiting my nostrils like smoke. My body and mind became internally luminous, and the world appeared as a vast, hollow void, everywhere pure and transparent like lapis lazuli.
As the appearance of smoke gradually vanished, the breath from my nostrils turned white. My mind opened and my outflows were exhausted;
all inhalations and exhalations transformed into radiance that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions. I attained Arhatship, and the World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain Bodhi.

T'i. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By means of the methods of calming and observation, through long-term cultivation of stillness, illumination was manifested; this illumination became perfected and extinguished outflows. This is the foremost method.
Sundarananda—whose name translates as "Handsome Joy"—was the Buddha's own younger brother. Previously, he relied on counting the breaths according to the sense organs. Therefore...
Gathering the mind: this contemplation relies on consciousness as its white basis; this is why the mind is anchored here.

Respiration arises from wind and fire, which agitate the turbidity of afflictions; its appearance is like smoke. Those who are deluded do not perceive it, but through diligent contemplation one can see it:

when the sixfold intersections of perception ignite the fire, they consume the breath and produce black smoke and purple flames—all of which are manifestations of the turbid afflictions. This pure contemplation then arises.
When clarity arises, turbidity gradually dissipates; thus, the interior becomes bright and the exterior becomes empty, like smoke vanishing to become white.
Upon the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), there are no further afflictions; because the inner luminosity emits radiance, the inhalation and exhalation are transformed into light.

"The dissipation of the message" refers to the smoke vanishing to become white; "the extinction of the outflows" refers to the opening of the mind and the exhaustion of the outflows. All of this proceeds from the breath through the nose.
This is the elucidation. △ Fourth, the tongue-consciousness.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Since the distant past, my eloquence has been unimpeded. I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness, profoundly penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Thus, even regarding the secret dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I am able to reveal them subtly and exquisitely amidst the great assembly, attaining fearlessness.
The World-Honored One knew that I possessed great eloquence; He instructed me with the wheel of sound to propagate [the Dharma].

In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted the Buddha in turning the wheel. By means of this lion’s roar, I attained arhatship. The World-Honored One certified that my preaching of the Dharma was unsurpassed.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied that by means of the sound of the Dharma, I subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows; this is the foremost method.

The cause for being foremost in preaching the Dharma and possessing unimpeded eloquence is such that the subduing of demons and the extinction of outflows are both due to the power of the tongue-consciousness.
Regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of suffering and emptiness: all phenomena in the world are impermanent, all are suffering, and all are empty.
Yet, within them there exists that which is truly eternal, neither suffering nor empty—such as the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*. This is precisely the true reality.
Through the three wheels of body, speech, and mind, the Buddha responds to sentient beings without obstruction; his vocal resonance is the wheel of speech. △

"Upāli, these are the five [factors] of body-consciousness. Then Upāli rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world;
I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; and I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all the māras and establish [the discipline]."
All those non-Buddhists, having liberated themselves from worldly greed and all outflows (*āsrava*), received the Buddha’s teachings and precepts.

Thus, even down to the three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle points—including both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)—they were entirely pure. With body and mind stilled, they became Arhats.
I am the leader among the assembly of Tathāgatas; they have personally sealed my heart, and they uphold the precepts and cultivate the person. Among the multitude...

"I consider this to be supreme. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I began by focusing on the body; once the body attained mastery, I proceeded to focus on the mind, whereby the mind attained thorough penetration.
Thereafter, both body and mind became entirely free-flowing and sharp. This is why I rank it as the first."

Upāli is called *upasthāyaka*, meaning one who attends closely upon the Buddha. The terms "intimate following" (*pratisaṃvidita*) and "intimate observation" (*pratyavekṣā*), up to "having renounced desire to receive the teaching," all clarify the physical consciousness’s reverent reception [of the Dharma].
Regarding the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—there are two hundred and fifty rules for each;
these, when paired with the three aggregates (*triskandha*), constitute three thousand. Furthermore, these three thousand are assigned to the seven branches of body and speech.

The branches further correspond to the four categories of afflictions, forming eighty-four thousand [precepts]. As for "nature and action," these refer to the roots such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;

"prohibitory action" refers to the cessation of faults and transgressions arising from the secondary branches. The precepts serve as the guiding framework for the community, being personally sealed upon my mind—this means they are approved by the assembly.

Regarding the phrase "I take hold of the body, etc.": [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on Buddhist precepts (*śīla*), likely from a Chinese or Japanese scholastic work.]
It is said that by virtue of upholding the precepts, both body and body-consciousness are universally unimpeded. Among those who attained liberation through the Vinaya, Upāli was foremost;
among those who attained liberation within the Saṃgha, Kauṇḍinya was the first. Therefore, in this hall, Kauṇḍinya is placed, and on the altar, Upāli is placed;
each is established according to their original foundation. △ Sixth, the mental consciousness.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first went out on the road to beg for alms, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa—and they proclaimed to me the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions.
Instantly, I gave rise to the resolve for enlightenment and attained great penetration. The Tathāgata then bestowed upon me a kāṣāya robe, which I have worn upon my body."

My hair and beard fell away of their own accord. As I traveled through the ten directions, I attained unimpededness; my spiritual powers were so manifest that they were deemed unsurpassed, and I became an Arhat.
This was not only recognized by the World-Honored One, but all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have praised my spiritual power as perfect, clear, pure, sovereign, and fearless.

When the Buddha asked about the path of perfect penetration, I replied that I achieved it by turning back the turbid flow of consciousness to let forth the light of the mind from its stillness, like clearing a muddy stream.
Having long been pure and translucent, this is the foremost.
The profound meaning of its causal conditions is that it is not a coarse phenomenon of worldly conjunction; rather, it illuminates both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
By means of this, one arouses the mind [of enlightenment] and attains great penetration, with supernormal powers at will. "Whirling the stillness" refers to whirling the mind.
Consciousness is further wondrously profound; thus, it has long been pure and lucid. Its supernormal powers are perfectly bright, and it is pure, tranquil, and sovereign.
△ Fourth, the seven great elements and their realization (7). First, the fire element.
Ucchuṣma, before the Tathāgata, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I constantly recall that in the distant past, many kalpas ago, my nature was characterized by much lust. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja."

It was said that those who indulge excessively in lust become like a mass of fierce fire. This taught me to contemplate everywhere throughout my body—the hundred bones, the four limbs, and all the warm and cold breaths within.
As the divine light coalesced inwardly, it transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
From this point on, all Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained Arhatship and made a great vow.
When the Buddhas attained the Way, I was a powerful warrior who personally subdued the demonic adversaries. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied:

"By clearly observing that the warmth and touch within my body and mind flow through unimpeded, all outflows were extinguished; thus, a great jewel-flame arose, and I ascended to supreme enlightenment."
This is the first. Ucchuṣma means "Fire-Head," which is the Vajra Fire-Head. For those who are excessively lustful, [this fire] is fundamentally provoked by the sensation of warmth;
while alive, it becomes the fire of desire, and at death, it becomes the fire of karma. Because the power of karma increases and blazes intensely, it becomes fierce.
It is a mass of fire. To observe the pervasive warmth everywhere is to cause one to realize that the fire element flows through unimpededly.
Once all obstructions have dissolved, the spiritual fire coalesces within and forms the fire of wisdom, which blazes forth from the crown of the head; therefore, it is called "Fire-Head" (Huotou).
The "Great Jewel Flame" arises; this is the Fire-Light Samādhi. △ Second, the Earth Element:
Bodhisattva Earth-Holder rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall in the past..."
When the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.
I constantly leveled and filled all major roads, ferry crossings, fields, and narrow passes that were improper or obstructed the passage of carts and horses; I also constructed bridges over them.
Or they carry sand and earth; thus they undergo such diligent toil through the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas in the world.
There may be sentient beings who, at a marketplace, require someone to carry their goods; I first carry them for them until they reach their destination, whereupon I set down the goods and depart.
I did not take their payment. During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine. I worked as a porter;
regardless of whether the distance was far or near, I accepted only a single coin. Sometimes carts and oxen became mired in the mud, and I possessed supernatural powers.
To turn his wheel for them and uproot their suffering. At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast.

I leveled the ground at that moment to await the Buddha. Viśvabhū Tathāgata rubbed the crown of my head and said to me, "You must level the ground of the mind; then the ground of the world will all become level.
My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the minute particles of my own body and all the minute particles that constitute the world were identical.
They are equal and without distinction. The self-nature of atoms does not touch one another; even weapons do not come into contact with them.

Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I have realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attained arhatship. Now, having turned my mind, I enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
I have heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the wondrous Lotus Sūtra, the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. I was formerly a witness to these teachings and served as their leader.

When the Buddha questioned me regarding perfect penetration, I observed with clarity that the two objects—the body and the realm—are equal and without distinction; they both come from the Tathāgatagarbha.
When delusions give rise to dust, and the dust is cleared away, wisdom becomes perfect and the Unsurpassed Way is realized; this is the foremost [attainment].
Leveling the treacherous and preventing harm, one saves others and aids the oxen without the notions of "self" or "other.
This manifests the well-leveled mind-ground, which has no high or low. Viśvabhū means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All"; he was also so named because of his level mind.
"Everything is sovereign. "I" refers to the opening of the mind; what follows below is all based on the great perfect enlightenment of the Ground.

The two objects—the body and the realm—originally constitute the Tathāgata-garbha; they arise through false delusion, and therefore do not actually rub against one another. To realize that they are fundamentally false and delusive is to awaken to non-arising.
The ground of the wondrous Lotus Flower Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the Dharma-door of the Buddhas' mind-ground.

When practice is truly perfected and accords with reality, defilement and purity are both forgotten; this is called the "Wondrous Lotus," which transcends the three vehicles and deeply penetrates the one reality.
This is called the stage of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana-bhūmi*). That which is upheld by the Stage of Holding is exhausted herein.
Thus, the body and the realms of sensory objects vanish, and supreme wisdom becomes perfect. △ III. The Greatness of Water.
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Jaladeva. He taught all bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water."

Entering samādhi, I contemplated that the water element within the body is indestructible. Beginning with mucus and saliva, I traced it through the entirety of the bodily fluids, essences, blood, and the major and minor excretions, until the body was completely pervaded; the nature of the water was one and the same.
I saw that the water within my body and the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King lands outside the world were equal and without distinction. At that time, I—
When first accomplishing this contemplation, one sees only the water and has not yet attained the bodiless state.
Once, while a bhikṣu was practicing dhyāna in his room, a disciple of mine peered through the window to observe the room; he saw nothing at all, for the pure water completely filled the entire space.
"A young child, ignorant of anything, picked up a piece of tile or pebble and threw it into the water; it splashed and made a sound, and he looked around and walked away.
After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he was struck by a malevolent spirit. I reflected to myself:"
"I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions of illness. Why has a heartache suddenly arisen today?
Could it be that I am falling away? At that time, the youth came quickly before me and related the aforementioned matter; I then said to him:
"If you see water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris. The youth followed these instructions.
Later, when I emerged from meditative concentration, I saw the water once more, and the tiles and debris were still there exactly as before. I opened the door and removed them.

Afterward, when I emerged from concentration, my physical body was restored to its original state, and I encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing in this manner until I reached the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Penetrations of Mountains and Seas.

Only then did I attain the dissolution of the self-body. My nature became one with the void of the true reality of the fragrant water-oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions; they were non-dual and without distinction.
Now, before the Tathāgata, I have received the name "Childlike Truth" and am enrolled in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way, I say that through the single flavor of the flowing nature of water, I attained the patience of non-arising and fulfilled Bodhi. This is the foremost.
The Moon is the Yin essence of water. In the past, he took the Water Deity as his teacher and practiced the contemplation of water.

Because the nature of water is perfectly luminous, he was named Moonlight. To "practice the water-essence" means to contemplate the nature of the water-essence. Regarding the fact that the nature of water cannot be superseded:

internally there are the bodily fluids and blood, and externally there is the ocean of lands (*kṣetra-sāgara*). Although the manifestations of water differ, their nature does not conflict with one another. This is the cause.

The water represents the realization of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). "Floating Banner King Realm" (*Uḍaka-dhvaja-rāja-kṣetra*) is the general designation for all the fragrant oceans beyond the world-systems.
"At that time, my physical body returned to its original state" describes the conditions under which the visualization was performed. I saw only the water;
this indicates that while I was focused on a single visualization, I had not yet integrated the four great elements, and therefore I had not yet attained the bodiless state. Śāriputra, at that time—

On the banks of the Ganges River, he entered samādhi and was seized by a malevolent spirit; upon emerging from samādhi, his head ached because he had not yet attained the state of being "without body.
It was only when the Moonlight King attained sovereign mastery over the elements of earth and water that he achieved wondrous, perfect penetration.
Upon reaching this stage, he then dissolved the four great elements, and thus finally attained the state of being without body, while his nature—
This accords with the True Emptiness. Initially, it was simply because the nature of water flows as a single taste.
Master Shui Guan of Mianzhu County in Hanzhou was like Yueguang in his traces. When Chan Master Chou entered the fire-light samādhi, his room seemed to be ablaze;
this is also of that same category. △ Fourth, the Wind Element.
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after the passage of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Amitaghoṣa.

He revealed to us the wondrous clarity of the Bodhisattvas' fundamental enlightenment, teaching that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of the wind of false conditions. At that time, I...
At that time, I observed the establishment of the realms, observed the movement of the world, observed the movement and stillness of the body, and observed the movement and thoughts of the mind.
All movements were non-dual and equal, without distinction. I then realized the nature of these manifold movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
The deluded sentient beings, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, are all equally illusory. This extends even to the three thousand [great thousandfold worlds].

All sentient beings within the single world-system of the great trichiliocosm were like a hundred mosquitoes contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in disorder, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.
Not long after encountering the Buddha, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

At that moment, their minds opened, and they beheld the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction; they became Dharma-princes, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions with both body and mind.

"Radiant and penetrating, unimpeded. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I realized the Bodhicitta by observing that the power of wind has no basis, thereby entering samādhi.
I have united with the Buddhas of the ten directions to transmit this single wondrous mind; this is the foremost."

By means of the wind-element, he attained great enlightenment and perfection; his body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction, and he was named Vairocana-prabhāsa (Liu-li-guang) Buddha of Immeasurable Sound.

He also relied upon the wind-element to instruct the bodhisattvas, causing them to know that fundamental awakening is unmoving, while the movements of the physical realm are all driven by the power of the wind.
Vairocana-prabhāsa, through this, contemplated the realms, contemplated the world, and contemplated the body.
The mind’s shifting, flowing, moving, and ceasing are all solely the power of wind; therefore it is said that all movements are non-dual.
Through this awakening, one realizes that the myriad movements within the great trichiliocosm are all merely frantic toil—like a hundred mosquitoes buzzing within the space of a single inch-square.
Once this frantic toil is understood, one beholds the Buddha of Immovability (Aksobhya). While the east is the source of all movement, the Buddha is named "Immovable."
This is precisely that which is still within movement. Because one can be still within movement, body and mind are without obstruction.
One who transmits this wondrous mind knows that the power of the wind has no basis and that all myriad movements are illusory, thereby personally realizing the unmoving original enlightenment.
△ Five: The Great Emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I and the Tathāgata attained the body of boundlessness under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated the Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.
Furthermore, within my own mind, I manifested a great circular mirror, from within which [emerged] ten..."
The light of various subtle and wondrous jewels flows and pours into all the *dhvajarāja* lands throughout the ten directions, reaching to the very limits of empty space;
it enters within my mirror-like reflection and permeates my body. My body becomes identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction.

My body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust, extensively performing the Buddha-work and attaining great accordance. This great supernormal power arises from my contemplation that the four great elements are—
"Based on this, I observed that the arising and ceasing of false conceptualization and empty space are non-dual; the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical.

By illuminating this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: 'By contemplating the boundlessness of empty space, I entered samādhi.
Its wondrous power is perfectly clear and bright; this is the foremost.'"
Because he has realized emptiness (*śūnyatā*), all that exists within his nature is empty. His body and the ocean of worlds interpenetrate without obstruction;
thus he is named Gaganagañja (Space-Treasury). "Dīpaṃkara" refers to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Regarding the attainment of the "boundless body" under Dīpaṃkara:
the *dharmakāya* is like space, having no limits or boundaries; it can only be realized by relying on the tranquil illumination of the lamp of the mind.

This is the revelation. Regarding those who hold the four precious jewels and so forth: it is because they contemplate that the four great elements have no basis, and through their wondrous power’s perfect luminosity, they clearly perceive that the entire dharma-realm is entirely empty—namely, that space is non-dual and the buddha-lands are fundamentally identical.
Furthermore, regarding those who manifest the great round mirror within their own minds and so forth: this too is due to the four great elements having no basis and their wondrous power...
"Perfectly luminous. Within the heart of the circular cavity, it is internally brilliant and emits light, such that they interpenetrate, harmonize, and encompass one another.
"Dhvaja-rāja-kṣetra" (Crown Banner Land) is the name for a land within the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. △ Sixth, the Great Consciousness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall that in the past, after the passage of atoms of kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness;

yet my mind was weighted by worldly fame, and I delighted in frequenting the houses of the noble clans. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to cultivate the practice of mind-only consciousness.”
In meditative concentration, I entered samādhi. Throughout kalpas past, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with this samādhi;

the desire for worldly fame has ceased and no longer exists. When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*).
Even the entirety of the Tathāgatas’ lands throughout space—whether pure or impure, existent or non-existent—are all my own.

"O World-Honored One, these manifestations are produced by the transformations of the mind. Because I have realized that all is but mind and consciousness, immeasurable Tathāgatas have flowed forth from the nature of consciousness.

I have now received the prediction that I shall succeed the Buddha in his place. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the Dharma], I observed with clarity that the ten directions are but consciousness;

the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, entering the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), far removed from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature)."
The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the foremost.

Maitreya—here translated as "Kindly One" (*Maitreya*)—is so named because his kindness flourishes in this world and his compassion reaches the future kalpas; he takes pity on sentient beings who are deluded regarding consciousness.

Therefore, he manifested traces to illuminate this truth. Those whose minds value worldly fame and delight in frequenting the families of the noble are deluded regarding consciousness and attached to sensory objects;

thus, they look outward and seek in vain. Those who, following the teachings of Dīpaṃkara, cause their minds to suddenly cease their activity have realized that consciousness relies upon wisdom, whereby delusion and falsehood are naturally eliminated.
When the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared, they attained the wondrous perfection; for once delusion and falsehood are gone—
When [delusions] are removed, the lamp of the mind immediately appears. Once the lamp of the mind has appeared, then the myriad objects are wondrously perfected.

Having attained this wondrously perfect samādhi, one realizes that the triple world is mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only. Therefore, all Tathāgatas throughout space are transformations of my own mind;
the purity or defilement of lands is likewise a transformation of my own mind. Thus, immeasurable Buddha-nature is manifested from this. This is...
This means that immeasurable Tathāgatas emerge from it; even those who have attained the stage of a Bodhisattva on the verge of Buddhahood do not depart from this.

Regarding the phrase "the consciousness-mind is perfectly luminous, entering the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature)," etc.: by means of the wondrously perfect consciousness-mind, one realizes true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), no longer becoming deluded by consciousness or chasing after objects with various attachments.
△ Seven: The Greatness of the Sense Organs (*indriya*). Previously referred to as the "Greatness of Seeing," here it is called the "Organs."
As for the "Great" [Assembly]: whereas the previous instance cited one example, this instance cites the general while including the specific.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same class, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named..."
"Immeasurable Light. Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of a kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Surpassing the Light of the Sun and Moon.

That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like this: suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another person who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting."
Thus, these two people may encounter one another or not; they may see each other or not. Yet, the two remember one another, and their mutual remembrance is profound.
In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing. Thus it is with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
He regards all sentient beings with compassion, as a mother remembers her child. If a child runs away and flees, what is the use of the mother’s remembrance?

But if the child remembers the mother as much as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will never be separated or far apart. If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite his name, [the same shall hold true].
In the present and in the future, you will certainly behold the Buddha; you are not far from him. Without relying on expedient means, you will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense, whose body carries a fragrance. This is called the Adornment of Fragrant Light. At my original stage of practice, I...

"By means of the mind that recollects the Buddha, I entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, within this world-system, I gather those who recollect the Buddha and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I made no selection; I simply gathered all six sense-faculties together, maintaining a continuous stream of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining *samādhi*."

This is the foremost. Mahāsthāmaprāpta is also named Amitābha. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "By means of the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all, causing them to leave the three evil realms and attain supreme power;
thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. This now symbolizes the *nien-fo samādhi*, which is able to...
It emits the light of wisdom, causing one to leave behind the sufferings of the three miserable realms; its power is unsurpassed. The Buddha encountered was named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another throughout a single kalpa, the last of whom was named Surpassing Sun and Moon.

This represents that the self-nature Tathāgata of those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha is the immeasurable light of nature when pure mindfulness continues uninterrupted throughout the twelve periods of the day and night.
In the end, he personally manifested an enlightenment that surpasses the sun and moon. The *Contemplation Sūtra* states:

"Now, those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name must not, for even the duration of a finger-snap, think of the five worldly desires; this is called 'binding the mindfulness. If one can do so, remaining entirely free from any intermingling [of other thoughts]," it continues.
Then the immeasurable nature-light will spontaneously manifest. This refers to what was mentioned below: "not relying on expedient means, the mind opens of itself.

The analogy that follows demonstrates that one must fix the mindfulness before attaining resonance; if one does not single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name, then even if one encounters him, it is as if one has not encountered him, and even if one sees him, it is as if one has not seen him.
If one is stained by incense, one is permeated by its fragrance; if one recites the Buddha's name, then...

Because one beholds the Buddha, one is perfumed by the wondrous practice of mindfulness of the Buddha; this is called the adornment of the fragrance of light. As for attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through mindfulness of the Buddha:

it is because pure mindfulness dispels turbid thoughts and correct mindfulness extinguishes perverse perceptions. Once the perverse and turbid are eliminated, the mind and its objects are empty and still, and nothing arises;
this is called the patience of non-arising. In this way, the Buddha-land of one's own nature is purified. Therefore...
This may be used to gather practitioners and lead them toward the same goal.

*Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization Based on the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Ten.
