Zhì (zhílì qiè). Jié (jíyè qiè). Jī (pinyin jī). Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Eleven.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty;
with the assistance of the Śramaṇa Migaśrīka of the country of Udyāna for the oral interpretation;
and [revised] by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, formerly the Right Counselor (Zhengyidafu) and concurrently a member of the Secretariat (Zhongshu).
The Secretariat Director Fang Rong of Qinghe transcribed this, with the monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lotus Monastery in Wenzhong acting as scribe. [Seal] △ Five.
This specifically highlights the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Among all twenty-five methods of perfect penetration, this one is most suited to the needs of the present occasion; therefore—
This is a special designation. The text has three parts. First, the narrative of his original cultivation and realization. Second, the initial narrative of perfect realization.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named..."
Avalokiteśvara, I awakened the bodhicitta before that Buddha. That Buddha taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

"Avalokiteśvara" means the one who observes the sounds and voices of the world; it is a title for one who possesses perfect awakening and perfect response. Regarding the use of the word "observe" (guan) in relation to sound:

One contemplates this with wisdom; it is not heard by the auditory consciousness. What is called "entering the stream and losing the object" can thus be understood as being through contemplation rather than hearing.
That the Buddha whom one takes as teacher is also named Avalokiteśvara (Guanyin) shows that cause and effect correspond, and that the Way is one throughout past and present.
Initially, within hearing, one enters the flow and loses the object of hearing. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.

Thus gradually increasing, hearing and the object of hearing are both exhausted. With the exhaustion of hearing, one does not dwell; with the awakening to what was awakened to, that awakening is empty. When the emptiness of awakening is perfectly complete, it reaches its ultimate fulfillment.
When that which is empty and the emptiness itself are extinguished, and both arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

This explains how Śāriputra entered perfect penetration through the three types of wisdom. Hearing with the ears is called "hearing" (*śruta*); attachment of the mind is called "reflection" (*cintā*);

and the cultivation of habits is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). When these three are perfectly luminous, they are termed the "three wisdoms. To "enter the stream and lose the object" means not to follow [the sensory objects].
Regarding the sense-object of sound: one suddenly enters the stream of the Dharma, yet loses all trace of that entry.

Because the nature of sound is manifested through movement and stillness, once that which is entered has become quiescent, movement and stillness do not arise; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Having thus reached the ear—

Furthermore, fix this in the mind. Like water gradually filling a vessel and like soil being incrementally added, cause both the hearing and the perceived objects to vanish together, so that even the mind that hears reaches a state of non-abiding.
By thus merging with true awakening, one attains the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Once this has taken root in the mind, one returns to it to cultivate practice, enabling both the subject that perceives and the object perceived to merge with wondrous emptiness.

When emptiness and awareness are non-dual, this is called the ultimate perfection. When both the capacity to empty and the object to be emptied no longer stand, this constitutes the path of ultimate exhaustion.
This is the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). Only then does birth-and-death cease as birth-and-death arises;
subject and object are both exhausted, and the essence of true stillness and true cessation, which is perfectly penetrating, manifests before one. This is what is called entering *samādhi*.

To correlate this with the *Awakening of Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, the passage beginning with "entering the flow and losing the object" means that one should distance oneself from illusory and delusive realms. As it says:

This gradual increase and so forth—that is, the mind being like an illusion—is also further transcended. The emptiness of that which perceives and that which is perceived is the further transcendence of the transcendence of illusions.
The cessation of that which is emptied by emptiness is the further transcendence of the transcendence of the transcendence of illusions.
When arising and ceasing have both ceased, one attains that which is nothing to be transcended; this is the elimination of all illusions. Quiescence.
Cessation manifests before one. This is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the clarity appears.
Upon reaching this state, the essence of perfect penetration is perfected. △ Second, the description of the perfect function, in two parts: 1. General summary.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains universal clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of excellence:
first, above, one merges with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Tathāgatas;
second, below, one merges with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as all those beings.

Because the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, neither mundane nor supramundane phenomena can obstruct them; thus, they penetrate with perfect clarity throughout the ten directions of the Dharma-realm.
Precisely because of this perfect penetration, they harmonize seamlessly with all Buddhas above and with all sentient beings below.
Harmonizing with all Buddhas above, they are able to take pity on all things and give rise to compassion, responding to the capacities of beings to bestow happiness—this is the [first] three...
The "Twelve Responsive Manifestations" (shí-èr yīng) must refer to this. Because he harmonizes with all sentient beings below, one knows his compassionate longing;

accordingly, he bestows [benefits] and extracts them from suffering—this is precisely the "Fourteen Fearlessnesses. Part Two: A Detailed Explanation of the Three. First, the Thirty-two Responsive Manifestations.

These manifest bodies within the ten Dharma realms to perfectly respond to the various capacities of sentient beings. When expanded, there are thirty-two; when condensed, they comprise only the four noble classes and the six ordinary realms of existence. These encompass [all beings].
Exhausting all categories, the text has three parts. First, the general summary:
"World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation, which is like an illusion;
and because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become thirty..."
Second, one should enter all lands;
this is the activity of an illusory person, which is fundamentally non-active. Therefore, it is called the "Illusory Samādhi," while later it is called the "Sublime Power of Non-action.
This samādhi is accomplished through the cultivation of the wisdom born of hearing, and thus it cannot be obstructed or destroyed.
It is called "Vajra. Relying upon this samādhi, one manifests transformations according to conditions; all such things are merely like illusions.
△ Second, the detailed enumeration has two parts. First, the four sages have four [sections]. First, the Buddha.
“World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi, advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), and bring their resolute understanding (adhimukti) to full manifestation,
I shall manifest in the form of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.”
Correcting the meditative concentration and attaining the true fruit is called advancing in the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

When both object and wisdom are forgotten and both emotional attachments and intellectual interpretations are extinguished, it is termed the "manifest perfection of supreme resolve" (*adhimukti*). This is how one may attain Buddhahood; therefore, the Buddha-body manifests to preach the Dharma of the fruit.
The Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, seated upon the Flower King Throne, is on the verge of attaining perfect enlightenment;
yet he must still receive specific teachings from another Buddha to sever the final ignorance before finally realizing the Way of Buddhahood. △ Second, the Pratyekabuddhas.
If there are those in training who possess tranquil, wondrous clarity and for whom the supreme and subtle manifests its perfection,
I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
There are those who are śrāvakas still in training (*śaikṣa*). The Pratyekabuddhas are also called "Rhinoceros-like" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*), a metaphor for their solitude.
They appear in worlds where no Buddha exists; by observing the transformation of phenomena, they personally realize non-arising (*anutpāda*) and are thus termed "Solitary Realizers.

Delighting in solitary tranquility and seeking spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), they are called "Tranquil and Sublime Clarity. Because they can wondrously manifest all things through the clarity of their own nature, they are so named.
Exquisite and sublime. △ Third, the Pratyekabuddhas:

If there are those in training who have severed the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance, the sublime nature is fully manifested, I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
One knows that the supreme nature is obscured by the twelve links of dependent origination; therefore, one severs them therein.

From the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, the conditions are severed and the nature manifests. Because the nature manifests through the severing of conditions, it is called the "supreme nature resulting from the severance of conditions.
By contemplating conditions to awaken to the Way, it is named the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. △ Fourth, the Śrāvaka.
If there are those in training who have realized the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, enter cessation through the path of cultivation, and manifest the perfection of the supreme nature,
I appear before them in the form of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

To sever the coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) beneath the Four Truths is called "attaining the emptiness of the Four Truths. By relying on the cultivation of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one realizes the fruit of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*);

this is called "entering cessation through the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*). Because this has not yet been able to subtly discern phenomena and realize emptiness-nature (*śūnyatā*) independently, it is said that "the supreme nature manifests in its fullness.

The reason the four classes of noble ones (*ārya*) do not include the Bodhisattvas here is that they are already subsumed within the stage of Buddhahood. Part Two: The Six Classes of Ordinary Beings (Three Sections).
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds clearly so as not to transgress against the dust of desire, and who wish for their bodies to be pure,
I will manifest before them in the form of a Brahma King and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to attain liberation. If there are sentient beings who desire to become a Lord of Heaven...
He presides over the various devas. Before him, I manifest in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve accomplishment.
Because the Brahmā heavens transcend the realm of desire, his mind is able to attain clear awakening; he does not transgress against the dust of desire, and his physical faculties are pure.
They shall immediately attain rebirth there. Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, presiding over the thirty-three heavens.

If there are sentient beings who wish to travel freely through the ten directions with their bodies, I will manifest before them in the body of a Vaśavartin Deva and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal. If there are sentient beings who wish to fly through the void with their bodies at will...
"Emptiness. Before him, I manifested the body of Maheśvara and preached the Dharma for him, enabling him to achieve success and roam with mastery;

this is called Maheśvara, which refers to the summit of the Desire Realm (Kāmadhātu), namely Paranirmita-vaśavartin. Flying through the void is called Mahāmaheśvara, which refers to the summit of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu), namely Maheśvara.
First the Brahmā King was mentioned; now, reaching this point, it refers to [the deities] of the Desire Realm itself."

Regarding the celestial realms: from the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), my intent encompasses the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as well, to demonstrate that there is no land where I do not appear.

If there are sentient beings who desire to govern spirits and deities and protect their lands, I manifest before them in the body of a Great Celestial General (*mahādevasenāpati*) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success. If there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and provide protection...
For those sentient beings, I manifest before them in the form of a Caturmahārāja and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in the celestial palaces and to command ghosts and spirits,
I manifest before them in the form of a prince of the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
The former [section] cited the orthodox lineage; this cites the ministers and assistants. The Heavenly General serves as the supreme general of Śakra-devendra, commanding ghosts and spirits.
The Four Heavenly Kings are ministers to Śakra-devendra and command the world. The Princes of the Four Heavens—such as Nāṭa and his peers—are able to drive away ghosts and spirits.
△ Second, three types: first, kings, ministers, scholars, and commoners.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being kings of men, I manifest before them in the body of a king of men and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who love to be leaders of clans and are esteemed by the world, I manifest before them in the body of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal. If there are sentient beings who love to discuss names and terminology...
Dwelling in purity, I manifest before them in the form of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve perfection.

From the Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*) down to the minor kings, all are rulers of men. The "minor kings" (*kṣullakarāja*) are the small princes scattered throughout the world as numerous as grains of millet.
A householder possesses ten virtues, namely: noble lineage, high rank, great wealth, and majesty... [text continues]

He is fierce in resolve, profound in wisdom, advanced in years, pure in conduct, and complete in ritual propriety. Thus he is praised by those above and revered by those below; for this reason, he is the leader of the clan, esteemed by the world.
To "live in seclusion" means to seek one's aspirations; to "practice righteousness" means to realize the Way. He is called a *ju-shi* (lay practitioner);
"layman" (*ju-shi*) refers to elegant and refined speech.

If there are sentient beings who love governing territories and administering cities and districts, I appear before them in the form of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goals.
If there are sentient beings who love various arts and techniques for self-protection and maintenance, [I appear before them...]
I manifested before him in the body of a Brahmin and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve accomplishment and discernment.

Calculating the conjunctions and harmonies, as well as divining signs and tracking the movements of celestial bodies to determine their fullness or emptiness—all these are the arts of numerology and technique. △ Second, entering the path among the fourfold assembly.

If there is a man who delights in study, leaves the household life, and upholds the various precepts, I will manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve accomplishment.
If there is a woman who delights in study, leaves the household life, and observes the various prohibitions and precepts, [I shall likewise manifest before her].
Before them, I manifest in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I manifest before him in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve accomplishment.
If there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I manifest before her in the body of an upāsikā and...
He preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
"Precepts" refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus; for bhikṣuṇīs, they are double that number.

Regarding what is called "vinaya" and "prohibitions," these refer simply to the constant rules maintained by bhikṣus; however, for bhikṣuṇīs, the prohibitions are even more detailed and restrictive. As for upāsakas and upāsikās... [text ends]
The five precepts for male and female lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*) who draw near to the Buddha’s Dharma are: abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants.

These constitute the foundation of all precepts, the pivot of the myriad virtues, and the true essence of the fivefold division. The former four are capable of encompassing morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation;
the latter one is capable of encompassing the knowledge and vision of liberation. This is because it causes the murky to become luminous. △ Three: The Principal [Precept].
Regarding the stage of the Female Youthful Truth:
if there are women who establish themselves through internal governance to cultivate their households and states, I shall manifest before them in the form of a queen,
a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.
The Son of Heaven, the Three Dukes, and the Nine Ministers preside over external affairs; the Three Heir Apparents and the Nine Consorts preside over internal affairs.

Thus they cultivate and govern the family and the state. The "Female Ruler" refers to the Empresses and Consorts. The "Ennobled Ladies" (Mingfu) are the wives of the Dukes and Marquises who have received imperial investiture.
For example, Ban Huaiyi served as the Tutor to the Empress Dowager and was titled "Dajia" (Great Lady).
If there are sentient beings whose male organs are intact, I manifest before them in the body of a young man and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve fulfillment. If there are virgins who delight in remaining chaste and do not seek sexual violation,
I manifest before them in the body of a young woman and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
△ Third, the divine manifestations:
If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial status, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga status, I manifest a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own kind, I manifest before them in the form of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.

If there are gandharvas who wish to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success. If there are asuras who wish to be liberated from their kind, I [manifest before them...]
To those who manifest as asuras, I appear before them in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.
To those kinnaras who desire liberation from their own kind, I appear before them in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.
To those mahoragas who desire liberation from their own kind, I appear before them in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma...

I preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. If there are sentient beings who delight in being humans or who aspire to be humans, I manifest in human form and preach the Dharma for them, bringing them to fulfillment.

If there are non-human beings—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—who delight in crossing over their own kind, I manifest my body before each of them and preach the Dharma, bringing them to fulfillment.

These are the classes of the eight divisions of devas and nāgas. Regarding those who "delight in being human" and those who "cultivate humanity": these types resemble humans but are not actually human; thus, they take birth in the human realm.

As for the various non-humans (*amanuṣya*), this refers to those with form or without form, those with perception or without perception—namely, the classes of *xiujiu* (spirits of portents), *jingming* (luminous spirits), *kongsan* (empty-dispersing spirits), and *xiaochen* (dissolving-sinking spirits).
The reason the six ordinary realms do not specifically mention hell-beings, ghosts, and animals here is that these types... [text ends]
While they are still submerged in profound darkness and have not yet been able to hear the Dharma, he uses the power of bestowing fearlessness to pull them out. △ Third, the conclusion:

This is called the thirty-two wondrously pure responsive bodies that enter into lands; all are accomplished with mastery through the effortless, wondrous power of the cultivation of hearing and the permeation of hearing by means of samādhi.

His traces manifest as being of the same class [as ordinary beings], yet his mind is severed from craving and views; this is called "wondrous purity. Based on non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), he gives rise to great spiritual power;
this is called "wondrous power. Being non-active and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he responds universally according to conditions;
this is called "accomplishment of mastery. △ Twenty-fourth: The Three Fearlessnesses (1) General Summary.
World-Honored One, by means of the effortless and wondrous power of the Vajra Samādhi cultivated through hearing and practicing what I have heard,
and because I share in the same compassion and longing as all sentient beings of the ten directions and three periods of time throughout the six realms,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness within my body and mind.
Because I did not look back at my own ears, they were able to escape suffering; because I knew how to turn my faculty back upon itself, they were able to avoid being burned.
Therefore, it is said that they have attained the virtue of fearlessness regarding my body and mind. II. Detailed Enumeration (in three parts). A.
Escape from the Seven External Karmas. 1. Escape from manifold sufferings.
First, because I do not observe by means of an observing subject, those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions who contemplate my voice shall immediately attain liberation.
"Not observing the ear" means not following after the cognitions and views that arise from the objects of hearing.
"Observing with observation" refers to turning back the inverted faculty of hearing to reflect upon one's own nature. When cognitions and views do not arise, there is nothing false;
when reflecting upon one's own nature, all is truly quiescent, and no further suffering or affliction can be found. This is true observation; this is pure observation.
The contemplation of great wisdom can destroy the darkness of ignorance and subdue calamities;
thus, it causes suffering sentient beings to receive my true contemplation and immediately attain liberation. Part Two: Deliverance from the Three Calamities.
Second, by the reversal of knowledge and vision, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.
Third, by the reversal of observation and hearing, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they are adrift upon a great flood of water, the water cannot drown them.
The four great elements of the internal and external realms are constantly interacting and influencing one another. Vision and cognition belong to fire; hearing and listening belong to water.

Thus, when the karma of vision interacts, one sees fierce flames; when the karma of hearing interacts, one sees surging waves. Now, if one knows that vision is revolved back [to its source], there is no karma of vision;
if one contemplates that hearing is revolved back, there is no karma of hearing. Therefore, water and fire cannot burn or drown them. Regarding this:
"Listening to words and observing" means observing through sounds and words. "Drifting on a great flood" implies that the calamity of wind is also included.
△ Third, liberation from the harm of ghosts:

Fourth, by severing and extinguishing delusive thoughts, one’s mind becomes free from killing and harming, causing all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts where the ghosts do not [harm them].
It can cause harm.
From this point up to the matter of being released from prison and freed from enmity, all is due to the six sense faculties being extinguished and restored, such that the mind has nothing to summon;
therefore, external objects cannot act upon it. △ Fourth, liberation from physical execution.
Fifth is the permeation of hearing. When the six sense-faculties are perfected through this hearing, they are transformed until they function identically to the faculty of hearing.

This enables sentient beings who are on the verge of being harmed by weapons that sever them limb from limb to perceive those weapons as if they were merely cutting through water or blowing against light; their nature remains unshakable.
One uses the wisdom derived from hearing to permeate the faculty of hearing, thereby perfecting it. Once a single faculty is perfected, the six faculties are all transformed;

they become identical to the act of hearing sound, free from further physical obstructions. Thus, it is like cutting through water or blowing across light. △ Fifth, liberation from the obscure and the heterodox.
Sixth is the brilliant clarity of the permeation of hearing. When this clarity pervades the Dharma-realm, the nature of all dark obscurations cannot remain intact;
it causes yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, pūtanas, and other such beings to be unable to see with their eyes even when they draw near its side.
The brilliance of the permeation of hearing scatters that profound darkness; therefore, one cannot see. △ Sixth, liberation from imprisonment:
Seventh, when the nature of sound is completely eliminated and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back inward, one leaves behind all sensory dusts and delusions.
This enables sentient beings such that they cannot be bound by shackles or fetters.

When the nature of sound is completely dissolved, there is nothing within to which one is bound. When hearing is observed and turned back into itself, there is nothing without to which one is entangled.
Thus, shackles and locks are shed of their own accord. △ Seven: Liberation from Enemies and Robbers.
Eighth, by extinguishing sound and perfecting hearing, one universally generates the power of compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths unrobbed by thieves.
When sound and hearing stand as two, then self and others become adversaries; when sound is extinguished and hearing is perfected, then there is no dependence on internal or external. Therefore:

It can universally generate the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), such that there are no longer any enemies. △ Second, liberation from internal karma has three parts. First, liberation from desire:
Ninth, by permeating hearing and departing from sensory objects, one is not plundered by forms; this can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.
Sentient beings are plundered by forms because their desires habitually conjoin with sensory objects; thus they are "plundered by form.

If one can use the Vajra Samādhi to permeate the faculty of hearing so as to perfect its inherent nature, one will then be able to leave sensory objects behind. When the nature is perfected, desire and love dry up;

when one leaves sensory objects behind, the sense organs and their objects no longer meet. Therefore, even if there are seductive forms, they cannot plunder or disturb the mind. 2. Liberation from Hatred.
Tenth, its pure sound is free from defilement; the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, such that there is neither subject nor object.
It can cause all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to be free from all hatred.

Hatred arises from the violation of one's emotions and is produced in relation to external objects. When the nature of sound is pure and free from delusory dust, it is perfectly interfused and without contradiction.
Being without subject and object, and without contradiction or opposition, one does not become angry. △ Third, liberation from ignorance.
Eleventh is the "Dust-Dispelling Revolving Radiance. The body and mind of the dharma-realm are like lapis lazuli, transparently penetrating and unobstructed.
It enables all those with dull natures and hindrances, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of delusion.
Delusion arises from being obscured by false objects and shrouded by ignorance. When these objects are dissolved, there is no longer obscuration;

when illumination is turned inward, there is no longer concealment. Thus, the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind become crystalline, translucent, and penetrating, departing from the darkness of delusion.
The obstruction of one's nature is precisely this delusion. *Adīnava* means "lacking a virtuous mind. There are ten internal karmas that destroy and annihilate the Dharma.

In the physical body, it is only lust, anger, and ignorance that are most extreme; therefore, these three are cited to include all others. △ Third, showing the response of merit: Twelfth, "fusing the form and returning to hearing.
Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one enters into the mundane world without destroying the worlds.

One is able to pervade the ten directions, making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, and at the side of each Buddha, one acts as a Prince of the Dharma (*dharmarāja-putra*). One is able to...
It causes those beings within the Dharma-realm who are childless and desire a son to give birth to a son of merit and wisdom.
When form is dissolved, obstruction ceases; when it is further heard, its nature is revealed as true. Thus, though it enters the mundane world, it remains unmoving and indestructible.

It can pervade the ten directions, making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, receiving and upholding their teachings, and becoming a son of the Dharma for each, thereby making offerings to the Buddhas.

He possesses sufficient merit and, having received the Dharma, possesses sufficient wisdom. Thus he succeeds to the Dharma King and possesses the way of a man; therefore, he is able to respond to their requests.

Thirteenth: his six sense faculties are perfectly penetrating and clearly illumined without duality, encompassing the realms of the ten directions, and establishing the great perfect mirror-like emptiness.
The Tathāgatagarbha reverently receives and upholds the secret Dharma-gates of the dust-mote-like Tathāgatas of the ten directions without fail.
It can cause those childless sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who desire daughters to give birth to virtuous women who are upright, endowed with merit, gentle and compliant,
beloved and respected by all, and possessed of auspicious marks.
Because it is perfect, it is non-dual; because it is pervasive, it encompasses the realms (*dhātu*). Its luminous illumination is the substance of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*);
its encompassing of the realms is the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Possessing these qualities, it is able to accord with and follow the Dharma-gates, receiving and accepting them without error.
To "accord and follow" is the gentle virtue of the Earthly Principle (*kūn-yi*); to "receive and accept" is the capable duty of the inner chambers. Thus, she possesses the nature of a woman.
Because he follows the Way, he is able to respond to their needs.

Fourteenth: within this trichiliocosm, across ten billion suns and moons, there are currently sixty-two *koṭis* of *Gaṅgā*-sands of Dharma Princes dwelling in the world who cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings. Following...
To accord with sentient beings, the skillful means and wisdoms differ for each.
First, many Buddhas are mentioned; next, much merit is revealed. One world-system has one sun and moon;
ten billion suns and moons refer to ten billion world-systems.

From the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, I have developed this wondrous faculty of the ear. Thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

I can cause sentient beings who uphold my name to possess a merit equal and no different from those who uphold the names of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Dharma-Princes; O World-Honored One, my single name alone [is thus efficacious].

My title is no different from those many other names. Because I have cultivated and attained true perfect penetration (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), this fundamental root of perfect penetration wondrously encompasses the Dharma-realm; the one and the many are equal, and self and others are non-dual.
Therefore, by holding my name, one’s merit shall be equal to theirs. You should know that when one cultivates and attains true perfect penetration, then one body becomes many bodies.
In other realms and in this world, there is a single merit and a single name, each perfectly pervasive, without further boundaries or distinctions.
△ Second, the conclusion:
This is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness; it provides the fullness of merit for all sentient beings.
△ Section 34: The Two Inconceivables. 1. General Summary.

"World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable, unconditioned, and wondrous virtues."
He manifests a multitude of forms and recites each of the mantras to gather and transform sentient beings, perfectly responding to their needs.
This principle arises from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and his spiritual response is unfathomable; thus, he is named "Inconceivable and Uncreated Sublime Virtue" (*acintyānabhisaṃskāra-guṇa*).

Now, while he had previously manifested forms in response to requests, this alone is specifically termed "inconceivable" because the former was a brief manifestation, whereas this further clarifies the matter in depth. As it is said:
Within a single body, he manifests eighty thousand heads and arms; this is truly beyond the reach of thought or calculation. △ Second, the detailed enumeration has four parts.
First, the manifestation of his form:

"First, because I initially attained the wondrous and subtle mind of hearing, the essence of the mind abandoned hearing, such that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could not [function as before]."

By separating [the defilements], one attains a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening. Therefore, I am able to manifest numerous wondrous forms and can proclaim boundless secret and divine mantras.

From the truly wondrous and perfect, one again gives rise to the truly wondrous, which is called the "wondrously wondrous hearing-mind. By turning back the hearing, one is liberated from sound and returns alone to the true source;
this is called the "essence of mind leaving behind hearing. Because one has attained this wondrous state of leaving behind hearing, the various sensory objects do not create obstructions;
with a single awakening that is perfectly interfused, one manifests responses without impediment. The phrase "initially attaining" refers to the original cause.
Among them, some manifest with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads;
and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, or eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads.
They may have two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, or up to twenty-two arms.
Fourteen. Thus, up to one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, or eighty-four thousand *mudrā*-arms;

two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, or nine eyes, thus up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—whether manifesting as compassion or majesty, as meditative concentration or wisdom—he provides protection and salvation.
Sentient beings attain great mastery.
The head represents the totality of the six faculties; the arms symbolize the compassion that uplifts and receives; the eyes symbolize the wisdom that illuminates and discerns.
Each is filled according to its original number, up to eighty-four thousand, which signifies the reliance upon the fundamental roots of the six faculties.
Fundamental wisdom and compassion universally respond to the afflictions of the mundane world, attaining great mastery;
this is the wondrous practice of Equal Enlightenment at the eleventh stage. Prior to the ten stages of the *Avataṃsaka*, one still relies on fundamental wisdom to nurture great compassion;

upon reaching the eleventh stage, the cultivation reaches its consummation, becoming pure great compassion that constitutes the essence of the Dharma-realm. Because it manifests perfectly together with wisdom, contemplate it thus.
His voice, hands, eyes, and entire body pervade everywhere; he is praised for his great compassion.

Within this single essence, the myriad phenomena of worldly toil, as well as kindness, majesty, meditative concentration, and wisdom, are fully present without exception. Thus, he continues the manifestation of the twenty-four sages.
This clarifies what is manifested therein: although each aspect appears as a single end or a perfect circle, when brought together, they all culminate in this very point.
Thus, those who awaken and enter do not stop at twenty-five gates; they suddenly comprehend the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).

The phenomena and principles of the *dharmadhātu* never depart from the substance of my one perfectly interfused and pure awakening. It can be both identical and different, both one and many—boundless.
The ocean-like functions of the lands pervade everywhere; throughout the ten directions, the realms of body and land interpenetrate one another.

The arts of the heterodox and the orthodox, of good and ill fortune, and the methods for nourishing life and pacifying things—all dharmas are perfectly interfused, and every atom is fully endowed with them.
Someone may say: "The eighty-four thousand [dharmas] merely represent the Dharma; how could they be applied to a single body? This is simply because of conceptual thought.
"Mind" refers to the measureless and boundless realm of the Bodhisattva’s perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Now, the body contains the ten voids, and within a single hair-tip, entire lands (*kṣetra*) appear. Those voids and lands are no more extraordinary than one's head or arms;
even the manifestation of eighty-four thousand heads and arms is merely like the eighty-four thousand pores of a human being—it is nothing to be considered strange. Such is the word of the Sage.
It is both principle and phenomenon. Since it is called the inconceivable virtue, there is no way to limit it through thought or deliberation.
*Śakala* means "vajra," signifying firmness and indestructibility; *mudrā* means "seal," referring to the various wondrous seals.
The pure jewel-eyes are free from defilement and united with awakening. With compassion, they gather and transform beings; with majesty, they subdue them. This is meditative concentration.
"By returning to profound stillness, wisdom is opened and awakened. This refers collectively to the many wondrous manifestations. **2.

Reciting the Mantras.** Second, because my hearing and reflection have liberated me from the six sense-objects—just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction—I am able to manifest each individual form and recite each individual mantra. These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all beings.
Sentient beings. For this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, all name me "The Bestower of Fearlessness.
Because one is liberated from the dust of the senses through the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, one manifests forms and recites mantras;
these divine transformations and wondrous powers are each and every one unimpeded—this is called "wondrous capability. △ Third, gathering and transforming [beings].
Third, because I have cultivated this fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, in all the worlds where I travel,
I cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassionate pity.
Because the fundamental root is pure, there is no attachment whatsoever; thus, one can cause sentient beings to abandon all stinginess and clinging.
For those who seek my compassion, I accept them out of compassion and perform the work of a Buddha. △ Fourth, the request for [compassion].

Fourth, I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate. I am able to offer various kinds of precious jewels as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the Dharma-realm. If they seek a wife, they obtain a wife; if they seek a son, they obtain a son;
if they seek samādhi, they obtain samādhi; if they seek long life, they obtain long life—and so on, even until they seek great nirvāṇa, they obtain great nirvāṇa.
Nirvana is the realization of the Buddha-mind; this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃbhāra*). The offering of precious jewels is the perfection of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).

Because both merit and wisdom are perfected, their residual influence extends outward, causing all that others seek—whether mundane or supramundane dharmas—to be fulfilled according to their wishes. △ Second, the conclusion.
Ānanda replied, "Regarding the perfect penetration that the Buddha asks about: I attained samādhi through the faculty of hearing, achieving perfect illumination.
By gaining mastery over the conditioned mind, I entered the state of 'flowing-in' and thereby attained *samāpatti*, accomplishing *bodhi*. This is the foremost."
Initially, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object; this is attaining perfect illumination through the gateway of the ear.

Because of this perfect illumination, one attains great mastery in responding to conditions and manifesting transformations. Next, by gradually increasing this until reaching perfect emptiness, one realizes awakening and attains quiescence;
this is the phase of entering the stream that brings about the fulfillment of Bodhi. △ Third, the conclusion that clarifies the Perfect Name.

World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having skillfully attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. Within that great assembly, he bestowed upon me the prediction of my name as Avalokiteśvara.
Because I contemplate and listen to the ten directions with perfect clarity, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Because he is able to observe and hear, the fruit of his realization is named Guanyin (Avalokiteśvara). Because he truly penetrates the ten directions, his name is also said to pervade all realms.
△ Third, the auspicious response:
At that time, from the Lion Throne, the World-Honored One emitted precious light from his five limbs, which reached far to irrigate the ten directions.
The Tathāgatas within those atoms and the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-Princes likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs;
this light came from the atom-sized directions to consecrate the crowns of the Buddhas' heads, as well as the crowns of the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats in the assembly.
The trees, forests, ponds, and pools all resounded with the sounds of the Dharma; the interlacing lights meshed together like a net of precious threads.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; all universally obtained the Vajra Samādhi.

Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and variegated. The empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures.
In this Sahā world-system, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all vanished simultaneously;
only the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions were seen merged into a single realm, where the chanting of Brahma-songs and hymns was spontaneously performed.
The method of perfect penetration was previously explained; this [passage] manifests the auspicious signs of perfect penetration in response to it.

That the Buddhas emit precious light from all five parts of their bodies signifies that when the illumination of the realized nature reaches its ultimate limit, the precious awakening is perfectly interfused and its entire substance is manifested.
That they mutually confer empowerment upon one another—since the crown of the head is the sign of perfect ultimacy—signifies that the Buddhas have realized the perfection of the nature.
"Extremely so. Within this assembly, there are bodhisattvas and arhats—members of the twenty-four holy ones—upon whose crowns the Buddha’s light also descends;
this seals their cultivation and realization as being equal, without distinction of superior or inferior.

That the forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sound of the Dharma and interlace their lights is because when perfect penetration manifests before one, every sound is the voice of the Buddha. One.
All forms are the form of the Buddha; there is nothing that is not a point of awakening-entry, and nothing that is not the principle of perfect penetration.
That the great assembly universally attains the Vajra Samādhi means that, by this means, they are all able to shatter the obstacles of delusion and awaken to perfect penetration.
Heaven rains down precious flowers; the void manifests precious colors; the earth conceals mountains and rivers; and the realms encompass all dust-like lands.
This signifies the realization of the nature of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-gati*). Then, unconditioned wondrous conduct naturally unfolds;

the jewel-brightness of empty awakening naturally appears. Conditioned habitual outflows shall no longer arise; all dust-like phenomena become vast and clear, with no further obstructions or divisions. — *Brahma* (The Brahma King).

As for those who naturally perform the chanting and singing of hymns and musical offerings, they are able to cause the Dharma-realm to forever be free from all suffering and to constantly attain sublime bliss.
The profound meaning and wondrous benefits of the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration expounded by the Sage are as detailed as this;
therefore, various auspicious omens appeared in response to them in full detail.
