△ Section Four: Imperial Selections, Part Three. First, the Edict Addressed to Mañjuśrī.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī: "You should now observe these twenty-five..."

The various great Bodhisattvas and Arhats have each spoken of their initial expedient means for attaining the Way, all of whom said they practiced the cultivation of true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In their respective practices, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority.

I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening; among these twenty-five methods, which one corresponds to his faculties? Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, [which shall serve] the multitudes of this world?
Those who have been born [into this world], having entered the Bodhisattva Vehicle, seek the Unsurpassed Way. By what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?
Although there is no difference in returning to the source and realizing the nature, according to circumstances and responding to capacities, there are variations in difficulty and ease;
therefore, it is necessary to rely on great wisdom for selection. II. Carrying out the Command to Select (in two parts). A. Compilation.
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and,
sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
△ Second, the main text has two parts. First, the general introduction has four sections. First, the indication of the source:
"The nature of the ocean of enlightenment is clear and perfect; the perfect and clear enlightenment is fundamentally subtle.
The "ocean of the nature of profound enlightenment" is inherently clear and perfect; this indicates the perfect essence. This perfect and clear enlightenment is subtle among the myriad things.
The word "matter" (*wu*) indicates the function of perfection. This person is, from the very beginning, one who is perfectly penetrating. **2.
Narrating Delusion:** Fundamental clarity illuminates and gives rise to objects; Once objects are established, the nature of illumination perishes. Through deluded confusion, empty space arises;
Relying on space, the world is established. When thought settles, the land is formed; When cognition awakens, sentient beings arise.
From within the primordial subtlety, deluded luminosity suddenly arises; this is called "primordial luminosity. When there is deluded illumination, it is called "the locus of arising.

This is what is meant by the statement: "Awakening is not the object of illumination; it is because of illumination that a locus is established. Once the object of illumination is established, the nature of illumination becomes obscured.
"Non-existence" is not a state of nothingness; it is simply entering into non-existence. Once the true nature is obscured, emptiness and awakening become divided.

Consequently, the two realms of the faculties and the objective world are established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, when false conceptualization coagulates, it forms the insentient realm of the physical world (*bhājana-loka*);
when false consciousness perceives and cognizes, it forms sentient beings. Therefore, that which is limpid and wondrous can no longer be attained.
It is perfectly round, yet there is no way to penetrate it. △ Third, the Harmonious Integration:
"Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, Like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The myriad lands of outflows, as minute as motes of dust, all depend on emptiness for their birth.
When the bubble perishes, the emptiness was originally non-existent; How much more so the various realms of the three worlds?"

By citing the above, it is clarified that delusion takes the clarity and perfection [of the mind] to form the faculties and sense-bases (*indriya-āyatana*). When these faculties and sense-bases are dissolved, they return to clarity and perfection.

Within the great ocean of Great Enlightenment, there is fundamentally no existence of either emptiness or being. Due to the wind of delusion blowing and surging, false bubbles of emptiness arise, and thus all existences come into being.
Once the wind of delusion has subsided, the bubbles of emptiness also perish; consequently, the various existences upon which they depend can no longer be found.

It is attained; yet, as emptiness and awakening are perfectly interfused, one returns once more to the original mystery. "All three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*) refers to the three realms of existence within lands as numerous as motes of dust. △ Fourth, the Selection.
The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet the skillful means have many gates. The sagely nature is all-pervasive;
whether following the current or going against it, all are skillful means. When those with a beginner's mind enter samādhi, their progress may be slow or fast, differing in degree;
yet the twenty-five sages share the same perfect penetration. This is what is meant by "non-duality" and what is meant by "many gates"—it rests with the sage.

As for the nature [of mind], it penetrates both the contrary and the compliant; it admits of no selection or discrimination. However, for those at the initial stage of practice, there are differing requirements regarding speed;
therefore, one must exercise choice. II. Specific Selections (five parts): 1. Discerning the Six Objects of Sensation.
Visual forms and perceptions coalesce into dust; though refined with precision, they cannot penetrate through.
How can one attain perfect penetration by failing to see clearly into this? Sounds and mixed languages consist only of names, phrases, and meanings;
since one does not contain all others, how can one attain perfect penetration? Fragrance is known through contact.
If separated, they originally do not exist; the awareness of them is not constant. How can one attain perfect penetration?
The nature of taste is not inherently so; it exists only at the time of tasting. Since that awareness is not constant or singular, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Contact is clarified by what is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly contact.
The nature of conjunction and separation is not fixed; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? The dharmas are called internal objects;
since there must be a basis for these objects, the subject and object do not pervade all things. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Kauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, and others each attained realization through one of the six sense objects, yet all of these have been set aside here.
That which is called the "sage-nature" has nothing it does not penetrate; this so-called "initial mind" is of a different order.
Thus, whatever is not selected is because it is unsuitable for the initial mind; the intention is simply that the ear-faculty alone is suitable. Now, the six objects of sense are being distinguished.
Because visible forms (*rūpa*) can give rise to the fetters of conceptualization (*saṃjñā-saṃyojana*), they cause the essential nature of the mind to fail to penetrate through them.

Sound is restricted solely to names and phrases. Flavor (*rasa*)—where "rasa" means "taste"—is neither comprehensive nor pervasive; "yi" here means "only. Fragrance, taste, and touch are as explained in the text.

The object of dharmas (*dharma-viṣaya*) has no distinct form; it is perceived exclusively by the mind. Because it lies hidden within the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), it is called an "internal object. 2. Distinguishing the Six Faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Although the seeing-nature is brilliantly clear, it illuminates what is before but not what is behind; the four directions are each missing half—how can this be called perfect penetration?
The breath of the nose flows in and out, yet there is no mutual exchange with what is present before;

it is fragmented and does not involve a true entry—how can this be called perfect penetration? The tongue has no fixed point of entry; its function is without end. How can this be called perfect penetration?
Because of flavor, cognition arises; when flavor perishes, cognition has no existence. How can one attain perfect penetration?
The body and its objects of touch are each distinct from the contemplation of perfect enlightenment; their boundaries do not merge—how can one attain perfect penetration?
To know that the faculties are a confused mass of thoughts, yet to seek a profound clarity where ultimately nothing is seen.
Conceptual thought cannot be escaped; how, then, could one attain perfect penetration?
Because the nose lacks a central point of intersection, it is called "fragmented" (*zhīlí*). The tongue can perceive without depending on flavors, which is therefore groundless.
The body and its objects of touch each form distinct boundaries; this is not a state of profound union. △ Third, the elimination of the six consciousnesses.
Consciousness arises from the mingling of the three; when their source is examined, they are found to lack fixed characteristics.
Since its own essence has no prior certainty, how can it attain perfect penetration? The mind’s hearing penetrates the ten directions, arising from the power of a great cause.
Yet the beginner cannot enter this; how then can it attain perfect penetration? The contemplation of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device.
It merely causes the mind to be gathered and abide; once abiding is achieved, the mind has its place of rest. How does one attain perfect penetration?

By playing with sounds and texts when preaching the Dharma, one awakens those who have already attained success. Since names and phrases are not themselves untainted, how does one attain perfect penetration?
Upholding the precepts or violating them merely restrains the body; where there is no body, there is nothing to restrain.
Originally not pervasive throughout all things, how could one attain perfect penetration? Spiritual powers are fundamentally due to past causes;
what connection have they to the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness relies on conditions and is not separate from objects, how could one attain perfect penetration?

[This refers to] the "threefold harmony" of faculty, object, and consciousness. Regarding visual consciousness, if one investigates its arising through the conjunction of these three factors, it is found to be inherently without self-nature.

Therefore, it is said that they are not signs. Because Samantabhadra Bodhisattva employs the mind to hear, he is able to know the external affairs of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions;
this arises from the great cause of practicing the dharmadhātu-conduct and cannot be entered by those at the initial stage of the path.
When Sunda was distracted, the Buddha wished to collect and stabilize his mind by having him contemplate the tip of his nose; this was merely an expedient means for a specific capacity. Indeed...
The true mind has no abiding; to have an abiding is delusion. Pūrṇa’s preaching of the Dharma arises from the tongue-consciousness;
if awakening were achieved first, it would not be appropriate for the initial mind. Upāli’s observance of the precepts ensures that nothing is transgressed, yet he merely restrains his own person;
this does not encompass all things nor is it universal. Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers respond to conditions as he wills, yet they are fundamentally...

This pertains to long-standing habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) and is not related to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, to have thought and objects of perception is not the Perfect Penetration.
The discrimination of dharmas is precisely the mental consciousness. △ Fourth, the exclusion of the seven elements.

If you contemplate through the nature of earth, it is solid and obstructive, not characterized by penetration; as it is conditioned and lacks the nature of the sages, how can you attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate through the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not real, and suchness is beyond both thought and observation;
how can you attain perfect penetration? If you contemplate through the nature of fire...
Weariness with existence is not true detachment; it is not the expedient means of the initial mind. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate by way of the nature of wind, motion and stillness are not without opposition. Since opposition is not the supreme awakening, how can one attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate by way of the nature of space, its dullness and obscurity were originally not awakening.
Without awakening, one differs from Bodhi; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If you observe with the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining this mind is itself a delusion; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and the nature of thought is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing; thus cause and effect now yield different results.

How can the attainment of perfect penetration and the leveling of the earth be considered anything more than conditioned phenomena? They are not the true nature of the sages. The contemplation of moonlight and water has not yet transcended conceptual thought;
it is difficult to accord with suchness, for the principle of suchness is not a matter of vitarka and vicāra (applied and sustained thought). As for Ucchuṣma...
Śamatha. Upon hearing the discourse on the fire of desire, one gives rise to weary detachment; this is weary detachment from existence (*bhava*).

Vaidūryanirbhāsa, observe that the nature of wind is movement, which stands in opposition to stillness; where there is opposition, there is no true awakening. Obscuration and darkness constitute space; therefore, space is dull and insentient.
Maitreya cultivates the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*); yet the consciousness that is the object of his contemplation arises and perishes from moment to moment.

If even maintaining the mind in such contemplation is already false, how much more so is the attainment of perfect penetration? Śrīvajra (Śvetaketu) cultivates the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha; yet the nature of mindfulness is itself a phenomenon of arising and ceasing.
To seek the fruit of eternal constancy by relying on the cause of arising and ceasing is a case of a discordant response. 5. Selection of the Ear-Faculty (7).
First, he sets forth his own view:
I now address the World-Honored One: The Buddha has appeared within this Sahā world-system.
The true essence of the teaching in this region Is purity found in hearing and listening. If one wishes to attain samādhi, One must truly enter through the medium of hearing.
The Sages establish their teachings according to different circumstances. In some Buddha-lands, the work of a Buddha is performed through the light of the Buddha;

in others, it is performed through the Buddha’s bodhi tree; and so on, until there are those that use gardens, groves, and pavilions, or the open sky, or even silence and non-disclosure—as in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa.
This is explained by means of words; however, it is solely through various fragrances that the devas and humans are led to enter the practice of the Vinaya.

As for this region, the substance of the teaching necessarily relies on sound and hearing; the reason why one must enter right concentration through hearing is because each [being] follows their own specific conditions and capacities.
This is because in those Buddha-lands, there is nothing that does not benefit wisdom; thus, the conditions and capacities are intuitively realized beyond words and symbols.
Yet sentient beings of this Endurance World are deluded regarding their original nature and merely follow after sounds;

their ignorance and confusion are so heavy as to constitute a barrier that they must first dissolve through the cultivation of hearing and the practice of hearing, thereby eliminating dust and removing obstructions, before they may enter. However, to take hearing as the means of entry is merely to find its gate;
one must ultimately aim for the forgetting of hearing and the turning back of hearing, for only then does one reach the ultimate. Now, as for reaching the state where hearing is forgotten:
If one turns the hearing inward, then the Buddha’s radiance, the Bodhi tree, and even the state of ultimate stillness where there is nothing to be taught or demonstrated—all can be entered.
Caoxi and Shaoshi have certainly taken this as their Buddhist work. △ Second, praising Avalokiteśvara.
Free from suffering and having attained liberation—how excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as minute as motes of dust;
Having attained the power of great mastery, he bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings.
Avalokiteśvara of Wondrous Sound, with a Brahma-voice and a voice like the tide of the ocean, He brings peace and security to all who seek refuge in this world.

The first couplet, "Transcending the world to attain eternal abiding," offers a general praise of Avalokiteśvara’s voice, which delivers beings from suffering and grants them joy. "Throughout kalpas of dust-like lands" praises the thirty-two manifestations.
"Attaining mastery and bestowing fearlessness" praises the four inconceivable powers and the fourteen [meritorious qualities].

It is fearlessness. "Myōon" (Wonderful Sound) and "Kannon" (Avalokiteśvara) are names that praise his virtues; "Bongo" (Sanskrit Sound) and "Chōon" (Tidal Sound) are names that praise the reality corresponding to those titles.
He is called Myōon because his preaching of the Dharma is unhindered, and he is called Kannon because he seeks out sounds to rescue beings from suffering.
The nature of sound being unattached constitutes the Brahma-voice; responding without missing the proper time constitutes the Tide-voice. The final couplet summarizes all virtues:
it is able to rescue the world from suffering and able to bestow supramundane bliss. △ Third, the three aspects of true selection:
first, the perfection of truth.
I now address the Tathāgata regarding what Avalokiteśvara has taught:
"Just as when a person dwells in silence and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions, they hear them all at once in those ten places—this is the perfect reality.

This refers to the matters such as Avalokiteśvara’s attainment of true perfect penetration through the faculty of hearing, illuminating perfectly from that gateway. I shall now compose verses on this.
This is the perfect illumination of the true essence. II. Pervading the True:
The eyes do not observe what is beyond the barrier; The mouth and nose are likewise so. The body perceives through contact;
Only then does one know that mental thoughts are chaotic and disordered. Listening to sounds across a wall, One can hear them both from afar and nearby.
That which is not uniform among the five faculties is what penetrates the ultimate reality.
This first refutes that the eyes, nose, tongue, body, and mind cannot attain true penetration; it specifically highlights the ear-faculty’s attainment of true penetration through a partitioned wall.
△ Third, the Permanently True.

The nature of sound is movement and stillness; within hearing, it appears as existence or non-existence. When there is no sound, it is called "no-hearing," yet this is not a true absence of the nature of hearing.
Since sound does not exist when silent, there is no cessation; since sound exists when present, there is no arising.
Thus, both arising and ceasing are perfectly transcended; this is the eternal reality.

Movement and stillness, existence and non-existence—all these belong to the sense-object of sound. When the faculty of hearing is perfectly detached, it does not follow the cycle of arising and ceasing;
this is the true nature of permanence. "The absence of sound is called 'no-hearing'" refers to Ānanda’s experience of hearing the bell.

"Even if one is in a dream, it is not the case that [the hearing] does not exist when there is no thinking. Through investigation and contemplation (*vitarka-vicāra*), one transcends discursive thought;

body and mind cannot reach or fully praise the manifestation of the eternal nature. The five sense organs all depend upon mental intention (*manas-cetanā*); their existence and non-existence are not constant. Only the ear remains present even in a dream."

That one is able to hear the sound of the pestle is not because it is absent when there is no thought; rather, its function as *vitarka* (initial application) and *vicāra* (sustained application) arises from deliberation (*saṃkalpa*), thereby excelling the other sense organs.
△ Fourth, clarifying the resonance with the capacity of the listener.
Now, in this Sahā world, the science of sound and discourse has been proclaimed and clarified. Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing;
because they follow sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth. Even though Ānanda possesses a powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts.
Is this not because he follows wherever he is submerged? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.
Regarding those who study the science of sound (*śabdavidyā*): they rely on the treatises of sound to clarify the nature of original hearing through awakening.

Those who are deluded regarding this original state follow after sounds, falsely grasping at them and falling into decline—such as Ānanda, who merely devoted himself to rote memorization and mistakenly fell into perverse thoughts;
was this not the fault of following after sounds? Had he been able to turn back and listen inwardly, there would have been no such false descent. Among the scholars of this Sahā world, many...

They merely devote themselves to rote memorization; they fall into heterodoxy and sink into delusion, unaware of how to return to the source. Therefore, [the Buddha] entrusts this to Ānanda to warn them.
△ Fifth, the announcement to Ānanda, in seven parts: first, commanding him to listen attentively.
Ānanda, listen attentively! Upholding the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King,
the inconceivable and illusory Mother of Buddhas,
the True Samādhi of Vajra-like Illusion— namely, the illusory hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation bestowed by the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara.
This is the Vajra Samādhi. All Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge from this; therefore, it is named the "Mother of Buddhas. 2. Causing One to Turn the Hearing Backward:
"You have heard of the subtle dust of all Buddhas And all their secret gates; Yet you have not first eliminated the outflows of desire."
Accumulating learning leads to error; one should instead maintain the hearing of the Buddhas. Why do you not hear that which hears?
"Hearing of the Buddhas" refers to the Buddha-nature within the Buddhas; "hearing that hears" refers to the nature of hearing within oneself.

Ānanda has protected and maintained the secret treasury of all Buddhas, yet he has merely accumulated much learning in vain and has been unable to achieve reverse enlightenment. Therefore, he is rebuked for his empty retention.

Buddha after Buddha does not hear by means of hearing. For those who wish to enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the essential task lies in turning the hearing back toward one's own nature. △ Third, causing liberation from objects.
Hearing is not born of itself; it exists because of sound, which gives rise to names. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, who can there be to name that detachment?
Once one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.

"Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); "sound" refers to the objective field of the ear. Since the faculties exist because of their objects, they are all deluded dusts; therefore, one should turn them back.
Yet they are liberated from it; there is nothing that can liberate them. This is returning to the true source. Once the single source returns to the truth, all six are liberated from delusion.
△ Fourth, Attaining Pure Enlightenment.
Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. "Hearing" refers to the removal of the cataracts of the sense-organ;

"the dust having vanished, awareness becomes perfectly pure" refers to the illusory cataracts of seeing and hearing. These collectively indicate the deluded root. "The three realms are flowers in the sky" collectively indicates the deluded objects. This is because...

Because all are illusory, as soon as one hears [the teaching], the cataracts are immediately removed; when the dust is dissipated, awareness is purified. Thus, by returning once to the source, the six [senses] are liberated.
△ Fifth, showing the characteristics of liberation, in three parts: first, the Dharma.
The purity of ultimate radiance penetrates through; Quiescent illumination encompasses the void.
Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream; Mātanga is within the dream— Who could detain your form?

Purity reaches the extreme, radiance penetrates, quiescence illuminates, encompassing the void. This is the liberation of the faculties (*indriya-vimokṣa*). Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream.
"Affairs" refers to the liberation of objects. Thus, Mādrī was truly but a dream-object;
since she is utterly unobtainable, who could detain you so that you do not attain liberation? △ Second, the analogy.

Just as a skillful worldly illusionist conjures various men and women through illusions—though their faculties are seen to move, they are drawn by a single mechanism—when that mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, all illusions become devoid of intrinsic nature.
The illusionist represents the deluded nature; the single mechanism represents the deluded consciousness. Since nature is moved by consciousness, when the mechanism ceases, one returns to stillness.
Thus all illusions are devoid of self-nature and each is liberated. △ Third, the synthesis:
The six sense-faculties are also like this. Originally relying on a single brilliant spirit, they are divided into the six harmonious unities.
When they are unified in one place, there is restorative recovery; the functions of the six are no longer operative, and defilements vanish in a single thought.

When perfected as perfect, bright, pure, and wondrous, the remaining dust still belongs to those in training. When clarity reaches its ultimate limit, it is the Tathāgata—the single brilliant essence.
This refers to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Based upon this, the six sense organs harmonize with their objects to conjure all manner of delusions.

Therefore, when one aspect ceases and returns to the source, all six aspects fail to arise. Thus, the dust of conceptualization and the defilements of consciousness shall vanish with every thought, and one attains wondrous, perfect penetration.
That subtle delusions are not yet exhausted is called "remaining dust"; that partial realization is not yet complete is called "those in training" (śaikṣa).
When delusions are purified and clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata. △ Six: Conclusion on the Benefits.
Great Assembly and Ānanda, turn back the mechanism of your inverted hearing; by turning the hearing to hear your own nature, that nature will accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
Such is the true reality of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-āyatana*):
being able to turn back the inversion of delusion and turning the hearing toward one's own nature, one must rely on this nature to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way. This is perfect penetration.
This Dharma-gate is truly efficacious. Its nature is perfected, as in what is called the "nature of all minds.
△ Seven: Encouraging Progress. This is the single path to nirvana for countless Buddhas.
All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; all Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity.
"Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma; I too have realized it through this—it is not merely the gate of Avalokiteśvara’s Nirvāṇa.
It is the essential path for transcending birth and death and realizing the true and eternal. No one among those who have attained the fruit across the three periods of time [has done so otherwise]."
It is not by this [other means]. Therefore, practitioners of the future should rely upon this Dharma. 6. Sealing the Selection:

Truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Inquired of me regarding various skillful means To rescue those in the final kalpa who seek to transcend the world, To bring to fulfillment the mind of nirvana— Avalokiteśvara is the foremost.

All other various skillful means are the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; they involve abandoning worldly toil through immediate circumstances rather than through long-term cultivation and study.
Whether at a shallow or deep level, the teaching is the same:
to achieve the wondrous mind of Nirvana, which is neither born nor extinguished. Among these, the faculty of hearing is supreme; all others are [the teachings] of the Buddha.
Through the empowerment of majestic spiritual power, one is enabled to abandon worldly toil by regarding it as one's own immediate concern;

this is not a teaching for long-term cultivation where the shallow and deep are explained as identical from beginning to end. Yet, if one desires a method for long-term cultivation that explains these as identical, there is none like the Dharma-gate of Avalokiteśvara.
It is like Nārada losing his sight and then regaining vision, or Piṅgala being pricked by thorns and forgetting his own body, or Ucchuṣma becoming weary of desire and [attaining liberation].
Shengjue ascended to awakening; Chidi waited for the Buddha to eliminate his defilements—all were merely matters concerning themselves. △ Seventh: Conclusion, Praise, and Exhortation to Study.
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, Immaculate and inconceivable. May you bestow your grace upon those of the future.
In this gateway there is no delusion; The skillful means are easily accomplished.
It is fit to teach Ānanda and those submerged in the final age of decay; If one cultivates with this faculty alone, Its perfect penetration surpasses all others—such is the true mind.
This concludes the praise for the dharma-gate of the uncontaminated *tathāgatagarbha* and the samādhi of hearing and permeation.
It exhorts those of the future to rely upon this for cultivation and realization, whereby they may transcend other samādhis. Such is the essential core of the truth. △ Third:
The Assembly Attains Benefit.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly were clear in body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.
They beheld the Buddha’s bodhi and his great nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far on business and has not yet returned, yet clearly understands the path leading back to their home.
Thus it was for the entire assembled multitude—the eight classes of devas and nāgas, those still in training, the followers of the two vehicles, and all others.

There were ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of newly resolved bodhisattvas who all attained their original mind, became free from dust and defilement, and obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Upon hearing the verse, the bhikṣuṇī Śrī became an arhat.
Immeasurable sentient beings all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is peerless.
The wondrous gate of perfect penetration opens instantaneously beneath a single word; the true fruition of all Buddhas may thus be hoped for.
Therefore, when one contemplates the Bodhi and Great Nirvana of the Buddha, body and mind become clear and lucid; this is merely a slight advance toward realization.
It is like a long journeyer who, though not yet home, clearly understands the path. All those gathered—gods and humans alike—attained their original mind and even realized the Dharma.
As for the "purity of the eye," it is because one awakens to the original hearing, thereby dissolving the dust and returning to the luminosity.
As for the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīmitrā (Xing) attaining Arhatship, it is because her wondrous nature is perfectly penetrating and all outflows are forever exhausted.

As for the "unequaled," it means that while no thing can equal it, it is able to be equal to things; this is the attainment of wondrous, perfect penetration, which ascends to join with those above and descends to harmonize with those below.
This is the virtue thereof. That immeasurable sentient beings all give rise to this mind is because they hear of this Way and thus aspire to, long for, and delight in it.
△ Third, the rules for upholding [the teaching] has two parts. First, Ānanda’s inquiry.

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet. His mind and its traces were perfectly clear and bright; he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.

Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed low and addressed the Buddha: “O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood.
In practicing this path, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have often heard the Tathāgata speak in this way...”

He said: "To first deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the aspiration of a bodhisattva; to have awakened oneself to perfection and then be able to awaken others is the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Although I have not yet been delivered myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age.

World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha, and teachers of false doctrines are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. I wish to gather their minds and lead them into [the Way]."
Samādhi. How does one cause them to be established in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from all demonic activities, and attain non-retrogression in the mind of bodhi?

Regarding "the traces of the mind being perfectly luminous": having previously resolved the knots of the faculties and transcended the vessel-worlds, the traces are perfectly luminous. This is awakening.
Perfect penetration: as the sense-objects vanish, awareness becomes pure; this is the luminous perfection of the mind. Thereupon, one laments past delusion and rejoices in present awakening.
One intends to employ this Dharma to respond to the world and deliver sentient beings, yet fears that during the many calamities of the final kalpa, malevolent spirits and demons will act perversely.

It is easy to retreat from the awakened mind, but difficult to enter right concentration. Therefore, he requests the rules for establishing a pure site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) by restraining the mind and keeping it far from demons.
△ Second, the Buddha’s compassionate instruction has two parts. First, the praise and permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda amidst the great assembly: "Excellent, excellent!

Just as you have asked, regarding the establishment of the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall speak for your sake."
"Ānanda and the great assembly replied, 'So be it; we shall respectfully follow your instructions.
**II. The Actual Instruction, in Two Parts:** **A. The Internal Rules of Discipline (Vinaya), in Two Parts:** **1.
A General Presentation of the Three Studies:** The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You have often heard me, within the *Vinaya*, proclaim the three definitive principles for the practice of cultivation."

What is called "gathering the mind as the precept" means that concentration arises because of the precept, and wisdom is produced because of concentration; this is termed the Threefold Training in the Outflow-free (anāsrava).
Among the Three Piṭakas, it refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is the general designation for the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. [The Hīnayāna...]
The Hīnayāna takes the reception of the Dharma as its precept; it roughly treats the branches. The Mahāyāna takes the restraint of the mind as its precept;
it subtly cuts off the root. The Dharma-precept consists merely in not transgressing; the mind-precept consists in having no thought of transgression.

Now, if one can restrain the mind, concentration arises thereby, and wisdom is produced thereby. When these three are perfectly clear and bright, all outflows are forever exhausted; therefore, it is so named.
The three trainings in the absence of outflows (*anāsrava-śikṣā*) are the most supreme for upholding the rules of conduct. △ Second, the specific presentation of the four gravities.

These four gravities constitute the first part of the ten precepts; the four *pārājika* offenses are the fundamental grave sins. The text has four sections. First, regarding sexual misconduct: there are six [points].
First, by maintaining [the precept], one emerges from the entanglements (*saṃyojana*).

Ānanda, what is meant by "gathering the mind"? That which I call "precept" is this: if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful thoughts in their hearts, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
All sentient beings, because of lustful desire, establish their very nature and life; thus they are entangled in birth and death.

If the craving of desire dries up, then this residual physical form will not continue. This means that their minds shall not be lustful and their minds shall not be thieving, ensuring that there is no thought of transgression.
△ Second, if one commits [these offenses], one will fall into ruin.
As you cultivate samādhi, it is fundamentally for the purpose of emerging from worldly afflictions. If the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the path of demons—becoming a high-ranking demon king in the superior grade, or a demonic subject in the middle grade.
The lower-grade māras. These various māras also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have attained the unsurpassed way.
Though these māras possess great wisdom and practice dhyāna, because they do not sever lust, they do not achieve the holy path; they practice dhyāna while still harboring lust.
They will inevitably fall into this category. △ Third, [the Buddha] instructs them to be prepared in advance:
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma’s decay, many such demonic followers will flourish in the world.
They will widely practice greed and lust while posing as 'good spiritual friends,' causing all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views and lose the path to Bodhi."
Sentient beings in the final age lack the eye of the True Dharma and are frequently deluded by demons; they must therefore maintain vigilance beforehand so as not to be seduced and ensnared.
Merely craving and desiring while disregarding the peril of falling into ruin is called the "pit of attachment and views. △ Fourth, instructing them to proclaim and clarify the teachings.

When you teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, you must first sever sexual desire in the mind; this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.
In various sutras, the precept against killing is placed first, for the purpose of establishing transformation through taking compassion as the foundation.

In this sutra, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first, for the purpose of true cultivation through taking the departure from desire as the foundation. Indeed, the vapor of desire is coarse and turbid, defiling the wondrous clarity;

the habituation to desire leads to madness and delusion, making it easy to lose right concentration (*samāpatti*). Nothing is more extreme than this in terms of perpetuating birth and death and losing true permanence. Therefore, one must...
The foremost precept is the first pure and clear instruction. Observe how Ānanda, when he began his teaching mission, encountered defilement by the wicked;
yet from the very moment he first resolved his mind, he first loathed the turbidity of desire. Throughout the three gradual stages, he rectified each matter at its head.
Only then did his body and mind become wondrously perfect, attaining great peace and stability. At the initial stage of the ten faiths, the craving of desire was dried up.
Though withered, the nature of wisdom is perfectly luminous; thus one gradually ascends through the stages of Equality and Wondrous Enlightenment.

As for ordinary people of the world, because their minds do not flow into dissipation, a clarity and brilliance arise, and they gradually reach the six heavens of the desire realm. Therefore, true cultivation that encompasses within must first involve the departure from desire.
△ Five: Repeatedly Manifesting Faults (in two parts). One: Clarification by Analogy.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever lust while practicing meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope of producing rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will only be called "hot sand. Why is this? Because this is not the basis for rice; it is composed of sand and gravel.
The essence is not beautiful; seeking it is but vain labor. △ Second, the conclusion and clarification:

You seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body. Even if you were to attain wondrous enlightenment, it would all stem from the root of lust. With the very foundation established in lust, [how could there be liberation?]
One will inevitably cycle through the three miserable realms and be unable to escape them. By what path can one cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?
It is said that if one uses gold to make vessels, every vessel is gold; if one uses clay to make vessels, every vessel is clay.
Thus, one must be cautious regarding the practices undertaken as causes. △ Sixth, exhorting one to definitely sever [delusions].
One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, and even the nature of this severance is non-existent. Only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
"Mechanism" refers to what is spontaneously aroused by the lustful mind; it is not that the nature of severance does not exist, but rather that it is triggered upon contact with the mechanism.
What I have spoken in this manner is called the teaching of the Buddha; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
This is intended to cause one to believe these correct words. *Pāpīyān* is a name for Māra. II. Killing the Nine. 1. By upholding [this], one emerges from the entanglements.
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
"You owe me my life; I shall repay you for your debt"—this is why there is continuity. 2. If one commits [killing], one falls into ruin.
As you cultivate samādhi, it originally aims for liberation from worldly toil; yet if the intent to kill is not eliminated, you cannot transcend the mundane world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the habit of killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Those of superior grade will become powerful ghosts.
Those of middle capacity shall become flying yakṣas and various leaders of ghosts; those of inferior capacity shall become earth-walking rākṣasas.
Those various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have realized the unsurpassed way.
If one practices meditation while harboring the intent to kill, one will inevitably fall into the class of spirits.

Third, [the Buddha] preempts this by issuing a warning: "After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma’s decay, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that eating meat provides the path to Bodhi."
You must prepare yourself in advance; do not fall prey to seductive teachings. △ Fourth, to cause them to understand expedient means:
"Ānanda, I have permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat. This meat was all produced through my supernatural power and transformation; it originally possessed no life-force.
In your land, O Brahmin, the ground is mostly damp and humid, further compounded by sand and stones, such that grasses and vegetables do not grow. For this reason, I..."
It is through the empowerment of the great compassionate spiritual power, and because of great compassion, that it is provisionally named "flesh.
Since you have tasted its flavor, how can you, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, eat the flesh of sentient beings and yet still call yourself a son of the Śākya?
The Buddha’s initial teaching was transformative, gradually establishing precepts in accordance with specific circumstances. As a provisional concession, he permitted the "five pure meats":

those not seen, not heard, not suspected [to have been killed for oneself], those that died naturally, and those pecked by birds; these were termed "pure" because they were produced through supernatural power and lacked the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

This, however, was a provisional expedient of the Hīnayāna. If one seeks true compassion and true liberation, all such things must be abandoned. Therefore, when the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* was first expounded, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*...
The conclusion: there is nothing that does not strictly prohibit [these acts]. Herein are listed the five purities;

yet in other sutras they may be three or seven, and in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* they may be nine—these are merely variations of inclusion and exclusion. "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is a general term for those who practice pure conduct.
△ Fifth, showing the root of evil.
"You all should know: even if these meat-eaters should attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, they are all great *rākṣasas*.
When their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha.
For such people, who have not yet ceased killing one another, devouring one another, and eating one another, how could they ever escape the three realms?"
If the root is unwholesome, it can never become wholesome in the end. That which resembles samādhi is not true samādhi;
because its root is delusion. △ Sixth, instructing them to proclaim the clear teachings.

When you teach the people of the world to practice samādhi, the next step is to sever the taking of life; this is called the Tathāgata’s second definitive, pure, and clear instruction following the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
△ Section Seven: Manifesting the Faults in Seven Layers, Part Two. First, the illustration by analogy:

"Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, yet seeks for others not to hear them.
This is called 'seeking to conceal, yet making it even more manifest.'"

To cultivate meditation in order to avoid transgressions, yet instead commit acts of killing; to plug one's ears to avoid others, yet instead raise one's voice loudly—this is to seek concealment only to make it more manifest.
△ Second, the conclusion and clarification.
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not even tread upon living grass when walking on a forked path, much less pluck it with their hands.
How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?
One must not step on them by mistake, nor pluck them intentionally. The utmost benevolence extends even to grasses and trees; how much more so for sentient beings who provide food.
△ Eighth, a detailed explanation of the conditions and their counterparts:
If there are bhikṣus who do not wear silk, cotton, or fine cloth from the East, nor the boots, furs, or woolen garments of this land...

"Milk, curd, and clarified butter—thus, O bhikṣu, having attained true liberation in the world, you have repaid your karmic debts from former lives and shall no longer wander through the three realms. Why is this?
Because by partaking of their physical remains, you have become bound by those very conditions. It is like a person who eats the various grains produced from the earth;
their feet do not leave the ground."
In the East, furs and wool are not absent; in the Western lands, silk and cloth are not lacking. These statements are made according to what is most prevalent in each region.
At the beginning of the kalpa, human beings possessed a radiant glow on their bodies and could travel as if riding upon clouds. This was because they consumed the "earth-fat" and ate fragrant rice.
However, due to these foods, their bodies became solid and heavy, and their feet no longer left the ground. △ Ninth: Exhortation to Sever [the Afflictions] Thoroughly.
If one can ensure that for all sentient beings, neither one's own body nor its parts, nor both the body and mind, are used as clothing or food, I declare that such a person is truly liberated.
What I have spoken thus is called the teaching of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
The body consists of blood, flesh, marrow, and brain; its parts include hides, wool, milk, and curd. One’s body serves as the vessel for food, yet the mind greedily seeks it;
hence these are called the "two paths" that must both be severed. Pure and clear instructions regarding evil conditions are as restrictive as this.
Yet nowadays, many people take cow's milk to assist in their vegetarian feasts, devouring it with voracious gluttony and without avoiding pungent or impure things.
What kind of mind is this truly? When one calmly reflects on its origin, it is the discharge of the mingling of stench and filth, a chaotic mixture of pus, blood, and residual fluids.
It is the essence of lustful evil and the richness of fat and flesh, produced from a body of excrement and impurity;
it is the ultimate in uncleanness. To consume its essence is to crave the true flavor of lustful evil; what difference is there, then, between that and eating its fat?
As for fatty meat: is it truly the case that those who are pure and authentically liberated act in such a manner? Even the five pungent herbs and their kin are forbidden to be eaten;

compared to these transgressions, [the former] are immeasurably more grievous. One should swiftly eliminate them, rather than greedily seeking a savory taste for one's own palate and intestines, thereby openly violating the pure instructions.
Some may say: "In the past, the Great Awakened One accepted the offering of a cowherd’s daughter and permitted Ānanda..."
What is meant by this seeking? It is said: "This is a provisional expedient of the Hīnayāna, established for those suffering from the ailment of withered hunger;

it is a matter of responding to circumstances upon a grass seat, a practice currently in vogue in the defiled age. How could such a thing exist within the diamond-like essence beneath the tree of seven jewels?
One does not take the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna as the standard, but instead adheres to provisional expedients."
Regarding this doctrine of non-comprehension: it is not merely a matter of taking milk to assist in the fast; rather, one should adhere to the provisional names of the five pure foods.

To place these upon the sacrificial tables and ritual seats of the pure assembly, yet act as a great rākṣasa, is a grave error. △ Third, the theft of the eight [precepts]. One who upholds them shall emerge from the entanglements.
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in the world, if their minds do not steal, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
Taking what is not given constitutes theft; even exceeding what one has been paid and still demanding the remainder is considered theft, let alone actual stealing.

[They] take [them]. Because they obtain [these things], there is no further challenge to their claims; this is why birth and death continue in succession. Second, as for transgressions leading to falling:
"When you cultivate samādhi, its primary purpose is to emerge from worldly toil (*saṃsāra*). If the thieving mind is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever this thievery, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths—becoming either high-grade spirits or mid-grade demons."

Low-grade heterodox individuals are possessed by various demons; these groups of heterodox practitioners also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Because of the deceit and fraud of these heterodox paths, those who steal [from them] will inevitably fall. △ Third, providing advance warnings and preparations.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world. They will secretly harbor deceit and fraud while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
Each will claim for themselves to have attained the dharmas of a superior person (uttaramanuṣyadharma), deluding the ignorant and causing them to lose their minds out of fear.
Wherever he passes, the households there will suffer depletion;
one must guard against his seductive influence. △ Fourth, rebuking his greed and theft:
"I have taught the bhikṣus to wander for alms according to their direction, so that they may abandon greed and accomplish the path to Bodhi. All you bhikṣus..."
One does not cook for oneself; one merely borrows this残余 (remaining) life to lodge as a traveler within the Three Realms, demonstrating a single coming and going from which there is no returning.
How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle like a merchant the likeness of the Tathāgata, performing all manner of karmic deeds while claiming them all to be the Buddha-dharma?

To claim that a fully ordained monk who has left the household life practices the path of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is a delusion that misleads immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. This is the method [of refutation].
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Begging for food is called 'parting' (*fenwei*). It means to distribute [alms] among the Saṃgha; it is to protect (*wei*) [the community]."
Regarding the power of protecting the Way, Master Zao said: "There are briefly four intentions for begging for food:
first, to bring benefit and merit to all living beings; second, to subdue arrogance; third, to realize that the body is subject to suffering; and fourth, to eliminate attachment.
In this sutra, the instruction to abandon greed and not cook for oneself corresponds precisely to eliminating attachment, thereby accomplishing the path to Bodhi.
This is precisely the power of the Way to provide protection and to bring benefit to all living beings. To know that the body is but a temporary lodging and that the world is but a transient sojourn;
to have no need for hoarding and no cause for attachment—this is what is meant by "following the proper direction. One who cannot follow this proper direction is not so.

Yet, out of greed and rapacity, they create karma; they destroy the Dharma and violate the precepts, and are therefore called "thieves. Though they wear the robes of the Buddha, they do not maintain a pure livelihood;
they merely don the Buddha's garments as a pretext to attach themselves to the Buddha-Dharma, seeking only to trade for gain and offerings.
△ Fifth, the instruction to repent and renounce.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to practice samādhi and is able,
before an image of the Tathāgata, to light a single lamp with his own body, burn a finger joint, or apply a single incense stick to his body.
I say that such a person has repaid their karmic debts from beginningless time all at once; they bid a long farewell to the world and are forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they have not yet clearly realized the path to supreme enlightenment, their mind is already resolved regarding the Dharma.

If it were not for this minor cause of sacrificing the body, even if they had attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they would inevitably have been reborn as a human to repay those old debts, just as I was with the horse-barley.
They are truly equal and without distinction.
The body is the root of karma and the condition for outflows (*āsrava*). Since beginningless time, one has greedily sought after it and accumulated debts because of it;
now, being able to renounce it constitutes the unsurpassed karma, whereby one can repay past debts and be liberated from all outflows. Indeed, all...

It is difficult to relinquish; nothing is more difficult to relinquish than one's own body. If one can relinquish what is so difficult to relinquish, then all other attachments and cravings will certainly be abandoned.

Therefore, it is said that such a person has attained a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma. If one can indeed relinquish the body, yet the mind does not resolutely relinquish [attachments], [it is not true relinquishment].
This would merely increase the suffering of karma and provide no benefit for the Path; therefore, it is said below that one must "cause both body and mind to be completely relinquished.

Because the Buddha was once reviled by a bhikṣu, he had to eat horse-barley; thus, after attaining the fruit of enlightenment, he ate it at the village of Vairaṇā to demonstrate that past debts must necessarily be repaid. △ Sixth: Instructing him to proclaim the clear teachings.

When you instruct the people of the world to practice samādhi, they must subsequently renounce stealing; this is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
△ Seventh, the manifestation of faults.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease stealing yet cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup while seeking to fill it;
even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.
If the vessel for the Way is incomplete, the fruit of the Way will ultimately leak away. △ Eighth, the exhortation to renounce:
"If any bhikṣus do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls, and give whatever remains from their begged food to hungry sentient beings..."
In the great assembly, one should join the palms and pay homage to the multitude. Whether someone strikes or reviles one, it should be regarded as identical to praise.
One must ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished; one’s flesh, bones, and blood are shared with all sentient beings.

One shall not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into one's own interpretation to mislead beginners. The Buddha seals such a person as having attained true samādhi, just as I have taught.
This is called the teaching of the Buddha; if it were not spoken thus, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyān.
One does not store robes or alms bowls, and regards disparagement as praise. In this way, regarding both benefit and harm, one relinquishes both body and mind.
When one shares one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings, one no longer treats the body as private and disregards one's own life;
this is the ultimate form of renunciation. When one’s practice can reach such a state, it may be known that the mind is free from theft.

The *Āgama* states that the goods one possesses may be used to sustain the body and advance on the Path; the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* permits the possession of one unit of each of the hundred types of items.
All of these are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). △ Four: The Six Delusions. First, transgression leads to downfall and loss.

Ānanda, although the beings of the six realms in such worlds may have perfected their physical and mental abstinence from the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, if they engage in great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*), their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views, losing as [they did before].
These are the seeds of coming [rebirth]: namely, claiming what has not been attained as attained, or declaring what has not been realized as realized;

or seeking worldly honor, supremacy, and preeminence by saying to others, "I have now attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin)."

Those who seek the path of the Arhat, the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, or the various stages of the Bodhisattva— from the ten stages down to those prior to them— and yet, out of greed for offerings,

perform prostrations and repentances while claiming to have attained what they have not actually attained— namely, the four fruits of arhatship or the ten stages— are guilty of a great falsehood. They do so out of greed for offerings and a desire for themselves.

The "Venerable and Victorious" is named the Mara of Attachment; to falsely give rise to perverse views, claiming to have attained equality with the Sages, is named the Mara of Views. Both are great falsehoods.
Such a person is an icchantika who extinguishes the seeds of the Buddha, just as a person uses a knife to cut down a tala tree. The Buddha has given this prediction regarding such a person.
Their roots of goodness are forever destroyed; they possess no further knowledge or vision. Sunk in the ocean of the three sufferings, they do not achieve samādhi.
*Icchantika* is the same as *icchantika*. Just as a *pāṭala* tree severed by a blade will never revive again.
This is like a great liar who has forever severed his roots of goodness; it refers to the three sufferings and the three miserable realms. △ Second, citing the true to reveal the false:
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command all the bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest their response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) within that age of the final dharma (*mappō*).
They manifest in various forms to deliver beings from the cycle of rebirth;

they may appear as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, officials, boys, or girls, and so on, even down to courtesans, widows, thieves, butchers, or merchants, working alongside them in their common affairs.
They praise the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi; yet they never say of themselves, "I am a true bodhisattva" or "I am a true arhat.

They do not leak the Buddha’s secret causes or speak lightly of those who have not yet studied, except when, at the end of life, there is something entrusted to them in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
How could such a person delude the masses and commit a great falsehood?

A true sage who manifests in response to conditions ultimately maintains a state of concealment; they do not lightly disclose the secret causes to those who have not yet studied. △ Third, it is appropriate to provide clear instruction.
When you instruct the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, you must subsequently cause them to sever all great false speech.
This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
△ Fourth, further manifesting the faults:
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great false speech, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood.
To seek fragrance while lacking [the source] is impossible.
To practice dhyāna while harboring delusions will never result in a pure essence. △ Fifth, a profound rebuke of falsehood:
"I teach my bhikṣus that the site of the Way is the straightforward mind. Within all activities during the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense whatsoever."
How can one falsely claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person? It is like a destitute man who falsely styles himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution;
how much more so for a Dharma King—how could one falsely usurp such a title? Because the ground is not true, the fruit will result in a crooked path. Thus one seeks the Bodhi of the Buddha.
It is like the man who bites his own navel; whom does he wish to accomplish?
This refers to one who, having not yet attained it, claims to have attained it, seeking for himself matters of honor and superiority, and is thus deeply censured. Vimalakīrti said:

"The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because it is free from falsehood. The four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) are walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. In the *Zhuozu Zhuan*, there is the account of "biting one's navel."

This means that, in the end, no one can ever equal them. Nowadays, there are many who claim to have attained the dharmas of those beyond the ordinary person (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*) and who recklessly usurp the title of Dharma King;
they should take the words of the sūtras as a warning. △ Sixth, exhorting them to be truthful.
If there are bhikṣus whose minds are as straight as a bowstring, who are entirely truthful and enter samādhi, they will forever be free from the works of Māra;
I certify that such persons shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva.
Because the former is circuitous, it ultimately fails to achieve success; because this [latter] string is straight, its success is certified.
What I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyas.

The preceding passage provides a general explanation of the four grave precepts. Although it initially sets forth the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), it concludes with only the four precepts because the aspects of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have already been fully detailed in the previous text.
