Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Thirteen.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī;
orally received by Fáng Róng of Qīnghé, former Grand Master for Rectifying Discourse and concurrently Minister of State Affairs, and disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling explains:

△ Second, the external rules of conduct for gathering [the assembly]. The preceding section demonstrated internal gathering; this section demonstrates external gathering. The text has two parts: first, citing the internal gathering as a point of inquiry.
Ānanda, regarding your question on the gathering of the mind, I shall now first explain the sublime gateway for training in the entry into samādhi.
One who seeks the Bodhisattva path must first maintain these four kinds of discipline as clearly as ice and frost; then, not even a single branch or leaf of transgression can arise.
As for the three actions of the mind and the four actions of the mouth, they will have no cause to arise at all. Ānanda, if these four matters are not lost or neglected...
If the mind does not even take form, sound, smell, taste, or touch as its object, how could any demonic activities arise?
Internal restraint is the essential; therefore, the sublime gateway is taught first. One must first uphold the fourfold discipline (*catur-śīla*);

these four disciplines are the root, while the remaining precepts are the branches. Thus, when the fourfold discipline is pure, the twigs and leaves do not grow. When one does not encounter sensory objects, demonic activities [cannot arise].

[The afflictions] are submerged and eliminated; one may then enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). The three [aspects] of mind are identical to the three [aspects] of intention; this fully enumerates the ten stages.
△ Second, the actual instruction on the external inclusion has four parts. First, the exhortation to recite divine mantras.
If there are habitual tendencies that cannot be extinguished or eliminated, you should instruct this person to single-mindedly recite my supreme divine mantra,
the *Mahāsitātapatra* (Great White Parasol) from the Radiant Light of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa. This is the heart-mantra spoken by the Tathāgata’s Unseen Crown-Mark (*anavalokitamūrdha*),
the Unconditioned Mind-Buddha, who emits radiance from his crown and sits upon a precious lotus flower.
Present actions are easy to restrain; one’s own conduct can be altered. However, long-standing habits are difficult to eliminate and necessarily rely upon spiritual power.

Now, some practitioners prefer what is correct yet remain firmly attached to the perverse; they desire purity yet are biased toward defilement. They act without being taught and do so without intending to.
That there is something hidden, as if a physical frame or a mechanism, which one cannot help but follow—this is the compulsion of past habituation.
That virtue is exalted yet blessings are meager; that one performs good deeds yet the person suffers misfortune;

that obstacles and grievances abound, and illnesses and vexations recur incessantly—there is something like a constant tension or a ratchet that one cannot release on its own—this is summoned by past habituation. This is not the result of a single lifetime...
The conditions of the kalpas are those that have been perfumed moment by moment since beginningless time; therefore, nothing but spiritual power can liberate one from them.
*Mahā-sitātapatra*—which translates as "Great White Parasol"—is precisely the hidden mind (*garbha-citta*).

Its measure encompasses the *koṭi* of worlds, hence it is called "Great. Its essence is utterly free from delusive defilement, hence it is called "White. Its function is to cover all things, hence it is called a "parasol" (*chattra*).

Because the divine mantra flows forth from this, it is named the "Heart Mantra. As for the "One Whose Crown Is Invisible," the *Kalyāṇamitra* of the ninth stage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* himself declared her to be the Buddha’s wet nurse;
when he was first born, she personally cradled him and gazed intently, yet could not see his crown. Thus, she revealed the crown.
The Dharma cannot be seen by means of seeing. △ Second, showing the spiritual power of the mantra:
Furthermore, regarding your past lives with Mātanga, the causes and conditions spanning kalpas and the habitual tendencies of affectionate love were not formed in only one lifetime or a single kalpa;
yet, as soon as I proclaimed [the mantra], your heart of desire was forever severed and you became an Arhat. She was but a courtesan.
"Practicing without a deliberate mind, you were secretly sustained by spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

How is it that you śrāvakas now gathered here seek the Supreme Vehicle and resolve to attain Buddhahood? It is like raising a handful of dust in a favorable wind; what difficulty or peril could there be?"

Even one with the defiled nature of a *ḍākinī* can still swiftly realize [the goal]; how much more so for those who are vessels for the Śrāvaka path, who are naturally endowed with the conditions for spiritual darkness?
How could it be otherwise? △ Third, the ritual rules for reciting mantras.
If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment, they must first maintain the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu.
They should certainly select a preeminent śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher. Should they fail to encounter such a truly pure monk, [they should proceed as follows].
Your observance of the precepts will certainly not be perfected. Once the precepts have been accomplished, put on new, clean garments, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion.
Recite this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times, and thereafter perform the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandhana*) and establish the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
One should pray to the unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in lands throughout the ten directions to emit rays of great compassionate light and descend to anoint one’s crown.

For the teacher is the model for humanity and the source from which both the correct and the deviant emerge; thus, without encountering a foremost true monk, the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) cannot be perfected.
Reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times symbolizes the extinction of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
Ānanda, if in the final age there are pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors who extinguish greed and lust in their hearts, uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha,
and within a place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) make the vows of a bodhisattva; if they enter and exit for bathing and practice the Way during the six periods of the day and night,
remaining thus without sleep for twenty-one days, I shall manifest my own body before those people and stroke their heads.
He comforts them and causes them to attain awakening.

When the roots of their precepts are pure and their vows and practices are sincere, they are then able to evoke a spiritual response. △ Fourth, the ritual procedures for concluding the altar, in two parts.
Ānanda questioned in detail.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already been awakened.

I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When establishing a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) for cultivation during the Dharma-ending age, how should one perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*)?"

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose conduct is pure, was asked for a detailed explanation of the ritual procedures for establishing the maṇḍala. Regarding the statement "knowing for oneself the cultivation and realization," it means that one knows the mantra’s power provides secret assistance, and the holy fruit can be expected.
Part Two: The Buddha’s Compassionate and Detailed Response (in five sections). Section One: The Requisites for the Maṇḍala Site.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the final age wish to establish a site for the Way, they should first take a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the fatty, fragrant herbs of those mountains and drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle."
One may take its dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not a cow from the Snowy Mountains, its dung is foul and unsuitable for coating the ground;
instead, one should dig into a plain until five feet below the surface and take the yellow earth from there.
The preceptor [should take] sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, *kunduruka*, saffron, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *nīlāguru*, *turuṣka*, *kālānusāri*, and clove;
with these ten kinds, he should grind them into a fine powder, mix it with earth to form mud, and smear it upon the ground of the site.
The Dharma-king’s words on the Dharma accord with both phenomena and principle. Phenomena do not arise in isolation, nor are phenomena established in vain.

Just as a single word of the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-gate would exhaust the ink of the oceans without being fully written out, so too the characteristics of the five stages are manifested through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In every arrangement and provision, there is necessarily a symbolic representation; thus, every implement used in this ritual arena is none other than a manifestation of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the mountain represents high ground. The Snowy Mountains signify pure and supreme faith. The great powerful white ox symbolizes the pure and great root.
The fragrant herbs and pure water represent wondrous, excellent, and pure wisdom. The lush growth, fullness, and abundance signify the surplus [of merit].
Sandalwood is the foremost among the ten fragrances; it is the synthesis of the ten perfections and the crown of the myriad practices. Its origin is in the level [ground].
The earth signifies faith. The ground has not yet been purified. From among the five numbers and within the yellow color, one takes the "middle-of-the-middle" to signify pure faith.
The ten fragrances are the fragrance of the Dharma of the ten *pāramitās*. The fine silk is woven into threads;
by spreading them out, they constitute the subtle and wondrous myriad practices. Now, one who wishes to take up the site of the Tathāgata’s nirvana must necessarily base themselves upon this.
Vast faith serves as the support for pure wisdom; nurtured by wondrous goodness, it forms a single, great root.
Being so full and overflowing that it is sufficient to harmonize with the incense-flower crown of the ten pāramitās, it can adorn and perfect the site of nirvāṇa.
Since this supreme faith and great root are unattainable, one seeks the next best; therefore, the middle [faith] is taken.

Regarding the middle level of faith: although one may not yet be able to surpass the ten perfections and myriad practices, one who can nonetheless embody them will likewise be able to achieve solemn completion.
Construct an octagonal altar measuring sixteen feet square; at the center of the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood.
Place the alms bowl within the flowers. First, fill the bowl with dew collected during the eighth month; within the water, place whatever flower petals are available.
The altar represents the essence of tranquil extinction and ultimate reality. Since this essence is endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path, it is octagonal.

Because it can subdue the eight types of heterodox paths, it measures sixteen feet square. The lotus flower at the center of the altar represents the wondrous practice of the Middle Way. As for the lotus, its flower...
In reality, they share the same essence; defilement and purity originate from the same source. This expresses the general principle of sublime practice.

Those fashioned from gold, silver, copper, and wood represent the specific manifestations of sublime practice. Gold and silver, though refined a hundred times, become ever more pure yet remain unchanged;
copper is hard yet capable of being shaped—these are symbols of righteousness (*yi*). Wood can grow upward to cover what lies beneath—it is a symbol of benevolence (*ren*).
Now, relying on the essence to give rise to practice, one must be refined yet unchanging, firm yet capable of harmony.

Whether regulating through righteousness or encompassing through benevolence, one avoids both excess and deficiency; all such practices converge upon the Middle Way, and it is precisely for this reason that they constitute wondrous conduct.

The alms bowl is the appropriate vessel; it symbolizes responding to things according to their measure. The dew represents the moisture of the shade; it falls in the eighth month of autumn, the very midst of autumn.

The flowers and leaves upon the water represent the conduct of benevolent coverage; they follow wherever the moisture is bestowed, which again signifies responding to things according to their measure.
This is a manifestation of the latent transformation through the hidden benefits of the shade.

Take eight round mirrors and place each in its respective direction surrounding the flower bowl. Outside the mirrors, establish sixteen lotus flowers, with sixteen incense burners interspersed among the flowers.
Adorn the incense burners by burning pure aloeswood incense, ensuring that the flames are not visible.

The "perfect mirror" refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). The arrangement of flower bowls surrounding each [mirror] on all eight sides signifies that wisdom and its practice are mutually dependent, responding appropriately to every direction.
The placement of sixteen lotus flowers and incense burners interspersed outside the mirrors signifies...
Flowers symbolize wondrous conduct; incense symbolizes wondrous virtue. "Outside the mirror" refers to that which is beyond correct wisdom.

Through the establishment of skillful means, the heterodox and the orthodox are made to encompass one another, and virtuous conduct and practice mutually perfume one another. It is hoped that through this, over time they will both be transformed, such that both the heterodox and the orthodox are forgotten.
To burn pure aloeswood incense alone so that no fire is seen means to reverse the functioning of the treasury of virtues and extinguish and subdue both vitarka and vicāra;

only then can one accord with the ground of quiescent extinction. Someone might say: "While this may be so as a symbolic representation of the Dharma, how can it be that the ancient masters did not understand it?
Does this not constitute a mere speculative interpretation? I reply: That which I venerate is the *Avataṃsaka-mahā-śāstra*. If you examine it thoroughly, you will know this.
This is not a mere conjecture. △ Second, the ritual for the offering and sacrifice:
take the milk of a white cow and place it in sixteen vessels. Make pancakes from the milk, along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, and milk porridge.
Sūhaka, honeyed ginger, pure ghee, and pure honey— each of these sixteen kinds [of offerings] surrounding the exterior of the lotus flower were presented to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.

The outer layer represents offering the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna to the two Honored Ones. While the provisional teachings permit milk and curd, the ultimate teachings prohibit them;
yet they are taken here to be offered. This is intended to harmonize the provisional and the ultimate, and to unify the heterodox and the orthodox.

Furthermore, the eight flavors, each surrounded by sixteen [petals] outside the flowers, represent the joy of the Dharma that follows practice as it harmonizes the provisional and encompasses the heterodox.
This is the ritual arrangement.
At every mealtime, or during the middle watch of the night, take half a *śuṅga* of honey and three *caturaṅgula* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
In front of the altar, separately install a small fire-pit. Boil *turuṣka* incense to extract scented water, bathe the charcoal with it, and kindle it until it blazes fiercely.
[He] blazes. He casts this ghee and honey into the flaming furnace, burning them until the smoke is exhausted, to offer as a sacrifice to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Since the Buddha receives food at midday, he presents the offering every day at midday; the offerings at midnight follow the same pattern as those at midday.
Honey is produced from flowers; this symbolizes the harmonious practice of the Dharma. Ghee is produced from milk; this symbolizes the harmonious flavor of the Dharma.
"Half" refers to the middle number, while "three" refers to the completed number. The small furnace, one square inch in size, is the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*).

Using incense to moisten the charcoal is the method for awakening the mind. King Bhaiṣajyarāja first consumed *turuṣka* incense before burning his own body; this signifies that the intention is capable [of such sacrifice].

Flames burst forth; therefore, take charcoal from a funeral pyre and kindle it until it blazes fiercely. Cast ghee and honey into the flaming furnace and burn them until the smoke is entirely consumed.

Once the ritual practice is thus completed, one must not remain stagnant at the end. One should instead forge and refine the awakened mind with vigor, causing habitual tendencies to be melted away all at once and the shadows of conditions to vanish together.
Suddenly, it shall be as the saying goes: "Snow falling upon a red-hot furnace. Thus it is.
Later, he was honored by the Buddha. Now, for those who dwell in the field of quiescent extinction and partake of the joy of dhyāna, they should here exert their utmost effort.
III. Rituals for the Installation of Images.
Have banners and flowers suspended everywhere on the four outer sides. Within the ritual chamber, arrange images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions upon the four walls.

One should display an image of Vairocana facing forward; alongside it, place images of Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and the various great emanations of Avalokiteśvara, with Vajragarbha installed to their left and right.
Śakra, the King Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, along with Kṣitigarbha, the various Cundās, and Bhṛkuṭī,
as well as the Four Heavenly Kings and Pināyaka, were stationed on the left and right sides at the entrance.
The four outer banners and flowers represent the adornments of the outer practice. The four rows within the hall represent the four natural reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
Regarding the four reliances in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Mount Gushan’s verse states: "The five stages and the ten faiths constitute the first; the ten abidings are the second;
the practices, the directions, and the grounds are the third; equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment are the fourth. The true state of the tranquil site belongs to Vairocana and his peers."
The Lord. Maitreya is the True Lord who shall come in the future. Akṣobhya dwells in the East; Amitābha dwells in the West; they are the Lords of Wisdom and Compassion.
The various great transformations and forms of Avalokiteśvara are the Lords who harmonize with those above and unite with those below.
Vajragarbha constantly leads the Vajra-holders to protect those who recite mantras, subduing māras and severing obstacles; he is the True Lord. [Beside the Gate]...
The assembly surrounding him, including Śakra and Brahmā, provides powerful external protection. In the practice of the Dharma-ending age, all rely upon this;
if there is even a single deficiency, success will certainly not be achieved. Ucchuṣma, the Fire-Headed Vajra; Nīladaṇḍa, the Blue-Faced Vajra;
and Cundā, the Vajra of Various Names—these are alternative titles. Bhṛkuṭī is also one who possesses great supernatural transformations. Bhṛ...
The *Ruru-vikurvaṇa-sūtra* states: "On the left is Bhṛkuṭī, who has three eyes, holds a garland, and wears her hair in a topknot.
Piṇāka is the pair of messengers known as the Pig-Headed and Elephant-Nosed ones.
Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in the void, facing the mirrors installed within the ritual arena,
so that their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers.
The mirror within the altar is mixed with phenomena and has a support; this is the wisdom of the practitioner.
The mirror in space is detached from phenomena and has no support; this is the wisdom of the Buddhas. That which is mixed with phenomena and has a support can only reflect objects;

before it can fully reflect them, one must necessarily attain the wisdom that is detached from phenomena and without support. Only when these two function in mutual interdependence can [the practitioner] then [reflect all things].
I and others illuminate one another; mind and phenomena are both fused. The bodies and lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate.

Without moving a step and without waiting for a thought to arise, every dharma is omnipresent and every phenomenon is unimpeded. When one lifts the eyes, the thousand sages appear simultaneously; wherever one touches, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest.
With a single flower or a single incense offering, one makes offerings throughout all dust-like lands; with a single practice or a single characteristic, one expands and fills all space.
It is infinite. It does not rely upon supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), nor does it involve conceptual thought. In the place of quiescence, every dharma is fundamentally thus.
The cultivation and realization of the secret cause reach their ultimate subtlety here. △ Fourth, the ritual for holding the mantra.
During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat.

Constantly throughout the six periods of the day and night, one should recite mantras around the altar and practice the Way with a sincere heart, performing one hundred and eight recitations during each period.
During the second seven days, one should single-mindedly focus on making Bodhisattva vows, maintaining an uninterrupted state of mind. This is my Vinaya.
First, there is the instruction on the vow. During the third week, one should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s *pāṭala* mantra throughout the twelve periods of the day and night.

By the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will appear simultaneously; at the place where the mirrors reflect one another's light, one shall receive the Buddhas’ empowerment by being touched on the crown of the head.

Thereupon, one cultivates samādhi within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This enables those practicing and studying in such a degenerate age to purify their body and mind until they are as clear and transparent as lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
One transforms into seven, and seven transforms into nine; these are all yang numbers, yet seven occupies the center, being unsurpassed.
This is insufficient; therefore, the ritual site (dojang) takes seven days as its period, yet achieves completion in three.
All that is sought and directed toward is taking refuge in the Triple Gem as the primary expedient means.

Thus, during the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the names of the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats, so as to rely upon their inconceivable power to initiate and assist the practice.

This is the Way. However, without the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), there is nothing by which it can be sustained. Therefore, during the second seven-day period, one relies on the Vinaya teachings to single-mindedly generate the aspiration.
When practice and aspiration are firm and strong, one attains great valor; therefore, during the third seven-day period.

At that time, without interruption and without limit, one recites and maintains the mantra single-mindedly; thus, through sincere devotion, one moves the divine response, and through the power of progress, one achieves the goal.
Where mirrors reflect each other's light, the Buddha-wisdom arises to illuminate; this is the mutual resonance of the Way.

The body and mind become luminous and pure; this means that the subtle and minute obstacles of past habitual tendencies have been completely eradicated. This is the achievement resulting from the power of resonance.
One hundred and eight is the full number of the mantra; if one performs the ritual circumambulation, it is called a "circuit" (zà).
Ānanda, if among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor or the ten bhikṣus of the assembly there is even one who is impure,
such a site of practice will for the most part not be successful.
This is why there are few who obtain spiritual responses at this site of enlightenment today.
After the three-week period, one should sit upright in meditative seclusion for one hundred days. Those of keen faculties may attain the stage of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats;
even if their bodies and minds have not yet achieved the holy fruit, they will certainly know for themselves that their attainment of Buddhahood is unfailing.
Regarding your question on the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*):

it is established in this manner, with rituals complete and the precepts perfected. When one is certain to attain the fruit and realize the state of a *srotāpanna*, this means that one has succeeded in entering the stream of the sages from the stage of an ordinary person;
it does not refer merely to a minor fruit. Therefore, it is said: "Even if the fruit has not yet been attained, one is certain to know that one will become a Buddha. As it is said:
In the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra*, the fourth stage of the ten stages is named *srotāpanna*. This signifies the severance of that which is not a minor fruit.
△ Fifth, the actual exposition of the divine mantra has three parts. First, Ānanda’s sorrowful entreaty.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying: “Since my renunciation of the world, I have relied upon the Buddha’s affectionate love and sought much learning;
yet, because I had not realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I was obstructed by the evil arts of that Brahmā. Though my mind remained clear, my power was not free.
Fortunately, I encountered Mañjuśrī, who caused me to attain liberation. Although I have received the Tathāgata’s secret *uṣṇīṣa* mantra, I have only obtained its benefits in obscurity.”

We have not yet personally heard of its power. We only pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more, to piteously rescue those practitioners in this assembly, as well as all beings in saṃsāra in the future.
By receiving the Buddha’s secret voice, may our bodies and minds be liberated.
All that Ānanda has related serves to admonish those of later learning and reveals the wondrous power of the mantra.
At that time, the entire assembly prostrated themselves, awaiting the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret verses.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s correct exposition has four parts. First, the manifestation of transformations:
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred-jeweled light from his *uṣṇīṣa*. From within the light, there emerged thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses.
There appeared a manifested Tathāgata, seated within a precious lotus flower. From the crown of his head, he emitted ten streams of light composed of a hundred jewels;

from each and every stream of light, there were manifested ten *gaṅgānadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Vajrapāṇis, who held mountains and wielded vajra-clubs, pervading the entire realm of empty space.

The great assembly gazed upward, feeling both awe and affection; seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection, they listened with single-minded devotion as the Tathāgata Amitābha (the One Who Emits Light from the Unseen Summit) proclaimed this divine mantra.
The appearance throughout the light of the majestic and formidable forms of the Vajras demonstrates that this mantra possesses great divine power for destroying Māras and severing obstacles.
Furthermore, this mantra is constantly attended day and night by a retinue of eighty thousand Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
it is for this reason that they appear everywhere. Other meanings have already been explained at the beginning of the sutra and at the start of this volume.
