△ Third: Recording the Merit.
Ānanda, this *Siddhārthapratāraṇa* secret verse from the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya-ghana*, these subtle and wondrous phrases, give birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained supreme, perfect, and universal enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold fast to this mantra-heart to subdue all Māras and restrain all externalists.
The Way: The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, mounting this mantra-heart, sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond in lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, containing this mantra-heart, turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-heart, are able to bestow empowerment by stroking the crown of the head and grant predictions of enlightenment throughout the ten directions. Even when their own fruition is not yet complete, they likewise receive the Buddha’s prediction throughout the ten directions.

Record: The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying upon this mantra-heart, are able to rescue and deliver all beings from suffering throughout the ten directions—namely, those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
those who are blind, deaf, or mute; those suffering from union with the hated and the disliked; those suffering from separation from the beloved; those suffering from not obtaining what they seek;

those whose five aggregates are in a state of intense fever; and those afflicted by various calamities, both great and small. They simultaneously achieve liberation from the perils of bandits, the perils of armies, the perils of kings, and the perils of prisons.
Difficulties—those of wind, fire, and water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty—shall dissolve upon mere recollection.

Following this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions enable one to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions, making offerings according to one’s wishes during the four modes of deportment.

Among the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they shall be promoted as Great Dharma Princes. By practicing this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions [attain these powers]. At the ten...
This is precisely that which gathers the immediate causes, enabling those of the Lesser Vehicle to hear the Secret Treasury without giving rise to alarm or fear.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart; thereby they achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart, so that after their parinirvāṇa, the affairs of the Buddha-dharma may be entrusted and ultimately maintained, and the precepts may be strictly purified.
The precepts will all become completely pure. If I were to recite this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya-Pāṭala Dhāraṇī from dawn until dusk,
with the sounds linked together and the words and phrases not overlapping in the intervals, it could never be exhausted even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
What is called the "mantra-heart" (*hṛdaya-mantra*) is the Great White Parasol, vast and untainted, which completely covers the *dharmadhātu*.
It is the secret dharma-gate of the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind. Precisely because it is vast and all-encompassing, it is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
By upholding and relying upon it, one is able to give birth to all Buddhas, achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, subdue demons through transformation, and rescue beings from their manifold sufferings;
as for other merits, they could not be fully described even in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. "Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, etc.
briefly cites four of the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*); "enmity and hatred, separation from loved ones, etc. briefly cites four of the eight sufferings (*aṣṭau duḥkhāni*).

Furthermore, the *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* states: "There are nine great calamities and innumerable minor calamities. To "gathering those with whom one has a karmic affinity" means to gather all those who share a causal connection.
It is also said that this mantra is named the "Crown of the Tathāgata. You who are still in training and have not yet exhausted the cycle of saṃsāra must give rise to a sincere mind.

To attain arhatship without upholding this mantra, yet sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) such that one’s body and mind remain far removed from all demonic activities—such a thing is impossible.
The above reveals the realm of the Tathāgata; this clarifies that it also encompasses gradual cultivation. △ Four: Exhortation to Uphold, in three parts. First, the general [exhortation].
I exhort you, Ānanda: if, in any world, among the sentient beings of any given land, this dhāraṇī is written down on birch bark, conch leaves, paper, silk,
or white woolen cloth according to what is produced in that land, and stored in a fragrant pouch— should the minds of these people be clouded and they be unable [to recite it],...

Recite it from memory, or wear it on the body, or write it within one's home; one should know that such a person will, for the remainder of their life, be incapable of being harmed by any poison whatsoever.
△ Second, the manifestation of the benefits, in two parts.
First, the heading: "Ānanda, I shall now further speak this mantra for you, to protect and deliver the world, to attain great fearlessness, and to bring about the supramundane wisdom of all beings."
△ Second, the explanation: If,
after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite this themselves or teach others to recite it,
you should know that such sentient beings who uphold it through recitation cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by either great or small poisons.
In this way, even the evil spells of nāgas, devas, ghosts, spirits, earth deities, and māras cannot take hold;

the mind attains right concentration (*samādhi*). All curses, malevolent incantations, poisons, mercury-based poisons, silver-based poisons, and those derived from plants, trees, insects, or snakes [are likewise neutralized].
The poisonous vapors of the myriad things, upon entering the mouth of such a person, become the flavor of nectar.
All malevolent stars, as well as all ghosts and spirits who harbor cruel hearts and poison others, cannot give rise to evil toward such a person.
Pināyaka and all the other evil kings of ghosts, along with their retinues, shall all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.

This is what is meant by "protecting the world and attaining great fearlessness. Because one benefits others through the recitation of mantras, all the evil kings of ghosts perceive this as a profound kindness.
Furthermore, gold and silver, when incorporated into medicine, may potentially give rise to toxicity.

Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Ganges-sands of the family of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, each of whom has a retinue of vajra-beings.

Day and night he shall attend upon them. If there are sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind and not in a state of samādhi, remember this Vajra King in their hearts and hold it in their mouths, this Vajra King will constantly follow those sons of good family; how much more so for those whose bodhicitta is resolute!
These Vajra Bodhisattvas, Kings of the Treasury, with their refined minds acting with subtle swiftness, awaken that divine consciousness.
At that moment, this person’s mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons, comprehending them all-pervasively and attaining freedom from doubt.
This refers to the accomplishment of supramundane wisdom for the sake of sentient beings. The first section of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s enumeration of the one hundred and twenty great numbers states:
"One hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi; one koṭi times one koṭi constitutes one ayuta; one ayuta times one ayuta constitutes one nayuta.

This corresponds here to the Chinese system of counting: hundred, thousand, ten thousand, million, ten million, hundred million, billion, ten billion, hundred billion, trillion, ten trillion, hundred trillion, quadrillion, and quintillion.
One *śata* (姟) is ten million; one *koṭi* (洛叉) is one hundred million; one *kūṭi* (俱胝) is a billion; and one *nayuta* (那由他) is ten billion (*śata*).
"The subtle mind secretly and swiftly" means that the wondrous mind secretly and rapidly provides the impetus for development. △ Third, the extensive manifestation of the ten [qualities]:
first, not falling into the evil realms.
From the first kalpa until their final body, in every successive birth, they shall not be born as yakṣas,
rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and so forth, nor as any of the various hungry ghosts, whether possessing form or formless.
The realms of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and such evil places— good sons who read, recite, copy, transcribe, wear, or store [this],
and who offer various forms of worship, shall not be born in states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness throughout kalpa after kalpa.
"One kalpa" refers to the beginning of the practice of cultivation; "the final body" refers to the completion of the practice of cultivation. △ Second, the acquisition of a mass of merit:
Even if these sentient beings themselves do not perform meritorious deeds, all the merits possessed by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions [will accrue to them].

He gives all of these to this person. By virtue of this, for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—indeed, unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—he shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas.
His immeasurable merits will be like a cluster of akṣa fruits, cultivated together in one place, never to be dispersed.

One does not perform conditioned karma, yet spontaneously attains the merit of the untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the numerical scales of the *Avataṃsaka*: one hundred and twenty is called an *asaṃkhyeya*;
one hundred and three corresponds to an "unspeakable-unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*), which is one hundred and nineteen.
The name "akṣa-fruit" refers to those that must necessarily grow in clusters. △ Third, the accomplishment of the various practices.
Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of discipline; it enables those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them;
it causes those who lack diligence to achieve diligence; it enables those without wisdom to attain wisdom; it allows those who are impure to quickly attain purity;
and it enables those who do not observe the fast and precepts to spontaneously fulfill them.
That Mātanga attained the fruit [of realization] serves as irrefutable proof. Nevertheless, one must find the right person to uphold it;

thus, it was previously stated that if one is not pure, one cannot achieve success, and it was subsequently stated that if one maintains the precepts according to the Dharma, one will certainly attain mental penetration.
Practitioners should examine this; do not merely harbor vain hopes. △ Fourth, the extinguishing of light and heavy offenses:

Ānanda, when these good sons uphold this mantra, even if they have violated prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all offenses of breaking the precepts—whether light or heavy—are simultaneously extinguished after upholding the mantra.
Even if they should subsequently drink alcohol or consume [forbidden food], [the offenses are still removed].
Regarding the various impurities of the five pungent roots, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, spirits, and ghosts do not regard them as transgressions.
Even if one wears impure or tattered clothing, whether walking or staying still, they are entirely pure.
Even if one does not construct an altar, enter a ritual site, or practice the Way, if they recite and uphold this mantra, it is equivalent to entering the altar and practicing the Way.
There is no difference in their merit. If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution,
or the four parājikas and eight saṃghāvaśeṣas of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, once this mantra has been recited, such grave karmic offenses will be entirely eradicated—
just as a fierce wind blows apart a heap of sand— leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.

"Unreceived" refers to drinking, eating, and so forth prior to receiving the mantra; all such acts are said to be past transgressions. The four *pārājika* offenses for a bhikṣu are the aforementioned four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*);
having committed them, one must be expelled and may no longer dwell in community. For a bhikṣuṇī, there are eight *pārājika* offenses, which add the three:
touching [a man], the eighth offense, and concealing [another's grave offense]. △ Fifth: Eliminating Past Obstructions.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas past, have accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstacles,
which they have not yet had the opportunity to repent for since previous lives— if they can read, recite, copy, or write this mantra, or wear it upon their person,
or place it within their dwelling, house, garden, or villa— then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in hot water; before long, it shall all be exhausted.
They shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). △ Sixth, the fulfillment of what is sought according to one's vows:
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women who have not yet given birth to sons or daughters and desire to conceive, if they can [practice] with a sincere heart...
Recall this mantra. Or, if one wears this *Sītātapatrā* upon the body, sons and daughters endowed with merit and wisdom will be born.
Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who desire that their karmic rewards be swiftly fulfilled shall quickly attain fulfillment.
It is likewise so for the physical vitality and strength of one's life. After the end of life, one shall proceed according to one’s vows.

They will be born in the lands and kingdoms of the ten directions; they will certainly not be born in frontier regions or among the lowly, much less in various hybrid forms—referring here to such classes as ghosts and animals.
△ Seventh, they can bring peace and stability to their homes and nations.
Ānanda, if in any kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages there should be famine, pestilence, or the calamities of war, bandits, and strife,
as well as all other lands beset by misfortune, one should transcribe this divine mantra and place it at the four gates of the city,
as well as upon various caityas or the tops of towers. One should cause all sentient beings within that land to welcome this mantra and pay it homage.
With reverence and single-minded devotion, they made offerings and caused each of their people to wear it upon their bodies or place it within their respective dwellings;
thus, all calamities and misfortunes were entirely extinguished.
*Cetiya* means a place worthy of offerings; it is a general term for a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*). *Dhvaja* means a banner.
△ When the people are eight years old, they will be prosperous and happy.
Ānanda, in every place and in every land where sentient beings possess this mantra, the devas and nāgas will rejoice, and the winds and rains [will be timely].
The seasons will proceed in their proper order; the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will be peaceful and happy.

Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars, so that regional portents, transformations, and calamitous obstructions do not arise. No one shall suffer untimely death; they shall not be bound by cangues, fetters, stocks, or shackles.
Day and night they shall sleep in peace, never having evil dreams.
△ The nine calamities shall not occur. Ānanda, in this Sahā world-system, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous evil stars,
with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders, and furthermore, eight great malevolent stars acting as their sovereigns, manifesting in various forms.
In the present age, it can produce various calamities and anomalies among sentient beings; yet where this mantra-ground exists, they are all entirely extinguished.
Within a radius of twelve yojanas, it becomes a consecrated boundary (sīmābandha) that no evil omens or disasters can ever enter.

When Heaven reverses the seasons and things act contrary to principle, these are all causes for calamity; yet such reversal and contrariety are fundamentally due to human beings, while Heaven and the natural world merely respond accordingly.
What are called "calamitous transformations" and "malevolent stars" are responses to the disasters and evils of human beings.
The eighty-four thousand [deities] correspond to the afflictions and karma of sentient beings, while the twenty-eight [lunar mansions] correspond to the four...

Regarding the principles of the directions: there are eight, which correspond to the fundamental patterns of the Five Elements. As for Ketu, Rāhu, and Śani, if they move in accordance with the proper order, blessings will respond; if they move in opposition, calamities will respond.

This is what is meant by "following the path of kindness brings good fortune, while following the path of opposition brings misfortune. That they can produce portents of disaster is simply because they are responding to such opposition.
For instance, when comets, meteors, or flying stars appear as responses, it is due to their shared *bhāga* (division/destiny), not because of the actions of the stars themselves. Now...
Because the power of the mantra accords with a hundredfold auspiciousness, all malevolent transformations are utterly extinguished. Celestial calamities and portents do not enter its borders;
"portents" refers to the prior manifestation of good or bad fortune. △ Tenth, the concluding exhortation to the practitioner.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect all beginners and practitioners in future ages,
so that they may enter samādhi with body and mind at ease, attain great peace and security, and be free from all demons, ghosts, and spirits.
As well as the karmic calamities and宿殃 (past misfortunes) from beginningless time, and the old debts of karma that come to harass and harm you;
you, along with all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, shall rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma.

If those who have received the precepts from a master encounter pure monks and do not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart, then these good sons shall attain mental penetration within this very body born of their parents; otherwise, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.

It is said that when one’s precepts are pure and the mind is sincere and resolute, one can effect such a response. "The mind attains penetration" means that obstructions are eliminated and wisdom becomes luminous, as in the account of Vajragarbha’s swift awakening.
△ Third, the sixfold protection and maintenance through the vows of the assembly: 1. The Vajra Assembly.

Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *vajras* in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, we shall protect with sincere heart those who thus cultivate bodhi."
△ Second, the assembly of heavenly kings.
At that time, Brahmā-rāja, Śakra-devendra, and the four Great Heavenly Kings also simultaneously prostrated themselves before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this manner, we shall protect them with our whole hearts and utmost sincerity."
It causes all that one has done throughout one's life to be fulfilled according to one's wishes.
This accords with the account of Vinaya Master Daoxuan of the Tang dynasty, who, while practicing the Way, experienced a sudden movement of his feet.
△ Third, the hosts of ghost generals: furthermore, there were immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, and kumbhāṇḍa kings.
The King of the Piśācas, the great kings of the Vināyakas, and the various leaders of the ghosts likewise joined their palms before the Buddha and prostrated themselves.
I also vow to protect and sustain these people, causing their bodhicitta to quickly reach full perfection.
△ Fourth, the assembly of celestial deities.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sun and moon deva-kings, as well as the masters of wind, rain, clouds, and thunder, along with the lord of lightning and others;
the officials who cycle through the years and the retinues of the various stars likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I, too, shall protect these practitioners of the Way, establishing them in the *bodhimaṇḍa* so that they may attain fearlessness.
△ Fifth, the assembly of terrestrial deities:
furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain spirits, sea spirits, and all the numinous essences of the earth, water, land, and air, as well as of all myriad things.
Together with the Wind Deity King and the gods of the Formless Realm, they simultaneously prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi, forever free from the works of Māra."
The Wind Master (Vāyu) circulates the wind; the Wind King (Vāyu-rāja) presides over the wind. These are paired with the Formless Heavens (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Regarding the sequence of deities:
having previously raised Śakra and Brahmā, one then reaches the two heavens [of the Desire Realm]; subsequently raising Earth and Water, the elements of Wind and Fire remain unaccounted for.

Therefore, at the conclusion, the Wind Deity is raised to encompass the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the Formless Heavens are raised to encompass the three realms (*tridhātu*). △ Sixth, the Assembly of Bodhisattvas.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Ganges-sands of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, being within the great assembly, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, as for the meritorious deeds we have cultivated, we have long since attained bodhi; yet we do not enter nirvāṇa, but constantly follow this mantra to provide protection.”
"World-Honored One, regarding those practitioners of the final age who cultivate samādhi and practice correctly— those who thus cultivate the mind seeking right concentration,
whether they are in a place of practice, on a walking path, or even when their minds are distracted as they wander through villages—
we, the members of our assembly, shall always follow and protect such persons. Even if Māra or Maheśvara should seek an opportunity against them,"

It shall ultimately be impossible [to harm them]. All minor spirits and deities shall remain ten *yojanas* away from these virtuous people, with the sole exception of those who have resolved their minds to joyfully practice meditation.

World-Honored One, if such evil Māras or their retinues should wish to come and harass these virtuous people, I shall shatter their heads with my precious mace until they are like fine dust, so that the deeds of these people may always proceed unimpeded.

As you wish. Within the realms of desire and form, there is a deity named Maheśvara, who is none other than the celestial king Māra. This concludes the second section: The Section on the Factors of the Path.
△ Third, the Section on Realizing the Fruit. By practicing through the previously established secret causes and definitive meanings, one may realize the state of Buddhahood at a lofty level.
This is the fruit. Regarding this, Ānanda alone asked about the stages of cultivation and realization.
The World-Honored One’s response begins by enumerating the twelve classes of living beings, followed by the clarification of the fifty-seven stages.

The intention is to enable all sentient beings to rely upon this Dharma-door to enter the state of sagehood from the level of ordinary beings, investigating and perfecting it layer by layer until reaching the ultimate wondrous enlightenment and accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.
The conclusion follows. The text has two parts. First, Ānanda’s inquiry:
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;
regarding our minds subject to outflows (*āsrava*), we have not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation of body and mind."

"How joyful! We have obtained great benefit. World-Honored One, when one thus cultivates and realizes the Buddha-samādhi but has not yet reached nirvāṇa, why is it called the stage of 'dry wisdom' (śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi)?
Regarding the forty-four minds, at what gradual stage does one obtain the vision of cultivation?"

"To what place does one go to be said to have entered the stages? What is meant by an 'Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva'? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
The great assembly, with single-minded devotion, awaited the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him in rapt attention.
The ultimate fruit of the noble stages is called *nirvāṇa*. The initial cause is called "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

From dry wisdom, one enters the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and orientation, as well as the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), which constitute forty-four moments of mind; these are the stage of faith, understanding, and practice, designated as the "stage of cultivation."
Advancing further to the tenth stage is called "entering the stages"; this constitutes the initial realization. Reaching the eleventh stage is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*Samyaksambodhi*);
this is still a partial realization. Upon reaching *Nirvāṇa*, it is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*Miaojue*); this is the ultimate realization. To gaze fixedly is called "staring" (*deng*);
to darken the mind is called "blurred vision" (*meng*). II. The Buddha’s Compassionate Instruction (in two parts): A. Praising and Granting Permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You have been able to universally act for the sake of the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future age who cultivate *samādhi* seeking the Mahāyāna, starting from the level of ordinary persons."
He brings one to the ultimate Great Nirvana and reveals from afar the unsurpassed path of correct practice. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, emptied their minds, and silently received the teaching.

To hollow out and eliminate miscellaneous thoughts is to receive the teaching with a vacant mind. II. An Extensive Exposition in Five Parts. First, the Original Absence of Cultivation and Realization.
The Buddha said: "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there have been no worlds or sentient beings."
△ Second, cultivation exists because of delusion;
birth exists because of delusion; and extinction exists because of birth. Birth and extinction are termed "delusion," while the cessation of delusion is termed "truth.
This is called the Tathāgata’s supreme bodhi and great nirvāṇa—the two designations for the transformation of the basis.
Arising and ceasing, truth and falsehood, bodhi and nirvāṇa—all these are what are called various names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
Within the wondrous nature, they are fundamentally and perfectly detached. It is due to the causes of deluded appearances that there is cultivation and realization;

thus, one turns from non-awakening to rely upon bodhi, and turns from birth-and-death to rely upon nirvāṇa—these are termed the two "reliance-transformations" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). △ Third, causing...
There are two causes for the delusion of consciousness. First, a brief enumeration:

Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true *samādhi* and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world. When inversion does not arise, this is the true *samādhi* of the Tathāgata.
Samādhi. The preceding section clarified the three types of continuity; this section clarifies the two causes of inversion, speaking of them by way of expansion and contraction.

The subsequent statement, "perfumed so as to form karma," subsumes both karma and its fruit. However, while the former clarified the characteristics of arising, this clarifies cultivation and abandonment.
The essential point is that while the meaning is the same, the contexts differ. By cultivating *samādhi*, one can recognize the causes of inversion; only then can one sever and treat them.
When inverted delusions do not arise, one returns to the true nature. Therefore, it is said: "This is the Tathāgata’s true *samādhi*. Part Two:
A Detailed Explanation, in Three Sections. First: A General Account of the Causes of Inversion.
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the luminosity of the mind is perfect, the nature arises from that luminosity;
from this, deluded vision is produced. From ultimate non-existence, there is established ultimate existence. This existence is what they possess.

It is not that which is caused by causes, nor is it the characteristic of that which abides in what is abided upon; it is utterly devoid of a fundamental root. Taking this non-abiding as its basis, it establishes the worlds and all sentient beings.
"The nature is luminous mind" refers to the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The nature is luminously perfect" means that it does not abide in its own nature. Because of this...
Because it does not maintain its own nature, deluded luminosity gives rise to a deluded nature; because of this deluded nature, deluded vision arises.
Thus, from the formless reality, there is established the delusion of having form. Therefore, it is said that from ultimate non-existence, absolute existence is formed.
Yet, this capacity to exist and that which exists, this capacity to dwell and that in which one dwells—all of these are neither causes nor the objects of causes. All of them...
They are utterly without root; this is seen from their mutual relationship in the text. Based on this non-abiding, worlds and sentient beings are established;
thus one knows that these two are without cause and without root, being entirely nothing more than inverted delusions. △ Second, the branching out into two inversions.
First, the inversion of sentient beings.
Delusion of the fundamentally perfect luminosity gives rise to the false and illusory. This illusory nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it relies.

Deluded regarding the Truth, the false arises, and the myriad characteristics compete to manifest; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). This clarifies the root from which delusion arises; what follows clarifies the characteristics of their competitive manifestation.

Desiring to return to the True, one seeks the True; yet that which is sought as True is not the true nature of Suchness. Seeking to restore what is not-True results only in the manifestation of non-characteristics.
It is neither arising nor abiding; it is neither mind nor dharmas. Through successive occurrences, the power of arising brings forth illumination, and through perfuming, karma is formed.
Karmas of like kind resonate with one another. Because there is karmic resonance, they mutually extinguish and mutually give rise [to states]. For this reason, sentient beings undergo perversion;
because they are deluded regarding their original nature, a mind of longing arises in their desire to restore the true state.

Since they have already lost the truth themselves, it is said that "desiring the true" means that what was previously considered true is not actually the True Suchness (Tathatā). To seek to restore the true by means of that which is not true is, in fact, a delusion.

It transforms into delusion; thus it is said that "non-characteristics are fully manifested. Consequently, the mental dharmas of arising and abiding compete to develop and evolve through mutual perfuming and conditioning, so that various characteristics arise in competition.
That which is non-existent yet suddenly appears is called "arising" (*utpāda*). That which, having arisen, remains for a brief moment is called "abiding" (*sthiti*).
The continuity of objective reflection is called "mind" (*citta*). The differentiation between defilement and purity is called "dharmas" (*dharma*). Thus do sentient beings fall into perversion.
From this, they arise. △ Second, the inversion of the world. Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of the world?
It is that which exists as having something to possess; it is the false arising of fragmented divisions. Because of this, the realm is established;
it is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abode. It flows on without staying still, and because of this, the world is formed. The three periods of time...
The four directions intermingle and harmonize with one another, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.
This is explained by restating the preceding meanings: that "that which exists" and "all that belongs to it" are not caused by causes, and so forth.

Because there is "that which exists," there is temporal division; because there is temporal division, there are spatial directions. Since the realms constitute spatial directions, these realms are established on this basis.
Furthermore, where there is no cause, there is no abiding. Where there is no abiding, there is constant flux.
Because the world is characterized by flux, it is through this that the world is formed. The three periods of time and the four directions comprise twelve transformations;
thus, those who move within them all follow these changes. This is the origin of the world’s inversion. △ Third, a detailed explanation of the principles of transformation.
Second: The one source undergoes twelve transformations.
Therefore, in the world, sound arises because of movement; form arises because of sound; fragrance arises because of form; and touch arises because of fragrance.
Because of contact there is flavor; because of flavor one knows phenomena. These six deluded false imaginings constitute the nature of karma;
thus the twelve divisions revolve by means of this. Therefore, the world’s sounds, odors, tastes, and touches, exhausting the twelve transformations, form a single cycle of recurrence.
All things arise from movement to take on form. Movement produces sound; form is color. Therefore it is said that sound exists because of movement, and color exists because of sound.
Fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects all come into being through mutual dependence upon these.
From these six sense-objects, the six faculties are aroused; these are called the six deluded false thoughts. They constitute the very root of affliction and karma; hence they are so named.

The nature of karma: it is because of this that the twelve classes of beings transmigrate. "Worldly sounds, smells, tastes, and touches" refers back to the aforementioned six categories of deluded妄想 (vikalpa).
This means that since their divisions are each twelvefold, their transformations are likewise each twelvefold;

thus, the forms of the six deluded disturbances evolve from ignorance conditioned by volitional formations (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), finally [reaching the end].
And thus it begins again. Therefore it is said: "Exhausting the twelve transformations, they form one cycle and then repeat. △ Second, the analysis of the twelve classes [of beings], in three parts.
First, the general heading:
Because they ride upon this wheel of revolving delusion, there are worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth.

There are those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with form nor without form, and those who are neither with perception nor without perception.
These revolving, inverted characteristics are precisely the six types of deluded conceptualization. △ Second, a detailed explanation of the twelve [links]. First:

O Ānanda, regarding birth from eggs: due to the causes of the world’s false saṃsāra and its fluctuating inversions, the combination of vapors produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Thus there exist egg-born kalala beings, who transmigrate through lands as fish and birds.
Turtles and snakes abound in their species; their eggs are produced solely through thought.
This "emptiness" is precisely thought itself. The essence of thought is buoyant and swift, which is termed "agitated inversion.

The egg is formed through the intermingling of vital energies, termed "formation through the blending of harmonious qi. When thoughts frequently fluctuate between rising and sinking, it is termed "confused thoughts of flying and diving"; thus, they evoke fish.

Birds are of the category of those that fly and sink. As for the eighty-four thousand types within each of the twelve categories, these arise respectively from the transformations induced by the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
*Kalala* (羯邏藍) means "coagulated mucus"; it is the initial stage of entering the womb, the state when the embryo and the amniotic sac have not yet differentiated. △ Second, birth from a womb.
Due to the inversion of desire that causes the world to revolve in defilement, eighty-four thousand transverse and vertical disordered thoughts are combined and nurtured into formation.
Because of this, there is the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī* stages of the womb, as beings transmigrate through various lands—whether as humans, animals, dragons, or seers.
Their kind fills [the world]. The womb is caused by emotion; that which is defiled is precisely emotion. Emotion arises from craving, which is termed the inversion of desire.

The womb involves the union of semen, which is termed the formation through blending and nourishment. Emotion has its biases and correctness, which are termed horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts. Thus, one receives a human [birth].
The categories of horizontal and vertical birth include the *arbuda*, which is called a "bubble"; this refers to the stage where the embryo or egg gradually begins to differentiate.
Delusion, affliction, attachment, and obstruction are possessed by all sentient beings; however, they are born into specific classes according to whichever of these factors is predominant.

The *kalala* and other stages are present in both womb-born and egg-born beings, yet they are described in sequence because the preceding stage can possess the succeeding one, whereas the succeeding stage does not [possess the preceding].
As before. △ Third, moisture-born beings:
due to the world’s attachment to the inverted courses of saṃsāra, through the union of warmth, eighty-four thousand thoughts of overturning and confusion are formed.
Because of this, there are moisture-born *kalala* (embryonic stages) that flow and circulate within lands, containing crawling and wriggling creatures.

Their kinds fill and pervade all. Moisture acts through union and response; attachment is precisely this union. Union arises from the stagnation of craving; as one encounters objects and rushes toward them, it is called "perversion of the destination.
Moisture generates life through yang-energy; this is called "the formation of warmth through conjunction. Since the destination is not fixed, it is called "reversal and confusion."
Because of [the state of] ideation (*saṃjñā*), one is reborn among the class of wriggling and crawling creatures that turn over and over. "Bishu" (蔽尸) refers to soft flesh;
it is the initial sign of moisture-born beings (*samsvedaja*). All ten modes of birth are rooted in lustful desire and arise from emotional ideation.

Because deluded emotions become increasingly false, the principles of transformation become ever more discordant, leading to the point where they dissipate into emptiness or become as inert as wood and stone. Although the branches of delusion differ, the root of delusion is the same.
First. △ Fourth, birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Due to the false inversion caused by the world’s cycle of changing and transmigrating, eighty-four thousand new and old disordered thoughts are formed through the conjunction of contact.
Because of this, there are transformed *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through lands, shedding their forms and flying about.
These types fill the world.
Transformation through detachment and responsive change is precisely detachment (*vairāgya*). To leave this and rely upon that is called "false inversion.

To touch various categories and undergo transformation is called "the formation of contact through conjunction. Because the old turns and the new approaches, it is called "the confusion of thoughts regarding the new and the old. Thus, retribution is experienced.
It is likewise because one sheds the old to proceed toward the new. Just as when a worm becomes a butterfly, its movement shifts from crawling to flying;
or as when a sparrow becomes a clam, it sheds its flight for submergence. Generally, whenever one form is transmitted to another through transformation, it is a process of shedding and metamorphosis.

*Kalala* is called "hard flesh. *Arbuda* (蛻) immediately forms a body and lacks the characteristic of softness. From this point downward, those referred to as *kalala* are general designations for all classes [of beings].

This is the case up to the fifth stage, *peśī* (鉢羅奢佉), which is called "formation of shape," at which point each follows its specific appearance and is no longer a general designation. △ Five: Those with Form (*rūpin*).

Due to the obstruction of the world’s causal stagnation and the cycle of samsara, and because of inverted views, these combine and coalesce to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of radiant brilliance.
Consequently, there arise the physical forms of *kalala* (embryonic stages), beings that transmigrate through various lands, and spirits of auspicious and inauspicious power.

Their kinds fill and obstruct all space. True nature is fused and tranquil; fundamentally, it is neither obstructive nor luminous. Due to delusion and stagnation, it becomes obstructive saṃsāra, veiling and losing its fusion and tranquility.
It falsely unites with brightness and attachment; clinging to the tranquil essence, it emits light and thereby forms a refined radiance. Rest!
The three luminaries are their manifestations; calamities are manifested as *pō* (comets) and *suì* (meteors). All brilliant spiritual entities (*shénwù*) are characterized by such refined radiance.
Because their conceptualizations have already coalesced into this refined radiance, they consist of nothing more than form. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"The eighty deities all achieve their refined radiance through the fundamental element of obstructive conceptualization. Although these beings are supremely refined and divine, they have not yet transcended the realm of conditioned existence (*yǐng*).
That is the revolving of inverted perceptions. △ Sixth, the formless realm:
due to the delusions and inversions of the world’s dissolution and saṃsāra, a combination of darkness produces eighty-four thousand thoughts of hidden and chaotic concealment.
Because of this, there is the formless *kalala*, which flows through the lands, dispersing into emptiness and sinking away.

These types are so numerous that they weary of existence and cling to emptiness; by extinguishing the body, they return to non-existence, which is called the cycle of dissolution. To be deluded, leaking, and ignorant is called confusion and perversion.
To weary of existence and return to non-existence is because one relies on the dark and obscure void; through the conjunction with darkness, it is formed and named the *skandha* (aggregate).

"Hidden disordered thought" refers to those among the non-Buddhist practitioners of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Although they possess thought within the formless state, their karmic substance is not absent;

therefore, they are also called *kalala*. Furthermore, because their delusions and karma are heavy and obscuring, their physical form has been dissolved, their substance merges with the indistinctness of space, and consciousness clings to the subtle aggregates.
They belong to the class of those who are "empty, dispersed, and submerged. △ Seven: Those with Thought.
Due to the world’s causes—the revolving shadows of delusive forms and inverted perceptions—there arise eighty-four thousand latent knots of disordered thoughts through the synthesis of memory.
Consequently, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages characterized by conceptualization, as well as wandering spirits, ghosts, and numinous entities throughout the lands.
Their kind fills the world;
they are false and have lost their true nature. They are perversely attached to shadows and images, having no substantial basis for their form.

Born from recollection and thought, within the midst of the formless, they secretly fashion appearances. Their spirit is not luminous and thus becomes a ghost in obscurity; their essence is incomplete and thus disperses.
Spiritual essence has no substantial form; it exists only as the mark of ideation. △ Eighth, the non-ideational:
due to the world’s causes of dullness, saṃsāra, delusion, and inversion, a combination of stubbornness produces eighty-four thousand parched and disordered thoughts.
Because of this, there is the non-ideational kalala, which flows through the lands and transforms its spirit.
Earth, wood, metal, and stone—these kinds of things fill the world.
Failing to understand the principle of ultimate truth (tattva), they stubbornly cling to ignorance and delusion. When stupidity reaches its extreme, one becomes dull-witted and devoid of knowledge;

the spirit is transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone, and no longer possesses any feelings or perceptions. This is precisely what is meant by being withered and parched, as in the case of Gopīla.
The wood of the tomb of Shi Yan-zhao and the jade disc of Zheng-ren Huan are both transformations of the spirit. △ Nine:
It is not that there is form;
it arises from the false and inverted cycle of the world’s mutual dependence, through which eighty-four thousand defiled aggregates are formed.
Due to reliance on such disordered thoughts, there exist non-material forms that take shape as *kalala* (embryonic matter) and transmigrate through various lands;
these include creatures such as jellyfish, which use shrimp as their eyes, and such species fill the world.
The class of jellyfish takes water-foam as its body and shrimp as its eyes. Fundamentally they possess no color;
they acquire color only by depending on other things. They cannot function autonomously; they have utility only by depending on other things.

Having lost their innate truth and become entangled in floating falsehoods, these different substances combine through conditions of defilement; hence it is called "relying upon causes. △ Ten: Not Formless.

Due to the nature of inverted delusion that causes beings in the world to draw one another into the cycle of saṃsāra, they combine with mantras to form eighty-four thousand types of distracted thoughts for summoning.
Because of this, there exist non-material forms and non-material kalalas that circulate through the lands.
Curses, incantations, and life-suppressing rites abound in their various forms.

Depraved karmas draw one another in, causing the nature and emotions to become inverted. Thus, by means of spells, consciousness is entrusted [to these entities], not arising through natural physiological processes, but following delusively upon being summoned.
This refers to those born from worldly malevolent arts, such as curses, malevolent spirits, and life-suppressing objects.
It does not arise from the principle of physical nature; thus, fundamentally it is without form. Since it is moved by conditions to form a substance, it is not without form.
△ Eleven: Not Having Perception.
This arises because, due to the world’s conjunction with delusive transmigration and inverted views, various combinations produce eighty-four thousand [perceptions].
Through these reciprocal and confused thoughts, there arise the characteristics of the "non-existent yet existent" and the "perceptual formation of the kalala," which flow through various lands.
Among them, creatures such as the *pulu* (parasitic wasps) transform one substance into another; their kind fills the world.
Second, false appearances combine; their natures and essences are utterly obscured. Different substances mutually constitute one another, and their vital processes intersect.
It is like the *pulu* (a caterpillar), which originally is a mulberry worm; it does not possess the notion of a bee, yet it develops the notion of a bee. △ Twelfth: Not Non-Perception.

Due to the cycle of enmity and killing in the world, which arises from perversion, they conjoin with strange things to form eighty-four thousand beings who harbor the notion that their parents are their food.
Thus, there exist these non-non-perceptive, yet not entirely non-perceptive *kalala* stages, which circulate through various lands.
For example, there are creatures such as the earth-owl that take clods of earth for their offspring, and the mirror-breaking bird that takes the fruit of poisonous trees to raise its young;
once the offspring have grown, both the mother and father are devoured by them. Such species abound.
Enmity and injury are repaid in kind; wounding and killing are met with retaliation. Their natural disposition is strange and perverse, and they abandon the principles of human kinship.

Thus, they evoke the species of the earth-owl (*kukkuta*), which takes form through clods of earth and poisonous fruit. It is not that these creatures lack the perception of being birds, yet fundamentally they possess no such perception.
△ Third, the conclusion.
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.

They all fail to understand the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind; deluded and ensnared by emotional desires, they accumulate falsehoods that give rise to further delusions, revolving according to those delusions.
Without correct cultivation, none can escape or be liberated. Therefore, next, the method for eliminating delusion and attaining realization through cultivation is shown.
Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
