Luó (láng gè qiè). Chǔn (chǐ yǔn qiè). Ruǎn (ér yǔn qiè). Tuì (pinyin shuì). Xiā (hū yá qiè). Xiāo (pinyin jiāo). Kuài (kǔ duì qiè).

Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas. Scroll Fifteen.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣa from the kingdom of Ujjayinī;
orally received by Fáng Róng of Qīnghé, former Minister of Justice and concurrently Vice President of the Secretariat and Chancellery, and disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling explains:

△ Four, "Commanding the Removal of the Root of Delusion. This is the gradual sequence for realizing the fruit. Since the previous section already commanded the recognition of the causes of delusion, this section further commands the removal of the root of delusion;
once the location of the thief is known, one must immediately pursue and eliminate them, so that the hidden enemies are utterly destroyed.

The nature of the universe is tranquil and clear. Thus, one may proceed with ease toward realization without encountering difficulties or perils. This section has two parts. First, the restatement of the original cause:
"Ānanda, among each and every class of such sentient beings, each also possesses twelve inversions, just as..."
Pressing upon the eyes causes a chaotic profusion of flowers to appear, which distorts the wondrous, perfect, true, pure, and luminous mind.
Possessing such empty and delusive discursive thoughts, there arise the twelve inversions, ranging from the inversion of movement to the inversion of killing. Because of these delusions...
This disturbs the true mind and gives rise to eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts. △ Second, the actual instruction on eliminating delusion, in two parts.
First, the general announcement of the three dharmas:
"Now, as you cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, regarding these fundamental causes that originally gave rise to deluded thoughts, I shall establish three gradual stages."
Only then can it be eliminated. It is like a clean vessel from which poisonous honey has been removed;

one washes and cleanses that vessel with various hot waters, mixed ashes, and incense, and subsequently stores ambrosia within it. What are the three stages of gradual progression? The first is cultivation.
First, the elimination of auxiliary causes. Second, true cultivation, which involves excising the primary nature. Third, progressive advancement, which involves penetrating manifest karma.

The five pungent herbs serve as the auxiliaries, while sexual misconduct and killing constitute the primary factors; when these conditions are severed, they are contravened. △ Second, a detailed explanation of the three dharmas, in three parts.
First, the elimination of auxiliary causes.
What are these auxiliary causes? Ānanda, the twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves by their own power;
they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment, namely: edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. For this reason, the Buddha said that all sentient beings—
All abide by means of nutriment. Ānanda, all sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume what is poisonous.
These sentient beings who seek *samādhi* should sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world.
Regarding the four kinds of nutriment: for humans, there is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), meaning that what is consumed must necessarily be taken in morsels.

For ghosts and spirits, there is contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*); they are satisfied merely by inhaling contact. In the heavens of dhyāna, there is nutriment of volition (*manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra*); when nutriment arrives, they are satisfied simply by intending it.

In the heavens of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*), since there is neither form nor color, they subsist solely through the ideation of consciousness. This is intended simply to clarify that all sentient beings abide in dependence upon nutriment.

Furthermore, one should observe the precept against consuming the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*) because of their effects on food; this need not be cited from other sources. The five pungent roots are: first, garlic; second, leek;
third, scallion; fourth, onion; and fifth, asafoetida. These five are foul-smelling and impure; they give rise internally to lust and anger, and externally attract malevolent spirits and demons.
Therefore, they are called "auxiliary causes. Laypeople do not consume them during fasting retreats, let alone those who practice true cultivation.
These five kinds of pungent plants cause lust when eaten cooked and increase anger when eaten raw.

Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent plants—even if they can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures—will be loathed for their foul stench by the celestial beings and immortals of the ten directions, all of whom will keep their distance from them.
Various hungry ghosts (preta), following that food, lick their lips and mouths; they dwell constantly with such ghosts, their merit and virtue daily diminish, and they find no lasting benefit.
Such people who consume pungent foods practice samādhi, yet the Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals (deva-rṣi), and virtuous deities of the ten directions [will not accept them].

Because they do not come to guard them, the powerful Mara gains an opportunity; he manifests in the form of a Buddha and comes to preach the Dharma to them, disparaging the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance.
When their lives end, they become members of Mara’s retinue, and when their demonic blessings are exhausted, [they fall].
They will fall into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda, those who cultivate Bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots; this is called the first stage of progressive advancement in cultivation.
△ Second, excising the root of the correct nature.

What is the correct nature? Ānanda, when such sentient beings enter *samādhi*, they must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever sever the mind of lust, abstain from wine and meat, consume food purified by fire, and never eat anything that has not yet lost its life-force. Ānanda!
For such a practitioner, if they do not cease sexual desire and killing, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms.
One should contemplate sexual desire as being like a venomous snake or as seeing a hostile thief.
If one wishes to excise lust and eliminate killing from one's true nature, one must certainly uphold the precepts. Not drinking alcohol is the ultimate defense against disorder;

not eating raw meat is the ultimate defense against killing. Among the five types of fruit permitted by the Vinaya, all must be "purified by fire" to demonstrate that one does not consume living energy.
Lust is like a venomous snake or a vengeful thief, for it can harm the Dharma-body and kill the life-force of wisdom.

First, one maintains the four parājikas and eight *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* of the śrāvaka, holding the body so that it does not move. Subsequently, one practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva, holding the mind so that it does not arise.
One holds the body to ensure there is no transgression; one holds the mind to ensure there is no intention to transgress.
When the precepts are perfected, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing within the world;
theft and robbery shall not occur, nor shall there be mutual debts or burdens, and one shall likewise not have to repay past debts within the world.
Lust and killing follow one another; theft and robbery follow one another. Because there is no restraint, the accomplishment of precepts is absent and these two types of karma persist forever.
Such a person is pure and cultivates samādhi; without needing the divine eye, they naturally perceive with their physical bodies as their parents'.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they behold the Buddhas and hear the Dharma; personally receiving the holy instructions, they attain great supernormal powers and travel through the realms of the ten directions.
Their past lives are purified, and they encounter no hardships or perils.
When the nature of karma is completely hollowed out, the wondrous nature becomes perfectly luminous;
this is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
△ Third, contravening manifest karma.
What is present karma? Ānanda, such a person who purely maintains the prohibitive precepts has no mind of greedy lust;
regarding the six external sense objects, they do not flow or stray excessively.

The mind flows outward and rushes toward the dust of sensory objects, giving rise to manifest karma. Through the restraint of precepts and prohibitions, one attains non-distraction; thus, one is able to distance oneself from such tendencies.

Because of this non-distraction, one turns back to the source and returns to oneself. When the dust is no longer perceived as an object, the sense organs have nothing with which to pair. The flow is reversed and becomes entirely unified.
The six faculties ceased their functions; the lands of the ten directions were brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.
Body and mind were blissful, wondrously perfect, equal, and attained great peace and security. All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous qualities of all Tathāgatas appeared therein.
This person immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When flowing, it divides and merges with sensory objects; when not flowing, it returns to its source and is without peer.

Thus, one can reverse the turbulence of the six faculties and perfect the stillness of the single Reality. It is like the water of a river: by reversing the current and returning to its oneness, it naturally becomes clear from its depths.
The profound nature is deep and limpid; thus, the land, body, and mind are wondrously perfect, pure, and clear, merging with the Tathāgata.
Consequently, the secret, perfect, and enlightened mind and the pure, wondrous nature of all Tathāgatas are all manifested therein.

The third of the Ten Endurances in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is called the "Endurance of the Non-arising of Dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which means not perceiving the arising of even the slightest dharma, nor perceiving the arising of even the slightest...
The Dharma is extinguished; free from all emotional defilements, it is without action and without aspiration. To dwell securely in this path is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).
The term "Dharma-patience" is used to distinguish it from the "subduing patience" (*vinaya-kṣānti*) of the two vehicles.

From this point, one gradually practices; according to what is initiated, one establishes oneself in the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*). This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.
Only when karma is purified and the nature is luminous can one initiate practice and ascend to the noble stages. There are fifty-seven such stages, each corresponding to its respective practice.

Names are established based on characteristics, so that one may contemplate their meaning and understand what is to be cultivated and advanced. △ Fifth, the detailed exposition of the noble stages (āryabhūmi), in eleven parts.
First, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśanābhūmi).
Ānanda, these good sons have the craving for existence dried up; their faculties and objects no longer meet. Their remaining physical form will not continue to be reborn.
Their minds of grasping are empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom. The nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, illuminating the ten directions.
Possessing this wisdom alone, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi).
Sensual craving moistens delusion; the faculties, objects, and the karma they produce cause birth and death to continue in succession—this is all there is.

Therefore, when desire dries up and the objects fade away, the remaining physical substrate no longer continues. Being free from all turbid confusion, the grasping mind becomes empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.
However, at the initial stage of this position, one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma; thus, while one possesses this wisdom in a parched state, it remains incomplete.

Thus it is said. The Noble Stages (āryabhūmi) begin with the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), taking faith (*śraddhā*) as the primary cause. Furthermore, prior to faith, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) is established;

prior to the [Ten] Grounds (*bhūmi*), the Four Additions (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*) are established; and prior to the Sublime [Stage], the Vajra-like [Samādhi] is established. These three—the Dry Wisdom, the Additions, and the Vajra-like—are the essential pivots for shifting stages and the skillful means for ascending progress.
Initially, when one departs from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the nature of wisdom is not yet perfected, and thus one cannot enter into faith.
One becomes a Worthy One (Arhat). Once the conduct of the Worthy has been perfected, one cannot ascend to the stages (bhūmis) and become a Sage without applying further effort.

Once the stage of the Sage is concluded, if one does not employ the Diamond-like Wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) to sever the final subtle delusions and wash away the objective shadows of the preceding stages, one cannot manifest the wondrous state of Buddhahood.
Twenty: Regarding the Holy Stages of the Ten Faiths, faith is taken as the primary cause because it is pure and true. It is without... [text fragment ends]

To be free from delusion is called faith; furthermore, to be in accord is called faith. One must first examine the path that is central, perfect, and subtle, ensuring it is pure and without delusion, and only then initiate practice so that the mind and the Dharma are in accord.
Thus, although the ordinary and the sublime may be far apart, [they can be unified].
One may proceed directly [to the goal]. Section Ten: First is the Mind of Faith.

When the habitual tendencies of desire have begun to dry up, yet one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma, one should cause this very mind to flow into the center of that stream.
Perfectly wondrous and fully blossomed, arising from the truly wondrous perfection, it further gives rise to the truly wondrous. This wondrous faith abides eternally;
all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder. This state of pure truth in the Middle Way is called the Abode of Faith.
Having abandoned desire and transcended the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), one still remains on the level of ordinary beings and has not yet entered the stream of the Dharma;
therefore, one must flow into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom) without any partiality or stagnation. Only then will the nature of perfect wondrousness blossom.
Yet, as long as residual delusive habits remain, it is not yet true wondrous perfection; thus, one must once again give rise to [the resolve for] true wondrous perfection from within that state.
Truly wondrous! By abiding constantly in this wondrous faith, one causes all delusive thoughts to be extinguished without remainder.
This is the Middle Way among middles, pure and true, free from delusion; therefore, it is called the "Abode of Faith. All other stages advance by means of this alone, with no separate dharma.

One merely follows the respective stages in reliance upon the truly wondrous nature, purifying the habits of afflictions through single and repeated refinements, until not even a speck of dust remains.
He does not stand [in duality], and thus immediately ascends to wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). △ Second, as for the mind of mindfulness:
with true faith and clear understanding, the three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements—though all-encompassing—are unable to act as obstructions.
In this way, even throughout countless kalpas of the past and future, whenever he discards one body and receives another, all habitual tendencies (vāsanā) manifest before him.
These good sons are all able to recollect things without any omission; this is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness (*smṛti*).
When the mind is true and luminous, then all things are perfectly penetrating and the *skandhas* do not obstruct it;
thus they can clearly illuminate past habits and remember their remedies without omission. △ Third, the mind of diligence (*vīrya*).
Sublime, perfect, and purely true, this true essence undergoes transformation. The habitual tendencies of beginningless time merge into a single luminous clarity;
by means of this alone, one advances toward true purity—this is called the mind of vigor.
When the wondrous, perfect, and penetrating nature is both pure and true, then deluded habits are all transformed, leaving only a single brilliant lucidity that advances toward ultimate purity.
Because one's conduct is free from admixture, it is called "diligence. △ Fourth, the mind of wisdom.
When the essence of mind manifests before one, it consists purely of wisdom; this is called the "abiding of the mind in wisdom.
Since delusive habits have been exhausted, the essence of mind manifests, and its subsequent movements and functions consist purely of wisdom, free from habituation.
△ Five. The Abiding of the Concentrated Mind.
Grasping and maintaining the clarity of wisdom, it is all-pervasive, tranquil, and profound; tranquil, wondrous, and eternally still—this is called the abiding of the concentrated mind.
Since wisdom is already purely luminous, one must employ concentration to sustain it, so that its tranquil and profound essence remains eternally still and pervasive.
When the mind is concentrated and unchanging, it is called the "concentrated mind" (samādhi-citta). △ Sixth, the "non-regressing mind":
when the light of concentration illuminates and the nature of clarity penetrates deeply, advancing only without retreating, it is called the "non-regressing mind."
By maintaining wisdom through meditative concentration, one reaches profound stillness; thus, the light of the nature manifests, and one enters deeply into the Way.
△ Seventh, the mind that protects the Dharma:
when the mind advances with serenity, maintaining [the state] without loss, the vital energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interconnects; this is called the mind that protects the Dharma.

Being able both to penetrate deeply and to maintain [the Dharma], such that one’s Way is identical with the ten directions and one’s breath merges with that of the Tathāgata—this is called "protecting the Dharma.
△ Eighth, the mind of dedication.
The awakened clarity maintains this state; by means of its wondrous power, it turns the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha’s abode.
It is like two mirrors facing each other with their radiance, wherein wondrous reflections mutually penetrate one another. This is called the mind of dedication.

By means of the mind that protects the Dharma, one advances toward union with the Tathāgata and attains wondrous awakening and clarity. Because one maintains this protection without loss, one is able to perform wondrous dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
To turn back the Buddha’s compassionate light is to turn the fruit toward the cause; to turn toward the Buddha’s abiding is to turn the cause toward the fruit.
Thus, cause and fruit intersect, and essence and function mutually encompass one another. Therefore, they are likened to a pair of mirrors, and so forth. (9)
The mind of precepts:
the light of the mind turns inward in secret, attaining the Buddha’s eternal composure, supreme, wondrous, and pure. Abiding peacefully in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one achieves non-loss;
this is called the dwelling of the mind of precepts.
Because one attains this from me by turning back the light of the Buddha-mind, it is said that one "attains the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, unsurpassed, wondrous purity.
"Eternally concentrated" means being unmoved in the face of objects; "wondrously pure" means being unstained when encountering the dust of the world.
Thus, the mind of precept is perfected. △ Tenth, the Mind of Vow.

Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla-vaśitā*), one is able to travel throughout the ten directions; wherever one goes is according to one's vow—this is called "abiding in the mind of aspiration.
Being unmoved by objects and untainted while traversing the defilements is what is meant by abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline.

When there is neither movement nor defilement, there is nothing that cannot be attained; thus, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, going wherever one wishes according to one's vow. At the very beginning of practice, it is essential...
Exhausting and severing desire and craving so that the nature of the mind becomes empty and luminous; only then can one enter the stream of the Dharma and open the wondrous, perfect nature.
When the true nature is bright and perfect, subtle habitual tendencies will manifest. One must then initiate practice to treat them, ensuring that pure wisdom is free of habituation.

Furthermore, maintain this through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) so that profound stillness emits radiance, entering deeply into the Way and guarding it without loss. In this way, one is able to...
They turn back the Buddha’s compassionate light and attain the Buddha’s pure precepts; thus they traverse the world of dust without being defiled, proceeding wherever their vows lead.
This is the sequence of the Ten Faiths. 30. The Ten Abodes (*Daśavihāra*). From faith, one enters and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Relying on non-abiding wisdom, one never regresses; this is called "abiding. The text has ten sections. First: The Abode of Generating the Mind (*Cittotpādavihāra*).

Ānanda, these sons of good family, by means of true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds. Their mental essence radiates brilliance, and as the ten functions interpenetrate one another, they perfect a single mind;
this is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind.
This is true skillful means and wondrous wisdom. These ten minds are the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

When these ten minds arise instantaneously and are perfected as a single mind, one abides in the ground of Buddha-wisdom; this is called the "Abiding in the Initial Resolve" (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).

In the stage of the sages, the ten faiths constitute the primary cause, while the ten abidings, ten practices, ten vows, and ten grounds serve as the gradual progression, culminating in the Equal and Wondrous [Enlightenments]. All of these follow one another in succession.

Furthermore, one intends to lead the practitioner from faith toward entry and abiding in the stage of Buddha-wisdom, such that they initiate practice based on wisdom and sustain that practice through aspiration.

Thereby, they transcend the Three Sages (the ten stages of faith) and enter the Ten Holy Ones (the ten stages of abiding), ascending to the stages of Equality and Wondrous Enlightenment. This is the sequence of cultivation and realization.
2. The Stage of Cultivating the Ground (Caryābhūmi).

The illumination within the mind is like pure gold appearing inside clear lapis lazuli. Taking that prior wondrous mind and treading upon it to form the ground is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman*).

The illumination within the mind is such that both internally and externally it is refined and brilliant; this reiterates the meaning of the mind’s essence manifesting radiance. One treads upon this wondrous mind.

This is considered the true foundation and is called the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman*). It is like one who intends to build a house and must first prepare the ground before construction can begin.
△ Third, the Stage of Cultivating Practice (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*).
When the mind-ground and its cognitive objects are both clearly understood, and one traverses the ten directions without obstruction, this is called the Stage of Cultivation (Pratipatti-vihāra).
Because the mind-ground has been refined and perfected through internal and external purity, both what is traversed and what is known are clearly understood;
thus, one advances spontaneously in cultivation without hindrance. 4. The Noble Birth Stage (Janma-uttama-vihāra).

Their practice becomes identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual influence. Just as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) spontaneously seeks out its parents, their subtle faith communicates with the profound;
thus they enter the lineage of the Tathāgata. This is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).

When wondrous conduct is secretly in accord, then the wondrous principle responds in profound stillness. One is about to be born into the Buddha-family and become a member of the Dharma-king’s lineage;

therefore, this is called "Birth-noble" (Jōki). The term "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) illustrates the principle of profound response. It is named "intermediate existence" because it is the interval when the present existence has already ceased and the subsequent existence has not yet arisen.
△ Fifth: The Stage of Abiding in the Fulfillment of Skillful Means.

Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One— just as when the fetus has fully formed and its human features are complete— it is called the stage of "Abiding in the Perfection of Expedient Means.
Sharing the vital essence of wondrous conduct and merging with the intermediate state of the profound principle, this is "entering the womb of the Way and receiving the lineage of the Awakened One."
Thus, once the embryo of the Way has formed, the wondrous marks are complete and not deficient, and the skillful means of cultivation are fully realized. △ Sixth, the Abode of the Rectified Mind:
One’s countenance resembles that of a Buddha, and the characteristics of the mind are likewise identical; this is called the Abode of the Rectified Mind.
Their outward deportment is identical, yet their inner mental states differ; this is not yet the state of a correct mind. △ Seventh, the Stage of Non-retrogression:
Body and mind are unified, and they increase day by day; this is called the Stage of Non-retrogression.
Sharing the virtues of the Buddha, one advances without retreating. △ Eighth, the Stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūmi):
The spiritual characteristics of the ten bodies are simultaneously and fully perfected; hence it is named the Stage of Youthful Truth.
It is specific yet minute; therefore, it is designated as "Child" (*kumāra*). As for the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), they are:
the Bodhi-body, the Vow-body, the Transformation-body, the Power-body, the Adornment-body, the Majestic-body, the Mind-born-body, the Merit-body, the Dharma-body, and the Wisdom-body. △ Ninth:
The Abode of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra-vihāra*).
The formation [of the embryo] is like being born from the womb. Becoming a child of the Buddha is called the stage of abiding as a Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra*).

From the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the stage of noble birth (*janmakula*), it is called entering the holy womb (*āryagarbha*). From the fulfillment of skillful means (*upāyasaṃpanna*) up to the stage of the youthful prince (*kumārabhūta*), it is called nurturing the holy womb.
Since the merit of this nurturing has now reached its completion, it is metaphorically compared to a prince born from the womb. △ Ten Abhishekas (Consecrations).
The stage of "Abiding at the Crown" (*mūrdhan*) signifies the completion of becoming a person. It is like a great king of a country who delegates various state affairs to his crown prince;
when that Kṣatriya king’s eldest son has reached maturity, the consecration ceremony is performed for him, which is called the "Abiding at the Consecration" (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).

The Great King of the land is a *cakravartin* (Wheel-Turning Monarch); his legitimate heir is called the Crown Prince (*kumāra*). A *kṣatriya* king is a sovereign ruler; his legitimate heir is called the Heir Apparent (*yuvarāja*).
When about to entrust the sovereignty of the kingdom, he takes the water of the great ocean to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), thereby manifesting him as a king.

He ought to employ the wisdom of the multitude. Now, this position is already secretly endowed with all virtues and is capable of performing the work of a Buddha; therefore, it is manifested through the formal investiture of adulthood.

This refers to the "successive consecrations. To say that state affairs are entrusted [to them] does not mean the actual transfer of the national throne; it merely signifies that they have attained full adulthood.
This is because, in this land, one must reach the culmination of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) and fulfill the practices of the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) before being fit for the formal entrustment.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages receive their official positions from the Buddha, comparable to a Wheel-Turning King’s crown prince receiving his office.
Now, one must first resolve the mind to cultivate the stages; having cultivated the stages, one then practices; and through practice, one is subsequently born into the family of the Tathāgata.

Therein, one is endowed with the marks of awakening, possesses a mind equal to the Buddha’s, and fulfills the essence of the long path, perfecting the ten bodies. As a son of the Buddha, one undertakes the Buddha’s work. These ten...

This refers to the sequence of abiding from beginning to end. △ Forty: Having relied upon universal wisdom and abiding where the Buddhas abide, one is thus able to extensively manifest sublime practices for the benefit of oneself and others.
The text has ten sections. First, the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*).
Ānanda, once these sons of good family have become children of the Buddha, they are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas and act in accordance with the ten directions;
this is called the Practice of Joyful Conduct.

Possessing the wondrous virtues of a Buddha, one is able to accord with beings throughout the ten directions; there is nothing to which one cannot adapt. With the fulfillment of benefit for both self and others, both the capacity [of the practitioner] and the response [of sentient beings] are joyful.
This is called the Practice of Joy. △ Second is the Practice of Benefiting Others.
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called the practice of benefiting others (*anugrahacaryā*).
Skillfully inferring sublime virtues and benefiting others with those advantages constitutes the third: the practice of non-anger (*akṣobhyacaryā*).
To awaken oneself and awaken others, attaining a state free from opposition and resistance, is called the practice of non-anger.
Anger arises from opposition and resistance. Fourth is the inexhaustible practice.

It gives rise to all categories of beings, reaching to the end of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions; this is called the inexhaustible practice.

He touches upon various categories and extends his understanding; he responds according to the capacities of beings, providing beneficial practices without end. △ Fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion:
all things are unified, and he attains no error regarding the various Dharma gates; this is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
Not understanding phenomena is called delusion (*moha*). The confusion and error regarding conduct is called agitation (*auddhatya*).
Now, being able to unify with phenomena and attain freedom from error, one is thus free from delusion and agitation. △ Sixth, the excellent manifestation of conduct.
Thus, within the identical, a multitude of differences manifests; yet within each distinct characteristic, their respective sameness is perceived—this is called "skillful manifestation.
Because there is no delusion or confusion, one is able to manifest various dharma-gates in mutual correspondence, characterized by perfect fusion and sovereign mastery.
This is what is called "Excellent Manifestation. △ Seventh, the Practice of Non-attachment:
In this manner, even unto the atoms that fill the space of the ten directions, within each and every atom, he manifests the realms of the ten directions.
Manifesting the dusts and manifesting the realms without mutual obstruction or hindrance is called the practice of non-attachment.
This arises from the excellent practice of manifestation, which is expansive and perfectly interfused. Manifesting lands within the dusts is called "manifesting the realms";
not destroying the characteristics of the dusts is called "manifesting the dusts. △ Eighth, the Practice of Reverence.
These various manifestations are all the foremost *pāramitā*, termed "venerable practice.
All that is manifested is the nature and virtue of *prajñā*, the wondrous power of non-action, spontaneously and sovereignly accomplished;
therefore, it is called "venerable. The Vajra is designated as the foremost *pāramitā*, which is precisely *prajñā*. △ Nine: Wholesome Dharmas.
Practice. Thus, through such perfect integration, one is able to fulfill the norms of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-caryā*).
It is by means of this that the Buddhas of the ten directions attain the Way, and it is by means of this that they benefit sentient beings. △ Ten: The Practice of Reality (*bhūta-caryā*).
Each and every one of these is pure and free from outflows; it is the single, true, unconditioned state, for its nature is thus from the beginning. This is called "True Practice" (*bhūta-caryā*).

It subsumes all preceding practices, for there is nothing that is not the true nature. Although its manifestations are myriad and diverse, its essence is the single truth; therefore, it is named "True.
Thus, from these ten practices through to the subsequent stages, they do not depart from the aforementioned dharmas, yet they are all...

They follow one after another. Those established separately serve to cause the practitioner to advance through the stages, expand their innate awakening, purify the obstacles of delusion, and bring the fruit of Buddhahood to maturity.
△ The Fifty Dedications (Pañcāśat-pariṇāmanā), also called the Ten Vows:

In the preceding Ten Abodes and Ten Practices, the mind was largely oriented toward transcending the mundane world, while the practice of great compassion was deficient; here, it is necessary to supplement this with compassionate vows to remain within the mundane world.

Benefiting sentient beings: turning the ultimate toward the conventional, and turning wisdom toward compassion, so that the ultimate and the conventional are perfectly integrated and wisdom and compassion are non-dual.

This is called the sublime practice of dedication and progress; it is fully detailed herein. The text has ten sections. First: the dedication of rescuing and protecting sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being."
Ānanda, when these good sons have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of Buddhahood, they will be pure, clean, and genuine, far removed from all lingering afflictions.

They shall deliver sentient beings while extinguishing all marks of deliverance; turning toward the mind of non-action and the path to Nirvāṇa, this is called the Dedication of Protecting and Saving All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Mark of Sentient Beings.

The supernatural powers are fulfilled, reaching far and removing all lingering afflictions. This refers to the aforementioned matters, such as the manifestation of sense objects and realms without mutual obstruction;

it means that when these practices are fulfilled, one should cultivate the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Because the practice of dedication possesses the deepest compassion and vows, its function lies in the salvation of sentient beings.
However, if one perceives that there are beings to be saved, one immediately enters into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and turns away from *nirvāṇa*.

The path. Therefore, one must eliminate the marks of crossing over and dedicate [the merit] toward the unconditioned mind; this is the path toward Nirvana. △ Second, the Non-Destructive Dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).
To destroy that which is destructible and to remain far removed from all forms of detachment is called the Non-Destructive Dedication.

To destroy that which is destructible means to remain far removed from all false and illusory objects. To be far removed from all forms of removal means to be removed from the very act of removal and even further removed from that [removal].
When one attains a state where there is nothing to be removed, all illusions are eliminated, and one realizes the indestructible.
△ This is the third dedication, the Dedication Identical to All Buddhas.
Fundamental enlightenment is profoundly still; its awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas. This is called the dedication that is equal to all Buddhas.
It is neither destroyed nor indestructible, neither separated nor inseparable; thus it is profoundly still and equal to the Buddhas. △ Fourth, the dedication reaching all places.
The essence is refined and true, manifesting with clarity; the ground is like the ground of a Buddha. This is named the Dedication Reaching All Places.
Because awakening is profound and still, the essence is refined and true, manifesting with clarity; the ground is like the ground of a Buddha.

When the preceding awakening is equal to all things, it is the pervasiveness of the substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*). When this ground reaches all places, it is the pervasiveness of the realm of True Suchness. △ Fifth: The Inexhaustible Merit.
The dedication of the treasury of merit:
the worlds and the Tathāgatas interpenetrate one another without obstruction; this is called the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
Because both the true realm and the true essence are perfectly pervasive, they interpenetrate without hindrance, spontaneously radiating the function of their meritorious qualities.
Inexhaustible. △ Sixth, the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality:
within the stage identical to the Buddha-ground, one generates various causes for purity in each respective stage; relying on these causes, they are brought forth to take up the path to nirvana.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality.
Being identical to the Buddha-ground means that the preceding ground is like the Buddha-ground. In all places, one individually gives rise to pure causes and takes up the path to nirvana;
this is what is meant by "roots of goodness of equality. △ Seventh: The Dedication of Accordant Contemplation of Sentient Beings.

Once the true roots have been established, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own fundamental nature. When this nature is perfected and accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings;
this is called the dedication of merit through the contemplation that accords with all sentient beings.

The roots of goodness of equality are, by nature, truly and perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature.
Since my own goodness is perfected, I am able to bring to fulfillment the roots of goodness of all sentient beings without exception, without omission, and without distinction of high or low;
this is called "the contemplation of accordant equality. △ Eighth: Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness.

That is, all phenomena are free from all marks. When both "being identical" and "being detached" are without attachment, it is called the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because it is as-it-is, it is identical;
because it is true, it is detached. If there were identity and detachment, that would be a provisional True Suchness. Only when both are without attachment— [...is it the True Suchness.]
It is the true *tathatā*. △ Ninth, the Dedication of Unbound Liberation:
Truly attaining that which accords with suchness (*tathatā*), being unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the dedication of unbound liberation.
If one relies on the provisional *tathatā*, there will inevitably be obstructions; thus, there is bondage and liberation.
Only when one attains the true *tathatā* is everything unobstructed, which is then called "liberation without bondage. △ Ten: Dedication of the Infinite Dharmadhātus.
When the intrinsic virtues are perfectly accomplished and the limits of the *dharmadhātu* are extinguished, it is called the "Infinite Dedication of the *Dharmadhātu*.
At the initial realization of these intrinsic virtues, one considers oneself equal to the Buddha, identical to the Buddha, and as having reached all places, and so forth.
All these involve the perception of the finite. Thus, the nature of the Dharma-realm has not yet transcended the finite.
When the inherent virtues are perfected, one extinguishes the perception of the finite and attains the infinite. This generally counteracts the limited emotional views of the preceding stages.
Once this nature is perfected, one may transcend the Three Worthies and enter the Ten Sages. △ Sixth: The Four Degrees of Applied Practice. The stage of the Three Worthies reaches its culmination.
At this juncture, one must further apply diligent practice to enter the stage of the sages. This section has two parts: first, a restatement of the preceding to provide a general heading:
"Ānanda, these good men have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds; next, they accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*)."
Regarding the forty-one minds: there is one stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*); then ten stages each for Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Direction.

While the Small Vehicle and the Shared Teaching both possess these four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), they are neither wondrous nor perfect. Therefore, these are specifically termed the "Wondrous and Perfect Preparatory Stages.
II. Detailed Explanation of the Stages of Practice (4): 1. The Stage of Heat (*ūṣmagata*).
One immediately takes the awakening of the Buddha as one's own mind. Whether it has emerged or not yet emerged, it is like drilling for fire when one wishes to ignite the wood;
this is called the Stage of Warmth (uṣmagata).
The "Buddha-awakening" (*buddhabodhi*) is the awakening of the fruit. Although one was previously able to attain parity, one had not yet achieved direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).

Now, at the stage of the Ultimate Sage (*paramārthasatya*), as one is about to advance toward the fruit of sainthood, one must take the Buddha-fruit awakening as one's own causal mind (*hetucitta*). Furthermore, one must apply effort and practice to seek direct realization.

Fire is a metaphor for the fruit-awakening; wood is a metaphor for the causal mind; and drilling is a metaphor for applied cultivation (*prayoga*). Having first entered the stage of the cause, one has not yet [attained the fruit].
One attains the fruit; thus it is likened to drilling for fire, where one only obtains the sign of warmth after sustained effort. △ Second, the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).

Furthermore, by means of one's own mind, one treads upon that which the Buddhas have traversed. Whether relying or not relying [on external objects], it is like ascending a high mountain where the body enters into empty space, yet there remains a slight obstruction below;
this is called the Ground of the Summit.
Previously, one took the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind; now, one takes one's own mind to accomplish the practice of Buddhahood.

Thus, the causal mind and the resultant awakening are already adjacent to the ultimate. Therefore, it is like climbing a high mountain and entering into empty space; yet, cause and effect have not yet been fully integrated.

The traces of the mind still linger; therefore, it is said that there is a slight obstruction below. However, having already reached the stage of the Summit (mūrdhan), one need only wait for a moment to advance further, and the slight obstruction will be removed.
△ Third, the Stage of Patience (kṣānti).

The mind and the Buddha are identical; this is to skillfully attain the Middle Way. Just as one who endures an offense neither harbors resentment nor expresses it outwardly, this is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

When one’s own mind and the Buddha’s awakening merge into a single essence, it is called "the identity of the two. When cause and effect are both forgotten and the two extremes do not stand, it is called the Middle Way.
Since this fruit of the Middle Way is at the point where awakening is about to be realized but has not yet been realized, it is like one who endures an offense—neither harboring resentment.
It is not an emergence. △ Fourth, the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*):
when quantity and extinction are eliminated, and both delusion and awakening are found to have no objective referent within the Middle Way, it is called the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma.

The preceding stage refers to the two "identical" states; these already fall within the realm of numerical measurement. To perceive the existence of middle and extremes is to forcibly differentiate between delusion and awakening.

When both of these are extinguished, even names no longer stand. Having escaped worldly conceptualization and transcended the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*), it is therefore called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
If one advances to the ten stages of sainthood (*ārya*) and reaches the pinnacle of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), this is the "Supreme Transcendent Dharma. △
The seventy stages (*bhūmi*). By accumulating the preceding dharmas until they reach the state of perfected reality (*satya*), all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon them;

therefore, they are called "stages. From the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and below, each position follows upon the previous and mutually supports it as one proceeds directly toward wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Within this process, there is no absence of abandonment and realization; yet these are all instances of abandoning without abandoning and realizing without realizing. Or, it is said:

For each stage (*bhūmi*), one obstacle and two delusions (*moha*) are severed, and one *pāramitā* is cultivated; however, such detailed enumeration would result in a cluttering of names and forms, and the phrasing would become prolix and abstract.

Therefore, I shall now omit these details and provide an explanation based directly on the principle of following in the footsteps of the predecessors and mutually supporting one another, so that those who practice and advance may understand with clarity and ease.
The text has ten sections. First: the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Ānanda, these sons of good family have attained excellent penetration into great bodhi; their awakening penetrates that of the Tathāgatas and they exhaust the realm of the Buddhas—this is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Although previously his awakening was equal to that of a Buddha, he had not yet exhausted the realm of the Buddha’s bodhi.

Now, because his preparatory practice (*prayoga*) is wondrously perfected, he is able to thoroughly penetrate and exhaust it. Because his joy in the Dharma increases further on this account, it is also called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
△ Second, the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
When different natures enter into the same, and even that same nature is extinguished, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
It penetrates Great Bodhi and exhausts the realm of the Buddhas; thus, all obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment.
Sentient beings and their lands share the same *dharmatā*. This is "different natures entering the same. Yet, to perceive difference or perceive sameness is still [delusion].

When emotional defilements (*kleśa-mala*) are extinguished even at the level of their own nature, it is called "Freedom from Defilement" (*vimalā*). △ Third, the Ground of Radiant Light (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*):
when purity reaches its ultimate limit and luminosity arises, it is named the Ground of Radiant Light.
When the defilements of emotional views are purified, the clarity of wondrous enlightenment arises. △ Fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
When clarity reaches its peak and awakening is fulfilled, it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom.

Because clarity reaches its peak and awakening is fulfilled, it is like a great mass of fire; all shadows of objective conditions are completely incinerated and severed. Therefore, it is named "Blazing."
Prajñā. △ Fifth, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā-bhūmi).
It is called the Ground of Difficult to Conquer because it cannot be reached by any similarities or differences.

Although in the preceding stage, despite entering sameness from a state of difference, that [notion of] sameness was also extinguished, there still remained an object that could be reached. This [ground], however, is like a flame...
Because wisdom incinerates and severs [all obscurations], nothing—neither identity nor difference—can reach it. If even "reaching" it is impossible, who could possibly surpass it?
△ Sixth, the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi).
The unconditioned nature of true thusness (tathatā) is pure, luminous, and manifest;
this is called the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi). No person is without this pure nature of true thusness, yet it is constantly obscured by all manner of similarities and differences.
Therefore, when identity and difference do not arrive, clarity is revealed before one. △ Seventh, the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*):
Reaching the limit of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is called the Ground of Far-Going.

While True Suchness is present, partial realization is still limited; reaching the ultimate limit is what makes it "far. Because it transcends far beyond and reaches the ultimate pinnacle, it is named "Far-Going."
Practice. △ Eighth, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
The mind of True Suchness (*tathatā-citta*) is called the Immovable Ground.
Having reached its ultimate limit, one fully attains its essence; because True Suchness is concentrated and eternal, it is named "Immovable. △ Ninth.
The Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). It is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence because it gives rise to the function of *tathatā*.
Having attained the true essence, one now brings forth its true function; whatever is illuminated and responded to is entirely true, and there is nothing that is not so.
Because of this, it is called "Excellent Wisdom" (Sādhumatī).

Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas have completed their cultivation and their merit is perfected; therefore, this stage is also designated as the "Stage of Cultivation" (bhāvanā-bhūmi).

This concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows. The stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) are collectively categorized into five: first, the provisions (*sambhāra*), which refers to the three levels of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*);

second, the application (*prayoga*), which refers to the four stages of application; third, penetration (*prativedha*), which is the first stage (*bhūmi*); fourth, cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which is this very stage [under discussion];

and fifth, no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), which is wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). From the initial arousal of faith until the transcendence of the worthy ones and entry into the noble stages, all constitute the matter of cultivation. And...

This stage has already transcended the eight grounds and the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*). Since wisdom and compassion are both perfected, the work of cultivation reaches its conclusion here;
thus it is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), as it serves to bind together the causes for the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

What follows thereafter is the fruit of the ten grounds, wherein there is no further cultivation. In the *Avataṃsaka*’s exposition of the ten grounds, Vajragarbha represents the cause. Interpretation.
The liberation from the manifest fruit also consists in the fact that there is cultivation on the causal stage, whereas there is no cultivation on the resultant stage. Question:

Since there is no further cultivation in the subsequent stage, how can there still be the matter of severing hindrances? Answer: This refers to the culmination of the merits of wisdom and compassion, which results only in the attainment of the fruit of the tenth stage.
As for the severing of hindrances, however, even the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is still one of cultivation. Therefore...
Upon reaching wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one is then termed "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). △ Tenth, the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*):
The wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*; thus it is named the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.

The wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade refers to the fruition-virtue of the ten grounds; the ocean of *nirvāṇa* refers to the ocean of fruition of wondrous enlightenment. This is the tenth ground.
The fruits are fulfilled; wisdom, compassion, and merit are perfected. There is no longer any self-benefit; it is purely for the benefit of others.
Thus, the aggregate of great compassion pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Without thought or objectification, it responds to the thoughts and conditions of others, bestowing profit and benefit.

Yet, its essence is fundamentally quiescent and without action, perfectly conforming to the Tathāgata’s ocean of great nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is called "covering. △ Eight: Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).
Position:

The Tathāgata flows against the current; the Bodhisattva likewise proceeds in accordance with it until they reach the point where awakening and the limit intersect, which is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage mixes with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, being identical to the Tathāgata in this regard; however, they differ in that the direction of their movement—one flowing against the current and the other flowing with it—is different.

The "coming" is different. It is because the Tathāgata goes against the flow of birth and death and emerges together with all things; whereas the Bodhisattva follows the flow of nirvāṇa and enters toward wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Having already reached the limit of enlightenment, it is called "entering the intersection. Because there is no interval between this and Buddhahood, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samanvāgama-bodhi*).

This is precisely the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) preceding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Although this stage is equal [to that of a Buddha], it has not yet reached the ultimate subtlety. For indeed...
One can merely accord with and enter [the ocean]; however, one must flow against the current from within the great ocean of quiescent extinction.
Only when one is wondrously identical to the myriad things is it called "Wondrous Enlightenment" (Miaojue). △ Ninth: Vajra Wisdom.
Ānanda, from the stage of the Dry Wisdom Mind up until Equal Enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind.
This is called the path of subduing for the Sublime Awakening that follows the mind of Equal Enlightenment. As for the path of Sublime Awakening, it has no distinct characteristics; it is simply...
From the initial stage of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, one again gives rise to the Vajra-mind and re-traverses all the stages from the beginning.
By shattering and severing the subtle shadows of conditions and the final ignorance, so that not even a speck of dust remains, one may then enter the Sublime.
Because it begins again from the initial stage, it is called the "First Stage of Dry Wisdom within the Vajra Mind.
As for "the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness," this refers precisely to the Bodhisattva’s entry into the Vajra Dry Wisdom.

The former was called "Dry Wisdom" because it had not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma; this is called "Dry Wisdom" because it has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornment.
Yan Hai continues: Although the names are momentarily the same, their meanings are vastly different. △ Ten: Wondrous Enlightenment.
Thus, through these successive layers of single and double [stages], totaling twelve, one finally exhausts wondrous enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way.

The *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*) contains the meaning of both single and combined cultivation. Herein, proceeding through the various stages solely by means of faith is called "single" (*dān*).
Proceeding again through the various stages while concurrently employing the adamantine mind (*jīngāngxīn*) is called "combined" (*fù*).

The twelve [stages]—namely, dry faith (*qiánxìn*), abiding (*zhù*), practice (*xíng*), orientation (*xiàng*), warmth (*nuǎn*), summit (*dǐng*), patience (*rěn*), the worldly first stage (*shìdì*), and so forth up to the adamantine stage (*jīn*)—constitute the cause. Sublime enlightenment (*miàojiào*) is the fruit. Therefore...
Through these twelve stages, both single and manifold, one exhaustively reaches wondrous enlightenment and accomplishes the unsurpassed path.
All these various stages are characterized by the adamantine observation of the ten profound metaphors of illusion within *śamatha*.
By means of the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas, one purifies, cultivates, and realizes [the truth], gradually entering deeper and deeper.
This teaching is the method for accomplishing wondrous enlightenment through the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*). The "various stages" refer to the twelve positions (*dvādaśabhūmi*).
As for the ten metaphors: they are a magical person, a mirage, the moon in water, flowers in the sky, an echo in a valley, a city of the *gandharvas*, a dream, and a shadow.
It is like a transformation. When one realizes that all phenomena are thus, then emotional attachments and intellectual understandings are suddenly forgotten, and not even a trace of dust remains.
Therefore, it is called "pure cultivation and realization. *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are termed "stopping" (*zhi*) and "contemplation" (*guan*).
The term "Tathāgata" is used to distinguish [this teaching] from the Lesser Vehicle. △ Eleven: Summary of the Efficacy.
Ānanda, it is by means of these three progressive advancements that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice false contemplation.

The three "increases" (*vṛddhi*) refer to the three "gradual stages" (*anupūrvakrama*). All the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*) rely upon these to achieve fulfillment. The stages of faith, abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*bhūmi*) constitute fifty;
when combined with the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), and the [equal] and sublime [stages], there are fifty-seven positions.
To point specifically to the fifty-five as the "path to bodhi" is because the equal and sublime stages are the fruit of bodhi, whereas these [fifty-five] are the path by which one proceeds.
This refers to the realization [of the fruit]. Alternatively, it points to the Vajra-observation as well as śamatha and vipaśyanā as the three progressive advancements.

△ Fourth, the section on concluding the sutra. Although the main body of the teaching has not yet ended, the sutra is concluded prematurely because, from the initial revelation of the secret cause, through the subsequent opening of cultivation and realization, and culminating in the ultimate fruit, the formal structure of the sutra is complete; therefore, it is concluded here. Hereafter...
These two categories—preparing against errors through the precepts and deeply guarding against deviant mistakes—merely provide special assistance to the Path;

therefore, they are listed separately later on, which constitutes the distinction between the primary and the auxiliary. This section has two parts: first, the inquiry regarding the name of the sutra.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, rising from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?"
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s indication of the five [aspects]. First, the indication of the *dharmacakṣus* (Dharma-eye) of the *garbha-citta* (store-mind).
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is titled 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Sitātapatra Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions.'"
The Supreme Jewel Seal of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Sitātapatrā: its essence is utterly encompassing and protective;
it transcends emotion and is free from views—it is the heart-seal of the Tathāgata-garbha. To realize the essential core of the Buddha-mind, one must surely accord with this.

It is the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, which illuminates to the furthest reaches of the ocean of lands and is pure, utterly devoid of even the finest speck of dust—it is the akṣaya-koṭi... [vajra].
This is the Dharma-eye. To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one must certainly rely upon this; it is truly a matter of great significance and not a teaching for those of small wisdom.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī is employed to pose the inquiry. II. Explaining the wondrous power of salvation.
It is also titled "Saving and Protecting One’s Own Causes: The Deliverance of Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly, Who Attains Bodhicitta and Enters the Ocean of Omniscience.

Ānanda represents the "own" (the relative), while Mādrī represents the "cause" (the karmic condition). By citing these two, it is clarified that all who possess the necessary conditions are delivered. There is none excluded.
One attains supreme enlightenment through this sutra; one enters the ocean of all-knowledge through this sutra.

△ It is practiced together by those who have realized the fruit of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), and it is also called "The Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata’s true fruition takes this as its cause; the cultivation and realization of the provisional vehicles are all of expedient meaning (*neyārtha*).
△ Fourth, it clarifies that the great virtues are fully perfected;
it is also titled *The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*.
Its essence is ultimate and without exterior; it is square, upright, and impartial, pervading and encompassing all—thus it is named "Great Vaipulya" (Vast and Universal).

Cause and effect are simultaneously manifested, and it is unimpeded in both the defiled and the pure; it exercises sovereign mastery over all phenomena—thus it is named "Wondrous Lotus King. It gives birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions;
it encompasses all dharmas and upholds immeasurable meanings—thus it is named the "Dhāraṇī Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions."
Dhāraṇī. △ Fifth: The Causes and Conditions for Realization through Shared Illumination;
also titled "The Mantra-Syllables of Empowerment. This is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. You should uphold it with reverence.
By means of this, the Bodhisattva receives the rank of a Buddha; therefore, it is called the "Mantra of Empowerment. △ Fifth, the Section on Aids to the Path has two parts.
First, a detailed explanation of the various realms of existence, wherein the precepts are prepared to guard against errors. The text says:

"It causes those who uphold the precepts to be cautious, pure, and free from transgressions, so that they do not enter into false views. This is the meaning of "preparing the precepts. The text has two sections. First, [the section on] *āpatti* (transgression).
Second, the request for further instruction. First, the conclusion of the preceding section with praise and gratitude:
Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Paṭala*.
Furthermore, having heard the definitive titles of this sutra, they suddenly awakened to the stages of holy progress through the cultivation of *dhyāna*.
The supreme and wondrous principle: the mind becomes empty and tranquil, severing the six grades of subtle afflictions cultivated within the three realms.
This section concludes by describing the benefits obtained by the assembly at that time; what follows is the expression of praise and gratitude.

From "Revealing the Secret Seals" up to "the supreme and wondrous principle," this collectively points to the profound meanings of the preceding sutras. It serves as a seal of verification for the pure *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse mind), which encompasses and covers all things.
This is the definitive resolution. This is called the *Guhyamudrā-paṭala*, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Taking the illumination of the mind and the seeing of its nature as the cause, and taking the equal, wondrous, and ultimate realization as the fruit, not even a speck of dust is established; emotional understanding and intellectual interpretation are both forgotten; and the mind’s deliberations become ashen and still.

The subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*) are severed instantaneously; this is called the sublime principle of the superior progress in the cultivation of *dhyāna*. Regarding the innate subtle afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
in the Mahāyāna, they are permanently suppressed upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and are only severed at the stage of Buddhahood.

In the Hīnayāna, the three realms are divided into nine stages (*bhūmi*), with each stage containing nine grades. The fruit of the first realization (*srotāpanna*) severs the first six grades of the desire realm and realizes the second [fruit].

Regarding the fruits: by abandoning the final three categories [of afflictions], one realizes the third fruit; by abandoning the nine categories of each of the two upper realms, one realizes the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Because this [path] now abandons the superior [afflictions] all at once, it is said to abandon six categories across the three realms.

As for the remaining three categories, they must necessarily be abandoned at the stage of a Buddha. Although the three fruits are capable of abandoning these nine categories, they merely involve partial abandonment and gradual suppression.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha:

"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, whose compassionate voice is all-encompassing, you have skillfully opened for sentient beings their subtle and deep-seated delusions, causing my body and mind today to feel such joy and granting me great benefit."
This is the formal expression of thanks. Because they are innate and deeply hidden, they are called "sunk delusions. △ Second, the formal request for the subsequent teaching has three parts.
First, the formal question:
"World-Honored One, if this wondrously bright, truly pure, and wondrous mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect, then even down to the great earth..."
Grasses, trees, and all wriggling creatures that possess spirit are fundamentally true suchness (*tathatā*); this is the very essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood.
Since the Buddha-body is truly real, how can there further exist the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas?
It was previously stated that the truly pure, wondrous mind is fundamentally perfect and pervasive; thus, the dharma-realm is a single truth and the myriad movements are one essence.
Accordingly, there should be no distinctions among the various realms of existence (*gati*). Yet, as they currently exist today, this remains a source of doubt for ordinary people.
Consequently, some cling to the various realms and become deluded regarding the wondrously perfect essence, while others cling to the wondrous perfection and deny the karma of the various realms.
Consequently, one errs and falls. For this reason, I specifically inquire, hoping that practitioners may understand this clearly and know how to exercise caution and preparation.
World-Honored One, does this path exist inherently from the beginning, or does it arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings?
These arise from one's own delusions; they do not exist from the beginning. △ Second, citing an example:
"World-Honored One, it was as with the bhikṣuṇī Ratnavatī, who upheld the Bodhisattva precepts yet secretly engaged in sexual misconduct.

She falsely claimed that engaging in sex is neither killing nor stealing, and thus carries no karmic retribution. Having uttered these words, first, a great and violent [fever] arose within her female organ."
Fire. Later, his joints will be consumed by fierce flames, and he shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
King Virūḍhaka and the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—Virūḍhaka for slaughtering the clan of the Gautamas, and Sunakṣatra for falsely asserting that all phenomena are empty—both fell alive into the Avīci Hell.
Do these various hells have fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously? From each of those [causes], they arise.
Karma is each privately experienced;
the three types of karma are not severed, and each has its own private [consequences]. Within the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous class), there is no lack of a fixed location.

King Virūḍhaka, the crown prince of the Śākya king, deposed his father and established himself as ruler; harboring old grudges, he slaughtered the Śākyas. The Buddha prophesied that his life would last for seven days.
When he was about to enter hell, the King sailed upon the sea to avoid him, yet [the fire] was naturally extinguished in the water.

The Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was able to expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras and had attained the fruit of the four dhyānas; however, because he associated with evil friends, he falsely claimed that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no nirvāṇa, and thus was born to fall into the Avīci Hell.
All of these cases involve erroneously clinging to the wondrous and perfect [nature] and denying the existence of karma.
This is the section on those who proceed [to liberation]. △ Third, the conclusion and request:
"I pray that you will bestow great compassion and enlighten this ignorant child, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear the definitive meaning."
Receiving this with joy and reverence, one should maintain it with meticulous purity and without transgression.
