△ Second, the Tathāgata’s revelation, which has two parts.
First, the praise and approval: The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Excellent indeed is this question! It shall cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views. Listen attentively now."
I shall now explain this for you.
△ Second, the actual demonstration has four parts. First, the arising of habituation due to delusion, in two sections. First, the general heading:
Ānanda, all sentient beings are in reality fundamentally true and pure. Due to that deluded seeing, deluded habituation arises. Because of this...
Distinguishing between the internal and external divisions.
△ Second, the specific explanation has two parts. First, the accumulation of internal emotions:
Ānanda, the internal division refers to that which is within the realm of sentient beings. Due to various attachments and defilements, deluded emotions are aroused; these emotions accumulate.
It never ceases and is able to produce the water of craving. For this reason, when sentient beings recall delicacies in their minds, saliva flows from their mouths;

when they recall someone from the past, whether with pity or resentment, tears fill their eyes; when they greedily seek wealth and treasures, a flow of craving saliva issues from their hearts, making their entire bodies glistening and moist;
when their minds become attached and they engage in sexual intercourse, the two organs of male and female naturally discharge fluids.
The movement of the mind within is called *qing* (sentiment). Thus, *qing* constitutes the internal division. *Qing* is the Yin energy of man characterized by desire;

it arises from various attachments and defilements. Because of this accumulation of Yin, it can produce the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). This moisture of karma and moisture of birth cause the cycle of saṃsāra to continue without interruption. All functions [of delusion] originate from this.
Ānanda, although various cravings differ, their flowing and binding are the same. Moistening and unable to rise, they naturally fall downward; this is called the "internal portion.
Since these various cravings are not uniform, yet all can induce water-like moisture and binding delusions, it is said that "their flowing and binding are the same. The nature of water is to sink.
Below. Thus, the karma accumulated through such emotions mostly leads to sinking and falling.

△ Second, the external manifestation of thought. Ānanda, the "external portion" refers to that which is beyond the sphere of sentient beings. Due to various forms of longing and aspiration, they give rise to empty thoughts.

When these thoughts accumulate without ceasing, they can produce a superior vital energy (*vāyu*). For this reason, when sentient beings maintain prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure. When the mind maintains...

Regarding dhāraṇīs and mudrās: his gaze was majestic and resolute; his heart desired rebirth in heaven; in dreams he envisioned soaring through the air; his mind dwelt upon the Buddha-lands, and sacred realms manifested in profound stillness;
he served spiritual friends, even at the cost of his own body and life.
The mind’s engagement with external objects is called *saṃjñā* (perception). Therefore, *saṃjñā* constitutes the external constituent (*bāhyāṅga*).

*Saṃjñā* is the vital yang-energy (*yángqì*) of a person that possesses aspiration; thus, it arises from yearning and longing. Because yang-energy accumulates, it is able to produce superior energy (*shèngqì*).

Instances such as lightness, clarity, vigor, and courage are all examples of superior energy. That *saṃjñā* can produce the superior and that eggs are produced through *saṃjñā* is due to defilement (*rǎn*).

"Ānanda, although these various perceptions differ, they share the same quality of lightness and buoyancy; they soar and move without sinking, naturally transcending. This is called the external factor."
The various perceptions are not uniform, yet all are capable of becoming light and clear, enabling one to fly upward; therefore, it is said that their "light elevation" is the same.

Because of this light elevation, they are largely able to transcend. △ Second, the three sections on the karma experienced through habitual practice. First, indicating the time when the transformation is experienced.
Ānanda, throughout all worlds, birth and death continue in succession. Birth proceeds from habitual conformity; death proceeds from transformative flux.

At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and tactile sensation have been abandoned, the good and evil of one's entire lifetime appear simultaneously and instantaneously. Death is contrary to birth, while birth is conformable to it;
thus, these two habits intersect.
The nature and habits of human beings are such that they love life and hate death; they regard life as the natural order (*ruci*) and death as a transformation (*vikāra*).
The intersection of this natural order and its reversal refers to the interval between the moment of dying and the moment of being born.

At that very time, the karma of one's lifetime—whether good or evil—is immediately experienced as a transformation in accordance with the gravity of one’s mental states and intentions. △ Second, the analysis of the principle of transformation through response has five parts. First:
Pure ideation:

when ideation is pure, one immediately ascends and will certainly be born in the heavens. If within the mind of flight there is both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will naturally open, and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands; according to one's vows, one will be reborn therein.

Because the substance of their perception is light and buoyant, they ascend by flight as soon as they are pure. However, because this state is characterized solely by goodness, they merely attain rebirth in the heavens.
If one cultivates both merit and wisdom along with pure vows, then through the convergence of these two and the six periods of time, the resulting transformations will be doubly superior. △ Second:
those with little emotion and much perception.
With little emotion but much conceptualization, their lightness of movement is not far-reaching;
they become flying immortals, powerful ghost-kings, flying yakṣas, or earth-walking rākṣasas, roaming through the four heavens with unimpeded passage wherever they go.
Their superior perceptions are not pure, and they are slightly hindered by deviant emotions; therefore, they are reborn among these classes of beings.

If, however, there are within them those with virtuous aspirations and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma, or who guard the prohibitive precepts and follow those who observe the precepts, [they shall attain liberation].
Some protect through divine mantras, following those who uphold them; some protect meditative concentration and preserve the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
These beings dwell personally beneath the seat of the Tathāgata;
though they remain mired in deviant sentiments, they possess virtuous aspirations and thus encounter favorable conditions—namely, the eight classes of beings such as devas and nāgas.
△ Third, when emotion and thought are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans. When thought is clear, one is intelligent; when emotion is deep, one is dull-witted.
People differ in their faculties, being either sharp or dull; this principle is as such. △ Fourth, those with many passions and few thoughts flow into the realm of horizontal birth.
Those with heavy karma become members of the hairy flocks; those with light karma become members of the feathered tribes.

These six emotions constitute four types of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Because emotion is predominant, one undergoes immersion and transformation; because it carries conceptualization, one attains flight and elevation.
Yet, due to heavy karma, one cannot merely become part of the fur-bearing hosts. As for those born sideways with their heads turned to the side, this is because their conduct was not upright.

With seven afflictions and three delusions, they sink beneath the water-wheel and are born at the boundary of fire. Receiving the breath of fierce flames, they become hungry ghosts who are constantly scorched by fire.
Water can only harm them; without food or drink, they endure for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that at the very bottom of the great earth are the wheels of gold, water, and wind, upon which the eight cold and eight hot hells are situated.
This present text, however, speaks of sinking below the wheels of water, fire, and wind; furthermore, it appears as though the hells are beneath these three wheels.
I suspect that what is being referred to here is not the three wheels beneath the earth, but rather the three wheels [of suffering] pertaining to the hells themselves.

The phrase "the water wheel at the limit of fire" refers to the eighth cold hell. It is called "receiving the fierce fire" because one receives fiery vapors as one's body and is constantly burned by fire;
even if one obtains water to drink, it likewise transforms into fire. Hence it is said that "water can harm oneself."
With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of form, they descend through the wheel of fire; their bodies enter the ground where wind and fire intersect.
There are two kinds of hells: those with intervals and those without intervals. In the former, life is light; in the latter, life is heavy.
Because their emotional karma becomes increasingly stagnant, their retributions in hell sink ever lower. "Passing through the cavernous wheel of fire" refers to the eight hot hells.
"Entering the ground where wind and fire intersect" means transcending the cold hells and entering the hot hells. The eighth of these hot hells is named the Five Uninterrupted (Avīci);
those with interruptions are the remaining seven. △ Fifth: Pure Emotion.

Pure passion leads directly to sinking into the Avīci Hell. If one sinks within the mind, there will be those who slander the Mahāyāna, violate the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, preach deceptive and false doctrines, greedily crave offerings of faith, and unworthily receive respect;
they commit the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses, and are reborn in the Avīci Hells throughout the ten directions.

*Avīci* is translated here as "Without Interval" (*Mujian*). This refers to five factors—namely, the suffering of retribution, the instruments of torment, the physical dimensions of the body, the duration of the kalpa, and the lifespan—all of which lack any interruption or gap;
thus it is called the Hell of Five Uninterrupted Sufferings. Only those whose emotional karma is most heavy fall into this realm, remaining there until the kalpa is destroyed before they can emerge.
If one has committed additional offenses such as slandering the Mahāyāna, then even when this kalpa is destroyed, one shall enter another [hell] for ten [kalpas].
They shall dwell in the Avīci Hell with no prospect of release, because by slandering the Dharma and violating the precepts, they cause countless people to fall into false views.
△ Third, the conclusion summarizes the resulting retribution in response.
Following the commission of evil karma, although one invites this retribution upon oneself, within the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous class of beings), there is also an original ground.
Because the previous question asked whether hell has a fixed location or exists spontaneously, the answer states that it is created through pure emotion;
although one invites it oneself, it is induced by shared karma and thus does not lack a fixed location. "Original ground" refers to each according to its original cause.

△ Third, the classification of destinies (*gati*) according to karma. From the lowest, the hells, up to the highest, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). There are seven sections:
1. The destiny of hell; 2. A transitional section linking the preceding to the following.
Ānanda, all these things are what is brought about by the karma of those sentient beings themselves. They create ten habitual causes and undergo six types of intersecting retributions.
Previously, I briefly explained how emotions and thoughts induce transformations; here, I explain in detail the construction of the faculties and their objects. These ten habits are rooted in...
The ten delusions. Through habitual practice, they form evil karma. The six [delusions] intersect with the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), thereby giving rise to intersecting evil retributions.
II. A general inquiry followed by a detailed explanation in five parts. A. The ten causes of habitual practice (ten items). 1. The habit of lust (*maithuna*).
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, first is the habit of sexual intercourse. It arises from mutual friction;
as this grinding continues without ceasing, a great and fierce fire is thereby ignited within. It is like a person rubbing their hands together, where the sensation of warmth appears before them.
Because these two habits ignite one another, there arise such things as iron beds and copper pillars.
Evil karma arises from emotional delusions, and sexual desire is the most extreme of such delusions; therefore, it is explained first at both the beginning and the end [of the ten karmas].
Regarding the karma of the ten practices, each first describes the environment experienced as a result, followed by the specific retribution one receives.
Sexual desire gives rise to the karma of fire, which is ignited by the friction of a deluded mind in a state of intense fervor; thus, the environment experienced as a result is seen—
"A great, fierce fire. King Shu said, "When the habit of lust is practiced and rubbed without ceasing, it naturally consumes one's essence. Thus, the realm of fire blazes intensely.
While one is still alive, there are already ailments such as emaciation, thirst, and internal heat; therefore, it is only natural that upon death, one perceives a great, fierce fire.
When subject and object blaze together, it is called the mutual kindling of the two habits; hence there is the iron bed and the copper [cauldron]."
The retribution for this pillar [of karma] corresponds to one's habitual practice.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct with the same name: the fire of desire. When Bodhisattvas perceive desire...
It is like avoiding a pit of fire.
Because the Tathāgata is the guide, he designates it with a specific term to warn [beings] of it; because the Bodhisattva is the practitioner, he fears it deeply to avoid it.
"Designating with a term" (*se-mu*) is like naming or labeling something. △ Second, the habit-energy of greed.
Second, the habit-energy of greed intermingles with mental calculations, giving rise to mutual attraction.

As this attraction and grasping do not cease, there is consequently the accumulation of cold and solid ice within which one freezes. It is like a person drawing in air through the mouth, whereby a sensation of cold arises.
Because these two habits mutually oppress one another, there occur such phenomena as the *ṭha-ṭha*, *pa-pa*, and *ra-ra* sounds, as well as the blue, red, and white lotuses of the freezing cold.
The habit-energy of greed produces water; through the mind of craving and attachment, it is drawn in and brought forth.

The accumulation of wind results in cold, and the congealing of this wind and water forms ice. Thus, there exist realms of accumulated frost and piercing chill, which are the retributions for the "Tsa-tsa" (Chata) cold hells.
This refers to the Hell of Cold Ice (*hima-śīta-naraka*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that terms such as *tāpala* are sounds uttered by those enduring the cold.
The blue, red, and white lotuses are the colors of the cold ice.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking with the same name: "the water of greed" (*lobha-jala*). When Bodhisattvas perceive greed...
It is like avoiding a miasmic sea;
greed for water can moisten karma and nourish evil, while a miasmic sea can bring its poison to destroy the body. △ Third, the habit-energy of pride:
Third, the habit-energy of pride involves mutual disparagement arising from mutual reliance, flowing on without ceasing; because of this, there is soaring and leaping.
Rushing currents; the accumulation of waves forms water. It is like the human mouth and tongue, which through their mutual friction produce saliva, thereby giving rise to water.
As these two habits strike against one another, there arise such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, hot sands, poisonous seas, and the swallowing of molten copper.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize arrogance as "drinking the water of delusion. When Bodhisattvas encounter arrogance, they avoid it as they would [a dangerous place].
Great drowning.

The habituation to pride gives rise to arrogance and dissipation; it originates from looking down upon others and relying on oneself. Because one gallops toward dissipation, one experiences a realm of surging and turbulent rushing waters.
Because one has accumulated and brought about malignant poison, there is the retribution of being drenched and swallowed by rivers of blood. Pride is able to...

Because it nourishes delusion; like drinking the water of delusion, which can bring about profound harm, it is likened to a great drowning. "The water of delusion" (*moha-jala*) is the name of a body of water in the Western Regions.
△ Fourth, the habit-energy of anger.

Fourth, the habit-energy of anger clashes and surges forth as mutual resentment. This resentment binds without ceasing, heating the mind until it ignites like fire, forging the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into metal.
For this reason, there exist mountains of knives, iron spikes, sword-trees, wheels of swords, axes, halberds, spears, and saws.

Just as when a person harbors a grievance, their murderous breath flies and stirs, so too do these two habits strike one another, resulting in the punishments of castration, dismemberment, beheading, hacking, mincing, piercing, and hammering.
For all these reasons, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate anger as the "sharp sword.
When Bodhisattvas encounter anger, they avoid it as they would an execution.
The mind belongs to fire; the vital energy (qi) belongs to metal. When one becomes angry, the mind produces the energy, which in turn agitates the mind.

Furthermore, through this impact and resistance, the fire of the mind increases further, and the metal of the energy becomes harder; therefore, it is said that "the heat of the mind gives rise to fire."
To forge one's spirit is to become metal. To sever the body in punishment is called *gong*; to mutilate the flesh is called "cutting. △ Fifth, the habit of deception:

these five habits of deception involve mutual enticement, arising from reciprocal provocation and continuing without ceasing. Because of this, there are punishments of binding with ropes, wooden stocks, strangulation, and shackles.
Just as water soaking a field causes grass and trees to grow, so do these two habits perpetuate one another; thus, there are handcuffs, fetters, neck-locks, and chains.
Because of such matters as whips, staves, clubs, and cudgels, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate deceit and falsehood with the same name: "the slanderous thief.
When a Bodhisattva sees fraud, they regard it with the same dread as they would a jackal or a wolf.
The habit of deception arises from the employment of crafty intelligence to produce evil, which gradually spreads and entangles like weeds;

it is like water soaking a field where grasses and trees grow because they are drawn along and extended by irrigation channels. This gives rise to experiences involving the pulling and dragging of ropes and wood—experiences that result from slanderous, treacherous, and deceitful acts which subvert what is correct. △ Sixth, the habit of delusion.
Sixth is the habit-energy of deception, which arises from mutual delusion. When such false accusations do not cease, the mind soars to commit wickedness.
Because of this, there are impurities such as dust, feces, urine, filth, and uncleanness—like dust carried by the wind, where one can see nothing at all.
As these two habit-energies interact, there arise various occurrences such as drowning, tossing about, flying, falling, and drifting in the depths. Therefore, throughout the ten directions, all...
The Tathāgata designates deception as being identical in name to murder. When a Bodhisattva encounters such deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous serpent.
A deceiver uses mad words to mislead others; their intent is fraudulent and their mind is flighty, like wind blowing dust until people can no longer see.
Therefore, they receive the retribution of being submerged in or falling into realms of filthy dust and foulness.
Seventh, the habituation of enmity.

Seventh, when the habits of enmity intersect and provoke mutual resentment, it gives rise to harbored hatred. Because of this, there are flying stones, thrown rocks, objects stored in boxes, placed in carriage enclosures, or kept in jars and bags;
these are like those who harbor malice with hidden poison, as the two habits swallow one another. Therefore, there are [such things].

Because they engage in all manner of acts—hurling, seizing, striking, shooting, casting, and snatching—the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate such an enemy as a "hostile and injurious demon" (*viheṭhaka-piśāca*).
When a Bodhisattva encounters an enemy, he views them as if drinking poisoned wine.

Hateful habits harbor resentment; hidden and concealed, they cause injury. Thus, like harboring malice through dark poison, one invokes the retribution of flying stones, being crushed by sacks, or being thrown, tossed, and seized.
Flying stones, projectiles, chariots, caskets, and sturdy fences are all matters of the hidden.
△ Eighth, the habit-energy of views.

Eighth, the mutual illumination of the habit-energies of views: such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the karmas of false awakening, which give rise to opposition and produce contrary outcomes.
Because of this, there are kings, messengers, officials, and clerks who testify to and uphold written records.

Just as travelers on a road meet one another in their coming and going, these two habit-energies intersect; thus, there arise interrogations, deceptions, examinations, and investigations through cross-examination.
Investigating and examining, one penetrates and illuminates [the truth]. The children of good and evil hold registers in their hands and debate all matters.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate "evil views" by the same name: the Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas see all pervasive attachments to the false and illusory, they regard them as if facing a precipice of poison.
There are five types of views to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): 1. **Satkāyadṛṣṭi** (the view of a self-existing body). This is translated as "body-view" (*shen-jian*).

It refers to the various attachments based on the grasping that the body possesses a self. 2. **Antagrāhadṛṣṭi** (the view of extremes). This refers to grasping at all phenomena as either annihilated or eternal. 3. **Mithyādṛṣṭi** (false view).

This refers to erroneous understanding and mistaken interpretation that denies cause and effect. 4. **Dṛṣṭiparāmarśa** (clinging to views). This refers to regarding what is not a fruit as being a fruit; for example, taking the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) to be *nirvāṇa*.

...and so forth. Fifth is the grasping at prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which consists of regarding what is not a cause as a cause, such as observing the "dog-precepts" as a means for rebirth in heaven.
These five are collectively termed "evil views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), because they accord with the heterodox and oppose the correct. Thus it is said that they "arise from rejection and produce opposition.
Because of this contrariety, one encounters the realm of royal officials who testify and seize one, and the state of being subjected to deceitful interrogation.
"Retribution. Meeting on the road, one person departs while the other returns; this is a metaphor for the contradiction between what is seen [and reality].
These five evil views can sink the Dharma-body; therefore, they are called "pits of views. They can lead to the suffering of karma; therefore, they are called "poisonous ravines.
Practitioners should swiftly extinguish them. △ Nine: The Habit of Injustice.

Ninth, the habit-energy of oppression intermingles, arising from false accusations and slander. Because of this, there are mountains and rocks joined together that crush, grind, plow, and rub [the beings].
Just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrong the virtuous, these two habits collide; therefore, there are various matters such as pressing down, hammering, crushing, straining, and measuring.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate resentment and slander with the same name.
Slanderous tigers: when a Bodhisattva encounters such injustice, it is like being struck by a bolt of lightning.
To bend what should not be bent is called "injustice" (*wang*). This injustice is not a matter of true feeling; it arises from false slander.

Because it oppresses others, the retribution received corresponds to that very act. It means to push aside and suppress; to press down and crush is also its meaning. *Lu* (to strain) and *li* (to drip) [refer to the resulting suffering].

"Ying" (衡) means "horizontal" (橫). This refers to being squeezed and compressed in body, with one's blood drained away, and furthermore, being forced through narrow, agonizing instruments horizontally.
That which is called "passing downward through," "hanging in a net," or "suspended upside down by the head"—all these belong to the category of horizontal passage.
Because slander can wound and harm others, it is named the "slanderous tiger. Because it can cause shock and terror, it is likened to a thunderclap. △ Ten.
The habit of litigation:
Tenth, the habit of litigation results in clamorous disputes arising from concealment and hypocrisy. Because of this, there is the mirror that reflects and illuminates;

just as one cannot hide one's shadow in the midst of the sun, these two habits are laid bare before one another, and thus there is the "karmic mirror" and the "fire-pearl" that expose evil associates.
Because past karma manifests through various circumstances, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the concealment [of one's faults] as "the hidden enemy," giving it the same name.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates this concealment, they perceive it as if wearing a mountain upon their head while treading across a vast ocean.

"Sòng" does not refer to legal litigation; it means to publicly expose what has been concealed. This refers precisely to the exposure of habitual practice. When this concealment meets that litigation, it is called "mutual clamor.

Thus, there arises the retribution of being confronted by a bad friend within the realm of the discerning mirror’s illuminating vision. Secretly harboring malice and concealing [one's faults], their exposure brings about self-harm.
The act of concealing one's transgressions merely serves to weigh one down and cause one to fall; it is like carrying a mountain upon one's head.
This is like treading upon the sea. The ten habitual tendencies arise from the ten delusions, encompassing both the root afflictions and their secondary manifestations.
There are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): the first are anger, resentment, vexation, concealment, deception, flattery, arrogance, and injury.

Here, the habit of "fraud" is *flattery*; "enmity" is *resentment*; "injustice" is *injury*; and "litigation" is *concealment*. This is merely a brief illustration. △ Second, the sixfold mutual retribution.
2. First, the general introduction:
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, for all sentient beings, the evil retributions summoned by the karma created through the six consciousnesses emerge from the six sense organs.

Karma is created from consciousness; retribution is manifested through the faculties. The convergence of karma and retribution is called "intersection. △ Second, a detailed explanation of the six [faculties].
First, the retribution of seeing. Second, one: retribution induced according to the faculties.
How is it that retribution for evil emerges from the six sense faculties? First is the retribution of sight, which draws forth evil fruits.

When this visual karma intersects with other conditions, at the time of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions. The deceased’s consciousness flies and falls, riding upon the smoke to enter the Avīci Hell.
This gives rise to two manifestations: first, the manifestation of clarity, by which one can see all manner of evil things everywhere.
They give rise to immeasurable fear. Second, regarding "dark vision": being silent and seeing nothing gives rise to immeasurable dread.
Seeing that perception belongs to fire thus invokes a fierce fire; fear is directed toward the external object, while dread is hidden within the mind.

As for the statement that "the six intermingled [karmas] all lead directly to the Avīci Hell," this is said with respect to the most grave cases. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Neither the most excellent good nor the most extreme evil has an intermediate state."
The *āyatanas* (senses) are thus directly entered. △ Second, transformation according to the faculties:
seeing fire in this way can burn the faculty of hearing, acting as boiling cauldrons and molten copper; it can burn the faculty of smell, acting as black smoke and purple flames.
When it burns the flesh, it can turn it into scorched balls and molten iron mash; when it burns the skin, it can turn it into hot ashes and glowing coals;
when it burns the heart, it can produce sparks that scatter like shooting stars, fanning and filling the void of space.
The faculty of hearing belongs to water; therefore, when burned, it can become boiling cauldrons and molten copper. The faculty of smelling governs air;
therefore, when its breath is burned, it can become black smoke and purple flames. The tongue governs taste; "balls of gruel" are a category of tastes. The body governs touch;
"ashes and charcoal" are categories of touch. The mind properly belongs to fire; when burned, it becomes even more intense, thus scattering, overflowing, fanning, and blowing. △ Second.
There are two types of hearing-retribution: first, karma that arises based on the sense organs;
second, hearing-retribution that draws forth evil fruits. When these two types of karmic hearing intersect, at the time of death, one first sees waves and surges submerging heaven and earth.
The deceased’s consciousness descends, follows the flowing water, and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two distinct appearances.

First is "open hearing": when one hears various kinds of clamor, the spirit becomes muddled and distracted. Second is "closed hearing": when it is silent and nothing is heard, the dark soul sinks into oblivion.

Hearing belongs to water; therefore, when one contemplates that hearing revolves and returns to its source, water cannot drown them. If one relies on it to create karma, one will be moved by waves and surges.
"Opening and closing" is like "passage and obstruction. "Mǎo" means stupor or delusion. △ Second, transformation according to the sense faculties.
When hearing the sound of waves, it can act as a reproach and an interrogation; when seeing them, it can act as thunder and a roar, and as the breath of evil poison;
when smelling them, it can act as rain and mist, sprinkling poisonous insects that completely cover the body.
If one focuses on flavor, it can become pus and blood, various kinds of filth and impurities. If one focuses on touch, it can become animals and ghosts, or feces and urine.
If one focuses on mental objects, it can become lightning and hail, crushing the heart and soul.

The commentary states that "hearing" refers to the emission of sound; thus, it concerns the matter of reprimanding transgressions and interrogating the state of mind. The commentary states that "seeing" is capable of producing the roar of thunder:
hearing corresponds to the Yin (陰), while seeing corresponds to the Yang (陽); for thunder is produced by the mutual friction of Yin and Yang.

The commentary states that "respiration" becomes rain and mist, as water changes according to the qi (vital energy). The commentary states that "flavor" becomes pus and blood, as water changes according to flavor. The commentary states...
Contact becomes a beast or a ghost; water changes according to its form. Attention becomes lightning or hail; the mind emerges from the heart, as water and fire interact.
Among all physical phenomena, none do not undergo transformation by means of the five elements riding upon yin and yang.
These matters of transformation following the sense organs do not transcend this principle. △ Third, the retribution of smelling has two parts. First, the basis.
The sense organ of the nose experiences karma.

Third is the retribution of smelling, which draws forth evil fruits. When this karmic act of smelling intersects with others, at the time of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings.
The deceased’s consciousness leaps up from the ground and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs.

First is "obstructed hearing," where one is permeated by various noxious vapors such that the mind becomes extremely disturbed. Second is "blocked hearing," where the vapors overwhelm and obstruct the senses, causing one to fall to the ground in a state of fainting.

Because of craving for foul odors, one performs various karmas; as a result, one is affected by toxic vapors, manifesting various retributions. △ Second, transformation according to the sense faculties:
when such odors strike the breath, they can become a solid substance or a vessel; when they strike the visual faculty, they can become fire or a torch.
When it encounters sound, it can become drowning, submersion, surging, and boiling; when it encounters flavor, it can become hunger and distaste;
when it encounters touch, it can become tearing, rotting, and a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes that insatiably devour.
When the impulses of thought strike, they can become ash or miasma, or flying sand and gravel that shatter the body; this is due to substantial obstruction (*pratigha*).

To tread upon is to pass through. Since the basis of olfactory karma does not depart from the conditions of penetration and obstruction, the impulse of the breath can thus become substantiality and the act of treading.
When the impulse of sight becomes a torch, and the impulse of hearing becomes drowning in a surging, boiling ocean, then the perception of seeing belongs [to these conditions].
Fire. It is clear that hearing belongs to water. Hunger and emaciation result from flavor following the transformation of the breath (*vāyu*).
Tearing, splitting, and rotting result from the physical body following the transformation of the breath. Being gored and crushed results in ash and sand, which arise through the influence of earth.
△ Fourth, the retribution of flavors has two parts. First, karma experienced based on the sense organs.

Fourth is the retribution of taste. It draws forth evil fruits. When this karma of taste intermingles with others, at the time of death, one first sees an iron net with fierce, blazing flames covering the entire world;
the deceased’s consciousness passes down through it, and its head hangs suspended upside down within the net.
They enter the Avīci Hell, where two manifestations arise: first, their inhalation forms into freezing ice that freezes and tears their flesh;
second, their exhalation flies up as fierce fire that scorches and rots their very marrow.

The tongue-faculty belongs to the mind. It issues speech to deceive others and craves flavors to ensnare beings; therefore, it brings about the sensation of being covered by a fiercely blazing iron net.
This is the basis for the karma of the tongue. It is never separate from inhalation and exhalation: inhaling produces cold, while exhaling produces heat—this is the natural principle.
2. Transformation according to the faculties.

When tasting flavors in this manner, through repeated tasting, they can become capable of receiving and enduring; when seeing in this manner, through repeated seeing, they can become like burning gold and stone;

when hearing in this manner, through repeated hearing, they can become like sharp weapons; when breathing in this manner, through repeated breathing, they can become like a great iron cage covering the entire land.

When it encounters [objects] through touch, it can become a bow, an arrow, a crossbow, or a shot; when it encounters them through thought, it can cause flying red-hot iron to rain down from the sky, devouring living beings with its tongue and making them endure it.
Thus, by encountering [objects] through tasting, it gives rise to suffering and makes oneself endure it. This is based on [wrong] views.
Because greed is obscuring, it can act as a flame that burns gold and stone. Because listening to [evil] gives rise to malice, it can act as sharp weapons.
Because smelling indulges greed to capture various flavors, it can act as a great iron cage.

Because the flavor of touch harms beings, one experiences bows and arrows to wound oneself. Because the flavor of thought pursues objects, one experiences flying iron to satisfy that craving. △ Five: Touch.
There are two types of retribution. First is the karma that arises based on the sense organs.
Fifth is the retribution of contact (*sparśa*), which invites and draws forth evil fruits.

When this karma of contact intersects with other factors, at the time of death, one first sees great mountains approaching from all four sides, closing in so that there is no way out. The deceased’s consciousness perceives a great iron city, filled with fire-snakes and fire-dogs.
Tigers, wolves, and lions; ox-headed hell-wardens and horse-headed rākṣasas—holding spears and lances, they drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell.
This gives rise to two kinds of manifestations: first, the manifestation of contact, wherein mountains close in upon their bodies, crushing their bones, flesh, and blood.
Second is the separation from touch (*spraṣṭavya*). When swords and blades strike the body, the heart and liver are torn asunder;

one’s physical karma (*kāyakarman*) frequently experiences and frequently gives rise to painful touch. Therefore, the grasping that summons the great mountain to crush one, the iron city, the fire-dogs, and so forth, are all the result of the retribution of various painful touches.
The basis of the karma of touch does not transcend contact and separation, such as being slaughtered.
"Rending" refers to the characteristic of detachment. △ Second, transformation according to the faculties:
such combined contact and successive contact can serve as the path and as contemplation; it can serve as the hall and as the desk. Successive seeing can serve as burning and scorching.
Successive hearing can serve as clashing, striking, stabbing, and shooting. Successive breathing can serve as... [and so forth].
When experienced through tasting, it can become plowing, tongs, cutting, and slicing;
when experienced through reflection, it can become falling, flying, frying, and roasting.
The "path" refers to the road leading to hell. The "gate-towers" refer to the two watchtowers at the gate of the King of Hell. The "courtroom" is the place where punishments are administered;

these are all bases for tactile contact (*kāya-spraṣṭavya*). Being burned and scorched is visual contact (*cakṣu-rūpa*). Being struck and beaten is auditory contact (*śrotra-śabda*). Being placed in a sack is olfactory contact (*ghrāṇa-gandha*).

Having one's tongue plowed and clamped is gustatory contact (*jihvā-rasa*). Flying and falling is mental contact (*mano-dharma*). As for being impaled, shot, interrogated, and bound, these arise through mutual dependence.
"Beside him he raises it": this refers to thrusting a blade into the flesh. "The sheath" is that which serves to contain the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Because the karma of thought (*cetanā*) is turbulent and drifting, one consequently experiences matters of flying and falling. △ Six: The Retribution of Thought, in two parts. First: Karma Experienced According to the Sense Organs.

Sixth is the retribution of volition. It draws forth evil fruits. When this volitional karma intersects with other conditions, at the time of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land.
The deceased’s consciousness is blown upward into the air, then whirled down by the wind and falls into the Avīci Hell.
This clarifies two aspects: first, non-awakening; when delusion reaches its extreme, one becomes desolate, running about without ceasing. Second, not being deluded;
when awakening occurs, there is suffering—an immeasurable burning whose pain is so profound it is difficult to endure.

Because volition (*cetanā*) is attached to the upper realm and is thus drifting and turbulent, one perceives such phenomena as being blown apart by evil winds and the destruction of the physical world.

The basis of this karmic volition does not transcend delusion and awakening: frantic rushing is deluded volition; knowing suffering is awakened volition. △ Second, transformation according to the faculties.
Thus, when wrong thought is bound, it can become a direction or a location; when wrong view is bound, it can become a mirror for receiving and realizing [objects];
when wrong hearing is bound, it can become a great congealing stone, ice, frost, earth, or mist;
when wrong breathing is bound, it can become a great fire carriage, a fire boat, or a fire cage; and when wrong tasting is bound, it can become great wailing, regret, and weeping.

When contact (*sparśa*) is bound, it can manifest as large or small, as ten thousand births and deaths within a single day, or as lying face down or face up; this is because thought must have an object.

When volition (*cetanā*) is bound, it constitutes the place where one undergoes punishment, for perception (*dṛṣṭi*) is able to discern and verify. When perception is bound, it constitutes the matter of the person who witnesses the offense.
When hearing (*śruta*) is bound, it can manifest as the joining together of great boulders and so forth, through the mutual interaction of water and earth.
Furthermore, vehicles, boats, and enclosures are transformations produced by the mind’s distracted thoughts acting upon the breath. The tongue-root is that from which sound originates.
From "large" and "small" downwards, all refer to the body as a transformation produced by the mind’s distracted thoughts acting upon the karma of touch.
△ Third, the conclusion: these arise from the fabrication of delusion.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six effects of the hells; they are all created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings.
△ Fourth, a detailed explanation of the gravity [of offenses], in five parts. First, the most extreme gravity.

If there are sentient beings who collectively commit evil karma and enter the Avīci Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas, they are said to have "collectively committed evil karma" when they equally engage all six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) to create the ten causes, involving both objects and faculties.
Because their offenses are extremely grave, they enter Avīci, where they possess the five immediate retributions (*pañca-ānantarya*). Second, the gravity of the offense.

If one commits offenses through each of the six sense faculties, and those actions involve both the objects and the faculties themselves, such a person enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (*aṣṭāv avīcayaḥ*).
"Committing them individually" implies there is a sequence and intervals between the acts; because these are the most grave, one enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells—which are the eight hot hells.
If one has the intention but does not go so far as to commit the offense, then the object is not involved. If one commits an offense unintentionally or by mistake, then [the same applies].
Furthermore, because one commits these acts with multiple faculties, one specifically incurs offenses involving both [the body and speech]. Third, next:
if one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three faculties of body, speech, and mind, such a person shall enter the eighteen hells.
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct committed through body, speech, and mind are grave offenses because they do not pervade all six [senses] nor are they complete in ten [factors].
Furthermore, these are slightly less serious than the preceding ones. In the great hells, there are only eight cold and eight hot hells;
however, the sutras mention eighteen sub-hells (*kalpa*) and eighty-four thousand attendant hells, all of which are divisions of the great hells. △ Fourth: Slightly lighter offenses.
The three karmas are not all present; that is, in the interim, one may commit either one act of killing or one act of stealing. Such a person enters thirty-six hells.
"The three karmas are not all present" means possessing two while lacking one. △ Fifth, the minor offenses.
"Seeing with the seeing-faculty" refers to a single faculty; it constitutes the commission of only one karma. Such a person enters one hundred and eight hells.
In the preceding cases, two were complete while one was missing; here, one is committed while two are missing, and is therefore lighter. "Jian" (seeing) is pronounced as "xian" (manifest);
it is clear and distinct, yet not inclusive of others. △ Fifth, the conclusion that answers the question.
Thus, sentient beings act and create individually, entering the stage of homogeneity within the world; their deluded imaginings arise, yet they do not exist from the beginning.
Regarding those who create individual homogeneity: for example, some create extremely grave karma and together enter the Avīci hell, while others create relatively light karma.
And they likewise enter the one hundred and eight [realms]. This is it. △ Second, the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati), in three parts. First, the indication of the causal origin:
"Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings have not violated the codes of discipline, nor have they transgressed the Bodhisattva precepts, nor have they destroyed the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa."
All other miscellaneous karmas burn for kalpas on end; when their retribution is finally exhausted, they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts.
To violate the *vinaya* is to lack a correct model; to transgress the Bodhisattva precepts is to lack a correct cause; to disparage the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* is to lack a correct fruit.
Because these three are incorrect, all others are likewise deviant. When the punishment for falling into hell is exhausted, one immediately—
Entering the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati). △ Second, clarifying the resulting categories. These categories consist of the mixed characteristics of afflictions and habitual tendencies;
that is to say, other miscellaneous karmas do not necessarily correspond exclusively to the ten causes. The text and its meaning do not follow [a fixed order].

If, regarding their original cause, they committed the offense of coveting material objects, once that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter matter and take form; these are called *guàiguǐ* (strange ghosts).
If they committed the offense of coveting sensual forms, once that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter wind and take form; these are called *póguǐ* (drought ghosts).

Because one who covets material objects is stingy and attached, unable to let them go, they become attached to objects and turn into monsters. Because one who covets form is deluded by the seductive and perverse, they fall and become a *yaopie* (a drought-demon).
As for these demons: when a *biegui* (drought-demon) encounters wind, it takes form; when a *meigui* (possessing demon) encounters an animal, it takes form;
when a *ligui* (pestilence demon) encounters decay, it takes form—each transforms according to the principles of its own kind.

Lustful delusion constitutes an offense; when this person’s retribution for that offense is exhausted, they encounter the form of an animal and become known as a *mèi* ghost. Hatred born of greed constitutes an offense;
when this person’s retribution for that offense is exhausted, they encounter the form of an insect and become known as a *gǔdú* ghost.
Lust is a haunting spirit; hatred is poison. This is the fixed principle. A haunting spirit is a malevolent essence. Greed and remembrance constitute a transgression.
When such a person’s transgression is exhausted, they encounter decay and take form, becoming what is called a "leprous ghost. Arrogance born of greed is likewise a transgression.
When this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter the vital energies (*qi*) that take form; they are called a hungry ghost (*preta*).
Because those who were "remorseful" (*yi*) constantly harbored malice and cruelty, they become pestilential and tyrannical ghosts when encountering places of calamity and decay.
Because those who were "arrogant" (*ao*) were falsely conceited and relied upon their own vital energies, they ride upon the empty and vacuous energies to become a class of hungry ghosts.

To covet and deceive is a transgression. When this person’s retribution for that sin is exhausted, they encounter the essence of darkness and take on a form; this is called a *yān-gui* (dream-disturbing ghost). To covet light is a transgression.
When this person’s retribution for that sin is exhausted, they encounter the essence of spirits and take on a form; this is called a *wǎngliǎng-gui* (forest-dwelling ghost).
Those who are greedy for the obscure immerse their minds in the dark and hidden; encountering the profound darkness, they become nightmares—all of which are matters of the dark and hidden.
Those who are greedy for clarity harbor deluded thoughts of the lofty and bright; thus, they secretly attach themselves to refined spirits and become a class of *wangliang* demons.
If greed becomes a transgression, when that person’s retribution for the sin is exhausted, they encounter a luminous form; this is called a "servant ghost.
If greed forms a faction and becomes a transgression, when that person’s retribution for the sin is exhausted, they encounter a human form; this is called a "messenger ghost."
Regarding those who achieve their desires through greed: because they follow others' will with devious intent, they attach themselves to luminous spirits to serve as their minions;

that is, they rely on spirit shrines to act as their messengers. Regarding those who form factions through greed: because they sycophantically align with the wicked and flatterers, they take form upon meeting people to serve as their transmitters;
that is, they attach themselves to shamans and priests to convey omens of good and ill fortune. △ Third, the conclusion on their falsity.
Ānanda, these people have all fallen due to their pure emotional attachments; once the fires of karma have burned them dry, they emerge above as ghosts.
All of these are summoned and drawn forth by the karma of their own deluded thoughts. If one awakens to Bodhi, then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous nature is fundamentally nothing at all.
Because the water of emotional karma has accumulated, one sinks downward; when it is burned dry, emotional karma is exhausted, and one ascends again by means of the karma of thought.
All of this is the work of delusive ignorance. The perfectly luminous mind of awakening fundamentally possesses none of these things. △ Third, the three realms of animal rebirth.
First, the indication of the causal origin.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of the hungry ghost is exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty.
Only then, within the world, does one encounter the person from whom one originally owed a debt, meeting with that karmic adversary as a beast to repay its past debts.

The retribution of hell arises from the karma of emotion; the retribution of hungry ghosts arises from the karma of perception. Thus, when the karma of the hungry ghosts is exhausted, both forms of retribution become empty. One then repays the remaining karma of debt.
△ Second, explaining the types of beings thus induced.
The ghosts of anomalous creatures, when their retribution is exhausted and they vanish from their state, are born into the human world mostly as species of owls.
The ghosts of wind-demons (*pāpa*), when their retribution is exhausted and they vanish from their state, are born into the human world mostly as all manner of ill-omened anomalies.
The earth-owl (*kṣetrapāla*) clings to clods of earth; this is the lingering habit of its former attachment to evil. The *pūtanā* ghost was once a malevolent omen;

thus, its lingering habits again manifest as signs of calamity. "Signs of calamity" refers to precursors to misfortune, such as the flying squirrel calling out to people or the *śaṅga-rāya* bird dancing upon the water.
Those ghosts who harbored malevolent spirits, when their retribution for those deaths is exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as foxes.
Those ghosts who harbored insect-pestilence spirits, when their retribution for the destruction by those insects is exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as venomous creatures.
Because they were possessed by spirits inhabiting animals, their residual habits cause them to become foxes. Snakes, vipers, adders, and scorpions all belong to the class of venomous creatures.

Spirits of decay and pestilence, when their retribution for decline and poverty is exhausted, are born into the human world; they mostly become types of intestinal worms. These are the ghosts that receive [only] vital breath.
When their vital energy has dissipated and their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn in the world of humans, mostly as types of food.

As pestilential ghosts (*pūtana*), they afflict people; as *ārma* and *krimi* worms, they infest them. Among the hungry ghosts, they suffer from starvation; among the animals, they serve as offerings of abundance.
The ghosts of lingering obscurity, when their subtle dissolution and retribution are exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as types of clothing.
The ghosts of harmonious refinement, when their subtle dissolution and retribution are exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as types of responsive objects.

"Cotton" (*mian*) means "to adhere" (*zhuo*). It adheres to the hidden and afflicts people; thus it is categorized as a type of clothing. Furthermore, it adheres to people, referring to the categories of silkworms, oxen, horses, and so forth.

"Harmony" (*he*) means "to combine. By combining the residual habits of the essence, they can respond to the seasonal cycles; this refers to the categories of the social swallows, the cold-season geese, the crickets, and so forth.
The ghosts of the enlightened and numinous, when their enlightenment fades and their retribution is exhausted, are reborn in the world, mostly as auspicious omens among all classes of beings.
The ghosts that depend upon humans, when those humans perish and their retribution is exhausted, are reborn in the world, mostly as members of the same species.
They are luminous rather than obscure; thus they are auspicious omens (*xiuzheng*). They are of the same category as the magnificent phoenix and the auspicious qilin.

Because they formerly relied upon humans, they became tame and submissive to them, such as the categories of cats, dogs, chickens, and pigs. Generally, all these extraordinary creatures possess natures that are wondrously akin to the divine.
The spiritual capacity of beings surpasses that of humans. For instance, tortoises are skilled at examining auspicious omens, and horses are able to perceive the Way.
Even species such as the cold-weather wild geese and the cricket do not rely on the calendar to know the seasons; this is all due to residual habit-energy (*vāsanā*).

When it is said that each [species] possesses much [of a certain quality], this is spoken in terms of the predominant portion of their karmic habits; it does not necessarily apply to every single case. △ Third, the conclusion regarding delusive falsity.
Ānanda, these beings have all been withered by the fire of karma and must repay their past debts; thus they are relegated to the state of animals.
These, too, are all summoned and drawn forth by their own false and delusive karma. If one awakens to Bodhi, then these false conditions will fundamentally be found to be non-existent.
It is as you have said regarding those such as Ratnapadmagandha, King Vairōcana, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra. Thus it is.
Evil karma originally arises from within oneself; it does not descend from heaven, nor emerge from the earth, nor is it bestowed by others.
It is summoned by one's own delusions and must be experienced by oneself. Within the mind of Bodhi, all such things are merely the solidification of floating, empty, and false imaginings.
△ Four types of beings proceed to three destinies. First, explaining the repayment of karma; second, a counter-objection regarding their surplus.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when these animals repay their prior debts, if the one being repaid exceeds what was owed, [the remainder persists].
These sentient beings, having returned to human form, are in turn required to repay the surplus.

If they possess both power and merit, they shall not relinquish their human bodies while among men to repay that strength. If they lack merit, they will instead become animals to compensate for the remaining value.
One should provide them with their rightful compensation. If the compensation exceeds their share, then for the sake of others, one will instead be subjected to excessive demands.

This refers to unreasonable forced labor and immoderate consumption; all such acts will result in being counter-demanded. Thus, in whatever food or resources one takes, one should not exceed the proper measure.
II. Because of these counter-demands, enmity arises.
Ānanda, you should know that if one uses money or goods, or employs their labor, the debt is settled once it is fully repaid and then ceases.
However, if in the interim one takes their life or eats their flesh, then even after passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they will continue to devour and slaughter one another.
It is like a turning wheel, alternating between high and low without rest; it cannot be brought to a halt except through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Once the debt is fully repaid, it stops of its own accord; if the debt is not fully repaid, the enmity will not cease. Unless—
They correctly cultivate the power of right effort; let none obstruct or cut it off. △ Second, clarifying the resulting retribution:
You should now know that those of the species of owls, having received their full retribution and regained their physical forms, are born among the human race as members of the dull-witted class.
Those who exhibited those ill omens, once their retribution was exhausted and they resumed their physical forms, were reborn among human beings, yet mixed with the ranks of the foolish.

Those of the fox-like nature, once their retribution was exhausted and they resumed their physical forms, were reborn among human beings, yet mixed with the ranks of the cruel. Those of the venomous nature, once their retribution was exhausted and they resumed their physical forms...
Born among the human realm, they are integrated with the common class. Those of the category of *āhri* (the "worm-like") have fulfilled their retribution and resumed form;

born among the human realm, they are integrated with the subtle class. Those of the category of *āśī* (the "eater-like") have fulfilled their retribution and resumed form; born among the human realm, they are integrated with the gentle class.
Those who followed the worldly norms, having received full retribution and restored their forms, were reborn among human beings as members of the laboring class.

Those who responded to the moral order, having received full retribution and restored their forms, were reborn among human beings as members of the literary class. Those who possessed auspicious signs, having received full retribution and restored their forms, [were likewise reborn among human beings].

Born into the human realm, they are integrated among those of clear intelligence. Those who follow the moral order receive full recompense and restore their physical forms; born into the human realm, they are integrated among those of profound realization.
Because the owl feeds on lumps of earth, its residual habituation is stubbornness, stupidity, and unrighteousness.

Because the *pó* (drought-demon) deludes nature through lewd sorcery, its residual habituation is foolishness, simplicity, and lack of wisdom. Because the fox follows its own animalistic nature, it is headstrong and does not obey.

Because the *dú* (poisonous insect) is blinded by its own vermin-sorcery, it is vulgar, lowly, and lacks acuity. Because the intestinal worm attaches itself to decaying matter, it is weak and diminished.

The *bushi* (not-tooth) arises from the hunger for devouring; therefore, it is supple and timid rather than courageous. The *fulei* (clothing-pattern) arises from the persistence of cotton-like attachment;

therefore, labor and service never cease. The *yinglei* (response-pattern) arises from clarity and brilliance; therefore, culture and refinement are not crude. The *xiuzheng* (auspicious-sign) arises from spiritual awareness;
therefore, intelligence and wisdom are not clouded. The *xunlei* (following-pattern) arises from long-standing involvement in worldly affairs; therefore, one is perspicacious and not ignorant.
These are all not primary karmic retributions, but rather accidental occurrences resulting from residual habits; hence they are called "intermingled.

The latter three are merely clever and miscellaneous arts of worldly wisdom and eloquence; they are not the matters of the enlightened, the refined, the civil, or the luminous. △ Third, concluding that these are false and illusory.
Ānanda, these individuals have all fully repaid their past debts and have again taken human form.

Yet, because they have been subject to the inverted calculations of karma since beginningless time—mutually giving birth to one another and mutually killing one another—they have not encountered the Tathāgata nor heard the True Dharma. Thus, amidst the dust and toil of worldly afflictions, they naturally revolve in the cycle of rebirth.
Such people as these are called those who are to be pitied.
The wheel of perverse and inverted karma can only be halted by what is correct; therefore, those who do not encounter a Tathāgata are to be pitied.
△ Fifth, the three destinies of the rishis. First, the indication of the causal origin.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are those who follow others and do not rely on the Perfectly Awakened One to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts and fixate their mental images to preserve the physical form.
They roam in mountain forests and places inaccessible to ordinary people; these are the ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
"Xian" (仙) means "to transcend. It refers to the human form and spirit being able to transcend and not die. Therefore it is said: "By preserving one's thoughts, one solidifies the form.

Nevertheless, in the end, it returns to decay and ruin; compared to Heaven, it is inferior, but compared to ordinary humans, it is superior. Thus, it is categorized separately. △ Second, clarifying the categories of resonance.
Ānanda, those sentient beings who steadfastly consume medicinal elixirs without ceasing perfect the path of food and are called earth-walking immortals (*bhūmicara-siddha*).
Those who steadfastly ingest herbs and plants without ceasing perfect the path of medicine and are called flying immortals (*khecara-siddha*).
To sustain one's lifespan for a single period by means of medicinal elixirs, yet being unable to levitate, is called "walking on the ground.

To consume substances such as *huangjing* (yellow essence) and pine or cypress, whereby the body becomes light after a long time, is called "flying. This refers to the practice of cultivating meritorious deeds.
One who is as firm as metal or stone and does not rest, having perfected the path of transformation, is called a *vihāyasaga* (wandering immortal).
One who is firm in movement and stillness and does not rest, having perfected the essence of vital energy (*prāṇa*), is called a *khecaratva* (space-faring immortal).

Refining metallic elixirs such as the "returning cinnabar" (huandan) to transform the bones and alter one's physical form; gathering soil or touching stones to roam at will among humans—this is called "wandering travel" (youxing).

Riding upon the movement and stillness of yin and yang to regulate the vital breath and consolidate the essence, leaving the physical form behind to traverse the void—this is called "empty travel" (kongxing).
Solidifying the vital fluids without ceasing, one perfects the virtue of moisture; this is called a "Heavenly-Walking Immortal" (devayāna-ṛṣi).
Solidifying the refined essence without ceasing, one perfects the absorption of the pure; this is called a "Pervasive-Walking Immortal" (sarvagāmi-ṛṣi).

To beat the celestial pond and swallow the vital fluids, remaining as pure and refined as ice and snow, untainted by worldly desires, and thus being no different from the heavens—this is called "Heavenly Conduct" (tianxing).
To inhale and absorb the essence of colors, to wear the rainbow and drink the mist, so that the pure qi penetrates in hidden harmony—this is called "Pervasive Conduct" (tongxing).
If one maintains firm mantra-restraints without ceasing, and the methods of the arts are perfected, one is called a "Siddha of Path-Practice.
If one maintains firm contemplation without ceasing, and the recollection is perfected, one is called a "Siddha of Illuminating Practice."

To be able to employ ritual methods (*śūtra-dharma*) to describe the spontaneity of the Way is called "Practice of the Way" (*Mārga-caryā*). To clarify and concentrate one's refined contemplation so that it can long ago illuminate and respond is called "Practice of Illumination" (*Āloka-caryā*).

Alternatively, visualizing the aperture at the crown of the head to emit the spirit (*śuddha-ātman*), or binding the mind to the navel wheel (*nābhi-cakra*) to refine the elixir (*rasāyana*), all involve the perfect accomplishment of recollective visualization.
When firm union is maintained without ceasing, and responsive resonance is perfected, one is called a Perfected Immortal of Refinement (*viśuddha-caryā-rṣi*).
When firm transformation is maintained without ceasing, and awakening is perfected, one is called a Perfected Immortal of Transcendence (*atyanta-caryā-rṣi*).

Internally, they pair the male of the *kan* trigram with the female of the *li* trigram to form a husband and wife; externally, they gather yin to assist yang and preserve their vital essence (*jing*).
This is called the "practice of refinement" (*jingxing*). By contemplating and transforming through mental visualization, their minds follow perverted awakenings and achieve great transformations;
their conduct transcends the world, hence it is called the "transcendent practice" (*juexing*). △ Third, the conclusion on false delusions.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate Right Enlightenment. Instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence and live for ten million years.
They dwell in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands, far removed from the realm of humanity. This, too, is the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra;
failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.

△ Section Six: The Three [Categories] of the Six Celestial Realms. First, the six heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). Second, the first: enumerating and clarifying the six. First, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājakāyika).
Ānanda, the people of the various worlds do not seek permanence; they have not yet been able to relinquish their affection for their wives and concubines. Regarding the wrong [views]...
When one’s mind does not flow into or stray toward lust, it becomes clear, limpid, and luminous. After the end of life, such a person dwells near the sun and moon;
this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
One has not yet been able to leave desire behind; however, by being able to obstruct desire so that the waters of craving do not flow, the nature of stillness becomes clear and translucent.
Thus, one can be born in the first heaven. The six heavens are attained through the cultivation of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

Now, we shall merely discuss those who have slightly increased their excellence over desire. Desire and craving are the root of saṃsāra; as previously explained, even the process of falling and sinking begins here.

This clarifies that transcending and ascending also begins from this point. The intent is to enable those at the initial stage who have not yet achieved meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to swiftly sever the root [of affliction]; thus, they may escape from saṃsāra. △ Second: The Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Regarding their own wives, their lustful desire is slight; even when dwelling in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), they do not experience complete flavor.
After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm. This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This craving is thinner than that which preceded it; therefore, its retribution dwells above it. The subsequent stages follow this same principle.
"Pure Abodes" (Śuddhāvāsa) refers to the time when one dwells in purity for oneself. Yet, they do not possess the full flavor of complete purity because there remains a trace of subtle craving.

The sun and moon dwell on the waist of Mount Sumeru, while the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwells upon its summit. Because their clarity and brilliance increase, they are able to transcend [the lower realms]. △ Third: The Times.
The Divided Heaven (Vibhuṣita-deva):
upon encountering desire, they engage briefly; once it has passed, they have no further thoughts or memories. In the human world, their movement is slight and their stillness is great.
After the end of their lives, they dwell serenely and clearly in the midst of empty space, where the radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach upward. These are such persons.
They possess their own radiance. This class is called the Suyāma Heaven.

Because they do not give rise to lustful thoughts, their movement is slight and their stillness is predominant. Of the six heavens of the desire realm, the lower two are known as the earth-dwelling heavens (*bhūmiśaya*), and the upper four are known as the space-dwelling heavens (*antarīkṣa*).
They do not require the sun or moon to be constantly bright; day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of lotus flowers.
Because there is still night, it is called the Stage of Time (Kāmadhātu). Fourth, the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita):
at all times they are tranquil; though sensory contacts may arise, they have not yet been able to contravene their state. After the end of life, they ascend to a refined and subtle realm.
It does not reach down to the realms of humans or devas of the lower worlds; even until the destruction of the kalpa, it is not affected by the three calamities.
Such a class [of beings] is called the Tuṣita Heaven.

Although the mind may become increasingly tranquil, one still cannot avoid contact with sensory objects; this is the state of having few desires, yet not yet being without mind. In the Tuṣita Heaven, there are inner and outer courtyards.
While the three calamities reach up to the third dhyāna heaven, this [Tuṣita] is not included therein; this is said in reference to the inner courtyard.
Its subtle essence does not encounter external stimuli—all such matters pertain to the inner courtyard. △ Five: Delighting in Transformations.
"O Deva, I have no desire; I comply with your actions only because you are acting. At the time of our union, the flavor was like chewing wax.
After my life ended, I was reborn in the Realm of the Gods Who Delight in Emanation (Nirmāṇarati). This class of beings is called the Gods Who Delight in Emanation."

This state, in which objects spontaneously appear while one is without conscious intent, is called "laid out horizontally" (*hengchen*). To say it is like chewing wax is to describe its flavor as extremely thin.

All devas possess realms of retribution, yet the pleasures of this heaven are enjoyed through spontaneous transformation; thus it surpasses the lower heavens and is named "Surpassing Transformation" (*Yuehua*).
6. The Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
They possess no worldly mind, yet they engage in worldly affairs; amidst these interactions, they clearly transcend them.

After their lives end, they are universally able to emerge and transcend both realms of transformation and non-transformation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
"Clearly transcending" means that [the preceding states] are entirely devoid of flavor. "Transformation" refers to the fifth heaven; "non-transformation" refers to the heavens below it.

Without needing to labor to transform objects oneself, all realms of sensual pleasure are enjoyed with mastery through the transformations of others; thus they are named "Mastery over Others' Transformations.
△ Second, the conclusion regarding delusion.
Ānanda, it is thus with these six heavens: although their forms move about, the traces of their minds still intermingle. From this point downward, they are called the Realm of Desire (kāmadhātu).
Although they have emerged from the disturbances of the mundane world, they have not yet been able to sever desire; therefore, they are collectively named the Realm of Desire.
