Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas. Scroll Seventeen.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā of the country of Ujjayinī;

orally interpreted by the Bodhisattva-śīla disciple Fang Rong of Qinghe, formerly Grand Master for Regular Counsel and concurrently Minister of State Affairs in the Chancellery and Secretariat; recorded in writing by Fang Rong.
The Bhikṣu Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wénlíng explains:
△ Second, the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Although they are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form; therefore, it is named the Form Realm.

It is collectively termed the "Brahma-world" because it has already abandoned the defilement of desire. It is collectively designated as the "Four Dhyānas" because it has already abandoned distraction and agitation.
While the heavens of the desire realm are produced through the retribution of the ten wholesome deeds alone, these heavens are produced through the combined retribution of dhyāna-concentration.

Nevertheless, this consists merely of the sixfold practice of impure dhyāna-contemplation. As for the six practices: one feels aversion toward the desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and an obstruction, and one rejoices in...
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is pure, sublime, and detached; this is the mundane path by which ordinary beings suppress their afflictions.
This section has two parts. First, listing and clarifying the four [dhyānas]. First, the three heavens of the first dhyāna. First, the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*).
Ānanda, among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, there are those who do not rely on *dhyāna* and possess no wisdom, yet are able to restrain their bodies from practicing sexual desire.
Whether walking or sitting, they are free from such thoughts; because defilement does not arise, they do not remain in the realm of desire.
Such persons should consider themselves companions of Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārṣadya*).

Regarding the phrase "without relying on *dhyāna*," etc.: although this is not the correct cultivation of true *samādhi* and lacks true wisdom, by merely practicing the six modes of conduct (*ṣaḍvidhābhijñā*) to suppress desire and prevent the arising of passionate attachment, one will not remain in the Desire Realm.

Being untainted by coarse delusions, a pure retribution manifests before them, and thus they are reborn in the Brahma world. Initially, they are called the "Assembly of Brahmās" (*Brahmapārṣadya*), which refers simply to the common multitude.

Next is named Brahmā-purohita (Brahma-Minister). These are the ministers of Mahābrahmā, culminating in the rank of Mahābrahmā itself; their advancement follows a sequential order. △ Second, the Brahmā-purohita Heaven.

Having eliminated the habitual tendencies of desire, the mind free from desire manifests. Regarding all forms of restraint (*saṃvara*), they feel love and joy, and accord with them. Such persons, at that time—
Those who are able to practice the virtues of Brahma (*brahmacarya*) constitute one class known as the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (*Brahmapurohita*).

While the first heaven (the Heaven of Great Brahma) merely maintains physical restraint to subdue desire, these gods further attain the precepts coexistent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).

Because they practice the virtues of Brahma in accordance with the monastic discipline (*vinaya*), they transcend the former. The precepts associated with meditative concentration are called the "precepts coexistent with concentration. 3. Mahābrahmā (The Great Brahma)
"O Deva,
with body and mind wondrously perfected, his deportment flawless, and his pure prohibitions and precepts further augmented by clear awakening,
this person is able at that time to preside over the Brahma host as a Great Brahma King. This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven."
Through the aforementioned pure mind, dignified deportment, and moral conduct, one advances to the stage of wondrous, perfect purity;
further augmented by clear awakening and transcendent penetration, this constitutes the height of sublime virtue, and thus one becomes a Brahma King. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
Ānanda, these three superior classes cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although they have not yet attained the true, correct samādhi, because their pure minds are unmoved by any outflows (āsrava), this is called the first dhyāna.
These are indeed "flows" (*ogha*). There are the flow of ignorance, the flow of birth-and-death, the flow of desire, the flow of supremacy, the flow of the four fruits, and the flow of nirvana;
each proceeds according to its respective category of flow. The flow of desire leads toward birth-and-death;

even reaching the sixth heaven is not sufficient to be considered supreme. This heaven has already emerged from the flow of desire, for it turns its back on birth-and-death and proceeds toward supreme purity.
The four dhyānas are all termed "superior flows" (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*). Having already departed from the eight sufferings of the desire realm, it is said that "suffering and affliction do not oppress.
Having already departed from the restless and agitated mind of desire, it is said that "all outflows (*āsrava*) are unmoving. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*," meaning that one has departed from the mixed evils of the desire realm and attained the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) born of that seclusion. △ Second, the second dhyāna.
The third heaven is the fourth [level]. First is the Heaven of Limited Radiance (Parīttābhā).
Ānanda, next is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmās; there they fulfill the Brahma-conduct, their minds are clear and unmoving, and from profound stillness radiance is born.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Radiance.
This refers to ascending through the practices of Mahābrahmā, fully possessing precepts, concentration, and wisdom; hence it is called "perfect.

Because of this perfection, one is able to clarify and stabilize the mind so that it does not move following external objects, and from this profound stillness, light arises. However, at this initial stage, one is merely able to detach from clinging and restore the clarity of the mind;
since this light is still inferior, it is named "Limited Light" (Parīttābha). 2. Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha).
Light illuminates light in mutual radiance, shining forth without end; it reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, universally transforming them into lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.

The power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly luminous, and wondrous light issues forth. As the objective realm follows this light, it becomes pure and universally transforms into lapis lazuli.

△ Third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven) absorbs and sustains this perfect radiance, thereby accomplishing the essence of the teaching. It brings about pure transformation, and its applications are inexhaustible. Such is one class [of beings].
It is named the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).

Because the substance of the teachings differs across various worlds—the Sahā world employs written characters, while the Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*) world lacks written characters and teaches solely through various fragrances—this heaven produces sound from its circular radiance to proclaim and disseminate the Dharma; hence its name.
The Light-Sound Heaven. △ Fourth, the conclusion:
"Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any anxieties or apprehensions.
Although they do not yet constitute the true, correct Samādhi, because coarse outflows have been suppressed within their pure minds, this is called the Second Dhyāna."
In the second dhyāna, one is free from sorrow and attains supreme joy and bliss; therefore, it is said that "sorrow and anxiety do not oppress.

In the first dhyāna, one merely attains a mind free from outflows (*āsrava*), yet has not yet subdued them. In this heaven, having already subdued the coarse outflows, karma gradually diminishes and practice gradually excels.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration," meaning that the water of concentration moistens the sorrow of karma.
"Suspended, they are not constrained. △ Third, the three heavens of the third dhyāna, four [parts]. First, the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha).

"Ānanda, such celestial beings possess perfected radiance that forms sound; they unveil the wondrous by shedding their voices. Their development constitutes refined practice, and they penetrate the bliss of quiescent extinction.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity."
From the teaching-essence of the aforementioned radiant halo, the wondrous principle is revealed, giving rise to refined practice. Departing from the prior agitation of joy, pure bliss is produced;
this bliss is not an external object, but emerges from the pure nature. Serene, tranquil, and still, it is called the bliss of nirvana (*śānti-sukha*).
However, because the power of purity is still inferior, one can merely penetrate [it] but has not yet perfected it. It is for this reason that it remains inferior.
This is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parittasubha). △ Second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇasubha):
When the pure void manifests before one, it induces boundlessness; body and mind become light and tranquil, achieving the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity.
Regarding "purity and emptiness": it is a state of meditative concentration that is free from all agitation caused by joy and does not take external objects as its focal point.
By expanding this state until the mark of purity is boundless, one accords with the wondrous nature; thus, body and mind become light and at ease, and the bliss of the nature is realized.
Because it is boundless, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha). △ Third, the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna):
World, body, and mind are all perfectly pure; the qualities of purity are fully accomplished; supreme reliance manifests before them, and they return to the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity) devas.
Because the pure space is boundless, their worlds, bodies, and minds are all perfectly pure.
Having achieved this purity of virtue, their innate joy takes refuge and reposes therein. Because everything is perfectly pure, they are named Śubhakṛtsna. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure, and they obtain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained genuine *samādhi*, within their peaceful and secure minds, joy is fully present; this is called the third dhyāna.
Possessing the nature of refined conduct and delighting in [this state] is called "great conformity"; thus, it is immeasurably peaceful and secure.
As for "complete joy," this is termed the stage of "sublime bliss free from joy. This means that although the mind is free from joy, the bliss of joy is spontaneously present.

△ The four dhyānas comprise nine heavens. Within the retributive realms of the four dhyānas, there are only three heavens; the fourth, the Unconscious (asaṃjñi-sattva), is actually the third, the Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala).
This is separately established as the retributive realm for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana). Above these four are the five Non-returner (anāgāmin) heavens;

these are produced through the karma of noble ones (ārya) who have cultivated meditative concentration (dhyāna) specifically to support the Vast Fruit realm, and thus differ from that of ordinary beings.

The same applies here; therefore, they are listed separately. The text has two parts: first, the four fundamental heavens. The preceding meditative practices were solely for one's own benefit and were unable to benefit others.
Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, one concurrently cultivates the altruistic minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*);
these are called the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). From these, untainted insight (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and all dhyānas and samādhis emerge; hence, they are so named.
The Fundamental. The text has five sections. First, the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*).
"Ānanda, furthermore, for these devas, neither body nor mind is oppressed. The causes of suffering have been exhausted; pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably perish after a long time.

Both the minds of suffering and pleasure are simultaneously and suddenly relinquished. The characteristics of grossness and heaviness are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises. Thus it is."
One class is called the Heaven of the Birth of Merit (*Puṇyaprasava*).

Although their previous afflictions and sufferings have already been exhausted and they have attained immeasurable bliss, that bliss does not endure; the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*) will inevitably follow.

The devas of this heaven realize this, and thus they suddenly relinquish both suffering and pleasure. Because they relinquish suffering and pleasure, the characteristics of gross heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) are extinguished; this is called relinquishment (*upekṣā*).
Because mindfulness is pure, the nature of pure merit arises. Second, the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*):
their mind of equanimity is perfectly integrated and their resolute understanding is pure; within unobstructed merit, they attain wondrous conformity that extends to the end of the future.
This class of beings is called the Puṇyaprasavā devas.
Because they have forgotten both suffering and pleasure, their mind of equanimity is perfectly integrated. Because the mind is free from all burdens, their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is pure.

Consequently, their merit encounters no obstruction, and they attain sublime conformity; thus, from within contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), they give rise to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

It proceeds until it reaches its ultimate consummation; therefore, it is said to "extend to the limits of the future. Since the merit of meditative concentration is thus, it is called "lovable merit" (*puṇyapriya*).
△ Third, the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*).

Ānanda, from this heaven there are two diverging paths. If one dwells in the cultivation and realization of the previously mentioned immeasurable pure light and the perfect clarity of merit, such a class is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
From the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), there branch off two paths: one is the direct path leading to the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*);

the other is the circuitous path leading to the Realm of Non-Perception (*Āsaṃjñika*). If, regarding the preceding mind, one does not harbor divergent attachments but practices meditative concentration directly, causing the merit cultivated from the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā*) up to the Heaven of Merit-Love to abide in perfect clarity, then the meditative merit of this heaven becomes exceedingly vast. Therefore—
This is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala). △ Fourth is the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva).

If, regarding the preceding mind, one simultaneously becomes weary of both suffering and pleasure, and cultivates a state of equanimity (upekṣā) with continuous, uninterrupted application, thereby fully perfecting the path of equanimity;

Body and mind both cease; the mental faculties become like ashen stasis. For five hundred kalpas, because this person takes arising and ceasing as their cause, they are unable to manifest the nature that is neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
For the first half-kalpa there is cessation, and for the latter half-kalpa there is birth. This class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Thought (Āsaṃjñika-deva).

Although the preceding mind was able to subdue afflictions and cultivate dhyāna, it involved delusion and retained dualistic distinctions. It took the presence of mind as birth-and-death and the absence of thought as nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, it came to simultaneously loathe both suffering and pleasure, focusing exclusively on the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) to advance toward the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi*).
By relinquishing external objects, then the body, and finally all mental conceptions, one is said to have perfected the path of equanimity. This is the [state of] mind...

"Contemplating the congealing of ash" refers to the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). By means of this, one receives retribution and is born in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), with a lifespan of five hundred *kalpas*.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that when first born in this heaven, one has not yet entirely ceased conceptualization; it is only after half a *kalpa* that it ceases.
As the retribution is about to end, one again possesses conceptualization for half a *kalpa*, and only then does the retribution expire. △ Five: Conclusion.
Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure.
Although they are not the unconditioned truly immovable stage, because the mental effort of those who still possess a grasping mind has reached full maturity, they are called the Four Dhyānas.

The mind of conceptualization consists of vitarka (coarse thought) and vicāra (subtle thought). In the first dhyāna, both of these are present in the two heavens; in the Great Brahmā heaven, there is vicāra alone without vitarka.
In the second dhyāna, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra, but there is joy and bliss. In the third dhyāna, one is free from joy and bliss, yet there is inhalation and exhalation.
Vitarka and vicāra give rise to fire; joy and bliss give rise to water; and inhalation and exhalation give rise to wind. In the fourth dhyāna, one is free from all of these.

It is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) because it cannot be shaken by the three calamities. Nevertheless, that vessel-world is not truly eternal; it arises and perishes along with sentient beings.
Although it is not the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) true realm, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) application of effort has here reached a state of complete maturity.
II. The Five Non-returner Heavens (*anāgāmin-deva*). 1. General Summary.
Ānanda, herein there are further five types of Non-returners (anāgāmin). Within the lower realms, their nine grades of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are extinguished simultaneously;
both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and since they no longer dwell below, they establish their abodes within the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) of equanimity (upekṣā-citta).
The person of the third fruit, having exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, is reborn in this heaven and will not take birth again in the desire realm;
therefore, they are called an Anāgāmin (Non-returner). They are also called the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*), meaning the dwelling place of those with pure bodies who have abandoned desire.

Regarding the "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-bīja*), these are the latent afflictions; since both these and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are extinguished, it is said that they are "exhausted together. This refers to the absence of continuity in the desire realm.
This refers to the karma of rebirth. Since both suffering and pleasure have vanished, it also indicates that there is no continuous karma from the fourth dhyāna downward.

Therefore, it is said that there is no place to settle below this level. These five heavens are established separately from the fourth dhyāna and are collectively named the Stage of Pure Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).
Therefore it is said: "The realm of those who have abandoned the mind. △ Second, the specific enumeration of the five [heavens]: First, the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*).
Ānanda, where both suffering and pleasure are extinguished, and where contentious minds do not interact—such a class is named the Heaven of No Affliction.
If one previously possessed equanimity and disenchantment toward suffering and pleasure, then the mind would struggle with its objects and could not be free from vexation.
Only when both the mind and its objects are relinquished do afflictions cease. △ Second, the Heaven Without Heat (Atapa).
The mechanism of their minds functions in solitude; there is no ground for them to cultivate intimacy.

This class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Heat (*Atapa*). Intense heat is termed "affliction" (*kliṣṭa*), while subtle heat is termed "heat" (*tāpa*). Although those above [in the heavens] have hearts that struggle with one another, they do not engage in social intercourse.

It might seem as though there were still some ground for interaction, yet they have merely attained the state of "No-Affliction" (*Atapas*) by extinguishing coarse characteristics. Here, moreover, the mental mechanisms are further enhanced and superior, such that there is no counterpart; they investigate and refine [their minds] until...
There is no ground for interaction; because they can extinguish the shadows of conditioned objects, they attain freedom from feverish distress. △ Third, the Sudarśana Heaven (Good-Seeing Heaven):
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, their wondrous vision is perfectly clear and serene, with no further traces of dust or any defilements.
This class of beings is named the Sudarśana Heaven.

Because it can extinguish the images of conditions, the wondrous vision becomes perfectly clear and pure; thus, the defiled mind, the images of sensory dust, the accumulated habitual natures, and the submerged impurities are all absent.
Seeing the ten directions perfectly, it is therefore called "Good Vision" (Sudṛśa). △ Fourth, the Heaven of Good Manifestation (Sudarśana).
Refined vision manifests before them; they mold and transform things without obstruction. This class of beings is called the *Sudṛśa* (Good Appearance) Heaven.
"Refined vision" refers to the illumination of wisdom. Previously, they were hindered by defilements and unable to manifest transformation;

now that they are clear and perfect, they appear according to conditions like a bright mirror—this is what is meant by "molding and transforming without obstruction. △ The *Sudarśana* (Ultimate Color) Heaven.

They exhaustively investigate the ultimate limit of the manifold and thoroughly penetrate the nature of material form until they enter the boundless. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha).

"Limit" (*ji*) refers to the subtlest point of form; "nature" (*xing*) refers to the basis of characteristics. If one has not yet fully realized this, one remains confined within the appearances of form.

It is limited and obstructed by itself; this [state] can exhaustively investigate and penetrate it, thus transcending formal obstructions and entering the boundless limitlessness, which is named "Ultimate Form" (Rūpakāya-paryanta).
△ Third, the conclusion on its excellence.
Ānanda, as for these non-returning devas, even the various kings of the four dhyāna heavens can only hear of them with reverence;

they cannot know or see them. It is just as in this world, where vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the holy path are all sustained by Arhats, such that ordinary people of the world cannot see them.
The deities of the lower heavens cultivate impure, mundane meditative absorptions (*sāsrava-vaipākika-samādhi*), whereas these deities cultivate pure, noble karma (*anāsrava-ārya-karma*).
Because there is a difference between the coarse and the subtle, they are unable to see [them]. △ Second, the summary.

Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without sexual union; yet they have not exhausted the burden of the physical form. From this point downward, they are called the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).

Because they are already free from the defilement of desire, they are solitary and without sexual union; because they still possess material substance, they have not exhausted the burden of the physical form.

The four heavens of the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack the matter of karmic fruition (*vipākaja-rūpa*), yet they possess the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhija-rūpa*).

This applies equally to both the environment and the inhabitants. Here, one extinguishes the body and returns to non-existence; it is the dwelling place of *śrāvakas* of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). Alternatively, there are those who are the distinct retributions of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) seeking the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), or those gods who dwell amidst humans out of weariness with existence.
Their types are not uniform, yet all are devoid of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). [The text consists of] four sections: first, the branching and transcending.
He emerges.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence, there are two further divergent paths.
If one illuminates wisdom through a mind of equanimity, and the light of wisdom becomes perfectly pervasive, one then transcends the realm of dust and becomes an Arhat.
Entering the Bodhisattva Vehicle—this type of person is called a "Great Arhat who has turned the mind.
The Akaniṣṭha Heaven resides at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), bordering the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it is termed the "limit of form" (*rūpānta*). There are two branches:
one is to exit the three realms, which is this present section; the other is to enter the formless realm, which is the subsequent section. All four dhyānas depend upon [the Akaniṣṭha].
"Cultivating meditative concentration through equanimity and mindfulness. This mention of "equanimity" refers to the causal mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

This causal mind can give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), exhaust all afflictions and delusions, and reach perfect clarity. Thereby, one transcends the three realms, does not abide in the minor fruits [of the śrāvaka], and enters the Bodhisattva vehicle;
this is called "turning the mind. II. Entering in Accordance with Meditative Concentration. Herein there are four heavens, all of which...
Practicing and advancing by relying on the exclusive emptiness [of the four formless attainments]: first, one detests form and relies on space; second, one detests space and relies on consciousness;

third, when form, space, and consciousness are all extinguished, one relies on the nature of consciousness; fourth, relying on the nature of consciousness, one exhaustively investigates until extinction, yet does not attain true extinction.
These are all superior wholesome fruits of the conditioned, which do not transcend saṃsāra and do not constitute the Path of the Sages. This section has four parts.

Regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*): if one abides in a mind of equanimity, having accomplished the relinquishing of aversion, one perceives the body as an obstruction; by dissolving this obstruction, one enters into space.
This class of practitioners is called the sphere of infinite space.

This [attainment] relies exclusively on equanimity (*upekṣā*) and does not cultivate wisdom. Having become weary of physical form and its obstructions, one vertically cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), whereby the body is extinguished and returns to non-existence.

This is the one who, weary of form, relies upon emptiness; it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Therefore, one is reborn in the sphere of infinite space as a result of this retribution. 2. The Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*):
Once all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; therein remains only the ālayavijñāna, together with the entire manas and a subtle portion thereof.
This single category is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).

When all obstructions have dissolved and ceased to exist, one no longer relies on form (*rūpa*). When even the non-obstruction of "non-existence" is extinguished, one no longer relies on space (*ākāśa*).
Only the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas* remain; this is the state of one who has grown weary of emptiness and relies upon consciousness.

This is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Therefore, those born in the sphere of consciousness possess the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*, and the seventh consciousness, the *manas*. [This is] the body.

Since the faculties have already been eliminated, the six consciousnesses no longer exist; thus, only two remain. Among these, the object of the manas consists of the triad of form, space, and consciousness.

At this stage, one becomes weary of form and space and relies upon consciousness; therefore, the coarse objects of form and space having ceased, only the subtle portions of the remaining [consciousness] persist. △ Third, the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana).
Since both space and form have vanished and the consciousness-mind has been entirely extinguished, the ten directions are silent and utterly devoid of any destination.
This category is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
While the preceding stage was able to eliminate space and form, it had not yet extinguished the consciousness-mind; here, that too is entirely extinguished, and thus the ten directions are silent.
Yet, it is utterly remote and has nowhere to go; because it is quiescent and has no destination, it is called "non-existence" (*akiṃcanya*).

Although this state lacks the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*), it does not yet lack the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Those who practice today do not penetrate the nature deeply and often stagnate at this point.

Though they may thoroughly realize that form is empty and extinguish their mental deliberations until reaching non-existence, they ultimately remain obscured by the subtle depths of the nature of consciousness.
Deep and vast, one cannot free oneself from the cavernous pit of birth and death; it truly resides herein. △ Fourth, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception:
the nature of consciousness is unmoving. By extinguishing and exhaustively investigating, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible. It is as if existing, yet not existing.
If one considers "exhaustion" to be non-exhaustion, such a class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

These have reached the limit of emptiness, yet they do not exhaust the principle of emptiness. Those who have reached the limit of the noble path from the Heaven of Non-Retumers (*anāgāmin*) are, likewise, a class known as "unregressing, dull-witted Arhats.

If they come from the various heavens of the non-Buddhist Unconscious (*asaṃjñin*) practitioners, having reached the limit of emptiness without returning, they remain deluded, leaking, and without learning.
One then enters into the cycle of transmigration.
As for the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is the profound root of the conscious mind. "Immovable" means being quiescent and having no destination.

If one can remain immovable and further investigate until it is extinguished, yet this extinction is achieved by relying upon consciousness itself, it is ultimately not true extinction; it is merely a forced negation of existence.
Within the ultimate exhaustion [of phenomena], one illuminates the full realization of nature. Thus, it appears as if existing yet not existing, and as if exhausted yet not exhausted.

Because it appears to exist yet does not exist, it is not the realm of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). Because it appears to be exhausted yet is not exhausted, it is also not the "realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This, moreover, is a subtle and profound state of being extremely minute. Because this subtle and minute state is not yet detached from existence, it is said that the principle of emptiness is not fully realized; and thus, sound...

If one hears this and takes it as the ultimate, one will ultimately achieve only a dull fruit. Externalists rely on this and have no place of refuge; they remain forever deluded within the outflows (*āsrava*).
When the supramundane mind is cultivated, it reaches its final limit; coarse karma is already gone, yet the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*) remains an obstruction.
If one can resolutely break free from this, one has emerged from the three realms. All the stages and positions of the various heavens are [of this nature].

Regarding the gradual sequence of samādhi: it is not merely a matter of explaining its characteristics; rather, they follow one another and support each other, being identical to the aforementioned stages of the sages.
This, however, merely demonstrates the ascent of the ordinary person from a shallow level. If one embodies this through profound wisdom, it can also be realized instantaneously.
△ Third, a general discussion of the ordinary and the sage.
Ānanda, these various devas among the heavens are each ordinary beings for whom the fruits of their karma have ripened as a response;

when that response is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth. Those celestial kings, however, are bodhisattvas who dwell in samādhi, gradually advancing along the path of practice dedicated toward the ranks of the noble ones.
This refers collectively to the heavens of the desire, form, and formless realms. Their multitudes receive retribution according to their karma and have not yet escaped saṃsāra.

As for the kings, they manifest through skillful means according to their conduct, occupying various positions as they advance. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the first bhūmi mostly become kings of Jambudvīpa;
those of the second bhūmi become wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) up to the six heavens of the desire realm; those of the third bhūmi become Brahmā kings. This is what is meant.

This concludes the vertical exposition; therefore, he summarizes and points it out. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the names and the revelation of their falsity, in two parts. First, the conclusion of the names:

"Ānanda, these four heavens of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are characterized by the total cessation of body and mind, with the nature of stillness manifest before them, and being devoid of the physical matter resulting from karmic retribution.
From this point until the end, they are called the Formless Realm."
The "extinction of body and mind" refers to the absence of the form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) and coarse consciousness. △ Second, revealing delusion:
all of this arises from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind. Through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of existence arise;
therein, deluded beings follow along with the seven destinies and sink into them. As *pudgalas*, each follows their own kind.
The three realms arise from delusion; the seven destinies result from deluded grasping and attachment.
The *pudgala* (individual self) is the profound root of such deluded grasping. △ Seventh, the destiny of the asuras.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms, there are four kinds of asuras.

Those who belong to the realm of hungry ghosts, yet by the power of protecting the Dharma, ride upon their supernormal powers to enter the void—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts.
If, among the devas, their merit is exhausted and they fall, the place where they dwell is adjacent to the sun and moon.
These asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the human realm; there are asura kings who uphold the world, whose power penetrates all and whom no one dares to fear.
They are able to contend for power with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings; these asuras exist by transformation and are included within the realm of the devas.
Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam through the void in the morning and return to their watery abodes in the evening. These asuras exist due to moisture and belong to the realm of animals.

Regarding the inclusion within the destinies (*gati*): *Asura* is here translated as "Non-Gods. Their power of merit is equal to that of the gods, yet they lack divine conduct because they are prone to much anger.

According to the lightness or heaviness of their karma, there are differences in the four modes of birth (*yoni*). "Water-hole" refers to the Tailgate (*weilu*), the outlet of the ocean. △ Fourth, the general conclusion.
The general answer consists of four parts. First, it summarizes and binds together the seven realms of existence:

"Ānanda, such as these—hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras—when one minutely examines these seven realms, they are all the characteristics of deluded, conditioned existence;
they are births resulting from false imagination and followings of karma through false imagination. Within the Wondrous [Nature]..."
The perfectly luminous, unconditioned original mind is like flowers in the sky; fundamentally there is nothing to which it clings, being merely a single delusion without further root or trace.

This is understood through precise investigation and thorough inquiry. Because dream-consciousness is clouded and dull, the delusion follows one through the seven realms of existence; yet when the awakened mind is wondrously perfect, then—
It is utterly without root or source. △ Second, a general answer to the previous question:
"Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind; they undergo this saṃsāra and, throughout immeasurable kalpas, fail to attain true purity.
This is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. If they turn away from these three, then non-killing will arise."

Regarding theft, sexual misconduct, and so forth: there are those known as the realm of ghosts and spirits, and those unknown as the celestial realms. Through the mutual intermingling of existence and non-existence, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of *samādhi*, then there is wondrous and eternal stillness; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even the absence of duality ceases.
Since there is not even the [conventional] non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct, how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?

The previous question asked how, within the wondrous mind that is perfectly pervasive, there can exist the various paths such as those of hell-dwellers, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; therefore, this section concludes by demonstrating the answer.
With the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—as the root, the presence of such karma is termed the "category of ghosts," meaning one will inevitably fall.
The absence of such karma is termed the "realm of devas," meaning one will inevitably ascend. To give rise to a state free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct is itself the realm of devas.
Thus it is. Of the seven realms of existence, two are mentioned here because they encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome. One falls due to existence and ascends due to non-existence;

therefore, it is said that existence and non-existence mutually incline one another, giving rise to the nature of saṃsāra. If one attains right concentration, then the wondrous nature is eternally tranquil.
There is no further saṃsāra. "Both existence and non-existence are non-existent" means that verbal characteristics are overturned and karma is severed.

"Even non-duality is extinguished" means that conceptual discrimination and emotional attachments are forgotten. When karma is severed and emotions are forgotten, the three kinds of delusive roots—the names and their traces—both vanish.
Therefore, if one wishes to sever the cycle of delusion, one must cultivate right concentration.
Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed; each has its own private [cause]. Because of these respective privacies, the collective commonality of these privacies has no lack of a fixed location.
They arise spontaneously from delusion; this arising of delusion is without cause and cannot be traced back to its origin.
The previous question asked whether hell has a fixed location or no fixed location, such that beings create their own karma and each receives it individually.
Therefore, this section restates and answers that point. The "three karmas" refer specifically to killing and sexual misconduct. △ Third, the exhortation to sever the three karmas.

You must exhort yourself in practice if you wish to attain Bodhi. You must eliminate the three delusions; if you do not exhaust the three delusions, even if you should obtain supernatural powers, they will all be worldly, conditioned functions.
Since your habitual tendencies will not be extinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra. Thus, though you may wish to eliminate delusion, [you will fail].
They redouble their hypocrisy; the Tathāgata calls them pitiable. You have fabricated these delusions yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi.

Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the roots of deluded karma, and are thus called the "three delusions. The preceding section clarified the various realms of existence and provided precepts to guard against errors, concluding with an exhortation to eliminate the three delusions;
this is the essential truth of guarding through the precepts. △ Fourth, the conclusion and demonstration of the correct [path].
To speak thus is called speaking correctly; if one speaks otherwise, it is the speech of Māra.
II. Detailed Examination of the Realm of Māra to Deeply Guard Against Error and Delusion. *Māra* here is translated as "the Killer" and also as "the Robber."
This refers to that which can kill the life-force of wisdom and rob one of the wholesome dharmas; there are five ways it opens [this path]:

namely, the māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), the māra of devas, and the māra of spirits. Taken together, these are reduced to only the māra of the aggregates and the māra of devas.

The māra of the aggregates is precisely that upon which the afflictions of birth and death depend, arising from within the five aggregates. The māra of devas arises because of practicing perverted meditative concentrations and taking pleasure in causing harm.
This refers to those who abide in the right path. Those who have not yet resolved their minds always accord with and follow [the path], and thus they have no enemies.
Only those who practice erroneously oppose and do not comply, causing partial affliction and harm; therefore, it is necessary to discern them. The text has two parts.
First, the proclamation and announcement, which has three sections. First, the proclamation.

At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session upon the lion throne, he took up a seven-jeweled desk from the Purple Gold Mountain, turned back toward it, and leaned against it once more.
He then addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying: "You who are still in training—the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—"
Today you have turned your mind toward supreme, wondrous enlightenment, the Great Bodhi. I have now already explained the Dharma of true practice;
yet you still do not recognize the subtle demonic activities involved in cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. When demonic realms manifest before you, you fail to recognize them.
Your purification of the mind is not correct, and you have fallen into false views. This is either the *skandha-māra* or the *deva-māra*.
Some become attached to ghosts and spirits; others encounter *chimei* (mountain goblins). Their minds lack clarity, and they mistake a thief for their own son.

Furthermore, within this state, they consider a small attainment to be sufficient, like the unlearned bhikṣu of the fourth dhyāna who falsely claimed to have realized the state of an *arhat*. When his heavenly retribution is exhausted, [he falls back].
The signs of decline have appeared before you. By slandering an Arhat, you shall undergo future existence and fall into the Avīci Hell. Listen attentively;
I shall now explain this to you in detail for your sake.
The preceding teaching having concluded, there was no one present who asked a question. Thus, as he was about to descend from the Dharma seat, he again took up the precious lectern;
turning his golden countenance, he spoke of his own accord without being questioned. This is a subtle demonic affair within true *śamatha-vipaśyanā*;

were it not for one possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), it could not be discerned. It can destroy precious awakening and ruin the house of the Dharma King; therefore, it must be specifically warned against—this is the very last [instruction].
This refers to deep compassion. Regarding those who have not heard the teachings within the four dhyānas, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
A bhikṣu who lacks the wisdom of extensive learning but diligently practices minor deeds may attain birth in the four dhyānas and then claim to have realized arhatship.

When his celestial retribution is about to end and he sees a place of rebirth, he subsequently slanders the Buddha, falsely asserting that arhats do not undergo future existence. Because of this, he falls into ruin.
"This is the fault of perverse delusion.
Ānanda rose from his seat, as did all those in the assembly who were fellow students; with joy, they prostrated themselves in worship and humbly awaited his compassionate instruction.
△ Second, the correct demonstration has four parts. First, the description of what the māras have initiated:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly: "You all should know that within the world of outflows, there are twelve classes of sentient beings."
The wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment is the perfect essence of the mind; it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the Buddhas of the ten directions.

It is due to the fault of your own deluded thoughts that you are confused about this principle. From this arises ignorance and craving; from their arising, universal confusion is produced. Thus, the nature of space comes into being. As this transformation of delusion does not cease, [the world continues to evolve].

There is the arising of worlds; thus, these lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions are not without outflows. They are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization.

The essence of the awakened mind is what is called the true source. Due to delusion regarding principle and turning one's back on the truth, delusion transforms and establishes falsehood, thereby creating existence.
The realm of outflows is the dwelling place of Māra; he transforms those who are deluded, changing according to their delusions.

You should know that empty space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so, then, do all worlds exist within empty space?

"Empty space arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean; it is further likened to a fragment of cloud to illustrate that the world is illusory, subtle, and easily dissolved."
If even one among you were to give rise to true resolve and return to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions would all be dissolved and vanish;
how then could the lands existing within that emptiness not tremble and shatter?
The essence of the True Source is fundamentally vast and open. The lands within the void are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false imaginings.
When one awakens to the truth and ceases to be deluded, there is nothing more to establish; thus, they naturally collapse and shatter of themselves. Someone may ask:

"The realm of the out-flowing void is a collective response of all sentient beings. How can it be that a single person is able to cause its dissolution? Moreover, throughout antiquity and the present, those who have awakened..."
The multitude of beings is real, yet the realm of emptiness remains as it was; how can it be said that they have been extinguished? It is replied:
They are moved by common karma and do not depart from the state of obscurity. When one develops the truth and returns to clarity, they may indeed be extinguished.

However, because sentient beings cannot be exhausted and worlds cannot be exhausted, even if a single person develops the truth, the multitude again experiences the binding of karma; therefore, it remains as it was.
If those of like karma were all able to give rise to the truth, then the mountains, rivers, and the physical world would, by a mere thought,
be transformed into supreme awakening and become a pure and wondrous Buddha-land.
"You all cultivate dhyāna and adorn yourselves with samādhi. The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various stainless Great Arhats have their minds and spirits perfectly integrated;
they remain profoundly tranquil in their respective states. As for the various Māras, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas—"
They saw their palaces collapse and crack without cause, the great earth tremble and split apart, and all creatures of water, land, and air take flight; there was none who was not struck with terror.

Yet ordinary beings, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive these transformations. They all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
"Because they are attached to these worldly defilements, how could you cause them to shatter that place?
For this reason, when you are in samādhi, ghosts, spirits, celestial Māras, and all manner of goblins and demons come together to harass you."
Māra relies upon obscurity and darkness. Now, by practicing dhyāna and adorning samādhi, the wondrous mind becomes refined and brilliant, uniting with Bodhisattvas and Arhats;
thus, one is able to shatter the realm of Māra and consequently bring about his affliction and harm.

This refers to the ordinary worldlings and the celestial Māra-kings, who have not yet attained the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). △ Second, awakening is free from delusion.
However, although those māras may harbor great rage within their afflictions, in your wondrous awakening they are like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water;
they do not touch it at all. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, [the ice will surely melt].
They will perish in no time.
The true essence of wondrous enlightenment is unmoving and indestructible; when the power of the Right is applied, evil influences naturally dissipate.

To rely solely on supernatural powers is merely to serve as their guest, resulting only in the accomplishment of disorder and ruin. This is due to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) acting as the masters within your own mind.
If the host is deluded, the guest will find its advantage. If you remain in *dhyāna* and awaken without confusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you.
When the *skandhas* dissolve and you enter into clarity, then all those various evils will receive only the dark, obscure energy. Clarity can destroy darkness.
Having recently perished themselves, how would they dare remain to disturb meditative concentration?
To "rely merely on supernatural powers" refers to various demons. "The master of the five aggregates" points to the mind;
"the aggregates dissolve and enter into clarity" points to one who has realized the truth. △ Third, being deluded leads to harm.
If you do not attain clear awakening and remain deluded by the aggregates, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a son of Māra and an accomplice of Māra, just like Matangi.
She was truly insignificant and inferior; she merely used incantations to violate your Buddhist precepts, destroying but a single precept among the eighty thousand practices.
Because your mind remained pure, you did not yet fall into ruin. This [present situation], however, destroys your entire body of precious awareness.
Just as when the family of a high minister suddenly encounters confiscation of their property, they fall into ruin and decay with no means of rescue;
so too, though Ḍākinī is insignificant, she can destroy the precept-body, and the various fierce demons can ruin the precious awakening. One must therefore guard against this deeply.
The confiscation of a minister’s property is a metaphor for being on the verge of the stage of awakening and yet falling into the evil realms. △ Four: Following.
The five aggregates are explained in detail. First, the aggregate of form has three parts. The first shows the characteristics of the aggregates:

"Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment and eliminate all thoughts, once those thoughts are exhausted, then all that is luminous and refined, free from thought, remains unmoved by motion or stillness;
recollection and forgetfulness are as one. You should abide in this state and enter *samādhi*."
It is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness; though their essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light.

This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). "The subsiding of all thoughts" means that through profound stillness, one turns back the false arising and ceasing. "The lucidity and brilliance beyond thought" refers to...
One attains the primordial luminous awareness whose nature is free from arising and ceasing. Because it is profoundly still and tranquil, movement and stillness do not displace it;

because it is free from discursive thought, recollection and forgetfulness are as one. Although the power of meditative concentration is thus, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has not yet been shattered; therefore, it is like having clear vision while remaining in darkness.

Although its essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light; this is the characteristic of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). "Aggregate" (skandha) takes the meaning of obscuring and covering.
It restricts and confines the true nature; therefore, it is called a "bounded realm" (quyu).

If one's vision becomes clear and bright, the ten directions open up completely without further gloom or darkness, and the aggregates of name-and-form are exhausted, this person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa.
Observing its origin, one finds that solidified false imagination serves as its root.

The characteristic of the exhaustion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) does not mean that the body is extinguished and returns to nothingness; rather, it means that through the power of contemplation, one penetrates and illuminates them so as no longer to be obscured by delusion.
Thus, it is likened to when the eyes are clear and bright, and the ten directions open up before one.

At the very first moment, when the perception of emptiness and the [perceived] objects are not yet distinguished, this is called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*); this is the essence of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Therefore, when the aggregate of form is exhausted, one transcends it. Form...
The aggregates (*skandhas*) initially arise from the union of the three false categories of father, mother, and self; therefore, it is said that "solidified deluded thought" is their root.
The five kinds of false roots are explained by the Sūtra itself at its conclusion. △ Second, distinguishing the ten manifested objects: 1. The body can pass through obstructions.
Ānanda, you should investigate this subtle clarity with diligent precision. When the four elements no longer entwine, within a brief moment the body can pass through obstructions.
This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the external realm; it is merely a temporary attainment of functional power and is not a realization of sainthood.

If you do not conceive the thought that this is a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm. If you interpret it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

Among these, the single aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is that which is fixed within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Its wondrous substance is fundamentally harmonious; it is only because of deluded matter that obstruction is formed.
If one exhaustively investigates its wondrous luminosity, then the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) will no longer entwine, and the body can emerge from obstructions.

However, this is induced by the power of a specific concentration, causing the essence of clarity to overflow; it is temporary and not permanent. Therefore, it is not a realization of the sages. 2. The Section on the Substance.

"Ānanda, when one further uses this mind to investigate the subtle brilliance until it penetrates the interior of the body, that person may suddenly pick out roundworms and maggots from within their own body;
yet the physical form remains intact, without any injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined spirit."

As for physical forms, these are merely temporary attainments resulting from refined practice; they do not constitute holy realization. If you do not conceive them as holy, they are called "auspicious states.
If you interpret them as holy, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

When the true, essential, wondrous clarity overflows into the external realm, there is nothing outside that can obstruct it; when it overflows into the physical body, there is nothing inside that can hinder it.
Therefore, one is able to pick out and extract intestinal worms from within the body. This, too, is merely temporary. △ Third, the secret meaning of hearing through emptiness.

Furthermore, as you investigate this mind with refined precision both internally and externally, at that time the *po*, *hun*, *yi*, and *shen* spirits—excluding the body which they sustain—will all interpenetrate one another, acting as both guests and hosts.
Suddenly, you will hear the sound of the Dharma being preached in the air, or hear the secret meanings being expounded simultaneously throughout the ten directions.
This is called the mutual separation and union of the refined spirits; it is the accomplishment of wholesome seeds, temporarily resulting in such an experience.

This is not a realization of sainthood; if one does not conceive of it as such, it is called a "wholesome state. If, however, one interprets it as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
The *po*, *hun*, *yi*, *zhi*, and *shen* are the presiding spirits of the five viscera. They grasp and receive the eighth consciousness, which serves as the aggregate of the seven consciousnesses.
As the sovereign of the five faculties, it is the presiding authority; therefore, it does not involve itself with anything.

Through the previous intensive cultivation, one was first able to become externally empty and subsequently able to penetrate internally. Now, through further intensive cultivation of both the internal and external, both are simultaneously empty and penetrating.

Because the five consciousnesses and the seven modes of cognition have all ceased, and because they were formerly constantly intermingling with one another, the habitual perfuming from former lives spontaneously manifests.

[The master] waved his hand and suddenly heard something. Now, when one concentrates the will and unifies the spirit to the utmost in their studies, even extraordinary writings and elegant compositions that have never entered the mind often emerge vividly within dreams and sleep.
Thus, it can be understood that such phenomena occur because the spirit, through intense cultivation and stimulation, occasionally manifests. △ Fourth, the silent manifestation of the Buddha-realm.

Furthermore, when this mind is clear, luminous, and transparent, its inner radiance shines forth, causing all ten directions to appear everywhere as the color of Jāmbūnada gold, and all species of beings transform into Tathāgatas.
At that moment, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon a terrace of celestial light, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas;
a billion lands and lotus flowers appear simultaneously. This is called the "soul of the mind" (citta-ātman).
When the mind is permeated by spiritual awakening, its luminosity becomes refined and clear, illuminating all worlds. To temporarily attain such a state is not yet a realization of the Sage;

if one does not conceive of it as a sage-like attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm. However, if one interprets it as a sage-like realization, one will immediately succumb to various forms of demonic influence.
The realms of purity and defilement always respond according to the mind’s perception. Thus, when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, the soul is imbued with spiritual awakening;
the Buddha-realm manifests within the light of the mind. This is identical to the way the sacred realm of the Buddha-land appears in profound stillness when the mind dwells upon it.
△ Five: Empty Form is Like a Jewel.

Furthermore, with this mind, one intensely investigates the wondrous luminosity, observing it without ceasing, suppressing and subduing it, and restraining it until it transcends [ordinary perception].
At that time, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures;
simultaneously filling all space without mutual obstruction, blue, yellow, red, and white each appear in their pure intensity. This is called the power of suppression exceeding its proper limit.

To temporarily attain such a state does not constitute a realization of the holy; if one does not conceive it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm. If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
By refining the subtle function and suppressing discursive thoughts, the mind is brought under control and its power transcends ordinary limits; thus, it is wondrously bright.
It manifests as an intense, radiant dispersion. △ Sixth, the dark room becomes like daylight.

Furthermore, by investigating with this mind until it is transparent and clear, its refined radiance remains undisturbed. Suddenly, when night falls and one is within a dark room, [the light appears].
One sees various objects no differently than by daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.

This is called the mind becoming subtle and dense, such that its vision penetrates the profound darkness. To temporarily attain such a state is not a realization of the holy; one must not conceive of it as a holy attainment.
This is called a "wholesome realm. If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, one will immediately succumb to various heterodox influences.
It is a fact that humans inherently possess a lack of clarity; it is not that they naturally give rise to darkness or are unable to be obscured by it.

Rather, it is only when the subtle mind of meditative concentration is clarified and kept from being disturbed that [these phenomena] can manifest. One must not eliminate the dark objects and claim that they are all real realms that do not change according to the state of concentration.
△ The seven parts of the body have no sensation.
Furthermore, as this mind enters perfectly into emptiness and fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood;
even when burned by fire or cut with a blade, there is no sensation whatsoever. Moreover, the flames cannot burn them, and even if their flesh is sliced, it is as if wood were being pared away.
This is called the simultaneous clearing away of sensory objects and the four great elements entering exclusively into purity. To temporarily attain such a state is not a realization of the holy;
if one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm. If one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

When the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is empty and harmonious, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are simultaneously extinguished and the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are cast aside. Pure awareness remains while the body is left behind;
thus, there is no injury from contact. Sustained by the power of meditative concentration, fire cannot burn it. This is the case for those in the world who sit upright and relinquish the self.
It can even cause the body to become like withered wood and the mind like extinguished ashes; how much more so the power of true samādhi!
△ Eighth, the ability to penetrate and observe:
Furthermore, by means of this mind, one achieves purity. When the merit of the pure mind reaches its peak, one suddenly sees the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions.
All have attained buddha-fields, complete with the seven treasures and filled with pervasive radiance.

Furthermore, they see Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filling the entire realm of space, with magnificent palaces and towers. Looking down, they see the hells; looking up, they observe the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision.
This is called the deepening of joyful and loathing contemplation; as the contemplation persists for a long time, it transforms into a manifestation. It is not a realization of sainthood.

If one does not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm. If one interprets it as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.
One grows weary of the coarse, turbid, and obstructive nature of matter, and rejoices in the pure, wondrous, empty, and harmonious state; this is called "achieving purity.

As one’s concentrated contemplation deepens, it undergoes spontaneous transformation over time, thereby enabling one to penetrate and observe all things without obstruction. △ Ninth: At night, one may see through obstructions.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate what is profound and distant, suddenly in the middle of the night, one may see from afar the marketplaces, streets, and alleys, as well as one's kinsmen and relatives;

or one may hear their voices. This is called "the pressing of the mind," for because the mind is driven to its extreme limit and flies outward, it perceives many things that are obstructed by distance.

This is not a realization of the holy; if one does not conceive of it as being holy, it is called a "wholesome state. If one interprets it as a holy attainment, one will immediately fall prey to various demons.
By investigating the mind to its furthest reaches and straining the spirit until the body is cast aside, one enters a realm of darkness where one arrives at a destination;

thus, one is able to see and hear events from afar. All of the above have not yet transcended the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); they merely rely on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to emerge beyond physical obstructions.
Sight and hearing reach far and wide. If the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, then the ten directions open up clearly, with no further darkness.

The six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are exercised with ease; even through mountain walls and barriers, one passes directly by—of this there is certainly no doubt. △ Tenth: The gradual emergence of demonic affairs.
Furthermore, if you investigate with this mind to the utmost degree of refinement, you may see the physical form of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) undergo transformations;

in a brief moment, it shifts and changes in various ways without apparent cause. This is called a deluded mind harboring malevolent spirits (chimei). Or, you may encounter a celestial Māra entering your heart and belly, preaching the Dharma at will and penetrating subtle meanings.
These are not signs of saintly realization. If you do not regard them as such and do not harbor thoughts of sainthood, the demonic activities will subside.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, one will immediately fall under the influence of various heterodoxies;

the knowledge and perceptions one encounters are but the manifestations of Māra. While the preceding nine sections clarify only the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this section alone clarifies the affairs of Māra:
when the power of concentration has not yet been perfected, one cannot move Māra; it is only when one’s investigation reaches its ultimate refinement that the affairs of Māra gradually emerge.
This is the case. Therefore, in the following text, the demonic activities become even more severe. △ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to guard deeply:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifestations that appear during *dhyāna* are all due to the interaction of the mind with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Thus, these phenomena appear. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these conditions, they are confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, saying:"
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood; one shall fall into the Avīci Hell.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Final Dharma, you all should proclaim this meaning so that celestial Māras may find no opportunity to exploit you. Maintain and protect it, and thereby achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
