Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣa of the kingdom of Oḍra;
the bodhisattva precept disciple and former Minister of Justice and Concurrent Vice President of the Secretariat and Council of State, Fang Rong of Qinghe, acted as scribe.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling explains:
Part Two, the Perception Aggregate (vedanā-skandha), Section Three. First, showing the characteristics of the aggregate:
Ānanda, when that good man, while practicing samādhi within the *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, has exhausted the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), he perceives all...

The Buddha-mind is like an image appearing within a clear mirror. If there is something perceived yet it cannot be employed, it is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet are perfectly present;
though they see and hear without confusion, their mind is struck by an external evil spirit and they cannot move.
This is called the realm of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

"Feeling" (vedanā) has the meaning of receiving and experiencing external objects. Having already shattered the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), the internal and external become empty and harmonious;
thus, one perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections in a mirror. The mind of all Buddhas is precisely my own wondrously enlightened and luminous mind.
"Like a reflection in a mirror" means that it is pure, empty, and coalescent, clearly devoid of physical obstruction. Although it possesses this wondrous essence, it is as yet unable to function.

This is because one is shrouded by feeling (*vedanā*). It is like a person who is asleep from a nightmare: though their limbs are fully intact and their six sense faculties are clear and alert, they are unable to move.
Such is the characteristic of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
If the affliction of nightmares ceases, his mind will detach from his body; he can look back at his own face, moving freely whether staying or departing, without further obstruction.

This is called the exhaustion of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). When examining its origin, one finds that empty luminosity and false conceptualization constitute its root.

As for the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*): one has already become free from physical obstruction; yet, because one is still "asphyxiated" by sensation (*vedanā*), one is unable to employ it.

Therefore, when the aggregate of sensation subsides, one is immediately able to detach from the body and turn back to observe [the mind], such that going and staying are unimpeded. When deluded views and perceptions arise, they turbidly disturb the tranquil nature;
this is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), which is the very substance of the aggregate of sensation. Thus, with the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation, one transcends it.
Because illusory objects of compliance and resistance give rise to false experiences of loss and gain, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has no substance;

it is merely a void that appears luminous. Therefore, it is said that "void-luminosity and deluded thought constitute its basis. II. Distinguishing the Manifest Objects (ten sections). 1. Suppression gives rise to compassion.
Ānanda, that good man shall therein attain a great radiance, his mind becoming luminously clear.

Yet, because he suppresses [the mind] excessively within, a boundless compassion suddenly arises from that state. Thus, even when looking upon mosquitoes and gadflies, he regards them as his own infants;
a heart of pity arises, and he involuntarily sheds tears. This is called the overstepping of effort through excessive suppression. If he realizes this...
This is "no fault," but it is not the realization of a sage. If one awakens to this and remains undeluded, [the affliction] will naturally subside after a long time.

If, however, one takes this to be the realization of a sage, then the demon of pity will enter one's heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, one will feel pity and weep boundlessly, losing right concentration and inevitably falling into ruin.
This refers specifically to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Since the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been shattered, there is no longer any darkness;
thus, one attains great radiance. Because one recognizes the aggregate of sensation as a fault, one internally subdues it to destroy it.

However, if this subduing is excessive, one loses their compassionate gentleness and becomes overly sorrowful and pitiable, thereby allowing the demon of pity (*karuṇā-māra*) to take possession. 2. Being moved to action gives rise to valor.
Ānanda, furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) becoming clear.
As superior signs manifest before them, they become excessively moved by emotion; suddenly, within this state, they give rise to boundless vigor.

Their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal to that of the Buddhas, claiming that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called "the overstepping of functional effort through rashness. If they awaken to it...
This is "no fault," yet it does not constitute proof of sainthood. If one awakens to this and remains free from delusion, it will naturally subside after a long time.
If, however, one takes this to be a realization of sainthood, then mad demons will enter one's heart and viscera. Upon meeting others, one will boast with incomparable arrogance;

one’s mind will reach such a state that above, one does not see the Buddha, and below, one does not see other people. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), one shall surely fall into ruin.
The exhaustion of form and the manifestation of sensation constitute the superior signs of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because success is achieved through joy, one is moved by a sense of urgency and stirred to action, thinking that the fruit of Buddhahood can be attained as easily as completing one's meritorious practices. This is the fault of overweening pride; thus, mad demons take possession of such a person.
Now, those who consider a little to be sufficient, who are arrogant and transgress their proper bounds, and who regard themselves as having no equal—all these are the faults of overweening pride.
Furthermore, regarding the third [category], those of inferior wisdom who are deluded by recollection:

moreover, within that state of meditative concentration, these good sons perceive that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become clear; yet they find no new realization before them.
Having lost his former dwelling, his wisdom and strength decline; entering into the midst, he falls into a desolate ground where nothing is seen.
Suddenly, a great parching thirst arises within his heart, which sinks into constant recollection without ceasing at any time. He takes this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind and losing oneself through lack of wisdom. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization.

If you mistake this for a realization of sainthood, then the demon of recollection will enter your heart and viscera. Morning and evening it will seize the mind and suspend it in one place, causing you to lose right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
One will inevitably fall into ruin.

In all cultivation of contemplative practice, one must maintain the equilibrium of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to be free from error. Now, in this case, concentration is strong while wisdom is weak;

thus, although the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted, there is no new realization attained through progress, and because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already dissolved, one falls away from the previous state.
In their coming and going, they have no reliance whatsoever; this is called the "Ground of Ruin in the Middle.

Because they lack reliance and lack vision, they become parched with thirst and sink into recollection, and thus the demon of recollection attaches itself to them. Because the mind of recollection is falsely bound, it is as if they were suspended by a cord.
△ Fourth, the failure to examine due to inferior concentration.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.

Because their power of wisdom exceeds their concentration, they lose its sharp intensity; yet, harboring various superior qualities within their minds, they themselves begin to suspect that their own minds are Vairocana.

To consider a small attainment as sufficient is called losing the constant discernment through the application of the mind and becoming submerged in intellectual views. If one awakens to this, there is no fault;
it is not a holy realization. If one takes it to be a holy realization, then the demons of inferiority and easy contentment will enter one’s heart and viscera.
Seeing someone claim for themselves, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth," they lose their right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) and shall fall into ruin.
Previously, concentration was strong while wisdom was slight; now, moreover, the power of wisdom exceeds that of concentration. In both cases, there is mutual deficiency;
therefore, one seeks meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). The general meaning is as outlined above. △ Fifth, losing one's guard gives rise to anxiety.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear;

yet, as they have not yet attained their new realization, the old mind has already perished. Surveying these two boundaries, they naturally encounter hardship and peril, and within their hearts, an inexhaustible sorrow suddenly arises.
It is as if sitting upon an iron bed or drinking poison; the mind has no desire to live and constantly seeks someone to end its life so that it may quickly attain liberation.
This is called "losing the skillful means" in one's practice. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; however, it does not constitute a realization of the holy state.
If one interprets this as a realization of the holy, then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow will enter their heart and viscera.

Grasping a sword or blade with their own hands, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span. Or, being constantly sorrowful, they will flee into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of people.
Losing right concentration, one shall fall into ruin.
Because one fails to maintain composure in both advancing and retreating, the mind gives rise to perilous difficulties, resulting in perverse anxieties that lead to personal harm and calamity.
△ Sixth: Deluded Attachment Gives Rise to Joy.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Once they abide in a state of purity with their minds settled in tranquility, there suddenly arises within them an infinite joy; their hearts are filled with such rapture that they cannot restrain themselves.
This is called "lightness-and-ease without wisdom," which is merely self-restraint. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy state.
If one takes it to be a holy realization, then a portion of the demon of "delightful joy" will enter one's heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, one laughs;
by the side of the road, one sings and dances alone, claiming to have attained unimpeded liberation. Having lost right concentration (*samādhi*), one shall surely fall into ruin.
The power of concentration is but temporary; lacking wisdom to sustain it, one falsely clings to it and incurs fault. △ Seventh, giving rise to pride through the perception of superiority:

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear and bright, whereupon they consider themselves sufficient.
Suddenly, groundless and great pride arises; thus, even pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, or overweening pride, or the pride of inferiority may all erupt at once.
Within their hearts, they still hold even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt.
How much more so for those of lower rank, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; this is called "superior vision without wisdom to save oneself.

If one awakens to this truth, there is no fault, but it does not constitute a realization of sainthood. If one takes this to be a realization of sainthood, then a portion of the great māra of self-conceit will enter one's heart and viscera.
They do not pay homage to stupas and temples, but instead destroy scriptures and images, saying to their patrons: "These [images] are merely made of gold, copper, earth, or wood;
these scriptures are merely made of tree leaves or woven silk. They themselves do not show reverence to the true, eternal physical body, yet they instead venerate earth and wood.

This is indeed a perversion. Those who have deep faith in it will, by its destruction and burial in the earth, cause deluded sentient beings to enter the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration, destined to fall into ruin.

There are seven types of pride (*māna*). To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"). To be arrogant toward those of equal virtue is called *māna* (pride). To strive for superiority over equals is called *atimāna* (excessive pride).
To strive for superiority over those who are superior is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride). To claim one has attained what one has not attained is called *adhimāna* (conceited pride).
To boast of oneself despite being inferior is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride). Not paying homage to stupas, temples, and so forth is *mithyāmāna* (false pride).
The deluded people of today do not observe the rites nor recite the scriptures; they are all demons of arrogance. They are like those who wrap their heads in fine flowers and precious silk scarves.
△ Eighth: being satisfied with a little attainment.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear and bright.

Within this state of brilliant clarity, they perfectly realize the subtle principle and attain great compliance. Suddenly, their minds experience immeasurable lightness and tranquility, leading them to claim they have become sages and attained great mastery.
This is called attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom; if one realizes this for what it is, there is no fault, yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then a portion of the "delightful light-and-purity" demon will enter their heart and viscera.
They will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such individuals mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings and cause them to fall into the Avīci Hell.
Losing right concentration, one shall fall into ruin.
Mistaking the dissolution of form for spiritual clarity and brilliance, and taking that clarity and brilliance to be perfect enlightenment, one then believes that great accord has been attained.
Yet, being light, pure, and self-possessed, they all consider a little to be enough; such are those who lack learning. △ Ninth: Denying by Clinging to Emptiness.

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) vanish and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear. Within this clarity of awakening, they...
One attains a nature of empty luminosity. Within this state, one suddenly turns toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect and entering exclusively into emptiness.

When the mind of empty space manifests before one, even if a long-standing understanding of annihilation arises in the mind, there is no fault in such awakening; yet it does not constitute a realization of the holy.
If one forms a sacred understanding [of this state], then the demon of emptiness will enter their heart and viscera;

they will then slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Small Vehicle, claiming that since Bodhisattvas have realized emptiness, what is there to be observed or transgressed? Such a person will constantly drink wine and eat meat before faithful donors.
They engage extensively in lewd and impure acts; by means of demonic power, they captivate those before them so that no suspicion or slander arises.

Once the ghost’s mind has long since entered [the victim], it may consume excrement, urine, wine, meat, and the like—all of which are equally void. Thus they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and lead others into sin through delusion.
Losing right concentration, one shall fall into ruin.
Because of attaining a state of empty clarity, one mistakenly clings to nihilistic emptiness, thereby incurring various perverse faults. All who act in this way are victims of the demon of emptiness.
10. Indulging in the flavor of meditative absorption gives rise to craving.
Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.

They savor this empty luminosity until it penetrates deep into their very marrow. Suddenly, infinite craving arises in their minds; when this craving reaches its peak, they lose their sanity, and it becomes greed.

This is called the state of meditative concentration where the mind enters with ease and compliance, yet lacks the self-sustaining power of wisdom; thus one mistakenly enters into various desires. If one awakens to this, there is no fault.

It is not a realization of the holy. If one takes it to be a holy realization, then the demon of desire will enter one’s heart and viscera, leading one to constantly claim that desire is the path to Bodhi, converting laypeople and practicing desire indiscriminately.
Those who engage in sexual intercourse under such conditions are called "sons who uphold the Dharma."

By the power of divine spirits, they will gather ordinary and ignorant people during the final age, numbering as many as one hundred, or even two hundred, five or six hundred, or reaching up to ten million; then the demons will grow weary and abandon their bodies.

Lacking majestic virtue, one falls into royal calamity; by misleading sentient beings, one enters the Avīci Hell. Losing right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), one shall inevitably descend into ruin.
Because much craving arises from compliance, the meditative state that accords with the mind results in the fault of perverse attachment. △ Third, the conclusion.
I urge you to maintain deep vigilance, Ānanda.

These ten kinds of visionary states that appear during *dhyāna* are all manifestations resulting from the interaction between the mind and the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). Thus, these phenomena appear.
Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these conditions, they fail to recognize them for what they are and say:
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood that results in falling into the Avīci Hell.

You all should likewise take up the words of the Tathāgata and transmit them during the Final Dharma after my parinirvāṇa, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
maintain and protect [these teachings] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

In all the textual passages concerning the fetters of the aggregates (*skandha*), the terms "sustaining," "preserving," and "protecting" appear; these signify the profound prevention of error and the assistance of the path.
△ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has five parts. First, the characteristics of the aggregate are shown.

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet extinguished, his mind is already separated from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.

He has already achieved the ability to ascend from this ordinary body through the sixty holy stages of a Bodhisattva and attain the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), moving everywhere without obstruction.
It is, for example, as if someone were sleeping soundly and speaking in their sleep; such a person...
Although there is no distinct object of cognition, the words themselves have already formed a sequence of phonetic rhythms that cause those who are not yet awake to fully comprehend their meaning;
this is what is called the realm of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
"Perception" refers to the floating characteristics of mental deliberation and the delusive habits of conscious emotion.

Because they can obscure the wondrous luminosity and obstruct the Path of the Sages, even though one attains the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation—such that the mind leaves the body and moves with freedom, having already achieved the cause for the "mind-born body" (manomayakāya) of a sage's station—it remains obscured by the aggregate of perception. Therefore, it is likened to the snoring and talking of one in deep sleep.
Although it is not yet immediately attained, because the cause has already been accomplished, it is like having mastered phonology even though there is no further object of knowledge.
Such characteristics of the cause can only be known by one whose conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted; thus, it is likened to how those who are not asleep all understand its meaning.
This is the characteristic of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, such that the awakened, luminous mind is like a heart cleansed of dust and grime,

and one’s entire cycle of birth and death is perfectly illuminated from beginning to end— this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*),
observing that their origin lies in the fundamental nature of pervasive delusion.

Because floating dust has been eliminated, there is no longer the defilement of cognitive clarity. When there is no movement, the notions of arising and ceasing vanish; when cognition is pure, thoughts of beginning and end are extinguished.
Thus, one cycle of birth and death is perfectly illuminated from beginning to end. Recollection, consciousness, recitation, and study give rise to cognition that manifests as sensory objects;
this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāluṣya*). It is the very substance of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Therefore, when perception is exhausted, one transcends it.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to effect transformation and fusion, causing the mind to follow objects and objects to follow the mind. It is like perceiving a sour plum; it can penetrate through material obstructions.
Therefore, it is called "perverse perception of fusion. II. Distinguishing the Ten Manifest Objects: 1. Perverse Perception of Skillful Attachment to Craving (3).
This is the fault of fixed concentration.

Ānanda, when that son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, within this samādhi where perfect concentration brings forth illumination, his mind comes to cherish its own perfect clarity.
He sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks after skillful artifice.

To attain the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is called "void and wondrous. To be already free from the demon of sensation is called "not encountering [it]. Regarding "perfect concentration":

this refers to the concentration within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). "Seeking skillful means through the love for perfect clarity" means that because of that void and wondrous state, one gives rise to a loving thought toward the essence of perfect clarity, thereby manifesting the function of *upāya* (skillful means). △ Second: The heavenly demons find an opportunity.
At that time, the celestial Māra awaits an opportunity to gain entry. He dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma.

The person, unaware that they are possessed by a demon, claims for themselves to have attained supreme *nirvāṇa*. They come to the dwelling of a seeker of skillful means—a son of good family—and spread out a seat to preach the Dharma.
In an instant, their form may transform, appearing as a bhikṣu for that person to see, or they may become Śakra.
Or they may appear as women or bhikṣuṇīs; or they may dwell in dark rooms yet possess bodily radiance.

Such people, deluded by folly, mistake them for bodhisattvas and place their trust in their teachings. Their minds become agitated, they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, and they secretly practice lustful desires.
Manifesting transformations to teach and convert others demonstrates the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of *uḍova*. "To attach to a person" means to attach to another person;

it refers to the person to whom one is attached. That person is a person who practices meditative concentration (*samādhi*). They are deluded and ignorant, possessing concentration but lacking wisdom.
△ Third, ghosts and demons attach themselves simultaneously.
They take pleasure in speaking of portents, auspicious signs, and strange transformations.

They may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in such-and-such a place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fires, or of wars and weapons, thereby terrifying people and causing their family wealth to dissipate for no reason. This is known as a "strange ghost" who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person.
Once it has become satiated and its mind turns away, it leaves the person's body; then both the disciple and the teacher [fall under its influence].
Both shall fall into royal calamity. You should attain prior awakening so as not to enter saṃsāra; otherwise, through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
In these ten sections, each first mentions the celestial demon (deva-māra) and subsequently clarifies the ghost-demon (bhūta-māra), yet the ancient commentaries did not distinguish them.
Now, following the scripture, they are divided. The preceding general introduction states: "Within śamatha, there are subtle demonic affairs—whether they be your skandha-māras, or..."
Furthermore, there are celestial demons (*devaputra-māra*), or those possessed by ghosts and spirits, or those who encounter *chi* and *mei* (goblins and specters).

The conclusion summarizes these ten kinds of demons: they either attach themselves to the human body or manifest their own forms. These demonic teachers transmit their lustful ways one to another, and their perverse essences bewitch the heart and viscera.

This is like the ten categories mentioned within the "receiving aggregate" (*vedanā-skandha*), such as grief and so forth; these are the aggregate-demons (*skandha-māra*). At the beginning of the "perception aggregate" (*saṃjñā-skandha*), ten [categories] are raised.
The "categories" (lei) refer to the celestial Māras. The subsequent mention of those who are "attached and associated" refers to ghosts, spirits, *chimei* (ogres), and *mei* (sprites).
The first passage in each case states that they "secretly practice lustful desires," which refers to the teachers of Māra transmitting their lewd doctrines from one to another.

The second passage in each case states that they "delight in speaking with their mouths," which refers to malevolent spirits and *mei* (sprites) infesting the heart and viscera. The "strange ghosts," "drought ghosts" (*baba*), and so forth, are all those previously mentioned.
△ Second, the experience of conceptual craving through three stages. First, the fault of concentration power:

"Ānanda, furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, yet within the samādhi of the luminous manifestation of perfect concentration, his mind craves wandering and flightiness;
he casts his refined contemplation about and greedily seeks out experiences."
They delight in roaming through strange realms. △ Second, the heavenly demons find their opportunity.
At that time, the heavenly demons wait for their chance; they send their refined spirits to possess people, who then speak the sutras and the Dharma with their mouths.

Those people do not realize they have been possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place of those good men who seek to travel [to such realms].

He spread out his seat and preached the Dharma, yet his own form underwent no change. Those who listened to the Dharma suddenly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into a mass of purple-gold light.
Each member of the assembly experienced this individually, attaining what they had never known before.
Such people are deluded by folly and mistake him for a Bodhisattva; their minds become licentious and they violate the Buddha’s Vinaya, secretly indulging in greed and desire.
Third, ghost-demons also attach themselves to them.

They are fond of speaking of various Buddhas appearing in the world, saying that a certain person in a certain place must be the emanation-body of a certain Buddha come here, or that a certain person is a certain Bodhisattva who has come to transform the human realm. When people see this, their hearts become filled with yearning and craving.
"False views arise secretly; the wisdom of all modes of being is extinguished. This is called the *pūtana* ghost, who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and confuse this person.
Once his heart is satisfied, he leaves that person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell."
△ Third, the fault of the convergence of perceptions and craving with the power of concentration in the three stages of dhyāna.
Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation is void and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration brings forth illumination within the samādhi.
The mind cherishes entanglement. It clarifies its refined contemplation and greedily seeks accord.
To "cherish entanglement" means to desire a secret alignment with the wondrous principle. △ Second, the celestial Māras gain an opportunity.
At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sends forth his refined essence to possess a person, who speaks the Dharma and the sutras with their mouth.
That person is truly unaware that they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvana.

They come to the place where the seeker of the Way—a son of good family—resides, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. Their physical form and those listening to the Dharma undergo no outward change; they cause those listeners to...
Before hearing the Dharma, their minds were spontaneously enlightened. From moment to moment, their states shifted and changed: some attained knowledge of past lives;
some possessed the power of knowing others' minds; some beheld the hells; some knew all manner of good and evil affairs among humanity; some spoke verses aloud; and some recited sutras themselves.
Each indulged in pleasures such as they had never experienced before. These people, deluded by folly, took themselves to be bodhisattvas;
their hearts were steeped in attachment, and they violated the Buddha’s disciplinary code while secretly practicing lustful desires.
Because they seek to achieve union, the māras grant them awakening. From "Having attained self-awakening" onwards, all concern matters of secret resonance.
"Clinging affection" refers to the arising of attachment in the mind. △ Third, ghost-māras concurrently possess [the practitioner].
They take pleasure in speaking of how Buddhas are superior or inferior, claiming that such-and-such a Buddha was first and such-and-such a Buddha was later;

they further distinguish among them as being true or false Buddhas, male or female Buddhas, and the same applies to Bodhisattvas. Because they perceive these distinctions, they defile their original minds.

It is easy to enter into deviant awakening. This is called a *māyā-ghost* that, having grown old, becomes a *māra* to harass and disturb this person. Once it has become satiated and its mind arises, it departs from the person's body;
both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
To speak of "male and female Buddhas" reveals a vulgar desire that misleads practitioners. △ Fourth, the analysis of the perception of love has three parts:
first, the faults of deficient power.

Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, within the samādhi of the "illumination of perfect concentration," the mind cherishes its fundamental source.
One exhaustively examines the beginning and end of the nature of the transformation of things, refining and clarifying the mind while greedily seeking analytical discernment.
Love reaches the root of the myriad transformations; therefore, one clarifies the mind in order to discern them. △ Second, the celestial Māra finds an opportunity.
At that time, the celestial Māra waits for an opening and sends his refined essence to possess a person, who then speaks the Dharma of the sutras with their own mouth.

That person was previously unaware they were possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained supreme Nirvāṇa. They come to the place where that good man seeking the source resides.
He spread his seat and preached the Dharma. His body possessed majestic spiritual power that subdued those who sought instruction, causing them to submit naturally even before hearing the teaching.
These people came to realize that the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi-dharmakāya* are none other than their own present physical bodies;
and that fathers and sons, succeeding one another in birth, are themselves the eternally abiding and uninterrupted *dharmakāya*.

They all point to the present as being the Buddha-land itself, claiming there are no separate Pure Abodes nor the golden-hued marks [of a Buddha]. Such people accept this with faith, losing their former resolve;
they take refuge with their very bodies and lives in what they have never experienced before. These are the deluded who mistake themselves for Bodhisattvas.
Upon investigating their minds, it is found that they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and secretly practice lustful desires.
Those who claim that the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and so forth take the physical body as the fruit of merit, or that his illusory birth is eternally abiding,
thereby repudiating the retributive essence of the Pure Land— all do so because they analyze the source of transformation and falsely attempt to conflate its distinct aspects.
Thus it is said. △ Third, ghost-demons also attach themselves.
They delight in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female sexual organs are the true locus of Bodhi and Nirvana.
Those who lack wisdom believe these foul words; this is called the "Goblin-Demon of Pestilence and Hypnotic Domination."

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people; once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body, and both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
To take what is defiled and stained as truly pure is also a mental inducement toward lewd desire. △ Fifth, the threefold dark resonance of conceptual craving:
First, the faults of meditative power.
Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is void and subtle, and one does not encounter perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration illuminates within the *samādhi*.

With hearts full of longing and yearning, they circulate through various teachings with meticulous study, greedily seeking a hidden resonance in the hope that their meritorious practices will yield manifest efficacy. △ Second, the heavenly Māras gain an opportunity.
At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to gain entry. He dispatches an essence that attaches itself to a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth.
That person has no awareness at all that they are possessed by a demon; they likewise claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place of the virtuous man seeking a response, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma, causing the audience to perceive their body as if it were a hundred thousand years old, thereby giving rise to feelings of attachment and desire.

They are unable to relinquish them; they become their slaves, providing the four types of offerings without feeling weary, ensuring that those in their retinue recognize these individuals as their former teachers and original spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), thereby giving rise to a distinct attachment to the Dharma that is as sticky as glue or lacquer.

This is something never before encountered. Such people are deluded by folly and take them for Bodhisattvas; they draw near to their hearts and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly practicing lust.

They manifest forms that have existed for hundreds of thousands of years, falsely claiming to be acquaintances from previous lives in order to appear as if they possess a hidden spiritual resonance. △ Third, the ghosts.
The Māra will also join him.
He will fondly speak of how, in a previous life, he first delivered certain people;
he will say that at that time they were his wife, concubine, or brother, and that he has now come to deliver them, accompanying them back to a certain world to make offerings to a certain Buddha.
Some claim that there exists separately a Buddha of Great Radiant Light who dwells therein, the ground where all Tathāgatas take their rest.

Those who lack wisdom believe this to be false and deceptive, thereby losing their original mind. This is called a *rākṣasa* ghost who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb such a person.
Once it has become satiated and its mind turns away from the person's body, both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity.
If you can awaken first, you shall not enter saṃsāra; but if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
These are all instances of manifesting in darkness through karmic retribution. To cite the case of the "Luminous Heaven" (Ābhāsvara-deva): it is about to lead one into the realm of Māra. △ Sixth:
The Tranquility of Conceptual Craving has three parts. First, the faults of meditative power (dhyāna-bala).

Furthermore, the virtuous son receives [this teaching]. His aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and he does not encounter perverse thoughts. Within the samādhi that illuminates through perfect concentration, his mind loves to enter deeply;
he disciplines himself with diligent effort, delights in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates, and greedily seeks tranquility.
Their love penetrates deep into quietude, and they cultivate supernormal powers through clarity. △ Second, the heavenly Māras find an opportunity.
At that time, the heavenly Māra waits for his chance; he dispatches an essence to possess a person, who speaks the Dharma of the sutras with their own mouth.

That person originally does not realize they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place of the good man who seeks the aggregates.
He spread out his seat and preached the Dharma, causing those who listened to each recognize their own past karma.

At times, at such a place, he would say to one person, "Though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal," and then command another to step on the person's tail from behind, suddenly rendering that person unable to rise.
Thus, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in humble reverence. If anyone gave rise to a thought, he already knew its very inception.

Beyond the Buddha’s discipline, he further imposed rigorous austerities upon himself; he slandered bhikṣus, reviled his followers, and exposed the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion.

His perverse concentration enabled him to possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). These two were his past karma (*pūrvakarma*); his rebirth as an animal was his subsequent retribution (*paścimakarma*). These two were his past [karmic results].

"Life" refers to the supernormal power of longevity (*āyuṣka-abhijñā*). "Knowledge" refers to the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). "Exposing" refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear and eye (*divya-śrotra-cakṣur-abhijñā*);
"exposing" (*jipelu*) means to reveal someone's private affairs. △ Third, ghosts and demons may both attach themselves [to these powers].
He delights in speaking of future calamities and blessings; when the time comes, not even a hair’s breadth of it fails.

This powerful ghost has grown old and become a demon, tormenting this person until he is satiated. Once his desire is fulfilled, he leaves the person's body, and both disciple and teacher fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
△ Third, the three [obstacles] regarding the perception of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*). First is the fault of deficient concentration.

Furthermore, noble son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, within the *samādhi* of the "perfect concentration that illuminates" (*cakra-samādhi-prakāśana*), there arise:
The mind cherishes knowledge and insight; it diligently and painfully investigates and seeks, greedily craving the knowledge of past lives.
It delights in knowing hidden and extraordinary matters as well as the destiny of previous existences. △ Second, the celestial Māras gain an opportunity.
At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sends a flying spirit to possess a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma.
That person is entirely unaware they have been possessed by a Māra, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He comes to the place where those seeking the Way are gathered, spreads his seat, and preaches the Dharma. This man, without cause, obtains a great precious jewel at the place where the Dharma is being preached. At times, this Māra...
They transform into animals, with their mouths holding pearls, various precious jewels, bamboo slips, tablets, and other extraordinary objects;
they first bestow these upon people and later attach them to their bodies, or they entice listeners to hide them underground. There are also moon-bright pearls.
It illuminated that place. Those listeners experienced what they had never known before. They consumed many medicinal herbs instead of fine delicacies;
at times they ate only a single sesame seed and a single grain of barley per day, yet their bodies remained plump and robust because Māra sustained them. Thus, they slandered the bhikṣus.
They revile the assembly, showing no regard for censure or suspicion.
They secretly conceal precious jewels, scriptures, and other extraordinary objects. Third, they are possessed by ghosts and demons;
their mouths are fond of speaking of hidden treasures in other regions and the secret abodes of sages and worthies throughout the ten directions, encouraging others to follow after them.

One often encounters individuals who appear strange and extraordinary; these are spirits of mountains, forests, local deities, city gods, rivers, peaks, and ghosts who have grown old and become demons.
Some preach licentiousness and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them.

There may be those who practice asceticism by subsisting solely on grasses and trees, yet their conduct lacks constancy and they disturb such practitioners. Once these beings have become weary and satisfied, they will leave the practitioner's body.
Both the disciples and the master will often fall into royal trouble. You should be aware of this beforehand so that you do not enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell. △ Section Eight:
The Spiritual Power of Conceptual Craving, Part Three. First, the Faults of Concentration.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, within the *samādhi* where perfect concentration brings forth illumination:
The mind loves various supernatural transformations and studies the source of transformation, greedily seeking spiritual powers.

The "source of transformation" (*huàyuán*) is the root of the myriad transformations; [the practitioner] desires to mount it in order to manifest divine changes. △ Second, the celestial Māras gain an opportunity.
At that time, a celestial demon (deva-māra) awaits his opportunity; he dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their mouth.
That person truly does not realize they are possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana.

They come to the place of the good man seeking spiritual powers, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma. This person may even hold a flame in their hand, or grasp that light with their hands and divide it among those listening.
Upon the heads of the fourfold assembly—those who were listening—flames rose from their crowns several feet in length; yet they possessed no quality of heat and never caused any burning.
Some walked upon water as if treading on level ground, while others sat cross-legged in mid-air, remaining perfectly still.
Sometimes he entered into a jar, or stayed within a sack; passing through windows and piercing walls, he encountered no obstruction.
Only regarding weapons did he lack mastery. He claimed to be a Buddha, wearing white robes and receiving the prostrations of bhikṣus, while slandering dhyāna and the Vinaya.
They reviled the assembly and exposed private matters without avoiding censure or suspicion.

Because they possessed the power of divine transformations through attachment, they manifested such feats as grasping fire and walking on water; yet if these were true divine transformations, they would not have feared weapons.
△ Third, they were possessed by malevolent spirits.
They constantly speak of supernatural powers and mastery from their mouths; or they cause others to see Buddha-lands from the side.

These are delusions produced by the power of ghosts and lack any reality. They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking various vulgarities as the transmission of the Dharma.
These are known as the mountain spirits of great power, the sea spirits, the wind spirits, the river spirits, and the earth spirits of this world.

They include the accumulated karmic ghosts and enchanters of all plants and trees over many kalpas; or dragon enchanters; or immortals who, at the end of their lives, have returned to life as enchanters;

or those whose immortal tenure has expired and whose years dictate they should die, yet whose forms do not decay because they are possessed by other monsters. As they grow old, they become demons that harass and disturb these people.
When a sense of satiety arises and they depart from the person’s body, both the disciple and the teacher often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Vulgar, lewd, and depraved matters. △ Ninth: The Three Aspects of Deepening Emptiness through Contemplation of Impurity. First, the Faults of Concentrative Power.

Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes void and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, within the *samādhi* where perfect concentration brings forth illumination:

His heart loved to enter extinction; he researched the nature of transformation and greedily sought profound emptiness, desiring to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in order to proceed toward empty stillness. △ Second, the heavenly Māras gain the opportunity.
At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sent a flying spirit to possess a person, who would orally preach the sutras and the Dharma.

That person never realized they were possessed by a demon, and likewise claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He came to the place of the good man seeking emptiness, spread out his seat, and preached the Dharma.
In the midst of the great assembly, his form suddenly vanished into emptiness; the multitude could see nothing of him, as he returned from the void.

They appear suddenly, exercising mastery over their presence and disappearance. Sometimes they manifest their bodies as transparent as lapis lazuli; sometimes they extend their hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood;
and sometimes their excrement and urine are like thick rock honey. They revile the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt.
Because they are fond of emptiness, they rely on it and become deluded by it. Third, malevolent spirits concurrently possess them;
they constantly say from their mouths that there is neither cause nor effect, that once dead one is extinguished forever, and that there are no further rebirths, nor any ordinary beings or sages.

These statements all arise from being driven by views of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). In recent times, heterodox sects have falsely claimed that "one must practice authentic cultivation and attain authentic insight.
Consequently, they dismiss as non-existent everything that is not personally witnessed—such as cause and effect, future lives, heaven, and hell.
Thus, those who adopt such views all conclude that good and evil are vague and distant, and that this transient life will not be experienced again.
Consequently, they forget the restraints of the precepts and indulge in licentious pleasures; intoxicated by drink and food, they bring about their own ruin through mere chance.
In public positions, they exploit and oppress others, truly believing that neither heaven nor hell exists.

I have always lamented this folly, and thus, upon reaching this point in my commentary and sub-commentary, I was moved to take up my pen with vigor, hoping that those who follow demonic teachings might awaken and not sink into self-destruction.
Although they have attained emptiness and stillness, they secretly practice lust; those who receive their desire likewise attain a "void mind" and deny cause and effect.

These are known as the vital energies of solar and lunar eclipses, which—like gold, jade, *zhicao* fungi, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes—do not die for thousands of myriad years and become spirits.
They are born in lands, and when they grow old, they become demons to harass and disturb these people until they become weary and satisfied, at which point the spirit’s heart arises.
When that person’s body perishes, both the disciple and the teacher will likely fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
During solar and lunar eclipses, the vital essence flows and infuses [the body], enabling it to become like gold and jade. △ Third, regarding the ten perceptions of attachment to long life:
first, the faults of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, within the samādhi of the "illumination of perfect concentration," the mind comes to cherish long life.

One undergoes arduous effort in investigating the subtle, greedily seeking eternal years; abandoning the coarse state of birth and death, one suddenly hopes for the permanence of the subtle marks of the transformation-death (pariṇāma-maraṇa).

Only when the delusions of the three realms are exhausted can one leave behind birth-and-death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) and attain birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*).

Now, while one's merit is not yet perfected, to falsely hope to immediately eliminate these delusions is a mistake. "Investigating the subtle" (*yanji*) means to investigate and exhaustively examine the minute and subtle in order to seek deep understanding.
"Subtle thoughts" refers to the desire to transform the coarse for the sake of subtlety, seeking to remain long in this world. △ Second, the celestial Māras find an opportunity.

At that time, the celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sends his refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person does not realize at all that they are possessed by a demon;
they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana. They come to the place where the son of good family seeking the Way resides, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma.
They love to speak of traveling to and from other regions without obstruction, or of traversing ten thousand li and returning in an instant.

In all such cases, they obtain the object from that direction; or, in a single location within a house, over a distance of only a few paces, they cause a person to go from the eastern wall to the western wall.
Even if this person walks with great haste, they do not arrive for many years. It is because of this that their faith arises.

Doubting that the Buddha was manifest before him, he realized that even ten thousand *li* could be traversed in an instant—this is the matter of one who has attained the power of transformation. △ Third, his demonic retinue also attached themselves to him;
he constantly said with his own mouth: "All sentient beings of the ten directions are my children. I give birth to all Buddhas; I bring forth the worlds."
I am the Primordial Buddha. My appearance in the world is spontaneous and not attained through cultivation. This is called the Sovereign Heavenly Demon who dwells in the world;
he causes his retinue—such as Cāmuṇḍā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Piśāca youths who have not yet resolved their minds—to exploit its empty clarity and consume the vital essence of others.
Or, without relying on a teacher, the practitioner may personally behold it.
They shall be called Vajradhara and granted long life. Appearing in the form of beautiful women, they will extensively promote lustful desires;

within less than a year, their livers and brains will wither away, and their mouths will engage in soliloquies that sound like those of demons or malevolent spirits. Those who do not discern them clearly will for the most part fall into royal calamities.
Before they even encounter their punishment, they have already withered and died; having tormented that person to the point of death, you should first awaken so as not to enter saṃsāra.
If you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
In the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, it is said that there is a Piśāca youth named Cchavinda, who is subordinate to the Four Heavenly Kings.
If he has already resolved his mind [on awakening], he protects people; if he has not yet resolved his mind, he harms them.

Because he uses the power of his concentration and its empty luminosity for his own benefit, he consumes their vital essence. Alternatively, those who do not rely on a teacher are not harmed because they are not possessed by Māra.
The Master said: "One may personally witness the manifestation of Māra; one may speak soliloquies, occasionally uttering strange words. △ Third, a comprehensive summary for detailed instruction:
"Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of Māras will, during the time of the final age, appear among those who have left the home life to practice the Way within my Dharma."

Some attach themselves to human bodies, while others manifest their own forms; all claim to have already attained the realization of Perfect Universal Enlightenment and praise sexual desire, thereby violating the Buddha’s Vinaya.
These former evil demonic teachers and their disciples transmit their lust from one to another. Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch the hearts and viscera of practitioners;
for as few as nine lifetimes, or for many more than a hundred generations, they cause those who practice true cultivation to become entirely part of the demonic retinue.
After their lives end, they will inevitably become subjects of Māra. Having lost the Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the final age, those belonging to the faction of Māra will manifest in the forms of bhikṣus, arhats, and so forth, to corrupt and destroy the True Dharma."
Do not disparage the precepts; your intention should be the same as this. △ Fourth, the command to propagate and proclaim:

"You need not first enter parinirvāṇa now. Even if you have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), remain by the power of your vow within that age of the final dharma, giving rise to great compassion to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, so that they do not fall under the influence of Māra and attain right knowledge and vision."
I have now delivered you from birth and death. To follow the Buddha’s words is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

Beginning with Ānanda’s initiation of the teaching and ending with his final entrustment to propagate it, one can fully understand that the profound origin and far-reaching influence of the Great Teaching were entirely due to Ānanda’s power.
Thus, [the events] such as encountering demonic obstacles, the investigation of the mind, and the discernment of vision were all [manifested through him].
Out of great compassion for the age of the Dharma’s decline, he causes [beings] not to cling to demons and to attain right knowledge and vision.

One should know that although in the past he manifested extinction through four schools, his current Dharma-transformation constantly endures; wherever there are manifestations and echoes, they are none other than bodies remaining due to his original vows.
△ Five: Conclusion and Exhortation to Deeply Guard Against [Harm].
Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states that appear before you all arise from the interaction between the mind and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations).

Thus, these phenomena manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering such circumstances, they fail to recognize their own confusion and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata as your guide regarding me.
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this to the age of the final dharma, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the unsurpassed path.
