The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Temple in Wénlǐng Explains the Four Categories of the Aggregate of Mental Formations (Saṃskāra-skandha) △ IV. 1. First, showing the characteristics of the aggregate:
"Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of mental formations (saṃjñā-skandha) is exhausted, this person’s ordinary dreams and thoughts..."

It is extinguished. Whether awake or asleep, one remains constant in this state. Conscious clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky; there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadows of external objects.
When observing the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they are like reflections in a clear mirror: as they come, there is nothing to which they adhere; as they pass, they leave no trace.
They are received in emptiness as responses, with no lingering habitual tendencies; there is only the single, pure, and true essence. From this, the root-source of birth and death [is severed].
Revealed: One observes all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.

Although one understands the individual origins of their respective lifespans, one perceives their common basis of birth as being like a shimmering, flickering mirage—a fundamental pivot and hollow for the floating sense organs and their objects.
This is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
This is a general description of the cessation of thought and the manifestation of activity. Floating and shifting are deluded habits: when the day is bright, there is thinking;
when the evening is dim, there is dreaming. These turbidities disturb the true nature so that it cannot be unified; they agitate awakened clarity so that it cannot be stilled.

Therefore, for one whose aggregate of thought (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, dreams and fantasies vanish; waking and sleeping are always one, and awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky.

Because the five aggregates are coarse at first and subtle later, when ideation (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted, there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadow-phenomena. Although one contemplates the myriad phenomena, there is no conceptualization;
thus, it is like a bright mirror that reflects without attachment or trace, receiving illumination and responding in emptiness, entirely free from habitual tendencies.
This singular, refined truth is such that its clarity is ultimate; therefore, the hidden *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is thereby revealed.

Furthermore, conduct is the root source of the birth and extinction of the myriad transformations; thus, when its characteristics are revealed, there is nothing of the origins of the twelve classes of beings that is not fully seen.
Each has its own destiny and the continuity of consciousness, while their shared basis is conduct.

It is agitated and obscurely hidden, and is therefore likened to a wild horse (mirage) that suddenly appears and suddenly vanishes; hence it is called "flashing" (*yi yi*). Since there is no longer any coarse shadow, [it is so described].
It is called "clarity and agitation. The movement and stillness of the faculties and their objects both originate from this; therefore, it is named the ultimate pivot-hole.

If this clarity and agitation—the shimmering primordial nature—enters the primordial clarity of its own nature, and once clarified, the primordial habituation ceases, like waves subsiding and transforming into clear water, this is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. One should observe the source of this.
Subtle, hidden delusions serve as its foundation.
As the habit-energies of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) become turbulent and form a nature, it is called the "original nature" and "original habit.

When one can extinguish these turbulent habits, one returns to the essence of clarity—the fundamental source—and the characteristics of flux and movement are exhausted. Thus, it is like waves subsiding and transforming back into still water.

Arising and ceasing without pause, the movement of karma constantly shifts; this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), which is the very substance of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Therefore, when the aggregate of formations is exhausted, one transcends it. Because the aggregate of formations shifts secretly without any conscious awareness, it is called "subtle and hidden deluded thought.
△ Second, clarifying the ten types of frantic misconceptions: First, calculating two causes within the perfect origin. Third, the initial general summary.

Ānanda, you should know that among those good men who have attained right awareness within *śamatha*, ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity because their minds are concentrated and upright.
Only then are they able to investigate with refinement the root of all living beings.

When the fundamental source of birth is revealed within that root, they observe that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source; yet, within that perfect source, they give rise to conceptual calculations.
This enters into and transcends the two types of causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*).
Dreams vanish; waking and sleeping are always one. Therefore, it is called "rightly knowing *śamatha*" and also termed "concentrated clarity and right mind.

These are all signs of the exhaustion of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Since external māras are all summoned by the mind, when conceptualization is exhausted and concentrated clarity is attained, [the māras vanish].
Then the celestial Māras will not approach. From this point on, there is only the loss of the path through the practice of dhyāna, involving frantic interpretations and false conceptualizations;

this is precisely the Māra of the aggregates (skandha-māra). The various classes of beings are fundamentally identical to the basis of co-arising. Within these fundamental classes, those for whom the source-element is revealed—
Having perceived the source of activity within the common basis of birth, one sees that the subtle, pure, and moving source is indeed the source of activity.
Once this has been seen, one concludes that all arising and ceasing is perfectly complete within this [source], and thus fails to further investigate the beginning and end of the *vijñāna-skandha*.
Consequently, one establishes the two theories of causelessness (*ahetu-vāda*). Part Two: A Detailed Explanation of the Two [Theories]. First: Calculating Original Causelessness (*mūla-ahetu-vāda*).

First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this? Because this person has already attained the complete breaking open of the life-faculty and rides upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-organ.

They see all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas; as their karmic currents wind and turn, dying here and being born there, they see only the sentient beings revolving in those very places. Since eighty thousand kalpas past, it has been dark and nothing can be observed. Thus...
They form this understanding: "These sentient beings of the world in the ten directions have existed spontaneously without cause beyond eighty thousand kalpas.
By such speculative reckoning, they lose sight of the Perfectly All-Knowing One, fall into the ranks of external paths, and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
Since the foundation of birth has been destroyed, the root is detached from its hollow; thus, the eye is purified and one is able to see through clearly.
As for those whose karmic streams form winding curves, they follow the flow of karma like water in a bay, swirling in that place and unable to emerge on their own.

Because their power of meditative concentration is limited before they have escaped the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), they remain in darkness and see nothing beyond eighty thousand kalpas. This is because...
Because there is nothing seen, one reckons that there is fundamentally no cause. One does not know that the fundamental cause resides in deluded consciousness.
This is what is called the loss of right universal knowledge. II. Reckoning that the derivative has no cause.
Second, this person perceives that the end has no cause. Why is this? Because this person, having already observed the root of birth, knows that humans produce humans and birds produce birds;
they know that crows have always been black and cranes have always been white; that humans and devas are fundamentally upright while animals are fundamentally horizontal;
and that whiteness is not produced by washing nor blackness created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further change or alteration. Now...
The exhaustion of this physical form is likewise so. Since I have from the beginning never perceived bodhi, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi?
I have always known that all phenomena today are fundamentally without cause.

They erroneously cling to the production of roots. Failing to comprehend the principle of transformation, they hold that from human one remains human, and even from black one remains black, with no further change or transition.
Consequently, they take this as an analogy for themselves: having originally not seen the Way, they will likewise have no realization at the end;
thus, the end has no cause. [Note: In the original text, the character "結" (jie) should be "未" (wei). △ Third, the conclusion on the error.
Based on these speculations, they lose the correct universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the first type of external path that establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
△ Second, regarding the four types of calculating [the self] as omnipresent and eternal within the Perfect and Eternal: 1. General Summary.
Ānanda, when these virtuous sons among the practitioners of *samādhi* concentrate their luminous and upright minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations within this Perfect and Eternal state—such persons...
This leads to falling into the four theories of universal permanence.
The previous statement referred to the "perfectly round source of agitation," while this statement refers to the "eternally agitated source.

Because the source of birth-and-death is perfectly round, one consequently clings to it as being eternal, thereby giving rise to the theory of universal permanence; "universal" (biàn) is synonymous with "perfectly round" (yuán). Therefore, this is the heading.

This is called "pervasive permanence. The subsequent conclusion is called "perfect permanence. 4. Second, specifically clarifying the calculation of permanence based on the single locus of mind and objects.
First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects and finds that these two locations are without cause.

Through cultivation, they are able to know all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas; seeing that these all circulate in a cycle and have never been lost, they calculate them to be permanent.

Due to the false conceptualization of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the fundamental source of arising and ceasing, one subsequently gives rise to false conceptualizations regarding the mind, objects, the four great elements, and the eight consciousnesses.

One may either negate arising and ceasing and conceptualize permanence, or preserve arising and ceasing while conceptualizing permanence, or identify the consciousness with a self-spirit and conceptualize permanence, or give rise to wrong views and conceptualize permanence. Now, this [text] exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects.

It is fundamentally without cause, meaning that there is neither arising nor ceasing. This is because the principle of arising and ceasing for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions is entirely cyclical;
fundamentally, nothing is ever lost. This is to deny arising and ceasing while calculating permanence. As for one whose aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted:
Because one cultivates contemplation based on the two factors of mind and mental objects, one is able to know events of twenty thousand kalpas through the power of such effort;
the subsequent cases of forty thousand and eighty thousand kalpas follow this same principle. △ Second, reckoning permanence based on the four great elements.

Second, this person investigates the fundamental source of the four great elements. Believing that the four natures are eternally abiding, they practice until they can know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas;
seeing that these are all essentially constant and have never been lost, they reckon them to be permanent.
Sentient beings arise and perish in dependence upon earth, water, fire, and wind; yet the four fundamental natures are originally eternally abiding.

Thus, all phenomena of arising and perishing are in their essence eternal. This is to conceive of permanence while remaining within arising and perishing. △ Third, conceiving of permanence based on the eight consciousnesses.
Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties and the *manas* that grasps and sustains them.

Because the fundamental source within the mind, intellect, and consciousness is eternally constant by nature, through cultivation they are able to know all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, following their cycles without loss.
It is primordially and eternally abiding; even at the limit of existence, it does not lose its nature.

To reckon this as "constant" refers to the six sense faculties and the manas, which together constitute the eight consciousnesses. Within the mind, intellect, and consciousness, the fundamental source is the very nature of consciousness itself.
Only a Buddha and a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage can thoroughly exhaust the origin of these eight consciousnesses. If one can truly exhaust them—

When [the former] is exhausted, one enters the realm of wisdom and transcends the admonitions of mind and thought. Now, within this very mind, intellect, and consciousness, one perceives the original source;
that is to say, its fundamental nature is eternally constant, and sentient beings rely upon it to dwell in cyclic existence, never losing it.
This is the deluded calculation regarding the divine spirit (*ātman*). △ Fourth: Based on the cessation of perception, one calculates permanence.
Fourth, this person has exhausted the source of ideation; in their fundamental nature, there is no longer any flowing, ceasing, or movement.

The mind of arising and ceasing has now been eternally extinguished, and within this principle, non-arising and non-ceasing spontaneously prevail. Based on what the mind perceives, they reckon this state to be permanent.
The "element of perception" (*saṃjñā-skandha*) refers to the aggregate of perception. The "principle of arising" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

To falsely claim that the processes of transmigration, arising, and ceasing all belong to the mind of perception, and to assert that now that these have been eternally extinguished, the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing naturally belongs to formations—this is to fail to realize that the aggregate of formations is itself the source of arising and ceasing.
This constitutes the giving rise to false views and making erroneous calculations. △ Third, the conclusion on the loss.
Based on this, they conceive of permanence, lose the correct universal knowledge, fall into the ranks of external paths, and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second type of external path: the doctrine of established circular permanence.
△ III. Regarding oneself and others, there are three [sections] concerning the four perversions. First, a general summary:
Furthermore, O virtuous sons within samādhi, when you stabilize and concentrate your correct mind, Māras shall find no opportunity; you will exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
If one contemplates that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source and gives rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others, such a person falls into the four inverted views,
specifically the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
Regarding the objects of self and others, they falsely give rise to inverted views; there are four such types, each reckoning one portion as impermanent and one portion as permanent.
II. Specifically explaining these four: first, the partial reckoning arising from both self and others.
First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate *puruṣa* (divine self).
From this, they reckon that their self pervades the ten directions, being a concentrated luminosity, unmoving; that all sentient beings are born and die within the center of their own heart.
Thus, they name their own mind-nature "constant," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.
It is wondrously luminous, perfectly still, and profound, free from "I" and "mine. Yet, the non-Buddhists falsely establish a "divine self" (*ātman*) therein.

From this, they calculate that the self is all-pervading, solid, and immovable, while sentient beings undergo birth and death within it; thus, they reckon themselves to be permanent and others to be impermanent.
2. Separating from the mind to contemplate the land, giving rise to partial calculations.
Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead surveys throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Where they see places where kalpas have been destroyed, they designate them as the nature of ultimate impermanence; where they see places where kalpas have not been destroyed, they designate them as ultimate permanence.

The former was contemplation based on the mind; this is contemplation based on the land. When various false conceptualizations arise, if even a single dharma is erroneous, then all dharmas are inverted.
△ Third, the specific contemplation of how the essence of the mind gives rise to partial conceptualizations.
Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and extremely minute, like a fine mote of dust.

It transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature remaining unchanging, capable of causing this body to arise and perish in an instant. This indestructible nature is called the permanence of the self-nature.
All birth and death flow forth from the self; this is called the nature of impermanence.
Because it cannot be identified with either the body or the mind, one must practice a distinct contemplation of them. The metaphor of "minute dust" refers to its subtle refinement;

that is to say, through the mind’s subtle and precise operation, the body is made to arise and perish, while the mind itself does not undergo destruction. Previously, one made a dualistic calculation regarding a single dharma.
This constitutes the dualistic conceptualization of what is of a single nature. △ Fourth, the error of giving rise to the conceptualization of division regarding the four aggregates:

This person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended, yet they perceive the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations flows constantly, they conceptualize it as having a permanent nature.
Form, sensation, perception, and so forth have now already ceased and exhausted; this is called impermanence.
These illusory aggregates are of one substance and possess the single characteristic of flux. Yet, you cling to what is delusive as being right and forget the past while seeing only the present;
thus, you take that which flows as permanent and that which shifts as ceasing. △ Third, the conclusion on the loss.
Because they speculate that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the third heterodox doctrine: the theory of partial permanence.
Nowadays, people regard intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) as real and phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*) as illusory; thus, while their reasoning is harmonious, their practice is obstructed.

They cannot avoid falling into these four kinds of partial conceptualizations. △ Fourth, regarding the calculation of the four states, there are three parts concerning the four extremes. First, a general summary.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their correct minds so that Māras find no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound,
pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, within these various states, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the four theories of the finite existence of the world.
There are four stages: namely, the stage of the three time periods, the stage of seeing and hearing, the stage of self and other, and the stage of arising and ceasing.
II. A detailed explanation of these four: first, the extreme views regarding the three time periods.
First, these people calculate that the source of birth flows and functions without ceasing; calculating the past and future, they call it "having limits";
calculating the continuous mind, they call it "being limitless."
The source of birth, the flow of activity, is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because of this shifting flow, one calculates across the three periods of time.
Since that which has passed has already ceased and that which is yet to come is not yet seen, it is called "having a limit. Because the present continues in succession, it is called "having no limit.
One does not know that the true limit (the *bhūtakoṭi*) is fundamentally neither limited nor limitless. △ Second, the calculation based on the limits of what is seen and heard.
Second, this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas and perceives sentient beings; yet prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, there is a silence beyond hearing or seeing.
That which is beyond hearing or seeing is called "boundless," while that where sentient beings exist is called "bounded."
Previously, not seeing was taken as "having a limit"; here, not hearing is taken as "being limitless. This is a case of inverted and contradictory reckoning.
△ Third, the reckoning of limits regarding self and others.
Third, this person calculates that because he possesses universal knowledge, he has attained the nature of boundlessness.

He thinks that all people appear within the scope of his own cognition, yet he himself has never known the cognitive nature of those others; thus, he claims they have not attained the mind of boundlessness, but possess only a limited nature.
I know that their nature is identical to my own. Now, because I have never known them to be different from me, I am boundless while they possess only limits.
△ Fourth, the calculation of the limits of birth and extinction.
Fourth, this person exhaustively investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Using the mental pathways he perceives as a measure, he calculates all sentient beings within a single body, determining that they are all half-born and half-extinguished; he thus clarifies that everything existing within the world is likewise so.
Half has limits and half is limitless.

Because they exhaustively investigate the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, seeing that what existed in the past is now non-existent, they consequently take one aggregate (*skandha*) to be half-born and half-extinguished;
and this applies to all internal faculties and external environments. They thus regard birth as having limits and extinction as being limitless. △ Third, the conclusion.
Failing to understand this, they speculate on whether existence is finite or infinite, thereby falling into the ranks of the heterodox and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fourth heterodox school that establishes the doctrine of finitude.

All have exhausted the Way and lost its true direction, revolving through false reckonings. This is what is called reaching such a state of delusion and error regarding the "mad liberation" of *dhyāna*.
△ Five: Regarding knowledge and views, there are four types of deceptive confusion. Three: First, a general summary.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, such that Māras find no opportunity,
they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, within their knowledge and vision,
they give rise to conceptual calculations, these people will fall into four kinds of perverse, "undying" equivocation and pervasive false theorizing.

Because of their perverse inversion, they possess a deranged understanding that lacks decisiveness within their knowledge and views, and thus they distort and confuse their speech. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that the heavens are eternal and name them 'the Immortal. They claim that by not engaging in deceptive confusion, one can be born in those heavens;
therefore, when questioned, they do not dare to answer truthfully, fearing it would constitute deceptive confusion. The Buddha said: 'This is true deceptive confusion.'"
...also. △ Second, the specific explanation has four parts. First, observing transformation and confusing the principle, leading to perversity and confusion.

First, this person observes the source of transformation and change; seeing the place where things shift and flow, they designate it as "change" (*pariṇāma*); seeing the place where things continue in succession, [they designate it as "continuity"].
That which is called "constant" refers to the locus where seeing is observed. That which is called "arising" refers to the locus where seeing is not observed.

That which is called "increase" refers to the locus where the causal nature of continuity is uninterrupted. That which is called "the middle" refers to the locus within the midst of correct continuity that is free from [extremes].

That which is called "diminution" refers to the various places where things arise; that which is called "existence" refers to their mutual presence; and that which is called "non-existence" refers to their mutual disappearance.
When observing through principle as a whole, yet perceiving with a biased mind, there may come those who seek the Dharma to inquire about its meaning.
To them, he replies: "I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and diminishing. At all times, his speech remains thus confused.
This causes the person before one to lose the essential passages of the text.

When observing the myriad transformations of phenomena and seeing their lack of uniformity, one subsequently gives rise to divergent interpretations. To employ the mind to perceive things differently is precisely what constitutes a divergent interpretation.

Consequently, one becomes unable to discern the truth and distorts the meaning with deceptive and confused speech. △ Second, observing the mind while clinging to non-existence and engaging in deceptive confusion.
Second, this person contemplates the mind with keen observation and finds that it has no location whatsoever; because there is nothing to be found, they realize its non-existence.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "non-existent. Apart from this non-existence, they have nothing further to say.
Because one contemplates this deluded mind, one perceives arising and ceasing; that they are mutually non-existent is the characteristic of moment-to-moment extinction.
As for "attaining realization," it means awakening to the fact that all phenomena are non-existent. △ Third, contemplating the mind’s clinging to existence and its deceptive confusion.
Third, this person carefully observes that the mind each has its own location, and through this, they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "It is so. Apart from this, they have nothing further to say.
Each and every one of these arises as a characteristic in every moment of thought. To say "yes" or "no" is in both cases an unclear answer.
△ Fourth, observing that the object distracts the mind and leads to deceptive confusion:
"Fourth" refers to the person who perceives both existence and non-existence. Because their object is fragmented, their mind is likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them...

He replied: "To say 'it both exists and does not exist' is itself to say 'it neither exists nor does not exist. Within that state of neither existing nor not existing, it is not the case that it 'both exists and does not exist.
This is entirely evasive and confused, leaving no room for further inquiry. It is like the branches of a tree, diverging and inconsistent. △ Third, the conclusion on the error.
Based on these speculative calculations, they engage in deceptive equivocation and nihilism, falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fifth type of external path: the pervasive false discourse of the "immortal equivocation" based on the four inverted natures.
Those heterodox persons of today falsely claim to have attained the Way, yet they lack internal rectitude and instead delude others with pretenses;
most are of these four types. △ Six: Regarding the continuity of practice, there are three calculations concerning the future. First, a general summary.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who stabilize their minds in upright concentration, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that source of constant agitation within profound stillness. Those who form conceptual calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow fall into the error of generating a mind that perceives signs after death.

The "inexhaustible flow" refers to the characteristic of the continuity of activity (*pravṛtti-saṃtāna*). Because birth and death cease while giving rise to one another in uninterrupted succession, one knows that there are characteristics [of existence] after death.
△ Second, the specific explanation has two parts. First, the actual calculation.
Some solidify their own bodies, saying, "Form is the self. Some perceive the self as encompassing and pervading all lands, saying, "The self possesses form.
Some perceive that preceding objects revolve according to the self, saying, "Form belongs to the self. Or again, they perceive the self as persisting in continuity within the midst of formations.
Thinking "I am in form," one speculates that there is a mark after death; thus, through such cycles, there are sixteen marks.

Because the mind is inverted, one stubbornly clings to the physical body, taking form to be the self. Furthermore, one claims that the essence of the self is pervasive and all-encompassing, whereby form becomes "mine.
The former object is the form before one's eyes; the continuity of formations is also form.
One forms these four reckonings regarding form (*rūpa*). It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*); thus, sixteen aspects are established.

All of these reckon that there is further existence after death. The reason the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is not reckoned [in this way] is that it is obscure and has not yet manifested. △ Second, the secondary reckonings.
From this point, some may reckon that afflictions (*kleśa*) and bodhi are ultimately two distinct natures that proceed side by side, each remaining untouched by the other.

They further reckon that all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas likewise proceed side by side. As for "ultimately proceeding side by side," they reckon that afflictions and bodhi do not overcome or extinguish one another, as both will continue to exist hereafter. △ Third, the conclusion on the error.
Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth heterodox school’s inverted doctrine of mind which posits the characteristics of existence after death within the five aggregates.
△ Seven: Regarding the denial of existence after the cessation of the aggregates, there are three parts. First, a general summary:
Furthermore, O virtuous sons within samādhi, when you firmly stabilize your upright mind, Māra shall find no opportunity; you will exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound stillness which is yet fundamentally subject to constant agitation, if one first eliminates form, sensation, and perception, yet continues to give rise to conceptual calculations within them,
this person will fall into the inverted state of generating a resolve for the signless after death.
△ Second, the specific explanation has two parts. First, the actual contemplation:
seeing that form ceases, one realizes that physical shape has no cause; observing that perception ceases, one realizes that the mind has no attachments; knowing that sensation ceases—
There is no further continuity; the nature of the aggregates (skandhas) dissolves. Even if there were the principle of life, it would lack sensation and perception, being the same as grass and trees.

Since this physical substance cannot even be found while manifest before one, how could various characteristics exist after death? By investigating and verifying this, one finds that the characteristics after death are non-existent.
Thus, through such repeated cycles, there are eight instances of the absence of characteristics.
The five aggregates (*skandha*) dissolve. This refers to the cessation of form, sensation, and perception. Physiological activity is precisely volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

This means that when sensation and perception are absent, volitional formations also cease. This is discussed in terms of the present causes of the four aggregates perishing and the future fruit ceasing;
since cause and effect are treated together, they constitute eight phases. △ Second, the secondary views.
From this point, some may calculate that the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.
While the former [view] speculates that all phenomena exist after [death], this [latter view] speculates that all phenomena do not exist after [death]. △ Third, the conclusion of the error.
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the heterodox and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox doctrine: the inverted view of mind within the five aggregates that asserts there is no sign of existence after death.
△ 8. Regarding existence and cessation, one calculates eight [positions] and three "neither-nor" [positions]. First, a general summary:
Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who stabilize their upright minds so that Māras cannot find an opportunity will exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
Observing that profound stillness as being fundamentally subject to constant agitation, while in the midst of active existence, they simultaneously suppress both sensation and perception;

by dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, their own essential nature and characteristics cancel each other out. Such a person falls into the inverted doctrine of "neither existence nor non-existence after death."

When activity exists, there are marks (*nimitta*); when sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) cease, there are no marks. By analogy with these preceding and succeeding marks, that which exists ultimately does not exist;
though it exists, it is non-existent. That which has ceased once existed; though it is non-existent, it is not non-existent.
Because the four aggregates (*skandha*) are dualistically reckoned, eight fallacies (*asat*) are established. △ Second, the specific explanation has two parts. First, the primary reckoning.

Within form, sensation, and perception, they perceive both existence and non-existence; within the flux of mental formations, they internally contemplate neither existence nor non-existence. Thus they cycle through these states until exhausting the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding the eightfold characteristics of being neither [existent nor non-existent], whenever they encounter any single condition, they all claim that after death there is either a mark or no mark.

Because the three *skandhas* (aggregates) possess the characteristic of cessation, one perceives existence as non-existence; because the [fourth] possesses the characteristic of flux, one contemplates non-existence as not non-existence.
Regarding "whichever single condition is encountered," this refers to whichever of the four *skandhas* is raised; in each case, conceptual attachment arises. △ Second, the secondary attachments.

Furthermore, because they calculate that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and distortion, their minds give rise to a false awakening. They conclude that both existence and non-existence are untenable, and that neither the void nor the real can be definitively established.

All conditioned phenomena are, by nature, shifting and flowing. Because they perceive that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is unstable and subject to change and distortion, they consequently develop this perverse realization, claiming that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent and cannot be pointed out with certainty. △ Third, the conclusion on the error.

Because they speculate that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, and because the future limit is obscured and beyond description, they fall into the ranks of external paths and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the eighth heterodox doctrine: the inverted view of mind established within the five aggregates, which asserts that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence.
In their ignorance and delusion, there is nothing they can rightly speak of; they are unable to clearly understand what occurs after death.

Nowadays, many people are confused by worldly discourse and harbor doubts as to whether or not there is an existence after death; all such individuals belong to the category of those who hold the eightfold "neither-nor" views. △ Ninth:
Regarding the subsequent non-existence, there are seven types of annihilationism, of which three are listed here. First, a general summary.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who stabilize their minds with right concentration, such that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound,
pure, yet eternally agitated source. If they subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding non-arising, these people fall into the seven theories of annihilationism.

Observing that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) perishes moment by moment, one designates this as "non-existence in successive stages. Based on this, one falsely calculates that even if one is born into the seven stations of humans or devas, all will ultimately be severed and extinguished. △ Second, the actual calculation.
Some reckon it as the extinction of the body; some as the extinction of desire; some as the extinction of suffering; some as the extinction of supreme bliss; or the extinction of supreme equanimity.
Thus they cycle through these until the seven limits are exhausted, manifesting their extinction before them; once extinguished, there is nothing more.
The extinction of the body refers to the two realms of humans and devas within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The exhaustion of desire refers to the first dhyāna.

The exhaustion of suffering refers to the second dhyāna. Utmost bliss refers to the third dhyāna. Utmost equanimity refers to the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). These are called the seven limits (*saptānta*).
This means that the phenomena and characteristics of these seven limits all manifest and then perish, never to arise again; they ultimately return to total cessation. △ Three.

This constitutes a failure of realization. Because of this speculative reckoning that there is annihilation after death, one falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and becomes confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the ninth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of the cessation of existence after death established within the five aggregates.
△ Tenth: Regarding the five views concerning future existence and three regarding nirvana. First, a general summary:

Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who stabilize and concentrate their correct minds will not be taken advantage of by māras; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound stillness which is constantly agitated at its source, those who subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding "subsequent existence" fall into the doctrine of the five nirvāṇas.
Seeing that activity ceases and then arises again, they designate this as "subsequent existence," falsely calculating the fruit of nirvāṇa within these five locations. II. △ Second.
They form a correct calculation:
either they take the desire realm as the true basis for transformation because they perceive its perfect luminosity and give rise to attachment toward it;

or they take the first dhyāna because its nature is free from sorrow; or they take the second dhyāna because the mind is free from suffering; or they take the third dhyāna because of its extreme following of bliss.

Alternatively, by means of the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure are extinguished; because one does not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra, one becomes deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (sāsrava) and conceives them as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Regarding these five abodes as secure and peaceful, one takes them as a supreme, pure refuge. Thus one revolves in cycles until these five abodes are ultimately reached.
As for "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): it is the transformation of the basis of birth and death into nirvāṇa.
Alternatively, one may realize the principle of perfect luminosity within the desire realm and thus take the desire realm itself as the locus of transformation.

Or, one may take the first dhyāna—free from sorrow—the second dhyāna—free from suffering—the third dhyāna—of supreme joy—and the fourth dhyāna—of supreme equanimity—as the loci of transformation. These are called the five nirvāṇas. [This concerns] delusion regarding existence and so forth.
They do not know that these heavens all belong to the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*), are not the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and are not the ultimate state.
△ Third, the summary of the error:

By means of this speculative reckoning, they conceive of the five [heavens] as present nirvana, thereby falling into the ranks of external paths (*tīrthika*) and deluding their own nature of Bodhi. This is what is called...

The tenth is the heterodox doctrine established by certain non-Buddhists, which posits that within the five aggregates there is a mind of nirvana manifesting through the perversity of the five [senses].
△ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to guard deeply:

"Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) in a state of mutual conflict. Thus they manifest."

Such is the awakening. Yet sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When encountering this which is manifest before them, they mistake their delusion for understanding and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The previous passage spoke of "dhyāna-manifestations," which are occasions when celestial Māras wait for an opportunity to exploit them.

This current passage speaks of "dhyāna-delusions," which are deep-seated evils arising spontaneously from the mind-māra. Whenever one’s realization of the Way is not genuine and one engages in manifold false conceptualizations, these are all instances of delusion;
this is what is called the mind-māra, and it must be guarded against with the utmost care. △ Fourth, the exhortation to propagate [the teaching].
"You must certainly carry forth the words of the Tathāgata after my parinirvāṇa and transmit them during the Final Dharma (mappō).

Cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning, so that the demons of the mind do not give rise to deep afflictions within themselves. Maintain and protect [this teaching], and suppress false views."

Instruct them so that their bodies and minds awaken to the true meaning, ensuring they do not encounter divergent paths on the unsurpassed way. Do not allow their minds to seek the small and consider it sufficient;
rather, cause them to become great awakened kings with pure and decisive resolve.

It causes those who propagate [the teaching] to take the Tathāgata’s words and extend them universally for the sake of all sentient beings, sustaining and protecting them so that Māra cannot invade, no calamities may arise, they do not fall into heterodox paths, and they do not settle for minor realizations, but instead ascend directly to the stage of enlightenment.
This is what is meant by acting as the guiding finger of the Great Enlightened King. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* bestows its teachings with profound kindness upon all sentient beings.
Those who look toward practitioners do not hold them lightly; we, his followers, ought to exert ourselves in this endeavor.
*Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle Nineteen.
