Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣā of the kingdom of Ujjayinī; orally received by Fáng Róng of Qīnghé,
former Grand Master for Rectifying Discourse and concurrently Minister of State Affairs in the Chancellery and Council of State, and disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
The Monk Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling Unfolds [the Meaning of] the Five Consciousness-Aggregates (5):
Part Five. First, showing the characteristics of the aggregates:
"Ānanda, when that virtuous man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the natures of all worlds become profoundly pure and serene."
The stirring of the homogeneous life-force suddenly shatters; the subtle cords of the *pudgala* and the deep channels that repay karma are suspended and severed.
As one is about to awaken to the great radiance of the heaven of *nirvāṇa*, it is like the crowing of a rooster at dawn, looking toward the east where the first brilliant colors appear.
The six sense-faculties become empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping; inwardly and inwardly they are profoundly clear, entering the state of non-existence.

As for that which is entered: one deeply penetrates the fundamental origins of the twelve types of life-sustaining breath throughout the ten directions. By contemplating these origins, one perceives that they are rooted in grasping;

thus, no such categories can summon one, and within the realms of the ten directions, one has already attained their sameness. One’s refined essence does not sink, and the hidden mysteries are revealed.
This is what is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

This is a general exposition on how the cessation of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) brings about the manifestation of consciousness. *Saṃskāra* is the essential nature of the world’s flux and movement;

it is the primary cord that agitates the mechanism of life, and the deep-seated channel through which the *pudgala* (individual) reaps the fruits of karma. It is capable of obscuring the celestial sky of one's true nature, causing the six sense faculties to gallop wildly, and turbidly disturbing the inner serenity.
It serves as the ultimate pivot and hollow for the floating sense organs and their objects. Therefore, when the *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, birth...
The mechanism of the governing threads suddenly snapped and split; the deep channels of *pudgala* were severed, and the resonance between stimulus and response was suspended.

Yet, the celestial nature (*dharmatā*) was about to be greatly awakened, and the six sense faculties no longer wandered in distraction. Because they did not wander, there was profound clarity within the innermost depths;

because there was no pivot-hole through which they could escape, one entered that which has nowhere to enter. Returning from movement to stillness, it became deeper and yet deeper; hence it is called "inner."

Internally, the *nirvāṇa*-nature sky is shrouded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), as dark as a long night. When the first three aggregates are exhausted, it is like the first crowing of a cock;
though this is a sign of dawn, one still remains submerged in the remaining two aggregates, and the subtle colors have not yet been distinguished.

When these mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, it is like the cock’s subsequent crowing; with only one aggregate remaining, one is on the verge of awakening through the Great Radiance. This is the primary source of receiving one's life-destiny.
This is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Because consciousness manifests through the cessation of formations (*saṃskāra*), one penetrates it deeply.

Because it lacks a pivot-hole, it can be observed; because it lacks flux, it can be grasped; because it lacks the mechanism of birth, it cannot be summoned. Consequently, one realizes that the ten directions—both the environment and its inhabitants—are all transformations of consciousness.

Thus, one has already attained the stage of the Heaven of Identical Nature (*sabhāgatā-deva*). Although the refined colors have not yet become perfectly clear and penetrating, the subtle and secret characteristics [are manifest].
The signs of this aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) have already begun to gradually manifest.
If, within the collective summons, one attains sameness, the six gates will be dissolved; through the perfection of both union and separation, seeing and hearing will penetrate one another.
Their mutual functioning is pure; the ten directions, the world, and their own bodies and minds are as transparently clear inside and out as vaidūrya.
This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life.
When one examines its origin, it is found that its root consists of formless emptiness and inverted false imaginings.
The simultaneous summons of the multitude refers to the *vijñāna-skandha*, the source-consciousness of the twelve categories of beings.

If, within this state, one employs the power of samādhi and wisdom to dissolve the six gates, such that the sense organs merge without division and their objective spheres open without obstruction, then seeing and hearing will become perfectly penetrating and the six faculties will function interchangeably.
Consequently, there will be no distinction between the external world and the internal body and mind.

Furthermore, there is lingering obstruction; this is the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Its nature is fundamentally one true reality, yet it is separated by sensory objects.

Between the nature and its functioning, the standards for identity and difference are lost, which is termed the turbidity of life-force. This constitutes the substance of the aggregate of consciousness; therefore, when consciousness is exhausted, one transcends it.
Consciousness is but a reflected luminosity of deluded awakening; it originally has no self-substance. It arises from inversion, and for this reason it is so named.

The *wangxiang* (phantom) is empty and non-existent; it is inverted false imagination. △ Second, clarifying ten types of deluded understanding. First, establishing a cause of true permanence leads to becoming a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).
Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness, thereby extinguishing birth and death.

Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, it is not yet perfected. This allows one’s own body to cause the separation and union of the sense organs, and to communicate with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions, such that their perceptions merge. One is able to enter the perfect source.

If, regarding this point of return, one establishes a cause of true permanence and develops a resolute conviction therein, this person falls into the attachment to a cause for what is itself the cause—namely, the *tattva* (ultimate principle) to which the Śābikāra school returns.
They form their own pairings, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the first establishment of a mind that seeks attainment;
it constitutes a fruit toward which they turn, yet it violates and distances them from perfect penetration and turns their backs on the city of nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of externalist paths.

Because consciousness flows from formative forces (*saṃskāra*), when formative forces are empty, it returns to its source. Since the aggregate of formative forces (*saṃskāraskandha*) is now empty, birth and death have already been extinguished;

yet, because one still relies on the source of consciousness, quiescent extinction is not yet perfected. Nevertheless, one can gradually break through the aggregate of consciousness and dissolve the six sense-gates.

Therefore, the six faculties of cognition (*ṣaḍ-vijñānendriya*) are already merged without separation; the nature of all categories of perception is universally interfused and non-dual. Thus, one is able to enter the Perfect Origin (*yuan-yuan*).
This Perfect Origin is precisely the source-consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) that fuses the sense-faculties and permeates the barriers between all categories.

If one takes this to be the true ground of return and establishes it as the "True Cause," one falls into the attachment to the cause and the object of the cause. For [this would mean taking] the True Cause...

All objects of perception are illusory. The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhist path regards the primordial state of the *ālayavijñāna*—the dark, indeterminate phase prior to its manifestation—as the true cause to which one returns; this is precisely the same [error].

Because the mind perceives something to be attained and there is something to which one returns, both cause and effect fall into the delusion of "objects. Consequently, this violates perfect penetration and turns one away from Nirvana.
Furthermore, when those who practice today give rise to the conscious mind within true nature, calculating cause and effect and producing views and understandings—
claiming there is something attained and something to which one returns— they all merely attain the source of consciousness and return to the obscure ultimate (mīṅdì).
△ Second, the calculation that one is born there,

which constitutes the attainment of pervasiveness and completeness. Ānanda, furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and thereby extinguished birth and death,

yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śānti*) is not yet perfected— if he regards that to which he has returned as his own self-body, then within the entire realm of empty space, among all twelve categories of beings...
If sentient beings all conceive the resolute conviction that they are born from a single category within my own body, such persons fall into the dualistic grasping of "agent" and "non-agent.
Maheśvara will manifest boundless bodies to become their companions; thus they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision.

This is called the second [stage]: establishing the mind as an agent, whereby the fruit of an agent's activity is accomplished. This violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one away from Nirvana.
In the city of Pāṇḍura, he was born as a deity of great pride.
He took the pervasive and perfect seed—the fundamental source of consciousness—to be his own self-nature, and claimed that all sentient beings flow forth from him.
Thus, he clung to the notion that "I" can produce them, though in reality he cannot; hence it is called "clinging to the capable as incapable. Maheśvara is [the embodiment of] form.
This is the summit of the Māra-king’s delusion. He falsely conceives that "I" can manifest as infinite sentient beings, and that "I" am both the capable and the incapable class.
He conceives that "I" am the agent of mental activity and its fruits, and that "I" can serve as their basis and accomplish those activities.
The "Greatly Arrogant Deva" refers to Maheśvara. Because he claims what he cannot do to be possible, he is called "Greatly Arrogant.
"Pervasive and Perfect" means he reckons his own essence as being perfectly pervasive throughout the realm of space. △ Third, reckoning that birth from him constitutes a perverted, perfect seed.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), one has not yet perfected it.

If, while seeking a place of refuge, one takes something as a basis for reliance, and suspects that one’s own body and mind flow forth from that [basis], and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it—then, regarding that very ground from which everything flows forth, one will conceive the understanding that it is a true, eternal body, free from arising and ceasing.
Within the midst of arising and ceasing, they prematurely reckon it to be eternally abiding; thus they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing.

Those who dwell securely in this delusion and yet conceive a resolute conviction [of permanence] will fall into the attachment to both permanence and impermanence, reckoning the Lord Creator as their companion.
Having lost the Buddha’s bodhi and forfeited true knowledge and vision, this is called the second [stage]: establishing causes based on the mind to produce deluded conceptual fruits;
it is far removed from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.
Because they take the source of consciousness as their basis, they suspect that it can give rise to both the self and all phenomena;

they consequently reckon that the place from which these arise and flow forth is a truly eternal and non-arising substance. This is to falsely reckon permanence within the midst of arising and ceasing.
Thus, they are deluded regarding the true nature of non-arising, and further confused about the presently manifesting phenomena of arising and ceasing, taking what is not permanent to be so.

Because it is eternal, it is called the "grasping at the eternal and the non-eternal. Since one calculates that it can produce the self, it is identical to calculating that Īśvara can produce all things.
Because one falsely calculates permanence based on the source of consciousness, it is said: "Establishing causes based on the mind results in the false calculation of effects.
The former calculation held that the self completely produces phenomena; this calculation holds that those [phenomena] completely produce the self.
Therefore, it is called "inverted perfection. △ Fourth, calculating objects and sentient beings constitutes inverted knowledge.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) into emptiness, one has already extinguished arising and ceasing; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, one has not yet attained full perfection.

If, regarding objects of knowledge, one establishes a conviction based on the claim that because one's knowledge is all-pervasive and complete, the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all called sentient beings and are no different from humans—
such that when grasses and trees become humans, and humans die, they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions—

if one gives rise to such a superior conviction without discrimination, this person falls into the attachment of knowing what is unknowable. This is the *Bāṣpa-Śākya*, who clings to the awakening of all things.
They form pairs with one another, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth reckoning:

calculating the mind as being perfectly complete, which results in false and erroneous fruits, violates and distances itself from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.

That which is known is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) that is observed. This means that consciousness possesses cognition, and all phenomena arise through the transformation of this cognition.
Because one reckons that the essence of cognition is omnipresent throughout all phenomena, a divergent interpretation is established:

it is claimed that even insentient things are everywhere endowed with cognition, without any discrimination. Therefore, it is called "non-discriminating universal cognition. Since this takes non-cognition to be cognition, it is so named.

To know "non-knowing" while clinging to it is the case with the two non-Buddhist teachers, Pāṭa and Saini, who cling to universal cognition—that is, they cling to the notion that all things possess consciousness.
This erroneous calculation takes perfect knowledge to be the causal mind; thus, the result will ultimately be erroneous.
To take non-knowing as knowing is inverted knowledge. △ Fifth: Venerating water and serving fire result in perverted transformations.

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, within the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, one has not yet attained full perfection.

If, amidst the mutual functioning of the perfectly fused sense organs, one has already attained conformity, then one will immediately bring about the manifestation of all-encompassing, perfect transformation.

Seeking the light of fire, delighting in the purity of water, craving the circulation of wind, and contemplating the formation of dust—each venerating these as supreme, they take these various elements as the primary cause of their arising and establish a view of eternal permanence. Such people fall into the attachment to birth within non-birth.

The various Kāśyapas and Brahmins, diligently applying their minds and exhausting their bodies to serve fire and revere water in their quest for liberation from birth and death, became his companions;
they were deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth attachment: the devotion to external services.

The deluded mind follows external objects, establishing false causes for seeking and falsely hoping for fruits. Thus it remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.
One for whom the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted has dissolved the six gates, and their various faculties function interchangeably.

Since this [state] has not yet been fully exhausted, one has merely attained compliance with it. Because of this compliance, they conceive that all phenomena can achieve perfect transformation and produce superior fruits;
they claim that fire can manifest radiance, and even that dust can accomplish the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). Thus...

Thus, they seek through the perverse and contemplate through the perverse, yet they diligently and reverently serve [their objects], clinging to them as being able to produce superior fruits when in reality they cannot;
therefore, this is called "clinging to the non-arising within arising. These are the likes of the three Kāśyapa brothers and other such heterodox practitioners.

They are deluded regarding the true mind and seek hope from external things; thus, both cause and effect are false, and their transformation of the principle is inverted—this is called the "species of inverted transformation."
△ Sixth, by the permanent extinction of all calculations, one achieves the basis for cessation.

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) into emptiness, you have extinguished arising and ceasing; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*), it is not yet perfected.

If, regarding this perfect luminosity, one reckons that the voidness within the light is not the cessation of all transformations, and takes this eternal cessation as a basis for reliance, thereby giving rise to a resolute conviction, such a person falls into the attachment of "seeking refuge in what is not a refuge.

They become companions among the *śūnyatā* (void) beings in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth [delusion]: the mindless state of perfect voidness.
One achieves the fruit of empty extinction, strays far from perfect penetration, turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of annihilationism.
Because one’s contemplation of principle is not authentic, one mistakenly falls into nihilism; thus, within the perfectly luminous nature, one calculates everything to be empty and void.
Thereupon, one severs all transformations and returns to eternal extinction, yet remains unaware that this is erroneous. This is called the attachment to "returning to nothingness."
*Śūnyatā* (śunyata) is translated here as "emptiness. To speak of "non-conceptual emptiness" (*asamjñi-śūnyatā*) refers to the externalist who clings to nihilistic emptiness.

Because they cling to nihilistic emptiness, they take the void and non-being as their causal mind, thereby producing the fruit of nihilistic extinction. This eternal cessation of the basis is the *nirvāṇa* of the externalists.
△ Seventh: Greed for permanence and attachment to the body result in the delusion of prolonging life.

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected.

If one develops a resolute conviction that, within this perfect permanence, one may make the body solid and enduring, identical to that subtle perfection so as to remain forever without decay or passing away— [This constitutes the second stage of the four stages of the "perfection of the mind."]
Such a person falls into the attachment of grasping at what is both craving and non-craving. They become companions to those Āsuras who seek long life;
they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh attachment, clinging to the source of life, establishing a cause of solid delusion.
They head toward the fruit of long-term toil, distancing themselves from perfect penetration and turning their backs on the city of Nirvana, thus giving rise to the seeds of delusive prolongation.
Relying on the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) to contemplate the perfect and constant, they grasp the source of consciousness as the perfect essence.

Consequently, they desire to firmly preserve their bodies so that they may coexist with them; they delusively crave solidity and longevity, unaware of their error. This is called "clinging to what is not greed as greed. — Āsita.
This is called "The Peerless One," who is none other than the Immortal of Longevity. Although his life was prolonged, it ultimately ended in destruction.
Now, if one seeks to solidify this delusory body in order to attain permanence, it will result in nothing but empty toil and vain extension of life. 8.
Clinging to desires to solidify one's lifespan results in becoming a celestial demon (māra).

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*), it is not yet perfected.

Observing that life-force is interpenetrating, one intentionally retains the defilements of worldly toil, fearing they might be entirely consumed. Thus, at this juncture, one sits within the Lotus Palace.

They extensively acquire the seven treasures and increase their many precious concubines, indulging their desires at will. Those who give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment to "the real as unreal.
They become companions of the Ṭakkirāja demons; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

This is called the eighth cause for giving rise to false thoughts, which establishes the fruit of blazing afflictions. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving birth to the race of celestial Māras.

Taking the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the root of life, it interpenetrates the three periods of time; yet when the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, one's life also comes to an end.

Thinking, "Who has realized the true and eternal? they then manifest various sensual objects within meditative concentration in order to retain their defilements and prevent them from being extinguished.
Relying on this perverted thought, they desire to realize the true and eternal without realizing it is not so; this is called "clinging to the non-true as true.
The *Ṭakkirāja* spirits can manifest sensual objects for their own amusement; they belong to the class of the *Kāmeśvara* gods at the summit of the desire realm.
Thus it is. Due to those perverse thoughts, one gives rise to celestial demons (*devaputra-māra*). Merely indulging in worldly desires is called the "blazing fruit of defilement.
"Yuánměi" (媛美) refers to a beautiful woman. △ Ninth: Realizing extinction brings natural rest, forming an entanglement with emptiness.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, you have brought an end to birth and death; yet, within this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

Within the clarity of life, you distinguish between the refined and the coarse, and resolve the true from the false. You regard cause and effect as a mutual retribution, seeking only to provoke a response through resonance.

They turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, the vision of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path. Having settled into cessation, they rest and no longer advance.
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the category of the śrāvakas of fixed nature; they become companions to those arrogant monks who lack learning.
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth stage of perfecting the essence.

This corresponds to the mind. It achieves the fruit of quiescent inclination, yet it remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

When one instructs those who are bright-witted, they investigate the ultimate limit of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), thereby gaining a profound understanding of the fundamental cause by which sentient beings receive their life-force.

Since birth and death arise from consciousness, while refinement and coarseness arise from karma, one relies upon the Four Noble Truths for analytical discernment; therein, suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are considered coarse.
This is false. To take cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as the essential truth, one then exclusively cultivates the causes for the path in order to seek the fruit of cessation.
Being content with little, one remains in cessation and rests there; such individuals belong to the class of *śrāvakas* of fixed nature who possess overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

In this context, "perfect essence" (*yuanjing*) should be taken as the causal mind, which achieves the minor fruit of quiescent entry. "Perfect essence" (*jingying*) refers precisely to discernment (*viniścaya*).
Coarse practice: seeking only the ultimate realization of partial truth, one remains entangled in emptiness and proceeds toward quiescence alone. △ Tenth:
Maintaining awareness to establish proof, yet failing to achieve transformation into perfection.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), it is not yet perfected.
If, within this perfectly integrated, pure, and luminous awakening, one initiates an investigation into its profound subtlety and establishes it as *nirvāṇa*, one will not advance further.

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction will fall into the fixed nature of pratyekabuddhas. Taking those solitary practitioners as their peers and refusing to turn their minds back [toward the Great Vehicle], they become their companions;
they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth delusion of the mind regarding Perfect Enlightenment.

This results in the fruit of "stilled clarity," which is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana. It gives rise to the seed of "awakened perfect clarity" that does not transform;

this fused, pure awakened clarity is precisely the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Although it is free from delusive habits and is perfectly integrated and pure, it has not yet transcended consciousness;
therefore, it is called "awakened clarity. If one were to take this as profound and subtle and establish it as a realized fruit, then it would be a fixed nature.

These are merely pratyekabuddhas and solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddhas*). This is because they take the "oceanic" (*yǒng*) as their causal mind, thereby achieving the stagnant fruit of "tranquil clarity" (*zhàn míng*).

Their awakening is like the mind reaching its ultimate penetration; their awakened cognition penetrates the limit of penetration. This means they merely penetrate with correct awakening but do not advance further.
"Tranquil clarity" is precisely the perfectly interfused awakening-cognition. That which is awakened to ceases.

Within the perfectly luminous essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-śukra*), one remains fixed in its nature without turning back; therefore, it is called the "perfectly luminous, unchanging perfect seed.
The fifty demonic realms described above are all products of conscious emotion, erroneous understanding, and perverse awakening.

Those who have not yet attained right view will fall into these states whenever they direct their minds or stir a single thought. Even those who have realized the stage of a Pratyekabuddha remain deluded regarding the Buddha.

Bodhi is lost when one’s knowledge and vision fail. For this reason, the Buddha-King, with bitter earnestness, bestowed his compassion, scrutinizing the matter with all his heart to analyze it for you, desiring that people not be deluded nor lose their way. If this is so, how then can it be attained?
One should examine and observe the categories of the fifty stages; once awakened, if one’s thoughts do not fall into them, then it is attained. △
Third, he exhorted him to guard against this deeply:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* lead to madness midway through their practice because they rely on delusion.

To perceive a state of fulfillment within what is not yet fulfilled is entirely due to the interaction of the mind with the *vijñāna-skandha*; thus, one arrives at this stage. Sentient beings are stubbornly ignorant."
Failing to examine themselves, they encounter these manifestations and each, according to their own cherished inclinations and previously habituated deluded minds, comes to rest therein.
Taking this to be the ultimate ground of refuge and peace, they declare themselves to have attained unsurpassed bodhi; thus, they commit the great falsehood.
When the karma of those influenced by externalists and malevolent spirits comes to an end, they fall into the Avīci Hell;
śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fail to advance further, exhausting the Way and losing its true direction, thus becoming deranged midway and wandering onto divergent paths.

This is because they rely on delusion and take what was previously practiced out of attachment—namely, the erroneous interpretations transmitted by heterodox teachers—to be the secret attainment of truth, and consequently cease their cultivation, regarding it as...
Since it is ultimately a place where one returns to rest, yet it only serves to mislead oneself, demons and malevolent spirits rely upon it, leading one to fall into the evil realms in the end;
those of the Two Vehicles rely upon it and fail to achieve further progress. One must guard against this most deeply. △ Fourth, the command to propagate and proclaim [the teaching].

"You all must maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata. After my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand its meaning.
Do not allow them to encounter demons or bring about their own ruin; rather, protect, sustain, and compassionately rescue them."

To eliminate false conditions and cause their body and mind to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they shall achieve this from the very beginning without encountering bypaths, false views, or erroneous interpretations that act as demons and calamities, causing the body and mind to stumble and fall; this is called the "demon of views.

The mind is the internal obstruction, while views are the external fetters; therefore, having previously guarded against the demon of the mind, one now guards against the demon of views—this is the essential method for assisting the Way.
It is finished. △ Fifth, exhorting them to reach the ultimate:
"Such a Dharma-gate as this has enabled the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in the sands of the Ganges throughout the past kalpas, to open their minds by relying upon it."
One attains the Unsurpassed Way. When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, your present sense faculties will function interchangeably.

From within this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). Within this state, the perfectly luminous and refined mind manifests its transformative power, like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.
In this way, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the four stages of preparatory application.
The Bodhisattva Mind practices the ten stages of the vajra-like path, attaining perfect enlightenment and luminous clarity;
entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornments, he fulfills bodhi and returns to the state of non-attainment.
The former sages mounted upon this mind and attained the Way; it is only fitting that later students should diligently investigate it.

When consciousness is exhausted, the six gates are dissolved; thus the various faculties function interchangeably. From within this mutual functioning, one enters adamantine wisdom and gives rise to the perfectly luminous mind—this is the matter of the mind opening.
Directly transcending the stages of faith and so forth, one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata and returns to non-attainment. This is...

This is the matter of attaining the Way. The Vajra-dry-wisdom (*vimalā-prajñā*) constitutes the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). The various stages of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the gradual sequence of progressive cultivation.

Those who are able to directly transcend these without passing through them do so because the progressive cultivation through the various stages was intended to remedy the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);

now that consciousness is exhausted and there are no more habits, they are able to transcend them. That Equal Enlightenment is perfectly luminous and returns to non-attainment means that from the beginning...

From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one has not yet attained perfect clarity; there is still something to be grasped because consciousness has not been fully exhausted.

Only upon attaining the Vajra-mind, when all subtle consciousnesses are shattered and eliminated, can one achieve perfect clarity and enter the ocean of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue-hai*), returning to the state of non-attainment.
This is the ultimate path of true cultivation. As for the Ocean of Wondrous Adornments (*miaozhuangyan-hai*), it encompasses all virtues and unifies all differences.
The Flow. It is majestic without being made so; it is the ocean of fruition realized without being realized.
What was previously called the "Ten Thousand Practices of Śūraṅgama" as the Path of Wondrous Adornment is simply the treading toward this. △ Third, the general conclusion.
This was the subtle demonic activity analyzed through the clarity and awareness of *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha* by the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
Now that these demonic realms have appeared before you, you are able to recognize them; thus, the defilements of your mind are washed away, and you do not fall into false views.
The māra of the aggregates is extinguished; the celestial māras are shattered; powerful spirits and ghosts lose heart and flee; goblins and imps no longer take birth.
Until one reaches bodhi, there shall be no lack of anything; those of inferior capacity will advance, and their minds will not be confused or distressed regarding Great Nirvāṇa.
As for the dull-witted and ignorant sentient beings of the final age who do not yet recognize dhyāna and do not know how to preach the Dharma—
Delight in the cultivation of samādhi; lest you fall into heterodoxy, single-mindedly exhort him to uphold this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra.
If he is unable to recite it, write it down in his meditation hall or wear it upon his person; then all māras will be unable to disturb him.
You should reverently honor the ultimate cultivation and final instructions of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
This concludes the analysis of the five aggregates and the intent behind discerning demons, so that you may know how to guard against them deeply. Regarding *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*:
this is the wisdom of meditative concentration. All demonic realms manifest because of the clarity of awareness (*jue-ming*). That which is called "awareness" [is as follows:]
"Analyze with clarity" means to analyze the luminous awareness; this is the syntactic force of the Western script. "Tǐ" (褫) is synonymous with "to lose.
△ Second, the detailed request for further instruction, in two parts: first, Ānanda’s request for further instruction.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, he prostrated himself in reverent acceptance and memorized it without loss.

In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "As the Buddha has said, within the characteristics of the five aggregates there are five kinds of delusion that serve as the fundamental source of thought.
In our ordinary state, we have not yet received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed exposition. Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates, are they [to be understood] collectively..."
To eliminate them is to bring them to gradual extinction. Thus, regarding these five layers, what constitutes their boundary?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion and clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, serving as a guiding eye for all sentient beings of the future age.
△ Second, the Buddha’s detailed explanation in three parts. First, a general account of the root of delusion.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essence of purity and truth is deluded luminosity; fundamental awakening is perfectly pure, leaving no room for birth and death or any defilements."
Even up to empty space, all are produced by deluded conceptualization. This is originally the wondrously luminous true essence of fundamental enlightenment;
through delusion, it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds, just as Yajñadatta, in his confusion, mistook his own head for its reflection.
The deluded karma of birth and death and the deluded conditions of dust and defilement leave no trace within the truly pure nature; they arise entirely due to delusion.
It is like being confused about one's own head. Thus, it can be known that among the characteristics of the five aggregates, the five delusions are the root.
Delusion has no fundamental cause; yet within deluded thought, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. Those who are confused about causes and conditions call it "spontaneity.

That very nature of space is like a real illusion produced from causes and conditions; both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings.

Ānanda, when one knows where delusion arises, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion. If delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then even the causes and conditions of delusion would fundamentally not exist.
How much more so for those who, lacking such knowledge, speculate that it arises spontaneously?
To clarify that delusion is causeless means it cannot be subjected to conceptual calculation. If one knows where delusion arises, one may speak of causes and conditions;
but if its arising is unknown, how can there be causes and conditions? Furthermore, to infer that it is "spontaneous" (svabhāva)—is this not itself a false conceptualization?
Therefore, the Tathāgata has clarified for you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but deluded thought.
△ Second, the specific answers to the questions, in three parts: First, answering the delusive origin of the five aggregates, in five sections. First, the fundamental nature of form as solidity.

Your body was originally produced from the perceptions of your parents; yet your mind is not itself perception. If it were not perception, it could not come into the midst of perception to transmit life.

As I previously said: when the mind perceives the taste of vinegar, saliva is produced in the mouth; when the mind perceives climbing a high place, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet.
There is no precipice present, nor has any sour substance arrived; yet your body is certainly not of a nature that transcends the category of delusion.
How could saliva emerge from speaking of the sour? Therefore, you should know that your manifest physical body is called the first false imagination of solidity.
Perception is a false and illusory image, the deep-seated channel of craving for desire that leaves behind the physical body.

Because it flows forth from one's own perception and craving, it is said that "the body arises from the perception of the parents. The aggregate-mind (*skandha-citta*) rides upon perception and craving, seeking in the darkness;

therefore, it is said that "the mind transmits life within perception. The analogy of the sour plum and other such examples serve to verify that the body arises from false attachments; thus, it accords with the principle of falsity. If...
If it were not for false conceptualization, then delusion could not produce an impression. The body arises because of thought; the mind arises because of thought;

life is transmitted because of thought. As various thoughts intersect and solidify, they form the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); therefore, it is called "solidified false conceptualization. 2. The essence of sensation is fundamentally empty and luminous.

This aforementioned mind that contemplates heights can cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness. Because this sensation arises from causes, it can move the substance of the body.
As you now experience both the favorable and the adverse before you, driven by these two manifest states, this is called the second deluded thought, "empty luminosity."

Facing the void, one imagines; yet the sensations of bitterness and astringency are truly experienced. Both the adverse and the favorable are illusory, yet the manifestations of loss and gain rush forth.

Thus, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has no substance, being a hollow manifestation of clarity; therefore, it is called "the delusion of hollow clarity. △ Third, the essence of perception (saṃjñā) is interpenetrating and harmonious.
It is due to your thoughts that they drive your physical body; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
It takes on various forms through mental projections, corresponding to those thoughts. When awake, it is the conceptual mind; when asleep, it becomes the various dreams.
Thus, your flickering thoughts and deluded sentiments are called the third false discrimination of "interfusion";

this refers to the empty sentiments of mental deliberation and the substantial reality of the physical body. That these two—emptiness and substance—which are of different natures, can nevertheless influence one another is [the third false discrimination].

It is through perception (*saṃjñā*) that they are fused. The mind gives rise to empty images, while the form grasps at substantial objects; though the functions of mind and form differ, they are able to correspond because they are made to communicate by perception.

As for waking and sleeping, or shifting and changing, causing the mind to follow the object and the object to follow the mind—all these are the fusion of deluded perceptions. △ Fourth, the root of conduct is profound and hidden.
The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and moves in secret. Nails grow and hair sprouts; vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles.
Day and night they alternate, yet one is never awakened to this. Ānanda, if this were not you, how could your physical form undergo change?
If it must be truly you, why do you have no awareness of it? Thus, your various formations ceaselessly stop at every thought-moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden deluded thought.
First, the subtle and hidden characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) were indicated. Below, Ānanda, the principle of their illusory nature is analyzed and established.
△ Fifth, the essence of the five consciousnesses is like a phantom.

Furthermore, that which is your own brilliant clarity, profoundly still and unmoving, and which you call "constant," does not depart from the body in its functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
"Exquisite and unshakable" refers to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" refers to the function of consciousness.
To grasp that which is not truly eternal as being eternal is called "permanence."

If one’s essence were truly pure and true, it would not admit the cultivation of delusion. For what reason, then, did you all once behold a strange object in years past, such that for many years thereafter there was neither memory nor forgetfulness of it;
yet later, upon suddenly beholding that same former anomaly again, the memory returned with perfect clarity?
It has never been lost or forgotten. Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, it is perfumed moment by moment;

how could there be any calculation? Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the ultimate truth. It is like a rapid current that appears tranquil at a distance; because the flow is so swift, it is not perceived.

It is not that they are free from outflows; yet if it were not the source of perception, how could one undergo the habitual tendencies of delusion? This false conceptualization, which arises from the mutual functioning, opening, and closing of your six sense faculties, can never be extinguished.
The essence of purity does not admit false habituation; yet now, it can conceal the past without losing a single trace—this is precisely false habituation.
Thus, although the profound stillness does not waver, it is perfumed moment by moment, and its capacity to harbor delusion is vast.

One should know that this stillness is not true stillness, but merely a state of deep-seated, unconscious latency. Therefore, it is likened to a torrential stream flowing silently and invisibly beneath the surface, which cannot [be seen].
This is the fundamental form of true recollection and the substance of delusive thoughts.
You must utterly destroy the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and dissolve the six sense-gates, so that delusive habits have no place to lodge; only then can it be extinguished.

Therefore, among what you currently see, hear, perceive, and know, how many are those that have been habituated through practice? They are the profound clarity within, which is internally formless, void, and non-existent—the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined ideation.
The above has all been introduced and described; here, the conclusion is made manifest. "Habitual" (*chuàn*) refers to constant practice. "Subtle" (*jǐwēi*) refers to the minute.

The brilliant, pure, and tranquil consciousness (*zhànshí*) serves as the fundamental basis for the habitual activity of the six sense-faculties. Therefore, when vision perceives the subtle, this is precisely the formless manifestation of that tranquil consciousness.

It is latent within seeing and cognition; therefore, it is called the "intermediate habituation-energy" (*antar-vāsanā-śakti*). That which appears as non-existent is called "the ungraspable" (*wang*);

that which appears as existent is called "the image" (*xiang*). Its substance is subtle and refined; therefore, it is named "the Ungraspable," "the Void," "the Inverted," and "Refined Conception. △ Second, answering regarding the limits of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of false conceptualization. If you now wish to know the depth of their causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form;
only contact and separation constitute the limit of feeling; only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception;
only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations; and the profound entry into the merging with stillness constitutes the limit of consciousness.

The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are also called the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-khandha*). Due to a single moment of delusion, one undergoes and grasps these, thereby concealing oneself.

Regarding the statement "conditioned by the elements" (*dhātu-pratyaya*): fundamentally, there are no elements; they exist due to the conditions of delusive appearances. Thus, form is not form by itself;
it exists as form because of emptiness, and thus the limit of form is established. This applies even up to cessation, which does not cease by itself, but [arises] conditioned by birth.
Because there is cessation, one reaches the limit of formations (*saṃskāra*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is termed "profound clarity" (*zhanliao*); yet this profundity does not clarify itself.

Because formations do not flow out or escape, the nature enters the fundamental clarity and merges with profound clarity, thereby reaching the limit of consciousness. △ Third, answering the sequence of the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
These five aggregates originally arise in successive layers; their arising is caused by consciousness, and their cessation begins with the removal of form.

In principle, they are suddenly realized through awakening, and upon that awakening, they are simultaneously extinguished. Yet in practice, they are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through a gradual process. I have already shown you this knot in the *kārpāsa* cloth.
What is it that you do not understand? I ask this again:
consciousness is like the *karpāsa* cloth, while form is like the final knot. Since the knot exists in dependence upon the cloth, [so too does form exist in dependence upon consciousness].

Arising occurs through the emergence of consciousness; understanding occurs through sequential progression. Cessation proceeds from the removal of form (*rūpa*). The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise from the subtle to the coarse:
from delusion regarding wisdom there arises consciousness, and so on, until from sensation (*vedanā*) there arises form. Cessation, however, proceeds from the coarse to the subtle:
one must first destroy form before sensation manifests, and so on, until one destroys formations (*saṃskāra*) before consciousness manifests. This is the principle.

"Those who attain sudden enlightenment find that both [delusion and practice] are simultaneously extinguished through awakening" means that one knows the handkerchief was originally without knots and never had them either.

"Matters are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through gradual stages" means that those of middling capacity, though they achieve sudden enlightenment, must rely on gradual cultivation. If one relies on awakening to forget cultivation, then there will be understanding without practice;
clinging to principle while being deluded regarding phenomena, one will inevitably fall into partiality and heterodoxy, and will ultimately fail to attain the true and correct path.
Samādhi. △ Third, the exhortation to propagate and disseminate:
You should take this root-source of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain liberation.

Transmit and reveal it to all practitioners in the future age of the Dharma’s decay, so that they may recognize its falsity, develop a profound weariness with their own arising [of delusion], know that there is nirvāṇa, and no longer cling to the triple world.
By means of this principle, one should awaken oneself and awaken others, forever severing the source of delusion and collectively returning to the ultimate fruit.
△ Third, the section on circulation, which has two parts. First, manifesting its excellence and exhorting its upholding.

“Ānanda, suppose there were someone who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a heart that never wasted its effort. What do you think?
By virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddhas, would that person obtain much merit? Ānanda replied, “The empty space is inexhaustible, and the precious treasures...”
It is boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to a Buddha; even after relinquishing his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.
How much more so when one fills the entirety of space before them with precious jewels as vast as the Buddha-fields—such that even contemplating it for an entire eon would not suffice.
How could the merit of this have any limit? The Buddha told Ānanda: "The speech of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is without..."
This is false. If there should be another person who has committed the four grave offenses and the ten *pārājika* transgressions,
and in an instant passes through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds, even exhausting all the uninterrupted hells throughout the ten directions without exception—

if such a person can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-gate and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa, that person’s karmic obstacles will vanish at that very moment.
It is extinguished; the causes for the suffering of hell that one has received are transformed into a land of peace and bliss.

One attains merit that surpasses that of the previous donor by ten thousandfold, a hundred thousandfold, a millionfold, ten millionfold, a billionfold, and even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
The giving of material wealth is finite; its merit benefits only a single person. The giving of the Dharma is inexhaustible, and its benefit extends to limitless beings.
Therefore, one not only acquires merit but also extinguishes grave offenses. The *pārājika* refers to the ten grave precepts.

By showing the Dharma to others, one can eliminate severe retribution and transform suffering into joy. Such is its excellence that it enables people to, through it, clarify the mind and realize their true nature (*xin-xing*).

Freeing oneself from attachment and returning to profound stillness, resolving the six to lose the one, breaking through the aggregates and stripping away demons—this is because one attains the fruit of the Treasure King without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Since that is so, then this [process of] eliminating severe retribution is merely a shallow and proximate description;
in truth, it shall lead to the same realization as that.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra— as I have explained at length, which would not be exhausted even if one were to speak for an entire kalpa—
and who follow my instructions and practice the Way according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi without further demonic interference.
The former [passage] exhorts the circulation [of the sutra]; this [passage] exhorts its recitation and upholding. △ Second, the audience joyfully accepts it.
After the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;

all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and the bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, holy seers, and youths from other directions, as well as those who have first resolved [to attain enlightenment]...
The powerful spirits and deities were all greatly delighted; they paid their respects and departed—all of whom were members of the assembly listening to the discourse.
As for the "holy seer youths," these are of the class of celestial rishis (*ṛṣi*).
The powerful spirits and deities who protect the Dharma, according to the measure of their respective realizations, all attained the joy of the Dharma.

Essential Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Twenty (End). Phonetic Transcriptions.
Bǐng (pronounced bǐng). Qí (pronounced qí). Yuàn (yúyuàn qiè). Xiàn (sūjiàn qiè). Tì (chī'ěr qiè). Chuàn (gǔhuàn qiè). [Yǒng-永+Huǐ] (pronounced mǐn).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the very marrow of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. It says:
"You should know that empty space arises within your mind, like a single fleck of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky.

When even one among you gives rise to true realization and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions will all vanish away. It further states: "How could there be anything further within this untainted, truly pure state?"
It accommodates other things. If one can master these things, one is identical to the Tathāgata.

During the Chen and Sui dynasties, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, hearing that this sutra existed in the land of the Five Indias, burned incense day and night and prostrated toward the west, vowing that it would soon arrive in China to prolong the Buddha’s life and open the eyes of humanity and devas.
It was not until the beginning of the Shenglong era of the Tang dynasty that it finally reached the South Sea. There have been several schools of commentary on its interpretation.
Only the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) by Master Zixuan of Changshui and the abridgment (*vyākhyā*) by Master Yuanyue of Suta have circulated widely in the world.

However, their texts and meanings are so vast and extensive that students merely skim across their waves, becoming increasingly ignorant of the fundamental source; they grow weary from the labor of reading them.

Chan Master Jiehuan Baosheng of Wenzhou attained a profound understanding of subtle principles at an early age and deeply awakened to the Mahāyāna, particularly excelling in his mastery of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

I once intended to lead those who had desisted midway directly to the Precious Abode; thus, I composed this Essential Commentary (*Yaojie*). It hooks the profound and seeks out the hidden, continues what is broken and cuts through the profuse.

Like a master wielding his blade with ample space amidst knotted joints and gnarled roots, its words are concise yet its meaning is rich; its expressions are fluent and its principles reach their ultimate point.
Upon unfolding his interpretations, one beholds the sutras; their literary patterns and principles are as clear as pointing at something in the palm of one's hand.

It is a pity that they did not reach wide circulation before the Chan Master passed away. The Elder Xingxuan of Sizhou had long followed him in his travels and, harboring a profound sense of longing, applied himself with focused dedication.
I have therefore raised funds to carve woodblocks for its printing, so as to broaden its dissemination. Alas! Who does not possess this Buddha?
Who does not possess this Sūtra? Yet people fight over their forehead jewels and become intoxicated and deluded by their silken treasures.

If students can rely on this essential commentary to clarify the Sūtra, and penetrate the True Sūtra to realize their own nature, then the wondrous, profound, and all-encompassing sovereign power of the Śūraṅgama’s myriad practices will not be obtained from others.
Thus we know that the "old woman’s heart" of Bao-sheng was indeed urgent, and that the "decorations" of Si-zhou were not in vain—truly adding legs to a snake.
Written on the fifth day after the Mid-Autumn Festival of the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era by the monk Xing-yi, residing at Wanan on Mount Hu. Respectfully inscribed.
